Rather annoying really, having to sort through all that red tape for Europe now. I mean, it's like... we used to be able to just wander off to France for the weekend, you know? Now it's suddenly a full-time process with forms, and insurance, and all this daft stuff.      Yeah, I understand the frustration. Having done a fair bit of EU travel for my PhD fieldwork, I had to get documents translated, too. I remember one time in Prague, I had to get a notarised statement just to present for an interview. Mad, really.      Right, but it's mostly just a pain for me as someone who uses Europe for holidays. Prior to this lot of turkey and Christmas madness, I was thinking of going to Barcelona. Probably go on the bus or something. But now I’ve got to remember to check if my passport is valid for two years after I get back—like it’s some kind of fancy HGV driving Licence! I had to tell him, “Cor blimey, mate, I’m just here for a few sunbathing sessions and some Mate’s Mate burger.” He didn’t find it very funny. A bit of planning, a bit of laughter, and all that.      A little mad, but I’m game if you are. Though I’m not getting on a bus again unless I can bring a digestive with me and the kettle’s on for proper tea.      Done. I’ll go talk to my nan—she’s got a few contacts at the camping association. If anyone can get us a group discount, bloomin’ nan can.

Rather annoying that the children won't play anything other than Monopoly. I know it's a classic, but it's the third time this week. Still, at least I can take their minds off dessert for a little while.      Mummy, what if I pretend to be a bank manager again and give you loads of money so you can buy all the properties?      That's a bit ambitious, love. The bank rules are a bit strict, aren't they, Simon?      Well, last time I got to be the banker when Alice spilled the sweets. You just have to spread out the money properly. I can show you.      That's very kind of you, Simon, but I think you'd be left with no money of your own to play the game properly. Still, I appreciate the generosity. Now, if you're both done arguing over Monopoly for breakfast, I've made some brownies. They're still in the oven, but you can have a seat, and I'll bring them out in a minute.      Yay! My favourite—personally I think they're better than chocolate cake.      I think they're better than cupcakes too. Especially when we can have extra icing on top from the left-over icing bottle.      I wouldn't mind that myself either, but we should be careful not to overdo it. You don't want to go out in the garden with sugar highs and then miscount someone's rent in Monopoly. I've seen it happen before.      Mummy, can we have a dessert and money talk chart like in school so we make sure we are fair? Miss Appleby showed us how to split the gold into the right piles.      That's an excellent idea, Alice. Maybe you and Simon can handle the dessert as well as the Monopoly money. That would keep you both occupied for a while.      Only if the brownies are the ‘rich man’s properties’ and we can trade little ones for big ones. Like how you trade houses for hotels in the game.      That sounds like a plan to keep the simulation consistent, you two. Now come with me to the kitchen—let's go over the map of desserts if you're going to govern over them.      Hopefully, we'll go bankrupt in the game and still have all the brownies at the end.      Yeah, I'm going to be the luckiest player this time.

Rather annoying this, innit? Traffic’s mental again, even at this time. Should’ve walked, like I said.      It wasn’t  that  bad earlier. You gotta give me some credit, I only took this road off the map wi’ a reason. Thought it’d be eeny weeny, yeah?      Ay, I’m all for trying a bit of a shortcut now an’ then, but this ain’t helping. Oh, and you’d better not be trying to impress me with fancy directions. You always say things like, “Turn left at the squirrel.” Where’s the squirrel even?      Okay, well, I can do without the sarcasm. I still helped, didn’t I? We’re only five minutes behind, not half an hour. Aye, and I think the squirrel might be real if I’m being honest. There’s been a load of ‘em lately.      Oh yeah? I didn’t notice any squirrels, didn’t see any of the map. I just sat here like a twat, looking at fields, thinking, “Is this it? Is this it? Is this it?”      Alright, fair enough. I should’ve double-checked the nav. You want me to turn back or just plough on?      Turn back. I reckon the main road ain’t too far now. If we go back we’ll at least get a better signal for the sat nav. This area’s suspiciously bad for anything wi’ electricity.      Yeah, this lot’s a bit remote. Anyways, at least no one saw us, eh? Not many about this time o’ day.      Oh I dunno. I swear I saw some farmer giving us the thumbs down the last time we passed ‘is land. He looked like ‘e’d just left the guest house after killing someone.      You’re overthinking it mate. He probably thought I was trying to steal ‘is sheep. We are lost in the midst of rural England. It’s always sheep with 'im.      Well, let’s hope you don’t try to shoot the squirrel later on. Don’t go wasting a map for a rodent.      I just might, mate. I just might. That bloke gave me the vibe all day.      Alright, soldier. Back we go. And try to keep the squirrel in view, right? For navigation purposes.      Aye, I’ll do me best. I might’ve brought a sausage roll in case I need sacrificial offerings to the squirrel gods.      That’s not a bad plan at all.

Rather chilly this morning, isn't it? I needed three cups of tea just to get out of bed. I remember the days when I'd be up at dawn for work, now I've got time to lie in, but my body doesn’t know what to do with it.      Aye, I know exactly what you mean, Ted. At my age, you'd think the body would let you sleep in a bit. But no, every creak in the house is enough to send me pulling the blankets tighter! My back was stiff as a broomstick when I got out of bed.      Honestly, you two worry me. I've got the same stiffness, but at least I made myself a turkey and stuffing for dinner! The others left themselves a chicken pot pie, and now I’m the only one who's fed in the whole house. Living with retired men is a full-time job, breakfast, lunch and then dinner!      Ha! Well, I'm not surprised! You always look after us both. Still, it's nice to have someone around to chat with, you know? I’d listen to the telly if you weren’t here to keep me company. Old habits die hard, but chatting like this always warms me up a little from the inside. How are the grandchildren treating you, by the way?      Oh, the usual! Now don’t go rolling your eyes at me, Derek. Last weekend, the younger one, Jessica, climbed out of the garden gate to chase the cat. I was a good half-hour looking for her! Some childminder I turned out to be in the end!      Look, as far as I'm about to fall off the perch, you did the best job of anyone I've known. I remember you taking my sister’s kids when you barely left the house. You were a rock to the lot of us for years. Still are, for that matter.      Aye, it's a shame you all can't get back to work, but I suppose there's not many jobs for a retired civil engineer these days. Still, we've got each other and the odd cuppa to keep the going in, eh?      That’s the spirit! Now go and make me another tea, Ted. If I'm going to be the active one, I might as well be the caffeinated one too!

Rather annoying, though—Facebook Marketplace. You know, I do talk about this in my classes. The language everyone uses there is so often informal and full of colloquial expressions. I've found that people rarely stick to proper measurements when listing things. For example, "half a litre" gets written as "500 ml" if you're precise, but some just say "bit over half a jug of milk." Rather unhelpful when trying to gauge quantity! I wonder if you've had any trouble with that when listing your skincare products?      Oh, honestly, it's the worst. You'd think people would just read the description  properly . I've had buyers ask, "Does this box have like a 'full size' tube in it?" and not even scroll down to where I clearly state the dimensions in centimetres and the net weight. I tried to make it all about authenticity and transparency with Honest Skincare—give sizes and ingredients in full, you know? But not everyone’s bothered to read! I mean, even when I say the serum comes in a 30ml bottle, half the time someone still asks, "Is that half a bottle or a full one?" and I want to scream!     That does sound frustrating. I suppose when people are buying online, they just skim read and often miss vital info. I know myself—when I see the photo first, I sometimes ignore the description and just assume. Which is probably why you need to make your visuals as clear as possible too. Do your photos show the measurements? Like a ruler beside the product or a comparison with something familiar—like a £1 coin or a bottle of water?      Oh, I try! I did that with the new face cream packaging. I stuck a 50p coin next to the jar to give a sense of size. I even have a short video unboxing to show how much product fits in the jar. It’s all about making it visual. I’m trying to think of new ways to make my posts pop. I tried using Instagram Stories recently with a quick demo on how to apply the serum. Let’s see if that drives more people to the website.      That’s smart. And remember, you’re not just selling a product; you're selling the  experience . If you can connect with your audience through your brand values and authentic language, that will go a long way.

Rather annoying this wet weather, don't you think, Charles? I've had to cancel my usual walk by the sea again. Never thought I'd miss the rain after I retired, but sure does make me feel cooped up.      Aye, I agree. Brighton gets quite the dreary days in autumn, doesn't it? Not as bad as Glasgow, I daresay. Though I reckon that's all too familiar to you after being born up there. Still, I thought we'd dump the hat and coat business and just curl up for the evening. Nothing wrong with a peaceful chat over tea and biscuits, is there?      Nothing at all, dearest. You know I like that best of all. I’ve been reading the newspaper this week—what a mess London is in with the transport strikes. Made me think again of my teaching days, actually, when the buses would stop and I’d have to walk an extra mile. Reminds me of Joanne, the girl from year 4, always turning up muddy and soaked, but grinning like the Cheshire cat none the less.      Ah, I remember her well! Still in touch with any of your old class, by the way? You always did have a way with the children. You deserve all the credit for preparing them for the real world. And it's a pity you retired the way you did. All that time and talent wasted.      I suppose we live in strange times, Charles. When I left the classroom, I didn't expect unemployment to follow. Harder to find meaningful work as you grow older, and I thought being a teacher would carry me through. But, well, at least I have you to keep me company now.      And I'm not going anywhere—that's for sure. I know I've only retired from teaching part-time, but I do enjoy preparing for the occasional lesson. Keeps the mind going, doesn't it? Just yesterday, a student asked me something so absurd I had to double-check it myself. You’d have laughed out loud, hearing their explanation.      Oh, do tell! That sounds just like the old days. Tell me, how's your back these days? Still giving you trouble when you go in too early?      Just a little twinge here and there. Nothing I can't manage with a bit of rest and your insistence on making me elevate my legs after dinner!

Rather chilly this evening, isn't it? I turned the heating on ages ago, but it's been like a sauna and a shower at the same time today. Blows hot air for ten minutes, then stops and leaves us shivering. I'll have to call someone about it.      Got a problem like that at my place last winter. Turns out the heating engineer had left all the valves half-shut. A complete mess. If you're struggling, I might be able to recommend someone. I know someone in the North East who was decent—hands on the whole gas, pipes, and underfloor heating lot.      Honestly, I don't envy either of you. I've been stressed about my PhD deadline since university reopened after the Christmas break. Speaking of which, did you hear the news about the retirement age increasing this year? If I don’t finish my thesis in the next six months, I'll be too old for a mid-life crisis!      Aye, thanks for putting that thought in my head, Mae. I was thinking more about how I can afford to retire with my current savings being what they are—there are days I struggle to afford both food and tools for the workshop, let alone a pension. Still, I’ve got a few mulberry bushes coming in. Might bottle some syrup or make jam. I know you, Eve, would appreciate some home-cooked marmalade to go with your whole grain toast.      That’d be lovely, Owen. Though I must say, I’m more of a crispy bread and blue cheese kind of person. Never really had the patience for cooking, and honestly, being a researcher leaves little energy for culinary experiments. Although, I have about five mulberries in a pot on the kitchen windowsill. We'll see if they survive the lack of attention.      I grew up near the North Sea, so the winters hit hard over there. If you're growing anything at home, you’ve got to drape the pot in a wool blanket at night. Works miracles for root vegetables, and I reckon could keep the berries from freezing.      That’s brilliant, Luke! I’ve got a couple of basil plants doing their best under a grow light. I’ve tried watering them the same way as I did when I lived in Swindon, but clearly, they’re bricking it in this house.

Rather annoying that half the cutlery’s missing again. I swear they vanish just when we’ve got guests over. Has anyone checked under the sink? It tends to go there with their organisational skills.      Not to start a, but it’s such a  rip-off . You buy it and then every single time you host someone, you’re handed a tin fork or worse— none  at all. A lot worse than just the cutlery, honestly. You’d think she’d get a reasonable amount. We’ve had to buy our own forks just to stop them arguing.      Right, I’ve sorted it. Last time I popped over and brought a supply of my own forks and knives and My turkey fork was missing again! So I left it on the counter. I’m not the only one who’s tired of this. A bit of organisation wouldn’t go amiss, really.      I’ve always said they’d lend a hand in there at least, you know, for once, but no. I told my sister the other day,  ‘Just label the drawer, you don’t need a Nobel prize for that.’  But no one listens to me. I’ve seen better organisation at war time. It’s not rocket science!      You’re all too harsh on them. Back in my day, we had to  wash up  the cutlery by hand and not even expect to use a plate. And we were happy enough for it! Now you just chuck anything in and expect it to work. You’d never have noticed a missing fork at  our  house—there was a  fight  for being handed the plate.      Haha, I do miss those times. I mean, not the fighting, obviously, but the vibes. Honestly, though, maybe we should take the plug and take the cutlery up for ourselves? I’m not  that  proud. Just less screaming if we’re not here for dinner at 6pm. It’s not like we can afford to keep buying forks.      We could compromise. Like, speaker_1 brings a tray of forks with her, I bring the knives, and someone else grabs the spoons.  That  way no one has to fight their way through the sink bin on arrival.      That might work—no one in the house has the sense to go box shopping let alone cutlery. Speaker_5 could have a big sign up on the fridge, in block letters: “ CUTLERY IS NOT EMPLOYED TO HIDE .

Rather annoying I had to take the afternoon off work, but Sarah’s promising to deliver the report by tomorrow first thing. Just need to get some breathing space before the trip next week. I found all the matching pyjamas and Aunty Karen’s knitted hat and scarf.      Oh, did you? That was thoughtful of you, love. Those pyjamas are a bit past their best, though. Might need a new pair. I can pop into Harrogate and pick some up tomorrow before I have that meeting.      Cans we have hot chocolate when we get to the slopes, daddy? Aunty and I watched a ski movie last night and she said they always have hot chocolate waiting when you come in from the cold.      Oh, posh, they probably do in the film! But I’ll make a pot once we get back from the shop tomorrow, just you and me, shall we? Might be a short break, but as long as you and I are together, I reckon it’ll be brilliant.      Be-because you’re my hero – even though you got shouted at earlier and were grumpy at dinner. Can we pick somethin’ to eat tomorrow as well? I want to get some crumpets for breakfast and some of those biscuits with the red bags!      Red bags – you mean the Jammy Dodgers? They’d better not be red and white this time, I still have a few of those St George ones in my coat pocket from last year! And you can help me decide what to buy for tomorrow’s cooking mission.      I know! I can write it all down on my to do list, like mummy does. She always gets things ready for work. Can I have a pencil and some paper?      Go on then, you can have my stationery case. As long as you don’t scribble out the insurance numbers with your glitter pen.      Posh, no, daddy. I’m a big girl now! I’ll be proper goody with it. Can I do a picture of us at the ski place as well? Like that art project we did with snowmen?      Now that sounds like a plan! Let’s get you started after dinner. And after that, maybe we can go to the park tomorrow and have a little pre-ski walk to get us in the mood.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it love? Thought I'd settle down with a film and a nice cuppa after the garden.      Yeah, I agreed with that actually. It's a proper sunny one. Not quite Cambridge spring, but it's getting there.      Got eeny idea what I fancy watching. Light-hearted, you know? Nothing too dramatic.      Oh, I've got just the one! I've been meaning to suggest this – there's a new comedy on BBC iPlayer, "The Lady's Talon." It's based in the 1920s, follows these two women solving a mystery.      Oooh, now that does sound a bit interesting! I like my films with a bit of crime, but if it's got some laughs, then I'm all for it.      Yeah, it's been a hit with the ratings and I found it quite a bit in my kind of taste. Only thing is, I saw the first two episodes so I know where it goes.      Oh, don't worry about that, pet. I like a bit of a surprise still. I'm off on my own binge tonight. You watching it tomorrow, then?      Yeah, maybe – but it's got five episodes, and I might just fly through them. Let me know what you thought, though.      Oi, don't be rushing, dear. Take your time. Spreading it out is more the way to go. Besides, I can do with some gossip about the plot before I delve too deep in.       laughs  Okay, fair point. I'll make sure to not give you the whole thing away. We can have our tea and twists together next weekend.      Perfect, love. That's the way to do it, like planning out the whole garden guest list.       laughs  Are you comparing films to event planning again?      Well, when you think about it, you've got your characters, your plot, your setting – it's not a bad analogy at all.      Alright then, I'll run with it. I’ll be the master of ceremonies of the pond life if you're hosting.      Now that, I'd like to see – you arranging the lily pads and all.      I might even build a stage for the ducks. We'll really make it a show.      Oh, very good, very good. Now that's the kind of team effort I appreciate. First films, now the garden. You're coming along nicely.      Likewise, Mum.

Rather annoying the wet weather isn't it?      That it is, love. We’d got the garden all ready for the weekend you know. I’ve asked Jane and Peter over for a little BBQ.      Oh, what a shame. They were just here last Saturday and it was hailstones the size of marbles!      It’s not going to last that long though, is it? The forecast said it’d be easier off by tea time.      It was supposed to for yesterday too. But, don't worry love, I can clear the table of clutter and we’ll give it a go.      That’d be lovely.      So, what’s on the menu then, or shall I do the meat and veg and you do the sides?      Cheerful of you, I’ll do the salad and brussels.      And I’ll do the burger hides, you know Mrs James is a vegan these days.      She is, yes. Rather annoying too—everyone I ask refuses to eat a normal meal these days.      Try not to be cross, it’s quite a thing now. You want to keep your friends.      I know, I know. I just miss roast beef and Yorkshire pudding.      Bless you, you cook that for me and I won't leave the house.      That's the idea. I've got an email from court saying I have a shift on Friday and it’s early too.      You told me about it last week though, right? I'll drop the kids off at boarding school and collect them again on Sat.      That's very unselfish of you. My day job gives me no time for anything.      It’s no problem. I'm a teacher too, I know how it goes. I miss out on a Saturday here or there. At least I have the academies to keep me busy.      They're such an interfering bunch, you remember when the last head teacher was thrown out for not wearing goody shoes on pond life day?      You’re not serious? I only had to wear a box jellyfish costume myself.      That was you? I thought it was one of the colleagues.      True to life, it was, and very sticky at the end of the day. I’m not entirely sure if I got all the custard out of my hair.      Right, right. Just make sure to wear the right shoes Friday, I don't fancy having to explain why you’ve arrived in flip-flops again.

You like that one, don’t you? Oh, I might ask if we can pop in to the electrical shop when we get back as well—  I need   a new kettle. The old one gives off that funny noise and it’s been boiling the water for like, 10 minutes now.      Again? That one couldn’t even survive the winter back home! Maybe we can just look for a couple of other things to get while we’re out—  like   shampoo, because I ran out last week and used some of yours and I thought it might be nicer if I had my own.      Yeah, okay. Just don’t spend too much. We were supposed to be cooking on a budget!   I shall   try and behave myself while we're there, but if the smell hits me from the baked goods aisle, well… you know what happens.      Of course. And don’t even get me started on them restricting the cake portion sizes again. Last time I had that sprite and cream bao, it was sad to see the big one had been   sold out   by 10 a.m.      Yeah, go for it on your own if you like.   I shall   go for the popcorn, I think. It always hits the spot after a lecture.      Right, I’ll manage the koi koi and you can handle the groceries.   This way   we can cover more ground without overloading one person.

Rather than share a text, let’s chat over the phone. I need to hear your voices properly. Okay... What's the plan for the weekend now that your parents are going to their friend’s birthday?      Not sure yet. Mummy said we might go to the park or make some cookies on Saturday if there’s nice weather?      Yeah! I want to bake muffins. Maybe we can read too. Do you have  Where the Wild Things Are ?      Oh, I’ve got it! And yes, the park sounds brilliant if the sun shines. I saw the forecast this morning—it might! But I also promised Lucy we could take some photos around the garden for her photo album. Just simple ones, you know, like having a picnic or pretending to be explorers.      I like the idea of playing explorers in the garden!      Me too! Can I wear my pirate hat from the toy box?      Of course, you can. I’ll get that out. And yes, we’ll try the baking, the reading, the photos, and maybe I can even squeeze in a trip to the hairdresser for a trim while you two read something quietly. I’ve got a few appointments all day, so we’ll have to plan carefully.      Mummy’s hair is getting too long. She tries not to go too often, but I think it splits at the ends.      You’re not wrong. It does need a little snip. It just feels oddly grown at the moment. But don’t worry, it’ll be back to ‘acceptable’ soon!      I had a haircut last week. Daddy took me to the man in the blue coat. He let me choose what shape my hair would be.      Did he give you superhero sideburns?      Yes! They’re still there.      Well, as long as you both don’t try to run off with the scissors, we’ll be just fine. Saturday sounds like it’ll be full of fun—baking with lunches, a little reading, some adventures in the garden, and maybe a trip to the cinema with Lucy if we have time.      Can we order pizza after the photos or after the park?      You might be in for a pizza on Sunday, your lucky day. But Saturday is about big kids' activities and healthy snacks, okay? Maybe with a dessert cup of chocolate sauce to finish off the baking?      Mmm, that sounds better than the cinema!

Rather annoying the queue at the supermarket, innit? Mebbe we could've just ordered online like I did... got the parcels round same day.      Erm, I dunno, online is a faff sometimes with packaging and stuff. But at least you can avoid the tills. I'm still trying to get used to paying for my own groceries now I'm living alone. Prior to I just mooched off my flatmates.      Oh yeah, you were in a place in Pembury, right? I heard Kent's got some nice countryside but the M20’s a nightmare. I prefer being in Cambridge—less traffic, more brains and better food options, if you catch my drift.      Ha! Yeah, Cambridge is brilliant for food. I reckon their kebabs are better than in Sunderland. Nothing beats a bit of proper North East hot sauce with it, though—bring it up to a whole nother level.      I agree, Sunderland’s got some mad-spicy stuff. One time I tried that fish shop over the road, and it nearly made me start crying I was laughing. Like a proper local prank.      Oh go on, tell us the story. I been out of the North so long I’ve forgotten the good bits.      Well, long story short, I went in for fried haddock and chips, asked for “medium spicy” hot sauce. Guy behind the counter just chuckles, then douses the plate in stuff like a chef in one of them fancy telly documentaries. Next thing I know, I’m gasping through my noodles like I’d swallowed a whole bottle of it.      Classic! That's the North East for you—always pulling a prank. We even do it with the weather! One week it's snowing, the next it's hotter ‘n' baked beans.      Hah! I remember that. I used to surf on the Tyne, and if you caught a wave on a sunny day while it was as hot as June, you'd swear you were in Cornwall.      Now that's a proper holiday for me, something different. I like a foreign trip now and then—Germany's got some nice coastal breaks too.      I’ve not really had a proper holiday, bloke. Family always says “we’ll go next year” but it never really happens. Instead we just potter about the garden with a couple of scoffs of pizza and chips ‘cause someone asked why we can’t just order in.

Rather a lot’s been going on, hasn't it, Mary? I was just reading ‘The Sun’... got the funnies out—course I did. I can't say I understand ‘em much these days, but it's nice to have a chuckle! Mind you, the election was interesting. I'm still voting Labour, if you ask me.      Oh, Harry, don’t start that again! I think policy changes so fast these days, it's confusing. Anyway, I was just talking to one of the old parents at the youth hostel in Cornwall, and they told me how lovely it is to see young people united over sports again.      Aye, football's still alive and kicking, no doubt. Still, enough talk politics. I tried to sell my car via eBay the other week, but no one in the world is interested in an old Rover nowadays. Cats would better fetch a price—mind if I have a coffee, Mary?      And what did you do, Grandad? I told you—those clunkers don’t sell. I do tell you—sell the house, not the car! You don’t need both to be living like a king, do you?      Easy for you to say, Tony. You’re a teacher – have it made with the job, and I know you're busy buying houses. I reckon you've got enough to worry about!      Now, now, no need to start squabbling at our age. Let’s talk about my trip to London last week. I went to see the horses at the weigh-in, and I thought it was absolutely delightful – all the flashing lights and people shouting. I about got run over by a taxi! Tony, do come over and taste this scone I made.      London's always a hive of activity. At least you're not buying a horse for the stables, Mary. Though I heard about a school up near Exeter trying to raise money for a new building by auctioning a rare edition from the school library. We could talk about that over the weekend.      Oh, and I heard ITV is running a show about the history of the road trip via eBay. Said it was a man from Birmingham cruising in his classic Ford. If I had a spare ten quid, I might just chuck in a bid.      Time to lay off your hobby, dad. It's about time you focus on your health, not some old jalopy.

So did you go and pick out a baby name yet, or are we just winging it like last time when we ended up with “Little Angel” because your goldfish died and we were emotional?      Haha, alright, Karen, we’ve moved on since then. We’ve actually narrowed it down to two names — we’re both very neutral about it, so it's easy… until my mother starts getting involved.      Of course she has. Oh no, she’s already pulling her “I know you’ll be sensible” and “You don’t want to give it a name you can’t spell” cards again?      All of the above, and now she’s managed to get Myra on board with her idea. Fun fact: Myra just had her first grandchild and already thinks they know better than every single one of us. It's like generational trauma at this point.      I mean, she did raise  you , so I get the confidence! But, you know, I’ve worked in language for over three years, so I can vouch, yes, some names are extremely inaccessible. I’m with your partner on this — keep it simple.      Honestly, I kind of wish we'd been taught baby names earlier in school — like alongside EVS or something. “This week, pupils study: names, babies, and basic baby food.” It would’ve saved me a lot of stress.      True. Speaking of, have you figured out the baby feeding thing yet? I know your brother’s doing a mix with his newborn, and it's a bit of a minefield. Can I come over one evening and help you prep some bottles and snacks?      Oh my god, that would be brilliant. I’ve already boiled some bottles into oblivion trying to be over-efficient. And let’s not talk about the time I tried to reheat formula and nearly set the kitchen on fire. I’m not cut out for this.      Don’t worry, I’ve had six practice babies in the lab. Almost like I’m being academically trained for this. We can multitask while I dole out wisdom about vowel sounds and you deal with the sippy cups.      You really are the lifeblood of our family, you know that? I just can’t imagine getting through this stuff without you.      Yeah, yeah. Just don’t forget me when your baby’s a grown-up and you’re all proud and ignoring me at the graduation.

Rather lovely to have you all over for weekend breakfast, isn't it? I made crumpets with potted shrimps, just how you like 'em, Michelle.      Oh, that is smashing of you, Julia. Look at the garden! The delphiniums are in bloom and the cat’s been sunbathing on the wall again. Someone needs to give her a lift inside—it’s getting nippy by midday.      She’s a free spirit, nan! You can’t just boss Miss Whiskers about. Didn’t you want to potter in the greenhouse later, Dad?      Aye, as soon as I’ve cleared my plate. You made that My turkey and leek casserole, didn’t you? Still tastes like the good old days, Vivian.      Oh, Vivian dear, you’ve got to put it in the slow cooker if you want it tender enough for me old bones. And Julia, the milkman delivered, so the fridge’s sorted—and I’ve chucked out those out-of-date tins.      Thank you for that! Honestly, your memory’s spot on. I’ve got a meeting today, but I’m watching for the post. The Royal Mail’s got a staffing issue at the moment—isn't it a bit ridiculous? It took  two  days just to get an NHS leaflet through.      Bless ‘em, they’re stretched thin up and down the country. Spent my morning dealing with a government grant appeal. Rude enough to have to email forms back and forth—where's the real civil servants?      Look on the bright side, Dad. At least there’s a web chat now to clear the backlog. I had to use it for my last tax stuff. Proper efficient.      Tax! That's one of those things they always manage to make worse, isn’t it? Still, I'm at the clinic all day tomorrow. Proper busy with trainee sessions.      You’re doing brilliantly, Vivian. More qualified than half of them! Just ignore the gossip machine in the staff room—some of it's more outlandish than a telly drama.      Honestly, Mags, your life would make a  proper  series! "Nurses in the making: between a rock and a hard place!"      Now that’s something I’d watch! Just as long it doesn’t turn those trainees into saints—after hearing some of Vivian’s war stories over tea, the lot of them sound like saints and sinners all rolled into one.      I’ve had my share, Reg, believe me.

Rather annoying this new rat puppet they've got at the village fayre, if you ask me. Mind you, I rather liked the old bumblebee one. I used to sneak up to see that with my missus before she passed.      Oh, well now, it was rather bright and silly if you liked that kind of thing—and the kids just adored it. But yes, this rat with the goggles and all? Not the best look for a place like Costessey. It seems a bit... misfitted.      Misfitted, or just glorified nonsense? I like to think of it as theatrical character-building. Now, forgive the harsh tone, but do you lot like that new turkey on the telly with his eccentric puppets?      Oh, yes, them ones. Rather sad in a way, really—puppets about a cat wearing a top hat, no less. I've been thinking of joining the Costessey bell-ringers again. There’s a new session at St. George’s. Good for the mind, keeping time and all.      Oh, I always admired that. Handbell ringing requires such coordination and discipline. You’ll have to pass on the details, Jack. I’ve been meaning to get my eyes tested too—Dr. Hinshelwood, I think it is, runs the surgery. His new staff don’t seem as polite as the last one.      Aye, they never are these days. Spoke to the bus conductor last week—good man, he was. Funny thing was, had the same name as a former commanding officer of mine in the Home Guard! Most people are surprised when I say I did that back in the war.      Oh, you've always been full of surprises! Going from that to running a provision shop up near Harrow? You’re quite the reborn entrepreneur. I’ve always said, if you’re going to branch out, do it with something you love. And you love the finer things in life.      We all have our passions. I just like to live simply. Now, what with the new bus route to the village, the young folk can travel cheaper, something I support.      That's noble of you, Tom. It's not often you meet a person who thinks of the community that way. And the rate of infrequent transport has always been a struggle for all of us in the countryside.      Well, I suppose that’s what retirement gives to some of us—time and perspective.

So did you go back to the gym after last week? I’ve been trying to get into a routine—basically, I’m either hitting the treadmill at 6 a.m. or having a full-on guilt trip for skipping. Not sure which is worse.      Honestly, I skipped again on Tuesday and went  full weekend runner  on Saturday. I think my calculator's dying… not my gym results. I’m just worried we'll become one of those people who meet at the bar and meet again at the bar because we don't know how to stop.      Then we’ll draw the line and finish with digestive gummy bears and a nightcap in my living room. Just like old times.      I’ll see if my ex does a work trip that week—if not, I’m breaking up with him purely for availability purposes.      You could just bring flu and act really sad. Trust me, it's foolproof.      Is it Friday or potion-making this time next week? Because this sounds like a very bleak and magical proposition.

Rather annoying the new bollards by the station, aren't they? You’d think they'd know by now not to obstruct the pavement with those plastic things.      Oh, absolutely! It is a complete shambles. Look, I’ve been thinking—my new book relies on writing about outsiders and bureaucracy, and I’m told the French have mastered the art of delaying anything productive. Though I’ve been to Spain too; documents in Seville and Cordoba gave me a whole new insight into how Philip of Spain and Mary Tudor dealt with their foreign entanglements.      Oh, you’ve been working on  another  book, have you? I had no idea. That's brilliant. My son, you know, he was born in Paris, and I can't tell you how much the French bureaucracy delayed our paperwork. A whole six months to get his birth certificate legalised properly!      I know! Anglo-French relations in practice, eh? And the property there hides its own challenges. I had a cousin who once tried to buy a farm in Provence—last I heard, it still hadn’t cleared the tax audit three years later.      Honestly, we’ve got local issues enough without looking overseas. Have you heard about the spire at Chichester Cathedral collapsing? I was in there last year for an open day. The exhibition of photos was moving—old hands-on images of the building and the work of that 18th-century architect, Porden.      Porden, yes. I remember a school friend who had a summer job restoring his work in Chichester. That collapse must’ve devastated people. And it makes me think of how our housing authority here manages such places. I’m watching this man from the council now—he’s not local, that’s for sure. Doesn’t know the history, doesn’t know the people.      It’s disgraceful, really. And it ties into the whole issue of land use, enterprise. We could do with some people who actually care about what the towns look like and how they feel. Even anarchists would probably do a better job on occasion!      That's where French visitors come in handy, if you ask me. They go straight to the pond in Kensington Gardens or the British Library and respect it. They seem to remember that art and history go further than bollards and bureaucracy.      I suppose they’ve had enough of it at home.

Rather do a newfit in the living room, ay, Mary? I know it's time they passed on... got to make some space for the dining table yet?      Oh, love, it is a right box of tricks, this place. But you’re right. We haven’t touched it eeny since Johnny was born. It’s sorely time we got onto it.      Aye, and if we’re redoing this lot, maybe we can stretch to a new coffee table as well. We’ve had the same one for thirty years — it’s about the age of the house!      Mary, when I were a gal we used to clear out likker once in a while. Now look at us, you lot! All this junk you cling on to, I reckon half of it ain’t used since the war!      What about the old gig? Like when you hover old bits up online and everyone goes mad for vintage stuff? Maybe we can sell some of the fai-in’s lot. I could help you take photos and that.      Oh, Jonathan’d love that idea, I’m sure. What with all his messing around with that laptop. Tell me, son, are we risking it? I’m rather put off by the tech side – all them ones and noughts and whatnot!      Don’t worry, Mary, it’s easy! You just load the photo and write a quick blurb and whamo, someone buys it. Though I’m not sure they’d consider this old wardrobe vintage. It looks outta a Dickens novel.      Anyroad up, I’ve had enough of the dust and the feeling about nowhere. We’re not all getting any younger! And what with this party comin’ up for Jonathan, it’ll be easier to sort the place while it’s up for bits to do.      Aye, well if you’re all going that route, maybe we could bin some of the old wooden chairs. They fell to pieces them!      Not to rush you lot, but Auntie Websites mentioned space in the lunches for a new big garden party. Could we clear the back room for that, too?      That’s a goon idea, son. I’ll start tomorrow, or at least rummage about in the morning, if I survive the boxset!      Reckon I’ll bring in the laptop and show you the ropes, Mary. No need to fear the new age!      ‘Tis good we’ve got them young ones round.

Rather a lot of changes in the countryside these days, don't you think? When I was working as a civil engineer, I saw roads popping up all across Norfolk. Proper countryside back then, now it's a madhouse with all sorts of development. Look at the children today — they can't tell a sparrow from a blackbird if their life depended on it!           That's a truth, Ernie. I used to take my grandchildren out to watch the meadow birds near the Broads. Now it's all hi-tech things and concrete... Not to mention the sound system in modern cars. I've got the oldest Land Rover you’ve ever seen — well-loved, if I do say so myself. The one you boys put together for me back in '72, and I still drive the little beauty. But I’d give a fortune to have something that doesn’t rattle when I go over a pothole!           I must say, dear, technology has some upsides. My grandson showed me this application on his tablet for spotting birds. It tells you everything — what they eat, how they sing. Absolutely fascinating, if you ask me. Of course, it's got a few fancy graphs and swiping actions, but I'm not entirely hopeless.           Oh, my students would laugh themselves silly to hear you call smartphones "fancy graphs and swiping actions," Gwen. But I can’t say I disagree with you — I do miss the simplicity of past technology. My lectures are now a mix of PowerPoint presentations and virtual meetings. I had to teach a whole module online last year because of the weather! I mean, it’s not ideal, but it works, I suppose.           Software, eh? I tried to get my daughter to install a security system for the house using this fancy monitor and sensor things. She said I needed “cloud integration,” whatever that means. I gave up after an hour — too many buttons! I prefer the good old fashioned lock on the door if you ask me.      I’ll stick with the Land Rover and a big old wrench if I can get them. But I have to admit, I looked at a couple of newer models for fun the other day — electric ones, you know? All that sound deadened and lights flashing green and blue like magic. Suits my lot I reckon.           Electronics and engines — they’re both just complicated these days.

Rather annoying this new schoolteachers bein’ so strict, innit? When I was at school in Costessey, the teachers had no time for nonsense, and I can tell ye, we knew our sums and our spelling. Not like now, where I hear children frightened to raise their hands lest they be called een outsiders.      Oh, I agree with you, dear. When I used to look after the children from the local area before I retired, I saw so many kids rushing into things without a Second thought. We had to teach them the very basics! Now it’s all about feelings and not too many rules. Bless 'em, but I can't see how they’ll make it in the working world.      Haha, you two are not wrong, but I think it works both ways. I teach at a school just outside Birmingham, and while the rules are stricter now, the children have far more opportunities—like learning about technology early. They can even tweet if they want, for goodness' sake! I remember ordering a pizza once and the delivery man had to tweet the order himself before it came, and I nearly fell off my chair I laughed so much.      Tweet? Hah! Tell me that isn’t on a machine that goes  ping-ping-ping  all day – Mate, I got enough interferin’ with that telly and these “binge drinking” programmes they got on them streaming services. If I weren’t careful, I’d be nursing a pint by this time at night.      Oh, don’t talk to me about binge drinking—my son used to have a right laugh over the bottle when he was young. I used to clean his room most nights about five times to get rid of the smell. And the National Health Service—glad it exists, but not always reliable when it comes to the cleanliness of it all, if you catch my drift.      Speaking of which, I had a funny one the other day. A student asked me if ‘azure’ was a colour or a spell from Harry Potter. I said, “It’s both if you blink.” And the class nearly flipped their wigs laughing. At least the kids today can still laugh, you know, even with all the pressure.      Aye, that’s about right. If we can laugh at ourselves, we’ll go far. I might be ancient, but I still know what a good joke is.

Rather annoying this snowfit, eh? You can’t even get outside without your boots crusting over in like five minutes. I were out in the garden today, trying to get a few bulbs in before the ground freezes for good. Not sure I'll have much luck mind you — this weather is a mither.      I know, it’s ridiculous. I reckon it’s more like "flurries with a side of chaos" than proper winter. I got stuck behind a delivery van on Newnham Road today. We were grinding along like two tortoises in a sleet storm. But you were gardening in this? That’s ballsy.      What can I say, I’ve got a bit of a green thumb. Still, I might not make it to the Come Dine With Me gig Oliver and Roxy are doing in a few weeks. Living in Cambridge, you’ve got to have culinary swagger, innit?      Haha, yeah — and I pity the poor sod that’s hosting the final dinner. I mean, once you’ve gone from fish stew with crusty bread to seven-course tasting menus, the pressure’s on. Was it one of those stakes and hens, by the way? Roxy mentioned something about it being quite a do.      Oh yeah, been mega posh, like, swank par-for-the-course. The hen do was in that swanky hotel near Ely, all canapés and mini proseccos. Our stag someone hired a limo and dropped him off at the airport with a rubber chicken. I’m still not over the rubber chicken.      Sounds like a bit much for a man whose idea of a good time is a pint and a curry. But to each their own, I s’pose. Anyway, moving on — are we still on for the week away? I was meaning to book the flights, ‘cos if we wait much longer, all the midweek prices’ll be blown out by the stag do crowd.      I dunno, I was thinking we could stick about for the spring and maybe do a garden-to-table bit here with lunches and a couple of whiskeys in the evening. That’d be proper chilled.      Maybe, but even goin’ on a weekender somewhere would be a change. I was thinking Cornwall — just us, the coast, the boxset binges.      You could have that in the sofa here, though, mind you. And with the garden starting to thaw... I’ve got a deck that needs pressure washing.

Rather good to have you all round for a bit of a feed. I've made my old favourite — potted meat and mash. Nothing fancy, but it'll warm the bones.      Oh, that does sound nice, dear. I always thought you were one of the few who could make potted meat taste like something more than just meat and salt.      Well, a bit of thyme never hurt, and of course I use top-quality pork — not the cheapest in the shop, mind!      Funny you should mention that, Dad. I was reading a paper the other day about how traditional British dishes like potted meat are fading, only still served in the most well-preserved corners of rural England.      Ten out of ten for academic musings, Dr. Ellis. But let me ask — if you're all about authenticity and traditional recipes, doesn’t your college teach you this kind of folk culture stuff in lectures?      Now, now — not everyone's so cheeky. I reckon your Dad’s recipe should be recorded, maybe even put in a museum next to that Wellington boots collection your Uncle Frank still has in the shed.      Ha, ha, very funny. But serious now, it's all about memories. This recipe’s been in the family for generations. My Gran brought the recipe over from Norfolk after the war. Seems like a strange time to start preserving meat, but we’d just come off food rationing, and leftovers weren’t to be thrown away.      That’s really interesting, actually. It adds a real cultural and historical dimension to the food — which is something I've been trying to weave into our curriculum a bit more.      Alright, so if you're going to start giving lectures on potted meat and preserve it as a national treasure, do you think they’d put it on the guest menu at the Oxford Moot Banquet?      Bless him, he's talking about worlds away. But bless you too, darling. It's a beautiful recipe — full of heritage and heart.      Aye, I suppose it is. Though you remember, after I had that back operation, the doctor said go easy on the salt. I’ve tried cutting it down, but it just doesn’t taste the same.      You know what your solution is, Dad — fermentation. The natural salts from curing could reduce the overall sodium while keeping the taste. I might be able to find you some curing salts over at the local food co-op.

Rather annoying the new oven’s taking so long to preheat. I blame this damp weather, it kills everything... What d'you think, love? It's not like we need superstitions, but this feels cursed.      No, I mean, it's fine. We've got mince and mash and peas, yeah? It's not like we haven't done this a hundred times before? I reckon that oven hasn't worked properly since the fifties.      Blimey, it’s just like when I was a girl. Didn’t take no fancy gadgets to cook a meaty meal. My gran baked Marylands in that oven and it never once let her down!      My turkey came out golden browned enough to dazzle a man’s eye, and I used the same oven, bless it. If it turned out a fine beast of a turkey, why would it not do the same for a bit of mince?      When I was the lad ye lot, you didn’t have no fancy programmes. One switch, on and off. Bake it, done.      Yeah, yeah, we all remember that. But this is the real kitchen. Nothing like the ones on telly, I can assure you. No spotless cupboards or knife blocks here.      Let it cook while we finish the potatoes, yeah? It’s not as if the whole family was coming. Just us four at our parents, which I suppose is someone to be grateful for.      I wish they’d been around when I was younger. Always at work. Or if not work, then travelling. I missed more Christmases than I can count about them two.      Aye, well, we’re here now. That's all that matters. Proper meal with proper people and no fancy gadgets to run out on us.      Let’s not sit here waiting for a miracle. Let’s open a bottle of red and pass the peas while the oven gets its way.      We could talk about that time Dad burned the Christmas turkey and tried passing it off as a new recipe from "around the world."      That was amazing. We had roast chicken with cranberry goop on it for weeks after that.      You’re all in on this, aren’t ye? That bloke could make carbon from steak and you'd all have it in.      That was a man with a proper sense of adventure. Or more of a charred sense of adventure.      It's a shame I can't remember the rest of those Christmases.

Rather than traditional university studies, what if we used social story-telling to engage students in learning? I was reading about how viral videos often go down well because they're relatable and shareable. If we could combine that with problem-solving techniques, students would not only absorb the material but actively apply it.      That sounds interesting. How would you structure that within the university curriculum? From what I've seen in education, students often lose interest once they're given a textbook. But involving interactive storytelling could keep their attention better. Have you considered what kind of content would be most effective?      Yes, the content is key. I've been thinking about tackling real-world challenges—like sustainability or entrepreneurship—through video narratives. Students could be split into small teams and tasked with creating their own mini documentaries or problem-solving scenarios, using storytelling techniques and entrepreneurial skills. Think of it as an EdTech start-up approach to traditional learning.      I love that! Incorporating teamwork like that helps students develop soft skills while learning content, which is always a bonus in the classroom. I remember when I was teaching high school, a group project on local environmental issues really resonated with the students. They ended up supplying the local council with some actionable insights. It was a win-win situation.      Exactly. And if we tap into new media channels, like TikTok or YouTube Shorts, we could even have students present their work as viral-style videos. If we gamify the process with views, likes, and even public votes, the students get a sense of audience and real-world impact.      That does make the learning process more engaging and real. But what about structure and assessment? We can't forget the academics in all of this. How would grading work? Would it still be marked externally or part of a peer-reviewed process?      I think a mix of peer assessment and mentor-led guidance would work well. We could create a platform where students can submit their projects, and have educators and the student community rate and provide feedback. It encourages reflection and iterative learning rather than just getting a grade.      That’s a good balance. It would also encourage students to learn from one another. I wonder, would you be open to developing a pilot program with a couple of local universities in Australia? I know a few educational tech start-ups here that might be interested in collaborating.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? That sun's been a treat after all that rain. Mind if I put the kettle on? Just a spot of tea and a bit of peace.      Please, do! I wouldn’t say no. It's been one of those days — coordinates for a supplier went wonky, and then one of the designers nearly missed his meeting. Classic Tuesday morning, really.      Blimey! I don’t envy your job, love. Seems like someone’s always losing their head these days. Still, you chase it, don’t you? You’ve a good head on your shoulders, just like your mums.      That means a lot coming from you, Nana. I remember you sorting out the parish council back in the nineties for their mishaps, all with just a cup of tea and a sharp mind. How’ve you been lately?      Oh, just about! Hobbled in this stiff old back, and Elaine says I should get to the doctor. Pah! I'm fine, just a bit over the hill, is all. I’ve been up in Cambridge two or three times as it is. Do tell me, what fancy bookshop was that on the High Street? I saw a few old faces in there — some cheeky faces, I might add!      You mean the one run by that old Irish chap? Seems like he was spotting some of the universities at that — he’s got coffee roasting going in one corner too. I might read up a bit more on it. Funny thing — you still looking at buying a place up here?      That I was, but there's a bit about Cambridge that’s quiet a bit snobbish! Not that I’m fussed — a house is a house. Just needs to plug me in and have a garden, not much to it. But I do like the chapel bells here. All that history about. A bit more class than the modern strip where you live, love.      I understand. I could see us visiting more as time goes on. With work getting busier with this new client, it's been tough to keep the schedule tight. Still, I’m happy with it. I think it's time I looked into my nan's old recipe book — got so many stories in there.      Stories and secrets, mostly! You know what your granddad used to say — "Cook it to the day and eat it to the hours."

Rather annoying this, innit? I mean, I knew it'd be chilly in France, but this wind’s got nuffink on it.      Honestly, I didn’t expect a blizzard in May. Chuffed we came out, mind you — wouldn’t miss it for the world. Right, so, how’s uni going for you again?      Yeah, aye. A lot of reading and essays so far. I’m doin’ sciences, y’know, lots of lab reports and whatnot. You on the same boat, or are you more artsy?      Not quite. I’m doin’ languages, actually — French and German. It’s a mix of literature, grammar, and cultural studies. Honestly, more talking than I’d expected, which is a bit of a faff sometimes.      Oi! Wait a second—yo’ speak proper French? Because I definitely ain’t got a clue. Only thing I can mumble is “bonjour,” and that’s if I’m in a good mood.      Haha, I can survive — just about. But I’ve been struggling with the idioms. Tryin' to translate stuff proper. Like, when someone says “tu as piqué ma curiosité” I almost lost it because I thought it meant “You stuck somethin’ in my curiosity.” Silly literal translations.      Oh, fair play. That’s proper funny. Honestly, I’d die tryin’ to translate that. I’m more used to the Yorkshire way of speakin’. Chuffed if I can make someone  understand  me, most o’ the time.      Oh come on, I get most of it. You sound like you know what you’re talking about. So, do you ever play any sports, like football or anything?      Aye, I used to play a bit. Not as much ‘cos I’m studentin’ and stuff, but I still watch a game or two. Leeds United’s me team.      Leeds? They’re doing alright this season, right? I think they got promoted last year or something. I support Arsenal, go on a bit too much about it. Sorry about that.      Nah, it's alright. Y’know, I might one day try and go watch a proper game in Leeds. Thought about it after I’m done with all this student stuff. You workin’ after uni or carryin' on with somethin’ else?      I hope to get into a teaching kind of thing, maybe interpreting or somethin' related to languages. Got to keep the brain used, innit? What ‘bout you, then?      I might give science communicatin’ a go. Or lab work.

Rather annoying when a spider turns up in the kitchen, isn't it? I just saw one scuttling across the counter the other day. Horrible things, really. I mean, sure, they keep the flies away, but honestly, do they have to hang about in the house like that?      Aye, I understand that. I get them in the house all the time too. Though I reckon they’re not too bad if you don’t mind a bit of unpleasantness. It's the mice you gotta watch out for. They’re the real problem. We had an infestation last winter up in my flat. Horrible mess they made—chewing through everything!      Oh no! Mice? That sounds dreadful. I’ve never had a mouse in this house thank heavens. I’d be out of there in a heartbeat. Do you have a cat or anything for that?      No, no cat. I used to have a tabby once, back in the old house in Peterborough, but she’s dead now. Used to adore her. She’d chase the odd bird, though—those little sparrows would always rattle the windows.      I actually quite like the birds around here. There are these robins that come to the garden every morning. They're very cheeky, fairly sidle up to the gate and wait for me to drop them some breadcrumbs. Little creatures are something else.      That’s nice. I wouldn’t say I've got the same patience for them. All that flapping and noise. But I do remember—years ago, when I worked in the café in central Peterborough—there was this giant bullying magpie that stole people’s crisps off the table! You couldn’t touch the chip packet once you opened it.      Oh that sounds like a proper cheeky bird! At least it’s not causing a mess like the mice you described. Although spiders will hang about even if you have them on the property. I assume you just sweep them up or something?      Aye, or good old fashioned hoovering. Websites say you should take 'em outside and let 'em live, but I don’t see why they should live around my floor. I mean, I clean for a living, for goodness’ sake.      You’re not wrong, I suppose. It’s the principle of the thing, really. Wildlife and home appliances don’t mix. Still, I suppose we’re lucky to live in a place where we don’t have to contend with cockroaches or something far worse.

Rather lovely to finally meet in person, Delyth. I've heard so much about you through the family... Our dear cousin James often speaks of the stories your mother used to tell by the fire.      A pleasure to finally have you in our home, Alice. And oh yes, my een used to glaze over when my mother warmed to one of those tales. She always claimed our ancestors were Welsh by birth and English by fate. Rather poetic, don’t you think?      Indeed. My own mother once traced our family through Dorset parish records. Her passing... it’s been a deeply strange chapter for me. She suffered from the same illness as your mother, wasn’t that Myra, if I remember rightly?      Yes, Myra had what the doctors called pick and mix of the body – a cruel condition she was far too brave to admit. I still miss her when I see a daffodil in full bloom. It brings back so many memories, you know?      I understand all too well. I still tell the children at school about her—how she put up with quite a few things for the sake of others, and still smiled through it all. Makes you think how little we prepare people for such things.      And you, young lady, you were a teacher all your time? Now don’t go making me feel old for retiring after thirty-five years in education.      No, no, your experience certainly doesn’t make me feel advanced in years oddly. I teach Latin and English—there's a fair stretch between the two subjects. You used to teach which one, if you don't mind me asking?      Oh, I had geography and Latin. I suppose you could say I was that sort of fixer of things. You know, the kind of teacher who got the local Gazette to drop by for an afternoon once a term. Kept them engaged.      Sounds like a bit of a trailblazer. I could see the two of you being quite a trio together, Myra, yourself and her.      She was a gem, you remember, even though she and your mother sometimes had their differences. But really, that life of theirs was full of so much colour and bristling with spirit that it's always a box of chocolates to remember what your mother was like.      I think we should start putting some of these stories into a book, perhaps to give to the next generation.

Rather lovely to be out here today, isn't it? The sky looks just right for a hot air balloon... if only I could afford one.      You say that every time we take this walk. But honestly, with those power lines overhead, you'd never get more than twenty feet in the air. Still, I understand the dream. Watching them float at sunrise is quite something.      It is. I wish more people appreciated the countryside like this. The noise and pace of London—it must be so different from your upbringing.      Oh, I came to appreciate the countryside eventually. Still, growing up in Islington, the idea of seeing deer in the woods and wild boar turkey on walks was amusing at first. Now I find it ridiculous that I didn't know what a woodpecker was until after university.      You’ve adapted well! And I still can’t believe you've never met my Hound, Max. He’s such a gentle beast, even though he looks like he could scare the woods away. He’d follow you over the hills if you told him to.      A hound, you say? I'd like to meet him. My neighbor's dog howls every time a car passes. So Max must be a marvel by comparison.      That’s an understatement. Anyway, enough about dogs—tell me something about your upcoming lecture. You've been working on medieval literature again, I imagine.      Yes. A course on Chaucer’s use of satire—quite something, really. It's amazing how relevant it stays. But I need more money in the budget for interactive displays about the period... or a real lantern slide to project the text. You’d find it as dull as I do if you were to sit through it.      I'd be there front row. Maybe with Max at my feet. And if you ever get that money, don’t forget a few lanterns for the students to take notes under. You know how your students are—hopelessly romantic about everything medieval. Even if it’s just about the campfires and the long walks in the forest.      Touché. Still, the proposal is pending. Hopefully, I’ll see improvements before next term.      I’ll keep that in mind. Who knows, maybe we’ll finish your research with a picnic at the edge of the woods. Just like the old times.      It's a date. Provided I remember where the woods are when I'm not on a leash.

Rather chilly for a midweek afternoon, isn't it? I was half expecting it to be warmer when I cycled over.      Aye, it's a textbook September, that's for sure—unreliable and a bit grudging with the sun. No sooner do you get your sweater out than there’s a heatwave somewhere else in the country.      It’s funny how the climate varies so much in this part of the UK. I mean, just last week there was a mist floating over the pitch like a ghost. Didn’t it get to you during your spin class?      Not really. Once you get the rhythm going, you don't even notice the temperature. Though I must say, I'd sooner spin in a blizzard than go to the gym in the city, if you get what I mean.      Oh, absolutely! This breakfast club—relaxing place, everyone here after class in their lycra, sipping tea and muesli. I've never seen anything quite like it. It's a far cry from the rows of cardio machines and solitary glares I used to see in gyms.      Tell me about it! I reckon the secret is rhythm and light music. You want people to associate working out with something fun, not like punishment.      That's an interesting thought. It reminds me of something I've been reading about in education. For language learners, context is everything. If they're enjoying the environment or the activity, they absorb more naturally.      Fair enough. So you're a language teacher? That must be fascinating. I’ve never been great with languages. I lasted two years of German at school and still can't say “Where’s the loo?” properly.      It's not uncommendable to step out of your comfort zone like that. My pupils often say they’re rubbish at languages and then, by the year's end, they're surprising themselves with their progress. I think your gym class could stick to that same principle.      Heh, thanks for the tip. I’ll have to keep that in mind when designing the next routine.      Oh, go on then, tell me about your work. Any big projects coming up?      Well, the box gym in Doncaster might be getting a facelift. I’m seriously looking forward to it. We're going for a cozier vibe—think better lighting and a games console for post-cardio cooling down.      Sounding like a gym to warm the heart, not freeze the feet.

Rather annoying this newfit in the boiler innit? Seems like everything sticks on.      What d'ya mean? Y'know, I popped by the gas man himself last week, and he reckons it's doin' fine. Maybe you're not sethin' it proper?      Aye, they 'ad one of them same in th’flats I used t’stay in. Got t'verify the top button; else, it’d go dump or nothin’.      Funny you're askin' 'bout boilers – reminds me of the one in our street back when I were a lad. Bloke next door, 'e turned it up 'igher than a kite, an’ left it on all winter! 'T was like a bloody sauna!      Oh no! So did it break?      Nay, 't just used up more gas than 'is whole family’s eatin'! 'e ended up with a £200 bill over th’ lot o’ us!      Oh老爷! I don’t fancy no £200 bill, especiall' since I'm already on a tight budget with grading work all week. Speakin' of, Lady – have we been out of water last night? The bath was flat as a pancake!      Oh, aye! I ‘eard the tank emptyed up. 'E someone turn the tap off again?      Maybe Grandad did it? He does seem to think it's a tap to pause and look at!      Hello! I was about to make泡t! Thought I’d just check the kettle, but it was th’cistern!      Oh for God's sake! Maybe we need a system, like stickers or something.      Aye, and maybe me and the old man could give ‘im a little refresher course, you know, on which taps stick out from the wall and what they do.      Haha, maybe with pictures! Grandad's good with pictures!      Pictures! I 'ad one go at binoculars once, 'e kept thinkin' it was a line of specs!      Oh bless 'im, your grandad’s still got charm though.      Oh I know, Grandad never changes! It's what I love about him!      Aye, 'e’s the granddad all of us wish we 'ad. Just a softie, albeit one who turns 'is taps into coat hangers now and again!      Well now, since we're on the subject, I've been thinkin' – would it be too much to ask if we could have a grand afternoon tea on Sunday? Would cheer me up grand!      That'd be lovely! We’ll lay it out proper! If you like, we can even see about gettin’ a real ‘ocker_cheers service?

Rather annoying this new satnav, isn't it? Seems to think the A66 is a better option than the usual route, but no—course it's closed for roadworks again.      Aye, we should’ve gone the long way round through Appleby. Satnavs 'ad all the sense of a newt with a brain injury sometimes.      Oh aye, I swear it's just trying to test us. Still, we're only a quarter o' an hour late. Which is sommat like twelve minutes short o' disaster, considering how late some folk get.      Well, no one’s got the patience for late these days. You'd think the postman'd be first through the door if someone's five minutes over, wouldn't you? D'you think Ewan'll be playing?      Aye, better than breakfast, he plays. I've been wanting to hear that new song he's got about the old lead mines, you know, near Kendal? They tell me it's a banger—though I don’t know what that means, really.      It means it's loud and deadly. Like a bagpipe on a washing machine. But it’s all good fun. Least we can knock about with folk at the end, maybe some ceilidh dancing.      Bless, you know I couldn't dance to save my life. Still, the tea and the scones at the tea rooms afterwards are worth the trouble. And the cake—don’t get me started.      You mean the apple tea cake with the hunk of clotted cream? Aye, I remember asking the barmaid what “apple tea” meant, and she said it was just apple and not tea. Properly confused me.      You’re not the only one! I took it for weeks thinking they passed it through tea bags. Still, they don’t do a bad job with it.      You're getting distracted again. Should we stop and get a map or something? Just trying to find the right turn off the main road here.      No, no. This way! The turn's up goin' on your left if you keep going straight for two fields and look out for the gate that's green with the box hedge by it. Proper old-fashioned thing.      There it is then, we’d better start looking out for it. It's a right laugh though—being sat in this car, heading to a gig like we're teenagers again.      Aye, and next thing you'll be trying to get backstage and chasing the lead singer for his autograph.

Rather annoying the new barista today, isn't she? I've been trying her patience by asking for oat milk in the soy latte mistake. Otherwise, how are we, love? Survivor after last night's chaos?      No, I mean—get over it. She'll make yours eventually. Right, now, more importantly—how was the   site visit   yesterday? I peaked at the   university project brief   this morning before heading out and got a headache just reading through it. Seems like someone's got a case of the block adequately for this new campus plan, don't you think?      Honestly, I'd rather be anywhere else, but the   site   was actually quite something. It's a   communal living   experiment, you know, ultra-sustainable, off-grid, co-working spaces, all very   '21st-century student housing'  . The problem is the brief doesn't specify how dorm and community space are balanced... I spent half the day arguing with the client's rep, thinking to myself—  "You want to reduce isolation but still expect everyone to do their own laundry?"        I know, right? It’s like trying to   juggle flaming coconuts in a wind tunnel  . But it does remind me of   Simon   at the practice down the road. He's still   struggling at work  , I imagine. His last email was something like:   "I’ve spent three days designing a door that isn't even in the brief. I miss doing my taxes."        Oh, I had a similar email from him the other day. So,   out with the client  , in with the panic.   Speaking of  , have I told you about Anna? Her   breakfast orders   have become increasingly elaborate. This morning, she ordered a   vegan smoothie bowl with beetroot, sesame seeds, and activated almonds  . I tried to laugh it off, but I passed out. Rather annoying I had to take a call just as I was slicing the onions, Richard. They think it's a proper emergency because some script format went wrong at work. At least it isn't making you miss your Friday crossword puzzle, is it? Well, let's see what this 14-year-old vintage has to say about itself. So far, it’s been 30 odd roles in my life — administration, transcription, bellyache, bard, bureaucrat — and now, wine taster.

Rather annoying me though, innit. Rather annoying when the barista at the weekend used my first name. I was just trying to order a flat white, and she insisted she knew me now because I come in every Tuesday. Do you think you'd get on better with a brand new person or is it just nostalgia?      It's like that old turkey soup saying, isn't it? The new one never tastes the same. I prefer the familiarity. When I imagine the barista as my soulmate, I have to see the uniform stained with coffee and hair in a messy bun, and it immediately changes everything.      You did it again. Looking for that perfect match with mismatched mugs, because really, that's where the magic is.      Silly, I know, but you know that whole spiritual journey thing is just someone looking for an excuse to avoid making a tough decision? It's like we're trying to outwit each other with vague terms. What would you say is your most desired trait in a colleague, or even a soulmate?      Loyalty without the clinging, I think. Someone who supports you and fails you alike. Not that I've met it, but it's out there. My idea of a party—whether imaginary guest list or real—would probably be just friends with similar preferences. No small talk, all substance.      You're getting your party on already! I was thinking about being in a different era. Do you think I'd fit better in the 1920s where people still wore hats?      Definitely go for 1940s or 1920s. You in a flapper dress with a feather, dancing the night away. I’d be the jazzy pianist lost to the rhythm and the drink.      You might be better off as the establishment, keeping the place in order.

Rather annoying the new tax rules, isn't it? Seems like everything's getting more complicated for small businesses. I got to inform some clients about it this week, and I can already see the heads nodding with worry.      No, I can imagine! I wouldn't know where to start with all that. I liked the idea of knitting the new baby a sweater, at least that’s not going to change. A bit stressful with work changes too—starting a new role in a couple of weeks.      You'll be smashing it, love. If it's anything like how you dealt with those IT issues last year, you'll be alright. I've been to a couple of culture events lately and they had some interesting topics around language differences too. Fun to reflect on what people think about East Anglia.      I think there are too many stereotypes about everyone, aren't there? Based on where you're from or what you do. I've noticed in HR that being from different places can lead to subtle biases even if you're not aware. Good to see culture events help break that.      Yeah, I remember one culture event we went to as kids and someone tried to stereotype us based on our accents. It was kind of funny and quite offensive, all at once. Though at the time it was new to me, and I had no context to respond.      All that aside, the whole idea of guns and violence in society came up in a meeting the other day. As someone in HR, I’ve had to deal with threats and bad language. It can affect the workplace morale badly.      That’s tough. I remember visiting a colleague at his hometown and we were near a graveyard. I found the tombstones quite interesting, the way people inscribe stuff on them and the local traditions that go with it. It felt very unifying for the community.      I like visiting places like that too. There's something about it that grounds you. It's probably also nice to escape talking about work once in a while. I did stick to my first aid refresher course as well, which always comes with lunches and a chance to meet people.      Defo, I did a day by the lake the other month away from work. I usually work from home or head to the building in town, so it was quite refreshing.

Rather annoying this new tax thing eh? You know, me an’ the flatmates had such a mither when we got our bill through. Yeah, it’s not bad. Bit cold, tho’. New boiler’s taken forever to get sorted and now we’ve got a leak under the floor. Fun stuff. It’s just us, the water, and the ghosts, I swear.      Sounds like it’s a bit of a character. Ours is alright, mind you. Not a mansion in the slightest, but at least it doesn’t fookin’ scream at us in the middle of the night. I mean, do you lot get that?      I do, quite a lot to be honest. It started after I put my bloody kettle on—it always goes  “HOO-HOOOO!”  like a ghost trying to get out. I nearly dropped it one time, and my mam texted me saying don’t be daft and turn it off if it’s doing that!      Haha, sounds like your kettle’s got a vengeful spirit in it. They had a full on electrocution moment, ended up with a little zap on the arm. Steve had to chuck them out of the house and now he’s banned them for life.      Sore thing for Tom, after he spent three quid on kebabs goin’ on that fookin’ spree again. But hey, at least it’s making the rounds. Word of warning, innit?      It really is. I’ve been thinkin’ about putting my hours in at that student bar, ya know? Just to see if I can’t make a few bob here and there.
