Rather do a bit o’ cyclein’ whilst I were down in Cornwall, dontcha think? The Yorkshire in a Day lot were absolutely brill. I’m more than a bit tired, mind you.      Oh, we do love readin' those sorts o’ things in the paper. Got eeny plans to go voluntin’ with the YHA up north any time soon?      I were actually just thinkin’ of this—do ya remember seein’ those photos o’ that little journey one man did in Yorkshire? Sounded lik’ a right pain in the ’ose to fetch everything to every village.      That’s the one, deary. You know, like that lighthouse journey? I’ve always wished to visit one myself. Ten o'clock on the dot and the lights go on and you think, blimey—what if it’s a misty morning and I see nothin’?      I used to live teachin’ science and we once talked about the lighthouse keepers—how they had to climb that spirally staircase with a ladder and everything, and listen for the impacts of the crabs outside as they scraped against the walls. Bit old-school, innit?      Oh aye, I remember that. Back in my day at school, I didn’t think it was all that interesting. Though I reckon the crabs did have claws as big as a large book ‘Baldrick might find useful in the old sketches.      Yes! That’s just the sort of odd detail that makes school lessons interesting. Also, I did a bit of talkin’ at a school once when I were a childminder. I told ‘em about a time I picked the little one up and she had a thimble full of lard in her coat pocket!      Crikey, that’s somethin’ else. I always tell the kids at school about funny things I learn—like the time I told ‘em all scientists once thought crabs had no heart. Imagine that! We know better now, obviously.      Heh, that’s a new one on me. Now, whilst you two were tellin’ tales, I were just thinkin’ ’bout goin’ on that cycle race up near Harrow next spring. You ever do one, Catherine?      Oh no, I’ve never been one for the race track, I’ll be honest. Although, after that trip down to Cornwall, I’m more keen to do a bit o’ ‘browlin’ again, just a little bit.      I’d support that, Catherine. I’ve done them sorts of shorties once or twice, very fit.

Rather skip the newfit sludge, innit? Eh Lucas, you know her—the one ‘ere—what d’ya fancy? Just bung it in the oven, ay?      I dunno, honestly. No idea what we’ve got. Just threw in a few packets when I saw the lass coming over.      Honestly, Lucas, sometimes you don’t even try. What if this was your mum’s house? She’d roll her eyes so hard, pulling out the same tinned soup again?      Okay, okay. You won’t get a three-star meal out of me—mind yer, Lucy. What’s in the fridge?      Just a bit o’ lasagne left. It’s from Wednesday, ain’t it? D’you know how I make it? Easy. Pasta, ground beef, a bit o’ cheese.      Like everyone, Hattie. But what’s the deal is you finish it, then puff it off so it goes nicely.      Naa, I know what I’m doing. I put two layers minimum. Want to come and help?      Nah, watching football tomorrow, innit? Be better off cooking it yourself.      I know Lucas, because you always say that. One time you nearly set the kitchen on fire trying to heat up a jacket potato!      That was just someone not using the microwave right.      Besides, we’re not here for the lasagne specifically. It's more the company and tea. Can I speak to you about something Hattie? about work actually...      Go on then, Charlie. Not like I’ve got anything else to worry about.      Quick reminder, eh? Before the chain ‘o hangovers begins.      Lucas, just shut up a sec. Charlie told me ‘bout it last night, so go on.      It's about this project I've been involved in. There've been a couple of spots of difficulty with team management and also… well you remember Jack?      From the warehouse goon show on your own?      Yeah, well he started sniffing around me. And he lives in the same area what your dad’s bar. It's awkward.      That’d be awkward alright, never had that happen to me. Just been in the ‘ole area, been working and them alone.      Arrr, Charlie. My advice? Keep it professional, keep it short, keep it far.      Or tell him she’s got a boyfriend before it goes too far.      No, no, babe. Irrelevant. All that does is lead to more awkwardness when it ends. Keep it minimal, keep it neutral.      Thanks, Hattie. Appreciate the advice.

Rather lovely to sit out here on such a peaceful Sunday morning. I’d forgotten just how beautiful the Cypriot coastlines are, really.      Not a bad view himself, eh? Being out of London for a few days has done wonders for the ears, if you know what I mean. The clatter, the chatter—it’s sorely absent here.      Oh I agree. A Sunday by the coast, no rush anywhere, it’s quite a treat. It’s interesting you mentioned London—what brought you to the Med this time?      You know, just needed a bit of a reset. I’ve been running my own business for nearly six years now and let’s just say, it’s not all jet-setting and high-fives. Most of the time I’m buried in emails, and I think I turned into a shade grayer in about a year. How about you, then?      Haha, hard to compete with you and your awards, I’m afraid. I’ve been a teacher for over 12 years now—about ten of those at the same secondary school up near Dorset. A bit different to your high-flying life, let me tell you.      I wouldn’t say “high-flying” – just survival of the fittest, really. Far from it, actually. Teaching must have been quite the experience—dealing with teenagers day after day.      There are pros and cons, but I’d say the pros often outweigh the chaos. Those years I had a group with a particular spark, some of whom I’m still in touch with. The gratitude I get from a note or a message about how I helped them makes all the headstrong years of my lot worthwhile. Not much like what you’re doing, is it?      Not at all. I do miss, well, the simplicity of things that didn’t involve spreadsheets. Though I have dabbled in education a few times—investing in a few start-ups for ed-tech. Nothing too hands-on, but I’ll admit to being a bit smug when one of them took off.      That must be satisfying, even from afar. Sometimes I wonder how I got go so far on the opposite end of the spectrum.      I say, that’s because we were given different tools—and different passions. Now, you don’t have to take it seriously, but if you ever wanted to start your own project in education, I’d love to talk sometime.

Rather annoying me a bit, eh? You know what me an’ the lads are like when it comes to cleaning up. Never bin no great shakes at tidyin’ up properly, ha!      Yeah, honestly love, the state of things at our flat is getting out of hand. I saw the bin  again  last night an’ just about lost it. I’ve had enough, I reckon we need a proper clean or summat this weekend.      Aye, you’re not wrong there. Me ma would.Fatalfanst me if she saw the mess. But how d’ya expect me t’do it when every week me flatmates are out at the bar? It’s like everyone else’s idea of a weekend is gettin’ pissed, not bein’ responsible.      I’ve tried talkin’ to them an’ all, but they’re better at gettin’ a pint up than they are with a hoover. Mebbe we should do it when they’re out then? I mean, I know it’s not ideal, but I’m getting sick of walkin’ in a place that looks like a bin exploded.      Haha, fancy that—just chuck on some tunes, bin it out, an’ get stuck in while the cheeky ones are elsewhere havin’ a laugh. You an’ me could deep clean an’ not have t’worry about anyone binin’. Just don’t expect me to dust the ceiling, someone’s gotta be practical about heights!      That’s a fair point—job for the scaffolders, then. But really, what I’m sayin’ is, it’s not just ugly about it. I’m startin’ t’get the sniffles every time I walk in now thanks to the dust. Properly tired of it.      Aye, an’ for the love of Pete, no one uses the rubbish bags. I swear me flat’s bin is a time capsule—stuff in there I’ve seen since uni. Archeologist’s dream come true, innit?      Yeah, we need new rules or summat. Some schedule o’ when things get binned. Mebbe like a cleanin’ timetable goin’ on the wall?      Ha, I like that—proper organisational vibes. Who’d’ve thought we’d be runnin’ a bloody NHS level clean in our own flat, eh?      Better than belly floppin’ on the mess, I reckon. Look, let’s just sort it up this Satur’day. You up for it?      Course, always up for a bit o’hard work for you and our sanity. Just don’t expect me to clean the loo—I’ve got standards, y’know!

Rather a lot to carry, eh, love? That supermarket do get the best of us sometimes. Mind if I put the parcels down by the fire? It's getting a bit heavy on the old bones.      Not at all, dear. Be as you are. I’ll give you a hand once I’ve got the kettle on. It was lovely to get out, wasn’t it? Bit of a grey day, but I think we needed that air.      Aye, it’s not often we get to stretch the legs. You always insist on the heavier bags, though. You don’t like to let me carry more than I can handle, do you?      Course not! You’re not a spring chicken, you know. And I’m not about to go back to the days of you doing all the heavy lifting. A little bit goes a long way nowadays, doesn’t it?      That it does. Less energy for everything these days. I remember the old days, shopping, then back for the tea and the papers. So much more pace to life.      I know, but I don’t mind the slower pace now. It gives me time to think, to reflect. The others would probably say we’re both too slow these days. Though I can’t imagine dragging any of them with me on these shopping runs!      Now don’t go making them out to be the lazy ones, love. We’ve been around the block a few times more than they have!      Possibly. But then we’re the ones with the stories to tell about it, aren’t we? Anyway, let’s not get too carried away there. We have about five minutes before the tea’s ready. Have you decided what we’re doing tomorrow?      Going to be one of those laid-back days, if we can manage it. Perhaps a bit of reading, the telly on in the background. Nothing that requires too much effort. I did think we might give that little walk by the river a try when the weather improves a bit.      That’d be nice. A bit of fresh air and scenery would do us both the world of good. Still, I won't be best pleased if the weather changes its go again!      Aye, you give the weather a hard time, but I think it does its best most of the time. Passes the test half-decent days in.

Rather annoying this newfit in the boiler innit? Seems like everything sticks to it, and it takes hours to shift the cobweb out of the dining room ceiling. I’ve asked Mum if we could put a notice up in the village to see if anyone fancies helping us for a few bob, but she says eeny weeny helpers will make the job bigger 'cos they'll need tea every five minutes.      Aye, I know what you mean, lad. And mind you, I’ve got someone coming round tomorrow to mend the step-stool under the outside light, but the bloke won’t fetch the part himself, even if it’s just down t’hardware store in Malton. You know the type — 'Can ye bring the bolts with you, Mrs. Preston? Tenpence ain’t far enough.'      That’s the same as the man who was at the old school yesterday. I was doing a Maths paper and happened to hear him on the phone — his missus had lost her phone, and he said to her, 'I’ll pop down to that new shop over the road, luv, and buy one up.' I thought, 'Up as in upwards?' and only realISED when I asked him in the break, 'Were you climbing a tree to get one?' He laughed – Mate, I got a ladder, and now it's on.'      Now don’t laugh at them, Silas. I remember when we were at your age, and the old man wanted to put in a TV aerial. All he had was a dictionary and a hammer. He tried to make the letters spell sense, and then hit it until it looked like a house of cards. Oy, nearly about blocked the chimney stack he was up so high.      Aye, and you was the one who fetched the plug and pushed the handle down the pipe, eh? Jus’ ‘cos the bloke from the telecom said the signal was funny. I thought me grandkids would laugh when I told them, but they fell about — you know when I started chucking the plug into the bin every week to see if it would improve the 'connection.'      Now, love, no need for that, I got this new TV that the son sent me goin' on the loo wall. If I sit wrong, I get line in the trousers, so I always go boxers up.      Grandma! Grandpa! I seriously think I'm gona throw up.

Rather annoying this, innit? We’ve been waitin’ ages for this internet company bloke to come fix the broadband. Never bin no luck since last week. I can’t even stream a pint of proper tea properly at this rate.      Yeah, well, at least it’s not eeny weeny TV, innit? Not like me mum’s rigmarole—switches on a box that only works when it’s sunny side up. I’m facin’ a right   p   e road journey just to tell som’un to check the cables outside when it don’t even rain hard enough to shift the sod!      Honestly, I’m just grateful I can do some uni work on MyMacBook here. Still, enough talk of bursts in the signal. I’m hearin’ Oliver’s brother is coming round in a bit? Is he still in Manchester at uni?      He is, but he’s returning after some right hard week. I hear the uni in hides, you know, near the canal? They’ve had some real blokes sabotaging the student-quarters—personally I’d just take one look and say “no thanks” and carry on.      Oh yeah, reckon the campuses up there been a right struggle. I’m at – MateCampus, fairly alright, least I’ve seen a decent amount of the city. Still don’t reckon they’ve got the facilities as good as Oxford or Cambridge, but what d’you want? Who wears full cricket dress anyway?      That’s oddly sour-mouthed—look, the key is   shakin’ and bein’ baked  , innit? If you’re fit and healthy about it, university is a right goldmine. Got the fitter lot here trying to do spin classes and fails at it. Not like me, I handle it all in the kitchen—banter, jaffles, baked beans.      Hey, health products are a bit of a buzz these days, innit? I tried some stuff from Amazon once—some dodgy supplement from Lagos and I swear I saw a glow in me toe nails. Bad idea.      Yeah, well you don’t see me trying anything like that. Fitness is more go out and get some life, you know? Any road, I reckon once the broadband’s back, I’ll be on box sets until the weekend. Anyone else fancy Shawshank Redemption again?      Only if we can pause it halfway and belly-laugh to some of the dodgy sound effects they added when we rewound it. I swear the warden’s got a moustache that talks in the next one!

Oh, and a couple of litres o' milk. What about you, Mum? Anythin’ else?     : Eggs, bread, beans, milk. Lakelands is always a bit short the day after the weekend. I'll put that on the list. What about you James, got any ideas? Don't go off and pick sweets again!     : Aye, can we get some chocolate biscuit things? And breakfast cereal—Granola bars!     : Oh don’t remind me of granola bars, you didn’t have any the other day and I had to endure your whingein’ for hours! Try savin’ up your allowance instead, eh?     : Haha, James, go on save up for the stickers. We will do healthy today. What about you –?     : You all know me, I’m set. But did you manage to kill that wasp in the garden yet? It been buzzing around for ages.     : Aye, my man, tried to swat it a couple times but it’d fly off. So I let the cat at it. The cat had a ballet, but it escaped.     : Classic! That's the problem with insects, they're like little Ronssens! Swat 'em once and they’re back the next day!     : True. Maybe you need a steady hand and a bug spray. I have some eco-friendly one at work. I can bring it by.     : Brilliant. We could spritz the garden. Though if it’s eco-friendly, do they not mention the fact that sometimes the eco stuff doesn’t work? Still, it’s worth trying.     : Fair point. I’ll see if it works on spiders too. Gave my kids a bite the other week. He were boxin’ on his leg for hours. What did you have, James?     : I was bit last Saturday by some big black one. It were itchy for a while, but when Mums cleaned it with that bactine thing, it got better.     : Right, so the first thing is cleanin' the area. Then, we can apply somethin’ like an antihistamine cream if it’s irritatin’. I have some on the side for things like that.

Rather annoying this cold, innit? I've been grumpy as a badger in a public library. I got the news off BBC2 about this Lloyd Grossman bloke—claims he can read body language off CCTV footage. Sounds like some sort o' dodgy magic trick to me.      Right, I heard of 'im. Lecturer at Cambridge if I'm not mistaken. Bit controversial. I’ve been huddled up on the sofa too, but it’s easier when you’ve got a hot cup o’ tea and no one to answer to. Didn’t you get the vaccination last week?      Aye, that made me feel like a wet Sunday morning, only lasted a few hours though. My turkey curry must have bin dodgy though. I 'ad to dash off to the loo like a shot, and I think the whole house smelled it!      Blimey! Health and hygiene gone 'orribly wrong. HOSPITALS these days, you ever looked at one? They look more like airports than places for people to get better. I mean, do they even have carpets anymore? All white floors and antiseptic air.      And speaking o', fancy turning on the telly for a bit? BBC1 was doing some piece on national health – Mate, have you heard about the new tech they’re trying to use in monitoring patients? CCTV in hospital wards to assess patients’ moods and states of mind using body language. Dunno if it feels a bit Spock-like, y'know?      Blokey, that’s hotter than the curry I ate. What if the cameras bin hacked? I don’t fancy people reading me like a textbook about how I’m feeling. And what if the machine misreads something? It might think I'm bored and not pain because I’m trying to read the housing manual again.      Could ‘appen. Maybe it’s not for expressing feelings, more for monitoring health? Like, if someone is holding something too tightly or trying to hide a tremor. You ever seen those deep-liar detection tests? I reckon this tech could be helpful – with caution.      Aye, but let’s hope it don't get pushed too far. I mean, I wouldn’t fancy bin on camera all day like some kind of livestock at the farm. Still, if it helps people get quicker treatment, I can see the value in it. Now, can I get you a cup of tea? I think I'm startin' to thaw out a bit!

Rather annoying this gridlock at the shopping centre. I couldn't get the milk for tea time.      I had no luck either today. Drove all the way from the other side of town for a loaf of proper sourdough and came back with a motorway-sized queue for the butcher’s!      It was the same where I was. I wanted to buy a few preserves but couldn’t find anything apart from that new brand of jam. Oh, and what was it, someone mentioned a music magazine in the queue?      Yes, I saw one on the trolley near the baked goods. Someone left it, so someone else just took it. Typical of these days. My visit was wasted, but I did get to reflect on the last time I queued – back in the '70s I think it was – for records at a shop by the old school.      I've been thinking about that music magazine ever since. I posted about it on Facebook, thinking maybe someone might have one to spare. I would love to see covers from the '80s again.      You did a great post. It stirred up some memories for me too. I remember watching concerts at Wembley in the late '70s. My father would take me there sometimes, and I used to get so excited.      Oh, what a lovely recollection! I remember taking care of children who’d be similarly excited at that age. It’s also the reason I read extensively and brought books to the children at school—shared experiences are what make a community.      That brings me to the scrabble game we have about once a week. I play it quite seriously now, especially after I had to document a complicated transcription and thought of it. Do you remember the time we had a word so obscure that the others refused to accept it?      How could I forget! I suggested "flibbertigibbet" and the others fell about laughing. I had to check the dictionary while you were quietly chuckling.      And what of the new word you all introduced last time? Wasn't it something to do with cooking and a method the French use? I still can't remember it properly.      You’re thinking of "basilic". We were talking about infusing oils and your suggestion was actually quite creative. I made it to the conference notes last week, where those culinary techniques were under discussion.      Oh, how very professional of you, Speaker_1.

Rather a lot of activity here today, isn't it, George? I was just down by the sheds and saw some nifty bits of machinery being sorted out. D'you remember when such things were novelty?      Aye, the days when things were simpler, Martha. Back in my time, I was running about Germany with a print system I'd just got off the ground—rolling out exhibitions like you might roll up a carpet! Got more stubble than smiles, mind you, what with all the engineering involved. But we had our moments. You always had more flair, of course. Gallery life suited you like paint on canvas.      Flair is the word, I suppose. Though I like to think of it as instinct, you know. When I opened that little art corner in Exeter, I wasn’t picky about what came in—just had an eye for storytelling. Cats would come in, see a Bucks-wool throw beside a Horsley print and walk out with five items! No, you didn’t have to prescribe a narrative to things, just let the character come out.      Remarkable really. I never did quite grasp that. Print systems and me—well, that was gear on gear. Germany, though? Absolutely a curious time. You landed in Frankfurt one morning with a box of samples, and by Friday, had a whole exhibition underway. Would set up in these dimly lit halls with a tape measure and a smile! The Germans, they appreciated precision, someone who could talk to a machine with a knowing eye.      I remember—piece of toast and a meeting in the café next door, and still managed to make your colleague wait ten minutes past the about-turn! You were a frustrating but very efficient man, George. I had to document a whole new world with my art that yours then brought to the masses. Rather a strange side to the business, don’t you think?      Strange, yes. But it worked. You documented beauty; I got beauty onto shelves. I always thought you knew when to let things speak for themselves. Like your yellow sunflowers from Somerset—enigmatic with a dash of charm.      Wasn’t that you once said something about ‘vivid prints and their silent companions go hand in hand’?      That was me—still do. Prints without context are like tea without sugar, inflexible.      So, have you made peace with your machine tools, George? Or are you still adjusting?

Rather annoying when the satnav says 'Mawrth', like it's her own name or something. It's "March". And no one calls it "Cornew" like it's spelt!      Aw, lass, that’s just how the Cornish pronounce it. Got eeny different dialect there, more like Breton 'cause of the history. You know, they've a funny way of listing stuff. Not like in this bit, where we stick to English.      Know what I was doing the other day? We had to analyse the  language  of a speech, like, how does the speaker use language to persuade people and all that hippo-cratic stuff. It’s turkey university, innit?      Aye, well if you’re keen on language, and I mean the whole history of it an’ all, uni might be better for you than just college. I hated exams. They didn't teach me a thing, but I looked after hides, you know, spare parts and such. Good money, but no help for the brain, if you know what I mean.      What did you read, like? Philosophical stuff, maybe?      Eh, not much. Was more into practical things – how to fix radios, deal with cheery customers, that sort of thing. More somethin’ to do than just sit about. Still, if you're thinking of linguistics or English, just make sure you're good with the boring bits like syntax and etymology.      Yeah, but it's cool how words come from Latin and Greek and all that. Like, "philosophy" is from Greek for "love of wisdom." And the spelling is chaotic. Why can "cough," "through"" and "bough" all have different sounds but the same "ough"?      That's the thing about language, lass. It's a bit of a mess. But that's the fun of it, you know. Like, did you know that “quinoa” came to the UK from the Andean people? I heard it was nearly the same as the Inca's name for it. Then it took off in the health stores as goody-two-shoes food.      True, I remember in the farmer’s market they had stalls with blokes selling it in ziplock bags. So weird.      You want to avoid service stations with broken toilets and belly-ups from dodgy sausages, ‘cause this is a long one, this drive. But the views are all worth it. Always stops pouring down in Cornwall when you least expect it. Lightning? Right handy for the drama.

Rather annoying the new oven’s still playin’ up, innit?      Yeah, got me confused half to death mornin’. Blows cold air an’ all. Thought I’d bin thrown into a moonshot or somethin’.      Haha, eeny munny, I used the one next door. Faster if yer use the heat straight up, aye? A lot o’ folk do that too.      Right, I know someone said that! Put the tray near the top. Didn’t even get the pot well under way. Get frozen to bits, even!      That’s because it only turns warm when yer put the heating turkey on. I’ve done enough oven lefts in this house! I’m startin’ to bin feel pickled I’ve been turned round so oft.      Yeah, breakfast, dinner—maybe need to bin rewire the kitchen in general. Bloomin’ modernisation!      Haha, well, I reckon we’d all need degrees in electrical faults before we bin finishin’ up. I never did quite make it to univesity myself, but I fancy I’ve got a degree in mess ups.      Poor lad—heard about it: got fairly sidled in college because they thought yer couldn’t even parse somethin’ written out. Seems Silly Stones!      Naa, fair enough. Who said life was fair? At least I can brew a good old-fashioned stew. Funny thing—job’s all out weighin’ and diggin’. Still, sod it all!      I do miss the old days back in Doncaster, touch wood. We bin had our own cooking on the hob! Proper old charm to that!      Maybe we’re all bin a bit over-civilized for our lowness here, innit? Signals me to the hob again.      I dunno, I’ve been sort o’ out of it as well. Mainly doing what I always did: lunches, a little bit of bobbins, but nae grand set-up, nae. Pensions! Haha!      Bless you! Always there for a laugh, innit?      And the box, the telly, your lot. Been watching all the old programmes again. Love how they’ve bin putting em back on, don’t like new ones to much.      Yeah, I reckon them modern ones bin a bit bleak for all of us. Always got somethin’ wrong in them, innit?      Oh, alright! So, who’s got the next task before it goes completely cold in this kitchen? I reckon I bin ready to bin done for tea, me!      Go on y’then, I’m nex’. I bet this brings us back on track, innit?

Rather annoying driving instructor I've got. You know what they do—drill it in, drill it in... got to pick up a gear after this road, downshift before that junction.      Aye, can be a bit much. But you've got to be cautious, haven’t een? I've taught English to a few people who were just beginning to drive. It’s not easy.      Fair dos. Proper confused I am. Oh, and she was waffling on about mirror checks and blind spots. You’d never run outta time with all those looks you’ve gotta do.      Well, it's the law, innit? On test they'll pin you on it if you skip. Fun fact—I've known people fail their test from not checking the mirrors, even if the move itself turned out fine. It's all about the procedure.      Procedure? I just want to get me in and out the road, no getting clocked, you know? I've worked in the pubs over the years, so I_DRIVER do know how a car works, but this feels different.      I_DRIVER remember when I got my licence. Goodness, I was terrified. But it does get better. You just have to remember that it's new to you, and that's natural.      Yeah, I reckon. You finished that module on idiomatic expressions yet? Still finding the homework a bit of a stretch at times.      Oh aye, did that module a week ago. They're handy things, idioms. Far more common in speech than in writing. If you understand them, people about you will respect you a bit more.      Could be. I_DRIVER hadn’t thought about it that way. I've only started taking the English studies seriously to improve me communication at work. Getting customers’ orders right can be tricky when you speak too quick or they don’t understand yer.      That's exactly why I chose teaching. We crack down on pronunciation and common expressions to help people fit in. Do you play sports much? Might help with the rhythm and clarity in speech too.      I_DRIVER do a bit go to the gym usually, if I've not got work. Gotta look the part, innit? Never really played a team sport though. Lift your ego and you'll be puffing in ten minutes.      Fair enough, I_DRIVER’m more of a reader myself. But that's overrated, anyway—everyone has their thing.

Rather annoying when the clock’s gone wrong, isn’t it? I was just about to brew a pot of coffee, and I thought it was half-past, and I’ve had to call Joan over to check. Seems it were only a quarter past, and we’ve frightened the cat!      Hasn’t been a normal day then, has it? I reckon Bill might be in town today, I saw a car from his garage just before I popped over. He was going to collect a donation box for the local church—said he was doing a bit of gardening outside the church too.      Right, I’ve sorted who’s doing what. I’ll handle the donation box and paint up some banners for the Gambia project. You know, dear, the one we tried to help with the clinic back in '08? Made quite the impact. But I must admit, it’s harder convincing people than it used to be—maybe I’ve been thinking too much about Munchausen’s Syndrome lately?      You always say the most interesting things, Bill. Munchausen’s? I get it, I listen—everyone I look after puts on a different face each week. But back to the today’s goings on—Elizabeth, would you mind getting that coffee started? I’m too old to wait for delays!      Of course, of course. I’ll set the kettle to boil and see if I can salvage the tea leaves. Still, the cat’s chasing the tail again—but at least it weren’t me this time!      Funny thing—cats and tails. Just like the bell ringing and being late. Can’t fault the dedication in the people, but I do wonder who’s finally managing the schedule round here! Anyway, Joan, mind looking at my driving Licence and checking if it needs renewing? I’m thinking of a trip to Norfolk to visit family.      Norfolk, well now—Costessey, wasn’t it? You know, I was told my gran once used to meet your family for picnics out by the river. Those were the days of doing things simply, without the lunches delivered or the big garden centres.      Oh you remember that? Then you must know about the old folks’ goings on with the plants! Elizabeth and I used to trade cuttings, even in the deepest winter. Never could beat a blooming geranium in your window, could we?      You never could, no.

Rather annoying when the new app we're all meant to use for everything crashes mid-purchase, don't you think? I've lost two shops worth now because of it. Honestly, what were they thinking?      Yeah, I know the feeling. Tried it last week. Went to order my usual Chinese, and boom, the app crashed. So I just walked to the shop instead. Cheaper than a new fridge, right? At least I got a free prawn cracker with my takeout.      Classic. Hey, did anyone catch the new horror film that came out last month? I heard it's a bit of a doozy. I've got the popcorn supply ready, but I'm not sure Myra can handle it after last time.      Oh, I saw the preview, and it looked terrifying. If you remember, I had an extended scene about the clown at the end when I was 12. Myra still laughs about it every horror season, thanks ever so much. You thinking of watching it together?      Yeah, I was hoping for a few company for the full experience—somebody to scream with, not just to mock. And maybe reassure me that the clown is probably not watching us right now.      I’m in – but only if we can pick the film, because the other day Anna was telling me her flatmate thought there were ghosts in their house. False alarm, apparently, but that made me curious. Our group could scare each other for a week with horror stories alone.      That sounds fun. Though, speaking of Anna, I wonder if she’s remembered to bring the housewarming gift for her parents in about two weeks. Anna tends to be quite the reliable one, but this time I'm unsure what she's got planned.      Honestly, if she's invited both her parents and her two older brothers, like she mentioned, I can only imagine the turnout. I remember her telling me they’re planning on serving traditional food. I wonder if I’ll be able to stomach all the sprouts and colcannon again. It’s always a test of culinary bravery.      I love going over there for these things. Then again, I’m the guy who once goaded someone on to see if jalapeno could go with milk—still wondering how that worked out between us. But, blokes, when it comes to food, we all have our quirks.      Well, as long as we’re not planning anything to do with the app or ghosts over dinner, we’ll be just fine.

Rather annoying this, having to rely on public transport when you're used to driving. Mind you, it's not got the seats it had twenty years ago, more of a bench with a cushion now. Still, better than nothing. Not sure I'll ever get used to it, mind.      That and the bloody timetable changes every time you look at 'em! I had to ring up the station just yesterday to make sure I wasn’t catchin’ a train that didn’t exist. It's a wonder anyone under thirty can manage it, the way it shifts around. But I suppose it's not too bad for a couple of retired old farts like us, is it?      You sound like Myra, bless her, she used to mutter on about the timetable every time I took her to town. Always thought I should get her one of them phone alarms for the buses. Probably better than breakfast, to be honest.      Oh, don’t remind me of getting people to places, I nearly broke a nail trying to pack Myra’s walking frame in the boot of the car once. I still don’t know how it fit. But as it is, I’ve started using that fancy new bus that goes to the High Street. The driver was from Manchester, which surprised me – but it stopped at all the right places, so I wasn’t going to complain.      You and me both. I’d rather catch a bus that goes directly than have to change twice at Sprowston. At my age, climbing stairs is not a good idea. You’d think they’d at least make the buses have steps that lower automatically, like they do on the mainland!      Ah, well, you can't blame the drivers, I imagine. It's what you've got to work with. Still, I reckon it's a better bet than trying to get a taxi for the price they ask nowadays. I passed one last week that wanted more for a trip to the shops than I paid for the whole fuel bill when I had a car.      Oh that’s right, I read somewhere they've increased the fares again because of fuel. Not that the drivers aren't hardworking, mind. Just tacks on the cost to the goer. I remember when you could get a taxi for practically nothing and they even gave you a cuppa.

Rather annoying this new traffic system on the M6, isn't it? I was trying to get up to Manchester last weekend and it took ages. I’m more used to navigating Dublin's clogged streets than this!      Yes, the motorways are a bit of a maze these days. Got stuck in the same traffic last week while heading to the airport. Makes me think about all the times I used to travel for oil projects. Back then, this road was practically empty; you could go as fast as you dared. We had to be moving quickly for those offshore rigs in Scotland.      I like to think of it as nature’s little vacation plan, slowing us down so we can finally enjoy the tea and biscuits you prepared, Mum!      Oh, well if I had known, I’d have brought the whole box of scones with me earlier! Cats are better at breakfasts—relentless about tea times. Haha!      Speaking of which, how are the back issues, Dad? I read over the weekend that taking regular breaks and keeping the body active is essential after 50. You did your teaching as if you were supplying brainpower, non-stop.      Well, I’m not sure about the “supplying” – but it was often fairly exhausting, and now that I'm retired, I'm trying to move more. Had to start walking every morning. Found it useful for keeping the old mind engaged and the old body upright at the same time!      Walker, not climber, preferably! Some of us are more focused on getting the tea and being able to sit down afterwards! Look, as someone who once spent about five years planning drilling patterns in Texas, the most important thing is efficiency—especially when it comes to your health.      Efficiency and reflection, if we're both to have peace, I suppose. Maybe you should guest-edit my will once in a while. I could do with it!      With your enthusiasm for retirement, I could see the two of you planning that ideally as well. Next topic: the house move. Grannie told me the surveyor came. How's it going, Mum?      That's still in the bureaucratic map pond, if you ask me. Just waiting for the final signatures and stamp of approval. It'll go further, but it’s already one of those projects that could have been made for a conservation conference seminar, not my kitchen.

Mum, I just wanted to say sorry again about what happened with your bike. I know it’s been piling up and I’m really grateful you got it back.      Aww, Evie, don’t worry about it, love. It’s over now. Honestly, I was so gutted when it went missing—it felt like they took   half of me   with it. You know I’ve been cycling since I was your age!      I know, and it’s like it’s part of your personality. I once saw you chase a guy down the road with a spanner like you were in some kind of action movie.      That was   spitefully well aimed  , by the way! I still talk to that man—he gave us a laugh afterwards. You should’ve seen the look on his face when he came to check if it was still parked properly! Ha! Anyway—how’s your bike going?      Oh, thanks! I’m getting used to the new lights and the panniers. I’ve even joined a cycling group on Instagram—personally I think it takes 10 minutes longer than just using Facebook, but   every little helps  .      That’s brilliant, Evie. You’re bound to see Mateo at one of them, and who knows, maybe even Anna. Let me know if you want to go together—might be fun to ride together and hit the hills.      Honestly, I’m more scared of falling over than him seeing me. I had a proper crash last week—  the helmet saved my life  , and I still look like a idiot with it on!      You walk around the house like the   cheese man   from the 80s—he had that little crown and scarf! I mean it, Evie, but that’s just a phase. When you’re 40 you will miss your cranium and wish you’d worn it religiously.      Ugh, fine. I’ll wear it. As long as he can’t see me wearing it. What with college and all that social whiplash—  I am not ready for him delivering a speech with a snack in the background  .      Oh you silly thing. Just give it time, love.      Thanks, Mum. You always manage to say the right thing at the right time. Even if it sounds like it was forced through a broken jaw.      That’s the sound of   mother’s love and a very old   metaphor coming together. Now, if you don’t mind, I’m going to go polish my saddle and dream of faster times.

Rather annoying that the train’s delay has messed up our plan. I was just about to hop on when they showed up and said it was delayed. I’m more than a bit tired of Wales’ transportation game!      Hey, speak for yourself—some of us actually live in Wales. Got on the 8:45 last week and didn’t miss it! But I get it, most people from down south have never dealt with the so-called “Welsh Timetables,” right?      Oh, bless, I don’t mind the chase when it’s with you lot. reminds me of the time when I took the train from Cardiff to London and the fire alarm went off. I managed to get the turkey I cooked for dinner all over my left leg. Never looked more glamourous.      Ha! I think I remember that. You told everyone it was a new ‘in’ breakfast, no doubt. I've been playing Ticket to Ride in my head the whole way here, actually. Wales, England, Scotland. Should have been a geography teacher instead, really.      Oh, I’ve got maps I can never keep up with as it is. I only started playing it today, but I must be disastrous at it. I blame it all on being born in Cape Town and then growing up in Bristol, and now barely getting around London without a GPS.      You know you have a better memory for geography than most! Though if we carry on chatting like this, we won’t get the boards set out in time for tea. I can already smell the roast potatoes from the kitchen.      Don’t forget the conversation  is  as good as most people’s games. I’ve spent the last thirty years talking to different people in the most mundane places doing charity work. Trust me, I know when a great conversation is unmissable.      True. Maybe we should guestimate the train times while playing. I have no idea if it’ll be any easier, but it could be amusing. I’ll nominally take Cardiff to Hereford first as a starter for being born there.      I think it's funny how proudly he calls it “being born there” after saying it three times! Still, I reckon go for Penzance to Liverpool. It’s a real ramble.      I suppose I could go from London to Glasgow through what little I remember of the UK. I might get to North Wales and think it’s Scotland.

Rather annoying that the beer’s all gone.      That’s it, is it? I suppose I should’ve stocked up before this week. Blows it all on wine      Aha, quite right. Look, I bet you picked this game out just so we’d have to use single malt instead of the lager, didn’t you?      I didn’t say that. But I  did  say I’d be easier to play with two sets of dice.      That and playing cards. But, come on, you know you can’t resist a good board game.      What’s that you said? That we like them more than university lectures?      Well, when you put it like that, I suppose it is very sad. A world where playing Risk with rules for nuclear collisions doesn’t seem far-fetched.      Honestly, I used to live in London, and I remember we used to play backgammon in the flat. That was real culture—drinking with friends, smoking, inappropriate music.      Right, as if you were supplying the real culture. Tell me, was that backgammon or Yahtzee then?      Mate, I got fairly drunk, and I barely remember the game. All the time, though, we did have strong conversations.      And I suppose the toilets overflowed in the middle of the discussions.      Possibly. But then we had a point—shared something meaningful at some stage. You can’t say Catan is meaningful.      Not in about forty years. That game does date quite far back, though. I remember first playing it in 1995. Not that I won, of course.      That’s because you took ages to get your head around the concept. The rest of us knew the minimal resources you needed to expand.      Right, because I was reading the instructions first, unlike certain individuals who jump straight in.      Well, I do like to be creative. Even if it does result in losing by a mile sometimes.      But it was more of a losing by two miles—no line in the sand, no betrayal.      And your insistence on playing fair doesn’t help much when someone randomly lands on one of your settlements.      True, but it made for better understanding over time. Rather annoying the new bins haven't arrived yet. I remember they said they'd be here by Tuesday. We're running out of space in the downstairs one already.      Yeah, I mean, it is a bit chaotic. I was trying to sort things at work, but the timing was pretty awful on their part. I've been keeping a few things under the sink.      Oh aye, I had the same issue when I moved here a decade ago. I'm still thinking about whether we should get the new dishwasher sorted before the new bins arrive.      I think the dishwasher is a good idea, especially if we're going to be having most of our friends over for dinner. Your breakfasts are practically legendary at this point!      Aye, you do have a talent, love. I always say so. As for appliances, I’d recommend Waterstone’s here, a bit pricey, but they’ve got decent after-sales support.      Thanks for the tip, Mam. I did my municipal engineering degree work placement in Brussels, got to see how they handle all their white goods fairly closely, and I can assure you, we are  certainly  not that efficient here in the UK.      Still, we live in the countryside, someone has to make up for the inefficiencies. At least the medical care is still top-notch out here. Also, have you seen the news this morning?      Which bit are you on about? I did see something about a new bridge being planned near the motorway. Could help with the commute into Swansea.      That's the one. They're promising it to be fully accessible for wheelchairs and stuff. It will make visiting family in London easier too, assuming the bin issue is sorted before Christmas.      I miss your grandmother's spoon cookies. She had a handmade recipe book full of them. Perhaps we could find a weekend to try one of the old ones?      That would be nice. I think the blueberry one go bad really quickly, unless you freeze them.      I do it differently. I spread them out on a tray and freeze them individual. Works every time. It's things like that, small and simple, that I miss those afternoons with friends helping her out more than anything.

Rather annoying this traffic, isn't it? I mean, do we need this many cranes and roadworks in North London in 2025?      I've been over this with you before, love. When you see the view from Hampstead Heath, you might start to forgive it. That and the fact that we're both inching closer to the shop where I promised to buy you a birthday present.      Oh! I'd forgotten. You said last week. I know you said you were going to be meek and get me something small, but I'm hoping you went a little splurgy on it?      Splurgy? You’re still using that word from your posh lectures, aren’t you? The TLS left it on the back seat, didn’t they? D’you know, I think I turned into a cultural critic in my old age. All those literary breakfasts and wine-tinged evenings at book fairs in Paris.      You went to Book Expo Europe again this year? I remember you texting me that famous Waterstones woman looked you up for some quote about print versus digital culture.      Print  is  real, love. You can’t press a button and feel the rhythm of a story. You can’t curl up with it in bed the same way. And it's not just me — the paper is thick, the ink smells like something real.      Okay, okay — I get it. You've made your point. But I still think my Kindle is easier to carry when I'm on the train. Also, it's 10.78pm at night, and your ballet flat is on my foot about five times now. Just trying to concentrate on the road.      I suppose you've not forgiven me for that driving mishap last summer. You remember? The man in the red delivery van cutting us off, and I nearly passed him a tea towel and a biscuit as a peace offering? That was  classy , if I do say so myself.      Like  Tom Courtenay  in  Doctor in the House . Grumpy man receives tea towel and calls you a madwoman. But I got it, truly.      Look, I know life is more about  Ibiza beach  than line edits, but I had a fascinating week with Tolstoy’s Russia emerging from behind the latest TLS pages. The way 19th century critics pooh-poohed him is like your university peers dismissing modern indie bands as ‘forgettable beats’.      It's understandable.

Rather skip to the part where you two tried to build a tent in the hurly-burly of Halton park and ended up with no luck, eh Jon?      Oh, that's where it gets good. We were only trying to camp as a fancy way to say it was too cold een to use the bloody tent we bought on the 'net. Ay, reckon it was only up for a grand total of five minutes before it collapsed in a heap of damp canvas and despair.      Oh, and you forgot the directions. You just tried to recreate it from the bloke’s head who showed you at a festival once. Jon, I reckon you'd struggle to put together a flat pack wardrobe now if your turkey depended on it!      Well, fair play, the wind wasn’t helping. But the rest of us did the smart thing—pitched up at a nice place with beer and proper heating. You need to learn some tips from me in the finer points of being lazy and comfortable, Sarah.      That was why I went directly to the Waterfront with me folks—proper chalets with wireless and hot tubs. Right idea as it were. I tell ya, ain't nothing like sittin’ in warm water while it's pissing it down outside.      I laughed, leastways, when Hayley told me the tent story. I met you near the top staggering back to the car, ‘cos you couldn’t walk another step. I thought you'd keeled over with a heart attack or a bag full of pottery.      A little bit of both, tbh. Those boots were a joke. Even looked good in the 'gram shots.      Some people, no respect for proper kit.      Still, laughable goings on on your own if you ask me. Just appreciated the camping trip even in the failure, I expect. Me, I'm happy with what your lot call a 'staycation'—run to North Wales and eat my weight in chips and Coronation Street belly up on the sofa.

Rather unusual to talk about wild winter camping on a Sunday afternoon with a decent cup of tea, wouldn’t you say, dear?      It might sound a bit mad, sure, but I’ve been doing it for years. There’s something so grounding about being in the wild when it’s at its rawest. Even if the weather is against you, it teaches you about limits.      Aye, I agree. I’ve been taking a group of students out since last year as part of a leadership journey. It’s not for the faint-hearted, but when the group survives a squall or two, you see a real shift in confidence and teamwork.      That surprises me, considering how harsh the Scottish winters can be. I’m a Londoner through and through; I’m far more used to a park pushchair ramble or the odd countryside walk with the dog.      I see what you mean, but once you get the basics right — shelter, fire, and hydration — it’s more about mindset than hardship. Of course, I always travel with a bivvy bag, a waterproof sleeping mat, and plenty of hot drinks. A nurse knows to keep the circulation going.      It’s brilliant for mental clarity. I remember when I got caught in a snow squall near the Royal Mile last January and ended up sheltering in a hollowed-out pine tree. All that isolation and silence, it was the best opportunity I’ve had to reflect on my own life.      Reflecting while trying not to freeze is quite a different beast. I’m flattered the grandchildren have continued the intergenerational bonding through outdoor adventures, but I must admit, they've outgrown about half the gear in the garage now.      You’re looking at it wrong, love. Give it to the school or a local youth group. Those kids in Edinburgh have just as much to gain from treacherous conditions as they do from fun days.      Exactly. My advice, if you ever fancy a go, is to start small. We did a series of twilight campouts to get used to the conditions with lunches delivered hot and fires pre-lit.      Still, I’m more likely to be booking the next family trip go-karting day or a coastal tour. But I appreciated your insight into the benefits, especially that mental side. Who knew blooming about in the cold could be good for the brain?

Rather than chuck a DVD in, I’ve been meanin’ to suggest this new streaming service ‘ere—what d’ya call it? The one with more box sets than a charity shop      You mean Netflix? I told her not to go wasting money on me—fine eyesight I got so far! Speaking of relatives, I’m seein’ Sue this boxun—should be interesting. She’s threatening to bring pesto pasta again.      Oh for heck’s sake! You gave her that recipe book for Christmas, ‘member? She’s not obligated to try   every single   recipe! Unless she’s got a new one?      Nup, it’s just the pesto. She swears it’s a new version—"with chilli". That, I'm not complaining about. I think I might last the conversation for a chilli pasta, as long as I don’t have to make it.

Rather than share a single sentence, I'll describe a broader scene. The room was dimly lit, typewriters and computers scattered across the small dining table, casting long shadows across the polished floor. Anon's bedroom in Comberton had become the makeshift command centre of our project. We were trying to translate old stories and ancient phrases into a format that was user-friendly and accessible.      The younger of Anon's sisters, just ten years old and wrapped up in a woollen blanket as if pulling comfort from the fiber itself, was quietly sorting through a pile of story books and toy Figures. Her small fingers fumbled as she tried to arrange the pieces into a square pattern.      On the other side of the room, Anon's younger brother left bursts of laughter echoing between the walls as he played what seemed to be a game of lights turned into a digital adventure of his own design. He had been tinkering with old Electronic Components to create some sort of Game in his own style, using the principles he had learned from building with Legos and working with his older sister.      "I remember reading once that a typewriter impacts the rhythm of your thoughts as much as your fingers," Anon said as we moved on from watching the children. "It adds a certain gravity to the words penned – very different from how they feel, say, in Excel." There was a thoughtful pause as she picked up a typewriter and started pressing the keys gently, the clack of the mechanical device reverberating through the quiet room.      Her younger sister noticed the oddly captivating sound and tried to mimic the letters typed by the typewriter. "Is that a piano?" she asked in a small, inquisitive voice, her fingers dancing in the air to the beat of the rhythm.      Anon's little brother stopped playing and looked over, his face lighting up in that way that happens when a child stumbles onto something new and exciting. "It's not a piano," he said, holding up a wooden block he used to tap out his own little songs on the desk. "It's like that sprite game we played last night – with special keys and magic letters."      Smiling at their curiosity, Anon adjusted the course of the evening's plans. "Tomorrow night is Brownie promise evening, isn't it? Perhaps we can bring in some stories to share with the Brownies that we've already formatted from our old collection.

Rather do I abandon my slippers for anything more dashing. Aye, just look at ‘em—what with the holes ‘n all. I’m more than a bit of a scruff, gotta say. But it were £2 in a charity shop, mind!      Aye, well if there’s one thing I’ve learned 'bout you, Janet, it’s that you don’t care what you look like if it's got a bit of character. Still, I’d rather see you in a spot of jam than in me pyjamas again.      You'd fetch the spread without a qualm. Last time I left me preserve unattended, you grabbed yourself a spoon like you 'ad a mortgage to feed!      Ten o'clock on a Saturday and I can feel the milk bubble in me head already. Living with a herbalist’s wife ‘n all breakfasts are practically sacraments.      Oh don’t start, Fred. You lot, you grow basil near the kettle and still grumble like it's taking tea leaves from the Crown jewels. Speaking of, I’ve got this plot next to a fruit farm and the apples are off-the-charts. Bet they’d be perfect for a jam rhythm of our own.      Should have got a ladder, Janet, because those trees sure as hell aren’t giving themselves up for love nor mortal coil. I daresay conversation is the gold standard these days, especially with this lotta th’ old ones about. Going stir-crazy with barely a youth to talk to, let alone to do something like ‘selling ANON’s old house’.      Aye, I know it well. Streets ‘ve changed. We grow ‘herbs’ in our windows now while the rest o’ the world sprite of ‘urban’ space. And 've been on the whistles with these roadworks. My grandad used to live around ‘village’ the size of a gothic room map. Talk about sufficin’ for rambling—no power lines, no phones, just a bit of soil and a heap o’ opportunity.      Ah, but how many of them’d you seen with a proper garden like this? Or a kitchen talk like ours ‘neath this Bradford’s sun? A fitting spot for a fruit-filled jam sandwich and a tale or two.      Listen, always take 'em for ANON's.

Rather annoying I had to take my paracetamol now. I was just watching the telly when it all got too much, really.      You need to try resting a bit more, love. You’ve worked hard enough this week. By the way, did you manage to buy that cheese your friend recommended? I seem to remember you telling me about it ages ago.      Oh, yes, I got the Comté last week, and it was delicious. It would go well with the red wine we still have left from Christmas. Do you want to test it tonight?      Sounds brilliant. That’s all right—your sense of humor is a pleasant change from the seriousness of work emails and things. What did you bring back from the city, by the way? That sounds fun, dear. Our daughter someone at our age would also be making a living from a computer screen and oddly-tossed-in-takeaway-chips.      Still, it’s good you’re in a better place now, about work I mean. I remember you mentioned the copywriting job had quite an exciting brief a few weeks ago. Going anywhere fancy for that new project?      I do plan to go to Malaga in March. It will be interesting, really. I have no idea what it will be like being on location there. I tried using Facebook to connect with someone there who might give good advice.      Just make sure your mobile phone isn't whining about being low on battery all the time. I lost a day once like that on a trip away.      Something about not losing contact at all makes me nervous. Imagine being in a Spanish town with no batteries or language skills.      That would be seriously stressful. Oh, but it could also be fun, right? Learning new things, like how to say, “Can I get the directions to the nearest café,” in the local language.

So, I heard you've been working on those surveys part-time. How's that going for you? It must be pretty different from being a full-time student, right?      Yeah, it is! I thought it would be more technical than it turned out to be—it’s mostly figuring out how to make questionnaires more engaging. It’s actually pretty fun if you like people as much as I do. I just wish I could fit in more hours without burning out. Oh, and how's your copywriting job? Still making people fall in love with shoes?      You know it! I’ve been writing brand narratives more recently—stories to go with the campaigns, not just slogans. It’s a bit of a shift, but I’m enjoying the creative freedom. Still, I’m constantly obsessed with what people actually care about these days. Did you catch the new series on BBC iPlayer? The one set in the 60s?      No, I missed it. Was it good? I’ve been swamped with university deadlines and trying to keep up with the weather here, which is frankly impossible. Do you have any recommendations? Or shall I just binge-watch it when I get the chance?      You should definitely give it a shot. It's one of those dramas that gives you a bit of history but really focuses on the characters. I found myself quite invested. Speaking of which, how’s the postgrad programme going?      It’s going—it’s definitely challenging. I’m trying to balance work, studies, and a social life without disappearing off the face of the Earth. It’s not easy, but I’m managing. I’ve started skipping a few late lectures to recharge a bit. I know it sounds terrible, but sometimes you just need to take a break.      I get it. No one can be productive 24/7. I’ve been doing that too—with work. My boss isn't happy about it, but I’m not either when I feel like I’m about to crash. My sister just started working as a project manager in Liverpool, which is interesting. Family’s been raving about her new role, but let’s be honest, I’m more interested in how she's coping with the goings-on on the North West coast.      That sounds amazing, though! I might need a change of scenery sometimes myself. London can be a bit much.

Rather annoying isn't it, how hard it is to find time to get any exercise in these days? With everyone working and the kids often popping in and out, it's like a full-time balancing act!      You're not the only one—definitely agree. I've tried doing some walks after work, but the weather tends to be so unpredictable here. One minute it's fine, next minute you’ve got a proper downpour! What do you do to keep active?      Oh, just some cycling and the odd bit of gardening during the day when the sun's up. I like to keep it low-key. I also throw in a short jog on the weekends if possible. It’s not the gym, but it keeps my legs moving.      You two are lucky, at least you're doing something. I find myself stuck most of the time, writing at the desk. When you're deep into a project, it's easy to forget about moving around. But I have started cooking more to distract myself. Cooking is great—it actually counts as exercise if you stand there chopping, don’t you think?      That's one way to look at it! Cooking can be quite a workout if you're making proper meals. Have you tried any new recipes lately, Sue?      Actually, I made this wonderful chicken and lemongrass curry last night—very spicy and full of vegetables. I got the recipe from that BBC cooking show. It was a bit of an arm workout with all the chopping, but it felt good oddly enough.      I've been trying to cook more too. Not as fancy as your curry, but I’ve taken about five baking classes—mostly trying to make the best scones I possibly can. You know, for the sisterly tea parties we barely have time for.      That does sound lovely. Maybe we can get together one weekend and swap recipes. I could use a bit of inspiration after the same old microwave meals. I tried making lasagna recently, but honestly, the pasta turned into something that looked more like a soggy cake with layers of cheese.      Some culinary experiments work out more than others, I suppose. But it's all part of the fun really. Speaking of, have either of you looked at the property market lately?      God, yes—far too much. It’s like watching someone play a game and all the rules change every five minutes.

Rather annoying the new budget, eh? You know, me an’ the lads down the uni kept talking about it last week. The government keeps on skimpin’ on arts an’ culture, which I reckon is a right shame. I’ve seen  Les Misérables  like five times an’ it’s still the bees’ knees.      I reckon it depends on your priorities. Being a civil engineer, I’m always thinking about infrastructure too. Roads, bridges, that kind of thing. But you know, a city like Cambridge needs culture and history just as much, don’t you think? I saw  Hamilton  last year, bloody pricey ticket, but worth every penny.      Yeah, well, you know I work with linguistic corpora. I’m always about words, language – I mean, even the way people say "budget" round here is different in the North. Cats say it like "boddjit," up me way. Down here it's like a posh, clipped thing.      Haha, I know what you mean. It’s funny how different things feel round Cambridge, isn’t it? I mean, we’re not that far from Kent and all, but it still has a very… academic kind of vibe. I remember when I got offered the job at the engineering firm here, I thought, "Blimey, this is a proper city."      Aye, it’s beautiful here, though. These gardens are a class apart from what we got in Sunderland. Although I’ve got to say, the Royal Northern College of Music put out a few decent acts. You into any musicals?       Phantom of the Opera  is about the only one I've seen, but the wife dragged me to  Wicked  a few years back. She still won’t let me forget I fell asleep during  Defying Gravity . My sister’s got tickets for  Mary Poppins  next month, you fancy tagging along?      Proper bloody pricey, innit? But if you’re waiting till I get a raise from the uni, that’ll be 2047.      Fair enough. I do the budgets for our household, believe it or not, so I can scrape us some goody tickets on the cheap if you like.      You’re on, mate. I’ll bring the boxset of  Les Mis  to study you with at the interval. Just to remind ya where the real culture is.      Haha, fair enough. But if you start crying at the barricade scene again, I’m not sharing my popcorn.      Pah! Coward! You know I kissed a girl after that very song.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh, lad? Thought we’d get a bit of a break ‘ere. Ruin the paint job proper if it’s like this all week!      Aw, it’s only Liverpool we’re talkin’ about—get used to it! Ain’t proper spring eeny if there’s more rain than sun. But at least we’ve got company in the gloom. A bit of fresh air and some telly paint’s got to be easier than stuck behind a tachometer all day!      Funny you say that, Jerry. Still plannin’ on takin’ up some actin’ classes, as we said? I’d lik’e to see you on the stage again. You’ve still got the left’s in you, boy, ain’t lost the spark.      Aye, I did actually, about a month back! Got a workshop near Liverpool Playhouse. Was daft alright—stood there in a shed wearin’ a hidesuit, recit’in’ Hamlet. Good time, mind. Feels like it’s been a lifetime since I properly used the words I learned at uni! Still, I’ve got me other hobbies. Tell you what, Marcus—what’s that book you been reading from Germany? The one about the old estate closin’ down, and the rich bloke rebuilding it.       Ah , you mean  Der Gutshaus ? Interesting read—shows the kind of urban development that happens in smaller towns. They replant the whole place, give it a gloss, but you still get this undercurrent of loss. It’s got me curious—I’ve been talking to a few of the lecturers about old developments in the city centre. New landlords, different areas... mind if I ask what you think as a cabby?      Aye, I’ll have a go. Burgers and development, that’s my hobby horse. You know them new flats on the old docklands? ‘Bout three of them gone up since I came back from tour in 2018. Look nice from out here, but the people who lived there? Gone—relocated, bought out, or just pricing’d out. Smart idea if you’re into the money goin’ in your own pockets, but not so smart if you’re into your community, innit?      You’re right ‘bout that. So, have you made peace with the direction the city’s movin’ in, or does it frustrate you more?      To be honest, I’m half-right. S’all my lot I got to worry for—my rent’s up, my old garage is flats now, but at least the kids in the neighbour’s want somethin’ better than what I had.

Rather lovely this stretch, isn't it? That view of the fields and mountains just gives it that peaceful vibe... What d'you think?      I know, it's so quiet out here. I've never really seen anything like this outside of places like Cumbria. It's nice not having concrete and exhaust fumes around every corner.      Aye, it's a bit of a slap in the face compared to that too-touristy Bialka Tatrzańska dump. Still, wasn't too bad for the money. Didn’t even want to spend a fortune on a hotel like you insisted, even if  you  were paying.      Well, I  am  the experienced one here, living off a budget left and right. Tenner a night is the new luxury, innit? I think it turned out worth it, actually, considering the mess of clutter we’re cleaning out of your flat this weekend. Honestly, I’m not sure what’s more worrying: the state of the room or the rats in the walls.      Ah, forget the rats—personally I’m more concerned about the two young lads we picked up back there. Hopped in as we were going through Zakopane, trotted in with all the confidence in the world – cheeky ones, I tell you!      Yeah, fair enough. We don’t often pick them up at home. Bit more suspicious back in the hills of Lancashire. Our parents always said, "If someone suspicious boards a vehicle, consider it your responsibility to not get killed."      Haha, sounds like a hillwalker’s mantra. Anyway, those boys were harmless. I about blocked the whole conversation with all my travel tales. Still, it gave me something to chat about.      Not that I mind the stories, but we should probably stop freeloadin’ for the day. Got guest speaker thing at 5 with that new language class I’m setting up – any chance you can pop in?      I could stick around for a bit. I’ll probably need a word with you about lunches, too. I told your mum I’d be bringing over soup for her, something around this time.      go on then, but let me warn you—there are at least six of your friends coming out of the woodwork today, all under the pretext of your soup. It's all going to get too much.      Well, I can never choose friends over food, so let it be that.      Exactly my point. I’m not entirely surprised either of us are still alive, considering where our priorities lie.

Rather annoying this newfit lot o’ toys, ay?
