I got me dad on there last year an’ he ain't as quick wi’ the tech as most, but once it clicked wi’ ‘im, he’s like a young’un again!  laughs  I reckon it's the same wi’ you.      Yeah, Gran, you just giff it a try. I gonno show you again, if you want. I think it's funny how even you can't hack a simple ‘in-app messenger.’      Well, alright then, if it eases you two o’ hides, I'll give it a shot again. Although I reckon I’d rather try and do a kebab wi’ a pint glass! I mean, what even is a ‘reaction’ and why do we need more than a ‘like’ for that?      You’re bound to adapt wi’ time, just like the rest o’ us. It’s part o’ life now.      Aye, well, while you lot are busy dawdlin’ ‘bout in apps, I’m off to read me a good old-fashioned book. Funny thing— The Importance of Being Earnest —horribly rude at times but witty as a ballet dancer! You two have about enough sense to walk a tightrope, talking sense into this chaotic lark.      Oh that book is barely a week old, gran! Maybe I’ll have a laugh ‘cos I just watched  Good Omens  last week. Brought it up to the house—along wi’ all me games. I dunno how long I’ve had those stick-likey things...      Ah, you've 've been meaning to clear out the garage, love. That's where you'll find a nice tuck o' sun an' go ahead binch your life if you don’t get a move on wi’ the chuckin’. I had a serious go ‘bout last week an’ found some old VHS tapes. Made me seriously question why anyone thought VHS was a good idea, never mind that it was a lark wi’ the ‘dub’ button!      S’all so stressful I ken’t tell me arse from a soft toy once all the clutter falls out! I've had a time ‘bout of it lately—mind’s just not quite ‘fit to be tied.’

: Alright lads, take a look at this beauty. I've been eyeing it for weeks — first-gen Ryzen 7, 16GB RAM, 1TB SSD, and a 4K display for editing. £1k seems like a decent price for a new machine. Thoughts?     : That does seem spec-wise very solid for the price. But are you sure they don’t include any bloatware? I once got this laptop, top of the line, but it came with like ten useless software packages grinding the OS to a crawl.     : Told you already — I’ve already baked it. Fresh Windows install, no corporate branding, no pre-installs. Just like that MyMac, if you catch my drift. All I need is some art apps and I’m good to go.     : You mean like you did for your uni project last year when you crashed your old laptop? I happened to lend you Gameboy while it was dead for five days! No, you didn’t have to remind me. Good times, real good times.     : Yeah, man, I owe you one — probably a week’s worth of grief. Anyway, let me open up this machine so we can see how it runs. Speak of “new tech,” – Mate, have you heard about these new PCs that store data on DNA? One drop of blood and you’ve got your Bitcoin wallets.     : Sounds more like a biology experiment in a lab coat. But hey, if they can read DNA like code, imagine the speed. You could backup your entire YouTube library in a test tube and be GDPR compliant at the same time.     : I mean, I’m not trying to win the Renaissance Faire this year, but I do like things that don’t fall apart easier than my old phone. The last one turned into a Jell-O sandwich for no reason. Remember that time my phone dropped in the kebab? Still works, minimal damage.     : I tried using it for a week, honestly? Not my thing. All that sprite and acadia waterlogged it with lunches and I walked out with digestive issues and a soggy screen. Still, I’m happy with my watering can and spade set go-to tools on the slab.     : True, true. I appreciate the old-to-new blend in tech, but sometimes I think your shovel’s better. It doesn’t need charged, software updates or a courtroom to sue for privacy breaches.

Rather lovely place, isn't it? You know, for a bistro that just opened, they've done a fantastic job with the décor. That pale pink wall and the wooden furniture gives it a really warm feel. I wouldn’t have thought Tarnow would have places like this.      Oh I completely agree! I mean, it’s very 'on trend' for the city — sustainability, clean lines, but with a touch of personality. It's like a nod to Scandinavian but with a Slavic twist. I must say, nothing like the greasy spoon joints back in Bury.      Yes, very different from the  pubs  I used to frequent back in Cambridge. You know, like that one near the station where they served enough gin to tide you over until morning. I was obsessed with escapism, I suppose. The gin, the escapism — both were my way of forgetful dreaming. But now I teach TEFL in the afternoons in a university here, you know?      Wow, that's a tough switch. I mean, I grew up with both parents working — teacher and shop owner — I understood early that your default as a woman back home is often to aim for stability. But you—what drove that change?      Hmm. Looking back, it was mostly the realization that I'd let myself get addicted to something that wasn’t feeding me. Not just the alcohol, but the  identity  that came with it — the woman drowning in her own loneliness. It’s funny, isn’t it? When you lose one identity, you're forced to rebuild from scratch.      Exactly. I mean, I  dream  of teaching abroad most of the time. I know I'm not living the most exciting life, but I've always been keen on routine. Going into that classroom each morning, laying it out step by step — that’s how I like to manage my world. To be honest, I think it borders on addiction too — the need to be in control all the time.      You mustn’t see it as such a bad thing. Having  goals , structure — it’s what keeps you whole. I’ve been thinking about going back to fitness, maybe something low-key but consistent. Maybe a yoga class or swimming? I think it would do me good.      That would, yeah. You need to focus on  your  body again — all of us women are so caught up in other people’s lives, we forget we also owe something to ourselves.

Rather skip the queue and just get us online tickets for the Dorset Steam Fair. Felt real busy on the phone and I don’t fancy hanging about at the gate.      Aye, I don’t mind paying online. Look, I’ve got a motor problem in me left leg again and standing in a crowd for hours is out the question. Any chance they’ve got easy access or wheelchairs? A lot o’ places nowadays have too much concrete to be easier but I’ve not been there before.      They do have disabled facilities, David. Let me check my phone... Yes, they’ve even got a special path round and a few benches near the main rides. Alice and I took Myra a couple o’ years ago and left her wheelchair by the food tent. It was brilliant, really friendly staff and I think there was even a dedicated bathroom for it.      That’s good then. I mean, I’ve been in the past with uni friends and it was amazing, but didn’t spare a thought for the accessibility. So glad that’s sorted. By the way, are we taking Lucy this time? I know she’s a bit to and fro with the pain, but today’s a better day than most.      That’d be nice, if it’s alright with her. I still think it’s a pity she’s had to give up work after that car accident. Silly thing, crashing into a lamppost in Rush Green. Our world’s changed in one go—her not working, me not contributing, and now we’re both out o’ the housing ladder. Prices up here in Bournemouth? Can’t even  dream  o’ a deposit.      Oh, David, it’s different for us now. I lost Ron last year and since then... well, I’ve just been drifting a bit. The council said I could apply for a re-mortgage, but I passed it up. The house’s too big for one person anyway. I’ve been trying to get someone to come round and sort the furniture out. There’s a lass on Gumtree whose moving business comes with a van.      That sounds good. You should let us know when she comes. I’ve got a cat goin’ on two legs if you don’t mind, Muesli, and I’d feel awful if she stressed out with big lads moving boxes.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh, love? Thought we’d get a bit of a break ‘ere Nan comes over, but it’s just bled on like. I’ve asked Jane to bring over that lemon drizzle cake she made last week. That and a bit of chat will keep us busy for a good eeny.      It was lovely of Margaret to offer to drive her in from Kendal. I don’t know if I’d have managed all the stairs with her walking frame. It is a bit of journey from her place to Yorkshire. Still, the chase is worth it.      Is Nan coming to see  me ? I haven’t got the maths homework done yet. I was meant to revise prime numbers, but I’ve been playing on my tablet. Ten more minutes on Twitter woulda been good too, and I only did the history work. It’s for tomorrow!      Fergus, if you want a better cricket net for the garden, you’d best do as Nan says, or she’ll have a go again. And I reckon she’ll mention that time with the jam—don’t ask. She doesn’t take short cuts, not as much as she used to.      Oh, I wasn't  that  bad then. Was I? I remember – Baptiste showed me a chap with a fake beard and a long beard. One was real and one was fake, and you couldn't tell the difference ‘til you touched it. It’s all in God’s infinite wisdom and mending the world. He’d a good sense of the silly at times.      It's been lovely this morning, catching up with Margaret after so long. She told me about about how she’s been helping the church bazaar. She said something quite deep—about how doing things for others leaves you with less to fix yourself. Rather theological, but true in its way.      Nan always says “not much” about the weather and “not much” about anything else. But when I once brought home a B for a test, she told me the whole story about how she failed her 11+ by one mark and how that changed her life. I took the next test and got an A.      Oh, I still go every Sunday, dear. I like the hymns and the gossip after. It’s the least I can do. The box might be empty most weeks, but it’s the principle.

Rather annoyingly, I've got to go to the dentist on Friday.      Oh no, don’t they often have the most terrifying gadgets? I can't even remember the last time I went for a hearing test.      Grandmum had a visit to the optician last week. She said they showed her some pictures by Monet.      I remember that—they always show those abstract ones to test colour perception, right?      Ashaad brought a whole bunch of Easter chocolates for everyone last week when he visited. He has the sweet tooth like you, gran.      Did he bring the ones with the little trinkets inside?      The ones left after school this week were, well, mostly trinket-free, and I think he saved the best for you two, by the way.      Ashaad said he’s visiting Hattie next week. I think they might plan to go on the school trip.      That’d be nice for both of them—personally, I think Hattie needs a bit of focus to keep her grounded. Hattie has been having some… issues with basic Maths.      Does that mean she missed out on any school trips last semester?      Actually, no. It was that weekend workshop for the Year 6 kids toward the end of term. Hattie's just someone who needs one-on-one attention. That said, she is quite animated when it comes to talking about her best friend.      Even so, I don’t see her as reckless. She seems about as mischievous as the goldfish the two of you had at home.      Going back to the school trip—Hattie does need a bit to do with her time over Easter.      Are they going somewhere fun? Like to the countryside or a museum?      It’s a little bit of both—a day visiting an estate and then a tour of a sculpture park. Recommended lunches include sandwiches and radishes—classic school trip fare.      Radishes are like rocket, but crunchier. Mm, très healthy if you ask me.      I don’t see it. I prefer crisps or something with cheese.      I can see both sides, though I think I'm going to stick with water for now. But I expect we can have a bigger discussion at the weekend, since both you and your brother have birthdays on the same day.      Right, so Grandmum, don’t you get us a gift that’s slightly more elaborate than a novelty keychain before that?

Oh my gosh, it's been ages since we last had a catch-up like this! How's everything with you and the kids at the hospital? I heard you were working with a new cohort of patients recently.      Yes, it's been what three weeks since we last grabbed a cuppa and a slice of  cake , if you can believe that! It's actually been really challenging but also rewarding. I've got a group of adults recovering from strokes, and it's incredible seeing how far some of them come. We've been focusing a lot on communication aids — it's fascinating.      That’s amazing! I couldn’t imagine doing that job, honestly. You’re always so patient with people. It must take a lot out of you emotionally though.      It does, I won’t lie — some days I go home absolutely drained. But most of the time, the positive impact we’re making is worth it. How about you? How's the writing life treating you?      Honestly, it’s a bit patchy. I've landed a couple of interesting campaigns, which is always a bonus, but the occasional dry spells don’t make it any easier. I’ve started working remotely more, which is good for saving the bus fare, but feels like I'm floating most days – no office camaraderie, no coffee machine chit-chat…      Oh don’t get me started — I  much  prefer working from home! Though the downside is the coffee is always  awful . Honestly, I miss my office coffee machine so bad.      Me too! I crave a decent cappuccino. Can I suggest we head in to that Italian place in about an hour? Or are the kids bugging you for attention?      Kids can wait! Let me just feed the cat and I'll be ready in ten. I do miss our ‘girlfriend days’ though — no kids, no work emails, just us, a bit of gossip and something sweet. Speaking of, I brought some brownies.      You are a  lifesaver . Websites and deadlines are one thing, but the chocolate void in the morning? It’s no way for a human to live.      Oh please go ahead and judge me, if you must — but you're eating those brownies in a second, aren’t you?      Fully guilty! Can you even  remind  me to breathe, or do we just go straight to the café?      Just go ahead and get over to the café, and I’ll follow in a tic!

Rather do a long cycle ride as a child, weren't we mad about that in our day? I once cycled from Almondsbury all the way to Bristol and back! Mind, I didn’t have gears on my bike then, only fixed. Was a proud as a peacock with my bell on the handlebars!      Oh, I remember that time! My dad used to say if I didn’t stop hollering on the way from Ramsgate to Broadstairs, he’d chuck me off the clifftop and I’d fall into the sea. But I still say those long rides helped clear the head, even if it made your knuckles as sore as a stone bruise.      Just you lot living for bikes! When I was young back in Manchester, I preferred the rail. But I used to love the NHS perk system—my dear, you’ve never forget the days when, if you were an oral surgeon, you got taken on these “lectures at sea”? I once gave a full lecture on root canals in a storm off the Cornish coast and the audience, a bunch of sailors, were too green to hold their dinner!      Hah! Tell that to my local dentist now—and he'd probably charge you for the session. Though I remember those good old days fairly well, and how cheap travel was back then. Last time I went to Prague, it was something like thirty quid for a weekend trip!      Oh, Prague sounds lovely. I’m glad you made it a habit to get out. Funny thing—my son told me about a quaint way to buy a property in France: all you had to do was make friends with about five locals and suddenly a derelict cottage in the countryside had “quiet vibes and a sunny outlook.”      Sounds more like a charming myth! Maybe we’re all just a bit over the hill now, but I hear the Jive Club is planning a big event at the old converted barn nearby. I wonder if they’ve thought about restricting the macarena or stick to the good stuff like the Lindy.      That barn idea is a good move—gives our town some life. We’ve got this entire rebranding proposal lined up. We really need to revive the place. If we restore the architecture and open some of the old shops, we could go from a dump to a gem in no time.

So do you think an online platform for sharing case studies in education would work? I mean, with so much reliance on moving images these days, it could make learning materials more engaging.      It sounds interesting. Do we have a clear idea of what kind of case studies we'd feature? Maybe we should start by targeting schools and teacher training institutions. They’re always looking for creative content.      Exactly. I was thinking of creating bite-sized videos where teachers can showcase how they’ve used moving images in their classrooms. We could also feature student feedback. It builds social proof and encourages networking.      Networking is important. I know a few Facebook groups full of educators sharing resources and strategies. My colleague, Sarah, even did a webinar last year on using social platforms effectively in teaching. You might find some of her ideas useful.      That’s a great point. Maybe we could include a section on this platform where teachers can collaborate in real-time. It would create a sense of community, not just a one-way delivery of content.      Absolutely, and maybe we can include some communication strategies tailored for different age groups. For example, younger teachers might be more tech-savvy, but others may need guidance.      Excellent. We can even provide downloadable resources. I know a production company in Wellington that specialises in educational content. It might be worth reaching out to them.      That could work. I also wonder if we could partner with universities. Many of my former students have gone into teaching, and they’d probably be interested in contributing case studies as part of their placements.      That’s a solid idea about leveraging their placements. We could offer a small token of appreciation or credit for their work. It would help grow our database of learning materials and also give teachers something to showcase on their CVs.      Definitely. And if we can make it interactive, maybe with peer reviews or ratings for the videos, it would increase engagement. Users would be more likely to come back.      Let’s not forget to add a section on best practices for developing these case studies. We should include tips for filming, editing, and structuring the content. It would go hand in hand with your expertise in education.      That would definitely complement the project. And since we’re house-sitting in Australia, we could use this time to reach out to educators and start gathering interest.

Rather lovely to be out here, isn't it? The sea’s practically whispering today, if you listen closely.      I’m more of a listener than a talker where the sea's concerned. You can feel it calm the mind, as if it’s saying everything will be alright eventually.      It’s one of the few places where I actually  switch off  a bit. A lot of the students I see this week were clearly feeling the pressure. It was quite interesting listening to their concerns—exam stress, the usual. Didn’t even want to imagine how some of them get through the day. Still, it made me think back to when I was at university, rushing from one seminar to the next like a headless chicken.      I know the feeling. You'd think after a decade of being a lecturer, you’d be used to it, but sometimes it’s breakfast, lecture, then straight to a coffee with a student in tears at the seminar room door. You try not to carry it all the time, but once in a while, taking a walk like this, maybe reading a book on the beach, it’s necessary.      It’s funny how friends seem to draw strength from different things. For instance, Julie from our department is always at the gym. Says it’s her way of clearing her head. Then there’s Tom, he walks quite a lot as well—on solitary hikes up in the mountains. Still, we’d better keep in touch.      Completely. You’d be surprised how many people are willing to open up about their problems if you just give them the time. I had a conversation with one colleague last week by the sea about how teaching university is a strange balancing act of talking the talk and walking the walk. To be honest, I think it’s easier to be a student now than when  we  were.      There’s less pressure in some ways, perhaps. But more in others. I remember when I was their age, there wasn't as much noise waiting for you at the crack of dawn as there is now. With emails and deadlines piling up, students are more anxious—more aware, too.      Then again, that’s the point of having go-to people, right? Being there for one another so no one has to struggle in silence. I suppose it’s the small things that matter most—sharing a coffee, a walk, maybe even just a quiet evening like this after work.

Rather annoying this new season’s trends, innit? Seems like everything’s trying to be ‘vintage’ yet ends up looking like someone’s minge nan’s wardrobe. I mean, sure, chunky knits is a classic, but do we have to see them on everyone at once?      Right? I swear I’ve seen a bigger coat handed down at least five times in one morning on the train. A lot of this “vintage” stuff isn’t even vintage—it’s just fast fashion pulling someone’s leg! You’d be better off going full new season than pretending to be a ’70s model.      Honestly, I love vintage when it’s done right. You know, like that My Fair Lady vibe with the high collars and bursts of colour. But I’m not obsessed with what’s trending this month. If it flatters you and you feel good about it, that’s what matters, innit?      Haha, yeah, e’s true. I remember one of my uncles always told me, “Daisy, don’t follow the fashion, tell the fashion where to go.” Cheeky old bugger, but he had a point. It’s not like I’m goin' to walk the Pendleton Fashion Festival, but I’d still like to look smart without havin' to spend a small fortune on a coat that’s just a duvet cut shorter.      For sure. And don’t even get me started on the “unapologetic” fashion—like oversized everything. I like room to move, yeah, but some looks make it look like you’re wearing your pyjamas out. I mean, your ballet flat or my sneaker, whatever, I’m not judging. But the shape still matters, right?      Oh! I know that one school I work at, the staff dress-up day was all “effortless glamour” and half the lads looked like they’d raided their mums’ charity shop bins. But I quite enjoyed it. I ended up in a little Aran jumper with a pencil skirt and ankle boots. Simple, but looked good.      Aww, do you do smart stuff like that for school a lot? Because I am dying for a bit of go-to outfit I don’t have to think about. Just slap it on, and it’s “me” but with a bit of class.      Shawna could have a few tips, innit? We went out last week and she looked bloody sharp in this tailored jumpsuit—like, where does she even find those places?

Mum, I just wanted to say, I think I’ve figured out what I’m gonna do for college. I got into a course at Hastings College for photography and art. I mean, I know you might think it’s a bit “airy-fairy,” but I’ve always loved taking pictures and it’s actually pretty technical!      Oh, really, darling? That  does  sound nice — a bit ambitious, but I think it's brilliant! I never had much of a creative bone in my body, truth be told. I was always the one dragging the camera when we went on holidays. You'd fetch the shots every time.      Honestly, the idea of only taking photos for holidays made me think — why not take it seriously? I got into a few courses, but the one at Hastings offers a special module on documentary photography. They even let us take photos for local communities and stuff. It doesn’t feel like just playing around anymore.      Documentary, you say? You know, Ken Loach’s got a documentary that came out last year that I adored — it shows a lot of working class struggles up close. If you ever want to do something similar, maybe that could be a way in.      I  do  like that sort of thing – showing people's lives through pictures, like, making real stories visible. I remember that time you told me about when you first started working at the surgery and got scared every time the toilets overflowed? You said you were terrified of the germs.       God , that was years ago! I was a right mess in the first year. Can’t even remember which colleague it was who told me about the plunger tip for the bin. But now the office is spotless most days — though you wouldn’t believe how many people still leave their coffee grounds down the sink.      That’s so funny. I hope you passed on your plunger tip to me — the one you told me was essential during the last plumbing disaster at home. You must be doing all the cleaning yourself now.      Something like that. I keep meaning to do your room, but the pile of towels you left by the door is growing like a mountain. Don’t go watching too many comedians if you don’t want to be messy and ungrateful, alright?      Well, if I can get a good photo of the mess, it might become art and you won’t mind cleaning so much.

Rather annoying this, having to fill in all these forms for that 3D printing company, if you ask me. Just because they want me to be a paid freelancer now! I thought I was just helping a little for fun. Not like I’ve the energy for being a proper employee.      Oh dear, William, I do hope they didn’t make you sleep on it all last night? I’ve been up myself, bless me, ever since I heard about Timmy’s bird-nest ordeal. That little screecher of a cockerel doesn’t chase the baby birds away anymore, not since Timmy’s miniature football habit!  Oh , I do wish he’d outgrow it!      My word, you’d think he'd grow up with a bit of structure, wouldn’t you? Oliver, I know how you feel—remember your class last term with the hand-me-down desks? They looked as if they belonged in a museum. Not a bit of shabby workmanship, no! Just hidesous, to be truthful.      Aye, I saw it when you brought me round for a visit. I said to my landlady, “Bet that lot cost twice what they were worth in repairs.” But what can we do? Beancounters only want to save – saves their faces, I expect, and none for the poor children!      All that aside, did you hear about the new housing development near the old town? There’s talk about someone buying up an entire block. Just sounds like another one of those bad investments to me. Some people still think houses are a golden egg these days. Still, at least it might bring in a few more jobs around abouts.      Now talking of jobs, Jane—did they officially tell you your childminder status is to be considered for housing support too? Maybe we’ll have better company for birthdays this year!      Aye, and I told them the day before yesterday. I think it might help, but I’m not waiting on them. We’re already making arrangements to get a birthday cake out of it!      More importantly, have we yet decided who's taking Timmy for a nice birthday snack later on? I reckon goin' on a walk abouts or something. Just don’t expect me to run after him again like I did the other day—far too near a sprained ankle.      Oh, we'll manage, we always do, dear. You gave him a right fright the last time he overstepped the garden and nearly landed in that hole near the fence—second to collision with that terrible cockerel!

Rather annoying this, having to bring my daughter to live with us. I know her mother would've handled it better, but I’m not complaining. I’m more than happy to help, you know. It's just that it's a new chapter for the lot of us.      I understand that, Mabel. You’ve always been one for helping family. I think it's a good move for her though. A fresh start. With the way things are abroad, especially with the economy she was in, it’s sensible. You and Bernard will look after her well, won't you.      Oh, absolutely! I've already made sure the spare room is clean and tidy. Bernard dusted off the old My Bed frame, bless him! He said he’s going to start calling her "Ladie Darcy", which of course drives me up the wall. But she’ll be staying with us until she gets on her feet, at least.      And what about the cost of it all? You know how tight things have been lately. I wouldn’t expect you to stretch yourselves.      Nonsense, Arthur. I never thought about it as a burden. She only needs a helping hand for a while, and we can spare a little in our budget. You’ve helped us enough over the years with the repairs, and now it's our turn. We’re a tight-knit family, aren’t we?      You're right about that, and I’m proud of you both. But also, maybe you can talk a bit to her about her future? Establishing something here is going to be tricky these days. Even as a teacher, I see it every day. Young people about to fall through the cracks.      Oh, I had a chat with her already. She's quite ambitious, you know. She mentioned something about starting a small catering business. That’s for the future though. Right now, she needs rest and somewhere to settle in.      That's a grand idea, if she can manage it. I could introduce her to a few people at the school. Websites and suppliers are the modern keys to success these days.      That's brilliant, Arthur! Then perhaps it's not such a burden after all. Just one of life's little journeys, isn't it? Another chapter to tick off the list.      Time to make the most of it, then. If you need me to help paint the room or anything else, just give me a shout.

Rather annoying to be honest, don't you think? Seems like everything's tied up in politics these days. I got to meet with one of the other lecturers down at Kent this week, and over a coffee, we were discussing how the referendum seems like it's being pushed on us yet again. Do you remember the last time there was talk of it?      Of course I do, Mark. I remember that clearly from when I was still teaching at Brighton Grammar. It felt like a backward step, pulling the rug under people's feet just after the Brexit deal was announced. It's like they think the country hasn't had enough of political jumbling already.      I couldn't agree more, John. It's a strange time for all of us to be having these discussions when there's so much else going on. But I digress — I wanted to check in with you, about the job interview. Your colleague, David, suggested I reach out. They're looking to expand the faculty, you know?      Ah yes, the interview. Good for you, Mark. I remember David mentioning you a couple of weeks back. You're in a different field now, from what I remember of your university days. You were in something else, engineering or something?      Actually, I'm doing something a bit different now, focusing on postcolonial theory. It's a new area of study that's been growing at universities. I understand it might be a bit unconventional, but the students are really into it.      That does sound unconventional, but oddly refreshing. You always had a good head for theory. I remember you being an intense student — all right angles and structured arguments. Not many about then who could walk us all through a lecture without the blinking slides.      Ha! That's very kind of you to say. But it does take time to step out of that structured way of thinking. My daughter, Sophie, actually, she helped me reorganize the whole presentation for the interview. She's finishing up her own thesis on gender performance in Scottish politics. It's been interesting talking to her about it all.      That's a good move, Mark. She's far too young, of course, but if she's into the field, she'd have some interesting perspectives. How does she feel about the present situation? I gather things are rocky for students these days.

Rather annoying when the traps don't seem to work, isn't it? I've tried placing cheese in front of them and everything, but no luck yet.      It's strange, isn't it? I remember reading somewhere that the effectiveness of those things depends a great deal on how clean they are. I suspect if the area is too dusty, the mouse won’t spring for it. You should try cleaning the base before setting them again.      Oh, I watched a YouTube video where someone used peanut butter and was so successful. Maybe that’s the trick? I mean, isn’t peanut butter far more appealing than cheese these days? I thought cheese was the classic, but clearly, some mice like peanut butter better.      Well, cheese is just more traditional, I suppose. D’you know, I remember my father once tried to make one out of a toaster and a spring when I was a child. He happened to be a bit of a tinkerer.      Do you have any idea how tough it is to work in a kitchen when there are mice running around? I mean, really, it’s a nightmare! I’ve seen chefs get so stressed, it's insane.      Yeah, I was just thinking—I had a friend who studied in America, and she told me stories about the way children there are raised. American kids don’t seem to be as afraid of exploration and making mistakes as British kids might be, she said. They just dive in and figure it out. That made me consider how different our upbringings can affect our approaches to problems.      That’s curious. I had a colleague who worked abroad for a few years. She told us about how differently the work environment is there—more informal and a bit more hierarchical at times. But she also said the children handle independence a lot sooner. I do wonder, though, whether that leads to less parent involvement overall here versus there.      It's something I've thought about as a librarian, too. You hear a lot of stories from parents about how they're being asked to read to their children more here than in other countries. They're trying to prepare them for school and for learning. But it's also quite lovely to see generations come together on weekends, if you ask me.      I think it’s brilliant. I mean, I'm learning from what your conversation inspires.

Rather annoyingly, I've bought us a whole bunch of new pyjamas.      What, another matching set? You've already got six sets!      I know, it's a bit excessive, but I saw them at a sale. They were twenty percent off and they were really cute.      I suppose it depends on your definition of "cute". A lot of your choices in that department tend to skew toward the... unusual.      Well, they're bright blue and have little ducks printed on them. I think they'd fetch like three times more if they'd made them for me to wear to a night class or something.      I don't know. I think I'd feel ridiculous in ducks on my pyjamas. But I'm sure you're the type of person who actually likes that sort of thing.      Look, just try them on for me, and if you absolutely hate them, we'll repackage them for charity tomorrow. Deal?      I suppose, if it makes you feel less guilty about spending that two hundred quid. But I'm not entirely sure "guilt-free spending on something ridiculous for fun" is something I want to encourage.      Well, I'm not entirely sure it's something I'm stopping. I found some quite fetching new loungewear as well. If we're already stepping out of our matching principles and into the world of absurdity.      Now, that just sounds oddly purposeful. What does "fetching" even mean in that context?      Look, it's silk and it flatters me. That's all you need to know.      I suppose you've also gone into that store that sells the really tight, unflattering things that do absolutely nothing for anyone. Just like always.      That wasn't me. That was you last time. Do I look particularly disappointed in your choices for your new wardrobe?      I'm being serious. Next time you want to buy a new set of absurd mismatched sleepwear, maybe consider telling me beforehand. Then I can be mentally prepared for the utter goonery I'm about to witness.      I just bought us some bright blue pyjamas with ducks on them. I can't be that bad at this. I seriously question why this continues to surprise you.      It's not the ducks I'm surprised about, it's the fact that I've somehow ended up involved in all of this nonsense.      Oh, stop being dramatic. You're probably going to end up wearing the ducks and then want a matching set of ducks and ducks as slippers and then as a hat or something.

Rather a brilliant game we had last Sunday, wasn’t it? That Munster match—the try they scored in the last five minutes, I nearly choked on me dinner!      Yeah, me mam and me were watching it too! Did you see the kid from our school who ran it in? They showed him on the TV!           You mean that young man with the ginger hair? I would know that freckle on his chin anywhere. Imagine what it’s like to be in the spotlight like that at school. Didn’t even get changed outta school gear before the game, I heard.           Aye, it must have made a nice change from classroom to field! Makes me think of when I was teaching, the excitement the kids would get when a rugby game came on the radio. Living in Glasgow, they were all about rugby back in the day—though I much preferred the cricket.      I love the rugby! Maybe I can go to training after school? Me mam, would ye be okay with that?      I don’t see why not if it’s not too much for you and you still get your homework done. But     , Padraic is okay with the idea—isn't he? I will write something heartwarming in there. My, time for the young ones always flies. I passed him in the park last week, and the boy is already taller than me!      I’ll pop in a note too. As for you     , you’d best not keep the whole team waiting with your birthday schedule. Me and you can deliver the cards after dinner.      Mind you, I think it’s best to leave   Oisin   in bed a bit longer. Last night was rough with the puppy barking through the house, and you know how sensitive that little one is.      Yeah, I heard it too—but it was cool to see the stars that night over the garden. We should go stargazing again some time; I read about constellations online.

Rather annoying that the new house doesn't have a proper playroom. I was hoping it would be easier once James got the hang of crawling. You've already sorted out a room for your baby, haven't you, Steph?      Oh, we did! We just converted the spare room. Got a nice cot and a bouncy chair. I must say, he settles there quite nicely. You should come round and take a look. I know you're always helping me out with childcare ideas.      Please! You're the one sorting out all the nappies and the formula. I just fetch the baby from the pram. Honestly, I'm learning more every day, only I think I've made a habit of wearing my sister's old stuff to save money. I suppose you've gone the same route, stealing clothes from your sister?      Oh dear, yes! Mummy definitely thinks I'm costing her more than I should. "You're in your early twenties, you should look like one, not thirty-something," was the phrase once I started wearing her vintage stuff. But tell me—how is your sister taking the whole sibling rivalry with your baby-free status?      Honestly, we’ve got a laugh about it. She insists she was always the “responsible” one and I was “charming, but scattered.” Now she’s the one with a baby and me learning to knit tiny booties for her next child already! It’s funny, isn't it?      Absolutely. And you're not missing a thing, honestly. I do wonder what it's all like for people in other countries. Any chance you’ve considered learning another language in tandem with raising your future about-to-arrive sibling's sibling?      I have! I mentioned French to my parents because it seems easier to get audio resources. You're up for helping me practice, right? And then I can pretend I speak it at the baby's first international playgroup.      Oh, I'd love to! I'm fairly fluent in Spanish myself. We could even study and practice together. Then we can always blame the lunches we keep missing because of "language study time."      That'd be nice. Truthfully, with the moving, the clothes, the life changes—it's good to have at least one thing to stay the same, you know?      Definitely. Pass the salad, would you? I can't manage both this and the conversation at the moment!

Rather annoying when people can't get my accent right, innit. I was in Cambridge the other week and someone got completely confused with me.      Mate, I've heard you speak a thousand times and I still can't quite pin down the exact Bedfordshire twang you've got. Got eeny influence from Luton or somewhere else?      Nah, not really. I’ve only ever been to Luton a few times, but I can tell you what it’s like to ride a bike through the High Street and hit the smell of hot chips and blokes walking around with chips in one hand and cans of cider in the other. That's real Luton.      Yeah, I’ve met enough people from there in this house over the years. I mean, my brother-in-law’s in the garden doing up the fence – again – and he’s definitely got that Luton-adjacent vibe.      Blokes planting evergreens in March, thinking the wind’s going to die down. That’s real Bedfordshire though – weather doesn’t get a say in what we do. I try not to let it put a damper on things, like today. Good for a walk, right?      You’re out walking – Mate, you got a job, and I’ve seen you trying to sell the odd somethin’ to cover your rent. You know what I got today? Smoked salmon, and I’m just someone who works in a classroom.      Man, I envie that. I had to work a tenner an hour and still got told off because I didn’t clip the hedges right. I mean, I’m a gardener, not Renaissance Leonardo da Vinci.      At least you know that. I barely know the handle of a wrench from my stepdad’s chain.      You should learn something about basic maintenance. I remember a time I had a landline, and the line fell out, and I had to sort it out while my kid was watching Dora The Explorer.      Yeah, speaking of kids – ever had the struggle of teaching a kid a board game with rules like a foreign language? My go-to is always Monopoly, but even that ends up with arguments about house prices in the real world.      You're what your mother’s lounge. It's like flu season 365, in here.      It's a family space. Got to embrace the chaos, the food, the fights about the volume on the telly.

Rather annoying driving today, wasn't it? That car in front of us was going so slowly through the roundabout. Honestly, sometimes I think half the road users don’t know how to drive      Yeah, it can be pretty frustrating, especially during rush hour. I had a similar experience earlier on the way to work. I’m just grateful my car is reliable. My old one would have broken down halfway through that ordeal.      I feel you. My commute into work is a bit of a nightmare at the moment. I’ve been looking into buying another car, but I just don’t have the budget right now. Have you ever thought about carpooling?      I have, but honestly, I enjoy my own space in the car. Still, I do hear the savings from splitting the costs and fuel make it tempting. But then you have to factor in the hassle if someone doesn’t show up or late starts.      Definitely a trade-off. I remember one time, I joined a carpool and the guy I was sharing with forgot his key and we got stuck outside his house. We missed half of the meeting because of that.      That sounds like a hassle! I reckon it's extra time and then the cost of being late at work. Maybe I should just deal with the noise and the other drivers instead. By the way, don’t you have your dinner sorted for the week?      I was just about to make a chicken curry. Want to join me?      Actually, that’s a yes! I have a red wine I thought we could try with it. I picked it up at a bargain price about a week back. Just trying to save where I can.      That's really kind of you. I know I've been tight on the budget lately with my student loan, but at least I've got my steady income now as an administrator.      It's something I really appreciate. Having a consistent amount coming in helps with planning your spending. As for me, I'm managing well as a project co-ordinator, but I definitely enjoy these small things we can still afford.      Agreed! Maybe dinner is the go-to event on most weeknights. If not for these little treats, the day would just fly by. Let’s start cooking then, I’ve got all the ingredients laid out.

Rather annoying this newfit in the boiler innit? Seems like everything sticks on for hours and it’s pottin’ out cold water again.      Eeh, I dunno much abe’ boilers meself love. Me and George usually just call the bloke from the village when eenythink’s wrong. He tends t’fix it quick if yer tell ‘im straight up whot’s gone on.      Aw, me George used t’make me go dump the water out t’the back meadow once when me kettle was hissing like a tea-pot with chips. Course, I couldn’t carry it no’way and the spout leaked sommates on me like well.      Ha! Me George, ‘e once told me the Hoover was Darcy, pick o’me auntie’s dogs. So I was about t’switch it on when ‘e grabbed me an’ said, "No Nan, Darcy e’s out the back! No, you didn’t see ‘im? Well he e’s off walking by himself agin."      Yer always rigin’ about your Georges innit nan and grandad?      Yer cheeky trot! Well, George got more sense than most – especiall’ with the water, leastways he kep’ his off while the tap was on.      Aye, well ‘e once tried to put a screwdriver in a plug socket when ‘e thought the toaster was broken.      Oh Mary, you shouldn’t be telling these tales at your age. Still, at least ‘e hadn’t gone fully bonkers in about forty odd years.      Y’know what, I thout you two and yer Georges are mental. Still, I’m glad it’s ‘oliday and I don’t ‘ave to do no lesson plannin’ or markers.      Good. You shan’t be needing the markers none if we’re givin’ you a crack to clear up and hoover properly. Even if it’s with Darcy or nan’s whispy old Hoover.      Aye, and if you don’t ‘oover, then I shall tell you more tales abe’ George and ‘is dentures, innit.      Now nan, leave the poor boy be. He’s done enough to help us carry the parcels in.      It’s alright I can talk ‘bout ‘oliday proper if we sort owt this boiler nonsense. S’all my faults I ken’t fix it, but I ken at least make us some proper tea once it’s working again.      Oh ‘e e’s right ‘bout that, needs teh make a pot like we used t’after school, with Irn Bru and sweet winks.      Aye, once you e’s made that, then ‘e e’s a Grandson!

Rather than share a text-based version of the request, let's talk about it. Pirates, real circuses... What's on your mind?      I saw a pirate ship in a storybook, Missy! It had a flag with a skull!      Oh, I bet that was  The Jolly Roger ! Pirates used that flag to scare people on other ships. Did I tell you I once watched  Black Sails  on TV, and it was quite dramatic!      Missy, what's drama?      Good question, little man. It means exciting or tense parts in a story. Like, in Shakespeare, people get in big arguments and sometimes even fall in love!      What's Shakespeare?      Oh, I love this! William Shakespeare was an English playwright who lived hundreds of years ago. He wrote plays like  Romeo and Juliet  and  Macbeth . And guess what—our school is doing Shakespeare Week next month!      Can I go with you, Missy?      Of course! We’re going to Stratford-upon-Avon, where Shakespeare was born. There’s a theatre where they put on his plays. And if we have time, maybe we can even go to the real Stratford Circus!      A real circus? Silly people on stilts and monkeys?      Haha, there are animals in circuses, but unfortunately, they aren’t monkeys doing acrobatics anymore. Also, some circuses now have magic shows, and guess what—we had a ballet-themed circus performance at school about a week ago.      Magic? Can I have magic for Easter too?      Well, I’m thinking of doing a stop-motion animation video with some Easter pictures. Maybe you can be in it? I’ll cut out paper bunnies and eggs, and you can pretend to find them. Then we can make little movies!      Like that sprite being chased by a space duck?      Well, not quite  that  weird... but maybe something a little funny. Now, shall we set the table? I think it’s time for tea.      Missy, I had a juice box three hours ago!      So? Tea is  British  tradition, and roles in society are based on certain rituals! You can have a third juice box  after  you’ve had some food and cleaned your hands. Now go wash up, both of you!      But Missy, can we keep talking about pirates after supper?      Only if you can convince your brother to let you have extra scones first. Deal?   Speaker_3 :   Cheater...      Not cheating, little man—negotiating. Now, bottoms up! Let’s go wash those little hands!

Rather do share a drink and tales. You know, once I taught English in Jeddah — quite a lively place, rather different from Gloucestershire!      Oh, really? I taught in a small village quite some distance from the city centre. The children were curious about so many things — outsiders, holidays, and especially about wine. Which puts me in mind of an amusing incident that most certainly involved wine — though not in quite the way one might expect.      Ah, you once journeyed to Cyprus by boat? Is this the chase when, I recall, you came too close to the coast of Jeddah and stirred up a bit of local interest, only to find yourself in hot water?      Indeed! We were a group of well-meaning Englishmen who thought we'd pick up a boat and head east. First evening in, we were sailing along quite merrily, and then suddenly this pair of local men — in full traditional garb, no less! — loudly reprimanded us. We politely offered to share our supplies, which was accepted with enthusiasm, and we were soon surrounded by their friends. Anyway, quite a while later, and we only realISED that the captain had neglected to inform us that it was illegal to sail from Jeddah. So – we were stopped, fairly summarily and, it must be said, while the others were quite tipsy and making polite conversation with our new acquaintances.      There’s also this other tale — one involving a suspicious sailing trip from Jeddah to Cyprus that had a curious twist. Much to your surprise, the wind changed and pushed you further than expected — but your curiosity as to what lay in about forty miles off shore pulled you toward a field of rocks — and then boom! Your boat ran into trouble!      I seem to recall a rather strange side to the incident, where for quite some time, you were expressing quite clearly your professional experience and qualifications to a group of smiling, curious locals. I could see the dental magazines piled up in your cabin. It was always a rather special cabin mate — one with interests in various materials and their applications under water pressure, no less.      Indeed! Though I daresay if you'd had a real incident, you might have started smiling quite a lot harder.      And your time in Saudi Arabia — what was that like, really, in terms of culture and those curious local customs?      Oh, the mix of cultures was enriching, and the openness astonishes.

Rather annoying this new toilet seat lid. You know, the one that sticks halfway up? I've been poked in the knee half a dozen times now.      Oh, you mean the “slippery seat” one they sell in the big DIY shops? They say it’s for elderly folk, but if  this  is what they get, I reckon it's not all that great for a clean old lady like me. I once had this one in my mother's house, she’d get so cross trying to sit down.      Blimey, that's a right pain. I’ve literally had it worse at home. My older brother keeps the seat down only when he's in a  good  mood. When he's moody , I've got to lift the whole thing every single time like a piece of gym equipment. Honestly feels like it’s breakfast, no matter when I use it.      That’s typical of teenagers! I remember you were still fairly young when I babysat for you once, weren’t you? Now you're being wilfully awkward—probably texting someone instead of going to sleep.      Fair enough, but if I don’t mess around in there a little, who will? I mean, Mateo from school said his parents still let him stay out late as long as he babysits his sister and “helps out.” If I could get that kind of freedom, toilets wouldn’t even be on my mind.      Now, now, don’t start bragging— you’d  have to babysit real young mouths to be traded like that! Look, when I was your age, I did work experience at the marketing company the summer before my A-Levels. It showed what you could do if you were proactive. I’d say it helped a lot when I started freelancing.      Geo., you passed A-Levels. I’m trying to pass GCSEs. That seems like a very different worlds apart.      Not to rush you over that, but academically speaking, the lunches we have on site with my job have shown me more than any set of books. Then again, I left school with nothing more than GCSEs myself. I’ve seen plenty of work done in person, and it’s no less valuable.      And what your mother’s saying isn’t wrong. The lives we build aren’t always about formal qualifications. I know people with PhDs who’ve never had a clue about understanding people—contrast that with someone who landed a job off the back of pure hustle.

Rather annoying driving up here in this traffic. I mean, do they all know it's Istria? We’d be there quicker if we’d walked, wouldn’t we?      Now, now, Lucy. Not all of us have got the legs you’ve got. And it was my idea eeny we went up through the hills today, so I reckon if it’s not easy, blame me.      Fair dos, Dad. I’m just joshin’ yeh. Honestly, the views ar’ sommat else. Those truffles they told us about… I’d kill for one of those right now!      That’s easily taken care of. There’s this wee restaurant round the bend, Marco told me about. His uncle owns it – proper truffle hunting folk, them! They say the truffles here taste summat different – earthier, more ‘nasty breakfast, really.      Haha, repulsive! I love truffles! We talked about ’em in school the other day. Did you know that chefs treat them like gold, and some people even use truffles for stem cells research now?      Blimey, Matthew, that’s brilliant. Never would have thought of that. Mind you, most of us just pop one on a bit of pasta, eh?      Truth be told, that’s what I’d use mine for. ‘Balderdash and truffles’ – old joke. Lucy, d’you remember me sayin’ that to your mum when we first got together?      Oh, yeah! Still cracks me up. I don’t know how you two have been together thirty years. I mean, not to touch the fact that I’m still young and all, but thirty years is an age.      Well, I’ll have you know Lucy, thirty years is twice as long as most of your American sods have been together. They’re all flash ‘n’ fancy, but no heart.      Not my mate Josh. His parents have been together for twenty years and they live in America. But he says it’s hard there because there’s too much freedom. You know, like the freedom to break up every other year!      That’s bollocks! Still, I’m glad you're all in school, Matthew. You’ve your future ahead. Lucy, you planning to stay in Bolton when you leave uni, or you off to London with all your ambitions?      Honestly, I dunno. I like Bolton. It’s got my lot of friends, and they’ve got this new restaurant opening, all about local cuisine. It’s got me thinking whether I could mix up being a chef with marketing, you know?

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? I mean, for Cambridge—it's got a bit of that crisp autumn air, and the sun’s just enough to make you think it might be summer again.      Not bad at all, I'd say! Though I'll be honest, I'm usually too busy checking my emails to notice the weather properly. Still, it's not as grim as most people here claim.      Honestly, I’ve barely stepped outside this morning. Between pulling spreadsheets and collating project updates, the view from my desk is just the interior corridor. You'd think the printing house had its own weather system—stories and stories of the same beige walls.      Fair point. I’ve only just taken a proper break this afternoon. I’m part of the language research team, and I’ve been buried in phonetics data for the last few weeks. It’s fascinating, honestly—tracking dialect shifts in Anglo-Saxon regions in real-time.      Oh, interesting. I work in digital marketing, so I’m more about algorithms and conversion rates, but I can see how both fields are about people, just viewed from different angles. Do you publish your findings as well?      Wait, seriously? You got into phonetics research? Mate, I got a humanities degree and now I just sort project timelines. You must have an absolute brain for all that depth.      It’s not as glamorous as it sounds, someone just with an ear for accents and a passion for language patterns. But oddly satisfying when you detect meaningful shifts—especially in a place like South and Eastern England where dialects are slipping into near uniformity because of TV and social media.      That’s actually something I grapple with a little too—hearing local accents water down to make campaigns seem more ‘approachable’ to wider audiences. It’s strange, the way communication is being standardised even in more traditional areas.      If you ask me, there’s something being lost there. I mean, who are we if we all end up talking the same way?      Exactly what I was thinking last week. That's why I believe the work we're doing—documenting dialects in real-time—is potentially future-proofing our linguistic identity. Not that anyone outside academia is likely to see it like that.      Maybe not. But in marketing, sometimes fluency means fitting in with the majority. It's a weird balance between authenticity and appeal.

Rather annoying this new European traffic system, isn't it? I've driven across France plenty of times when I worked in the language schools, but now everything seems more... complicated, don't you think?      Yeah, honestly, I didn't realize how different the motorway toll systems could be in each country. Even though I used to teach English in Kraków for a while, all that changed after Brexit.      I know! I'd never have thought registering a UK-numbered van abroad would be such a nightmare. And I don't mind admitting, when it comes to setting things up on my mobile, I'm rather hopeless. I've been fumbling around the past two days!      My uncle still lives in Tarnów though, so he said we can go the old-fashioned way, through Krosno and away from the toll roads. It's a slower route, but better for breakfast, no?      Sounds a bit longer, but a slower drive means I won't fumble the van’s gears so much. Good idea, and I do need the coffee, if nothing else. I’ve not driven since I moved back to Cambridge. Too many dogs and rain for a proper road trip!      You used to be such a regular on the national networks – doing weekend radio with your tips on grammar, right? You'd charm the pants off everyone with your soft Cambridge vowels.      Bless you, you make it sound like prime time! I just dabbled for a bit when I was teaching a bit here and there. Funny thing—job markets are tight now, but I sometimes get asked through word of mouth to do a private lesson or two. I do miss the classroom though.      I’m currently teaching in a secondary school in Manchester and often think of that soft charm! I mean, it does help when students are more... motivated. But hey, you always told me enthusiasm can carry a lesson on its own, even if it's a bit bumpy at the start.      You always did stick to my good advice and ignore the bad. And I always ignore the 'never retire' comment from my younger cousins! Anyway, Manchester's a proper city for a teaching career. I sometimes dream of cruising in that world again.      Well, at your age, you can always reinvent yourself. After all, I'm teaching through what your generation used to call "new media"!

Rather annoying this, innit? They’ve got the telly on but it’s muted, an' it’s got the football on. Just keeps on playing music and I can’t tell if we’re winning or not.      Aye, it’s a bit cheeky really. I mean, I understand if there’s somethin' important on at the same time, but just silence? Should a' let us know if they’re gonna keep this up or not. Oh, and what d'you think o’ this new lads' strip for Sunderland? Looks a right mess.      Right, I’ve seen it. They’ve gone all posh and glitzy, like some sort of posh turkey. I preferred the old one to be fair. At least that told the lads who they were playin' for. Now it looks like they're in it for the Maccy’s breakfasts and whatever that new advert says. "Look good in your kit while munchin' oversized breakfast burritos, lads!"      That’s real typical—McDonald’s, big brands always dopin' up the side mascot and puts a logo as big as the human eye on their shirt. Reminds me when I used to watch Liverpool as a kid. Back then it was just red and white stripes with a badge, and now it's all logos and neon. I reckon the lads are just mortal and their feet are meant to be on the ground.      Aye, but it’s also the crowd. They like a bit of flash now. I mean, you chuck in some sponsored shirts, and you get a lot more money in the till for the club. You can't argue with that. Still, the kits look the same the whole lot of them. It's like every team's gone gone to the same tailors and it's a £10 cut.      Aye, well if they’re gonna spend that cash on the logo, I’d expect something a bit more original. I dunno, maybe some mad designs or stick to their roots a bit more. Let’s face it, we've 'ad a couple of decent strips in our time, but no, now it’s all neon colours and sponsors.      Mm, I reckon if you've got a real heritage, you don't chuck it out the window for soddin' buns and whatnot. Still, I suppose it's better for them lads to eat well and look smart while they're doing it, eh?

So, I read this article today about the Matrix and how it’s basically like a metaphor for real life. It got me thinking—isn't it kind of like religion? I mean, like, where does your truth come from? Do we even know the real truth?      Interesting way to put it, dear. I’ve always thought religion was more about giving people something to believe in… especially with a child to look after, it’s comforting to know there's something bigger out there. It helps put life into perspective. We’ve been to church occasionally for the baby’s baptism, but the decision to follow anything... that’s personal, really.           D’you think it’s kind of the same as groups like Scientology, then? Like, if something doesn’t feel scientifically true, does it matter?      Well, you can’t discount that, can you? I mean, people believe in things for all sorts of reasons—science, faith, hope, or even just the people they hang out with. I’ve seen how close friends can change someone. My best friend at my age believed in practically nothing, then after she married her husband—he’s very into his beliefs—you know, like, daily prayer and all that. She started believing too. It did change her life.      But what if your whole reality is fake? Like someone manipulates it for you. If God made man, or if man made God, which one’s the real truth? It's like the Matrix being controlled by machines… but if your people are doing it to you, how do you even know the difference?      You’re looking at it like you’re not part of that system. Everyone is, whether it’s religious, political, cultural. The trick is knowing that you’re part of something bigger and making your peace with it. Or trying to change it. That’s what the nun I used to see for advice always said. We had to trust that we could do the right thing—enough.           I get it, like trying not to go wrong in the world even if you don't know what the rules really are. But it scares me sometimes. What if I’m just made for someone else’s purpose?      Then maybe choose your purpose. Or more accurately—like that nun used to say—find your own light. I’m not entirely sure what I believe, but I do know love and kindness aren’t meaningless, no matter what matrix we're in.

Rather annoying this new roundabout eh? You’d think in 2023 it would be easier to get from the motorway to the local road without feeling like we’re in a textbook traffic diagram!      Aw, don’t worry love—get used to it. We’ve been in eeny weeny villages where we’ve got to reverse   twice   just to get out of a car park. A roundabout feels like the height of sophistication by comparison!      Can someone turn the radio up or somethin’? Didn’t even get to finish my vegan chipolata like, ten minutes ago!  Mate, I’m dying here.       You like that vegan turkey one, don’t you? Fun fact—did you know there’s a music festival in nearby Pula this weekend? Just don’t expect me to spend a fortune on green food. I’ve got enough on my hands worrying about whether you two are going to get lost if we ever camp again in one of those center parks.      Just don’t fall asleep over the wheel, okay?

Rather annoying I’ve just lost me wi-fi, innit? Might need to pop down t’café for a bit o’ proper connexun.      Yeah, where are you? I’m just over the road at the library, mind if I come with? Rather nippy today, ain't it? That’s me tellin’ you, I’d kill for a mince pie an’ a cup of tea like it’s Christmas!      Aw, I don’t think we’re quite there yet, Simon! Rather annoying when a LinkedIn contact requests assistance with sorting out a query. I was just wrestling with a string of those last week. Never mind them sending messages at 2 a.m. on a Saturday. It's mad, really. Not quite sure they read the description—  L  ibrary   In  formation   N  etwork—probably more suited to somewhere else,   Social Media Enquiries  , as it were!      Aye, I've had my fair share of queries involving social media as well. A chap the other day asked how to create a Facebook page for his ancient cat. The cat isn’t old, but the profile page!  Ancient . I showed him the steps, only to find out he made a MySpace profile by mistake years ago. Fun stuff. It’s like we need to start teaching social networking basics again, and I’m not even 30!      Oh, honestly, it’s practically prime time therapy in here with these demographics in New Zealand. I had a group last month, you'd not believe. One man thought he had to wear a hat to Twitter and tell the computer his opinion before it would let him post! Another tried to “re-tweet” by actually calling someone and repeating the message… reminiscent of the telegraph days in a way. You folk here at Salford must often be experts, not librarians!      More like accidental social media support line than   Enquiries   Services. Last week, I had someone who was convinced their LinkedIn had been hacked because they weren’t given a Nobel prize. It just goes to show, some people think connection equates to   achievement   these days. Still, at least they  try  to better themselves!      That’s the spirit, man! Though I had this lass from a local college last month ask me how to “make a post on Instagram uncool.” I asked her what she  meant  by that, and she explained she did something silly and now feared peer evaluation. She told me she was  worried it looked unsparkly . I gave her a choice: “Either unpost it or consult a therapist.” She went for the former.      Some people, no doubt you remember, even come with entire scripts! I had a woman go in details on how to use Pinterest like a   mood board   for a holiday, but only include green stuff—flowers, gardens, anything green. She was going to depict sustainability through  monochromatic pastoralism . I had to start drawing her a PowerPoint because that's what she expected:  formalised representation via digitised silence !

Rather than going ahead prematurely, I think we need to take a step back and think carefully about  what to do with the tape , don't you? It's part of the consultation process, after all, and we owe it to the stakeholders to be thorough.      You're absolutely right, and I couldn't agree more. The business case must be robust if we're going to get buy-in. The rationale for the location is just as important too — Tunbridge Wells is a good choice, but not just because it’s convenient. We need to show how the new hospice will tie in with the organisation of local health services.      That’s the key, precisely. Our working model assumes that the new hospice will help reduce the load on existing services, especially when it comes to the nursing of people at the end of life. A good location would allow us closer collaboration with the hospices already in operation, and that’s something I’d want to highlight in the business case.      Absolutely, and collaboration is vital. From the political side, we’ll need strong relationships with both the local council and the clinical commissioning groups. Geography puts us in a good position to service the Kent and East Sussex region, but we must also consider how we manage existing estate services. You wouldn’t believe the number of estate agents I’ve spoken to who barely understand the long-term needs of a project like this.      I've dealt with that too! It's a case of misaligned priorities — commercial property is about short-term yield, not long-term care. But let's not lose sight of the core reason: patient health. The new building must reflect that — open, welcoming, uncluttered. It needs to feel like a sanctuary, not a hospital wing. I imagine something modern — modular architecture perhaps, with communal areas that encourage conversation and shared reflection.      That hits the nail on the head. And for the building to work, we’ll have to be pragmatic. If we assume the health budget is under intense pressure, then we can’t expect miracles in the funding request. We’ll have to clearly define the benefits: better outcomes, a more efficient use of NHS resources, and reduced pressure on care homes and A&E.      Exactly. And I think we can use the patient testimonials to highlight emotional benefits as well as the medical ones.

Fully of energetic minds and the occasional pest — I live to educate and manage the chaos. As long as I don’t forget to charge the tablet, I can fall sound asleep reading bed stories online to them!

Rather a lovely day for a walk through Brucefield Farm, isnae it? The light’s real golden like it’s right outta one of those poetry books ye love so much.      Aye, sun’s quite the mood, I ken what ye mean. Reminds me o’ that eeny wee place I visited in the Pyrenees. Small village, no trains, no shops, aye but the books? Ah, the old man who ran the bookseller had shelves o’ forgotten novels—ferns and dust and all. Ye’d have loved it.      Oh hell, I’ve been wantin’ to read mair travel lit lately, precisely the sort o’ thing. Did the lochans there glimmer like the ones here, do ye think?      A bit o’ a contrast, though. There, it was mountains, and the wind would breakfast the whole valley if ye left a page unflipped in yer book. I read _The Guide to the Mountains_ by torchlight one night. Good title, real misleading—nelped me fall off a hill t’boot.      Christ, and here I’ve been bogged doon in this essay on municipal policy for work. Ten thousand words on “stakeholder engagement.” Real riveting. Sometimes, I think I just need to chuck it all and somewhere like Sicily, read something scandalous on the beach and insult a fisherman in dialect.      That’s the spirit! I read _The Leopard_ there once, on an outcropping looking at a ruined church and smoking a cigarette—feeless as hell. Look, as yer employer in books about nowhere, I’m recommending the same.      Employed? Aye, and paid in cabernet and eggnog? I’m listenin’. Remember that festival in Berlin where Burgundy was treacle and every book had a fatal disease? I read _The Painted Bird_ in a wooden hut once. I swear, I returned to my flat speaking in hushed tones as if I’d seen Stalin’s ghost.      Aye, Berlin’s sharp like that. Reminds me, I’ve this travel course next week—will ye go? They’re runnin’ it alongside a book club. Gonna read travel lit, explore the greenbelts of Edinburgh, then summarise what your soul’s made o’.      Oh? Sounds like yer nipping off to teach people how to find themselves while we talk aboot where we’ve nearly lost them. A fitting irony.      Dark sense o’ humour, love. But yon course, it could be interesting. A week o’ wind, and ink, and flaked wallpaper, and maybe no wifie left at the door.

Yeah, I’ve sent them my last university projects and some freelance bits I’ve been working on. But I’m dreading the meeting now. That’s you—my mum saying that.      What did your dad say when you told him?
