You mean like overthinking or taking things too seriously?      Both. It can make people think you’re not as confident as they'd like you to be before they even meet you.      I suppose I’ve had a bit of that to learn as I’ve gone along.

Rather a damp day, isn't it? That’s the weather for you—too much of it in recent weeks, and I’ll not be mending no more bridges in me old age anyway!      Aye, truth told, I've been frightened half to death every time it’s poured een window. Thought me roof was comin’ down more than once! My estimatin’ of most a' that concrete lot these days tends t' be “I’m not bleedin’.”      Well, you two are always bleatin’ me to pieces, but the worst lot is the politicians. You’d think with property prices sky-high, they’d offer the elderly a few grants for roof and floor replacements.      Ha! Yeah, and what about housing, luv? You'd think they’d build a bit more for folks like us instead of all them fancy glass towers! Norf, where I’m from, half the folk are still in slums. I pity the lot!      Aye, and why do they expect blokes of me age to queue up for handouts? I’ve never worked in me life, as it is. I tell ya, it's time they stopped bowin’ to them big firms and started lookin’ after ordinary folk – especiall' with the cost of living what it is.      Now don’t go making them all out to be the enemy, dears! Though I’d say the Tory bunch aren’t helpin’—I’ve not seen me wages move in years, and I retired with a chuckle and a nod, not a pension pot!      Aye, and most people about now are havin' to work into the red just to keep up. Not much of what civil engineers like me are paid is spent on the houses we live in! Maybe I should have bin a ‘handyman’ rather than a high-falutin’ bloke with a degree.      Ha! You tried to build me a garden wall once and ended up with a leanin' pile of bricks and a sprained 'arm!      Well, let’s hope you don’t try t' tinker with the 'eaters goin' on in politics if you end up gettin' your hands into polities, Ronald! You might end up with a leakier government than your roof.      Touché, dear. But in all seriousness, with all the changes comin’ to housing, it’s madness they don’t make more affordable places for us old duffers. I’d pay for one of them tiny cottage flats in Harow, if they’d let a man with no credit get a taste of adventure!

Rather annoying to be honest, the amount of work needed in converting that old meeting space down by the fire escape. What do you think? Have we got the budget?      I’d say we’re just about within £2k or so, depending on how fancy we want the carpeting. Got a fella at Newton Park who does good deals on second-hand furniture. He's all self-employed, a bit of a haver but quality stuff.      Oh, right? I know someone similar. We used to do workshops at the depot in Stratford, and he’d donate some of the bits to keep it affordable. Not sure how our storage will cope once we supply tables and chairs for the space. My worry is if the tenants will co-operate with the storage plan – I had one who moaned for ages last year about not having enough room for his paintings.      Yeah, I see what you mean. The ones in the H Block are hard to deal with. But as long as we can convince them it's a shared benefit, I reckon we can manage. We could tell them it’s for educational workshops—there are plenty of young folks round here who might be interested. Marketing-wise, I might pass on a couple of leaflets to some of the students who hang out near the café?      That’s a good idea. We’ve been trying to boost the number of bookings, especially after the holidays. I understand one of the volunteers might be ill in December, so someone at the office will have to cover. You’d consider it, wouldn’t you?      Fair enough. I can handle the holidays—though I might need someone to swap shifts with because most of the staff are off. Pay's not a problem, the office budgets for it. Though I’ve already warned the folks in the manager's office that the handle on the fire escape in Block C is sticking. Burglars could get in if someone's not around. The health and safety man’s coming round on Thursday, so I’ll get it sorted then.      We should talk about maintenance and maybe arrange to get a proper survey done next spring. I’ve noticed the glass in the upper floor is tinted where it shouldn't be. Pigeons keep flying in through the gap between the panes, and our volunteer got hit by a bird at the weekend—so that’s a welfare issue, not just aesthetic.

Rather lovely to be here in Hereford, isn’t it? A bit of peace and quiet away from the classroom, and the kids’ parents. I’m more than happy to take a break from lesson planning!      Yes, the view from outside is smashing, but can we make this cottage eeny weeny bit more warm? It’s like living in an ice lolly!      Aye, but that's the charm, isn’t it? If it was as warm as Cardiff it wouldn’t feel like the countryside. Still, I say when it's time to cook up a feast like we're on  The Great British Bake Off , let's start with a fire first.      Just keep the cheese board out of the oven, right boys? I’m not cooking again if we burn the place down.      Ed, you’ve cooked for us before when we went camping. I think mastering the campfire was in your DNA.      Oh, don’t remind me of that. One time, we thought we were making stew, and it turned into a very sad crop of tentacle with no idea what to do. I think the squirrels still hide from me when I walk past.      You’re dramatic, but true. Speaking of food, I still think it's a pity Anna’s not a chef. It would’ve made things a whole lot easier. She could’ve whipped up something edible, and then you wouldn’t have to rely on supermarket ready meals.      I can do an okay nut roast, if it's a stretch to call it ‘whipping up’. I did ballet as a girl, not about to start doing any quick routines in the kitchen now.      Nancy, you and I need to be the calm ones in the kitchen. Otherwise, these two will have us eating ‘mystery baked treacle’ for weeks.      Aye, it's a cautionary tale I once heard about a man who tried to cook a chicken while being on the phone and ended up being asked out by the chicken farmer.      That happened? Was it in Singapore you say, Leslie?      No, go on then, man up if you don’t believe me. But I digress. I’m just wondering what we can do with the veg from the garden out back. We could have a real rustic vibe down to the marrow bones and stew meat!      Or we can talk about that ‘rustic vibe’ while someone else does the cooking.

Rather annoying this new ad on the radio innit?  "Come to the coast for your holidays — sun, sand, and sea..."  Like we all haven’t heard that before ten times today      Aye, honestly I’ve switched off the radio at half past seven every mornin’ eeny ad since  that  one started. 'Course I reckon it depends where yer from — if I’d grown up in Sunderland like yer, I might be lured by the sea. Imagine me, pulling up to a beach with nothing but me car and a tent. Y’know?      It's more likely you'd be bringing a tent, two fold out bikes, and a speaker in yer Renault My you're a bit posh for wild camping.      I reckon you're right, but still I think there's something about spendin' a few nights away from the grid. No Wi-Fi, no alarms, no boss breathin' down yer neck. And the odd bit of felling the wind or the rain? That’s actually quite satisfying, innit?      Y’know I might actually be persuaded. What about a road trip up the east coast? Like we go in me car, pull up by some West Country sea spot and just camp out for a weekend. No planning, no booking, just slap a map up and drive. Y’ked?      If we’re talking about a road trip — let’s make it a proper one. Start up here in Harpenden, a rush of caravans at the out-of-town Tesco, a stop at some strange village tea room for a fry-up, then end in Bude or about there. I hear the coast path round the area is well scenic this time of year — what d'ya think?      Sounds brilliant. We could nominate some playlists, like for each day. Me guest for Friday might be all folk — something to do with the sirens and surf sounds. Yeh, I dunno how long it’d take but I reckon Saturday we could do something rural as well. Y’ked with lunches and a couple of whiskeys by the fire.      Then Sunday it's a slow drive back — go easy on the petrol, if you don’t mind. And maybe some country line dancing? I reckon between us we can box a tune on the radio and some dodgy sandwiches at the roadside.      That’d be hours of fun. Just make sure the car’s got a bit more ‘oomph’ when we head back up north — wouldn’t fancy my old clunker getting stuck in some pothole next to the cliffs.

Rather annoying the queue at the surgery this morning, wasn't it? I had to get my blood pressure checked... What with my father's recent heart scare, I thought I'd better be sure      Aye, can be a bit of a grind at times, can't it? Me mum's been having a few more check-ups since the stroke. Still, better safe than sorry, they say.      Absolutely. Such a tragedy, really. My mother-in-law had a funeral last week. We've been helping the family sort out the logistics. It's been a lot to deal with, but I'm trying to stay strong.      I'm sorry to hear that. It must be tough, especially with young children involved. My niece tried to throw her dinner around the room the other night, and I think it turned out for the best she was at home and not out shopping when it happened.      Haha, I don't doubt it. Keeping children calm during such times is near impossible. I suppose they just don't understand death in the same way, do they?      You're quite right. They might mourn and miss the person, but they don't get it. My neighbour used to be very healthy, but she's lost a lot of weight recently. I asked her, and she said she's been on a new diet.      Oh? Which one is that? I might look into something for myself too.      Just a low-carb, high-protein sort of thing—more about the way she eats than any real fad, I think. She's talking about feeling better, not just about how she looks.      That's commendable. I'm a bit conflicted though—you know that new school healthy meal plan we've introduced? It's to do with nutrition and encouraging better habits.      Does it work? I remember when the school uniform was mentioned being too tight last year, but I suppose restricting calories must help. We all know how hard it can be to say no to the cake bar lunches, right?      It is, but you try delivering something around this time of year, with the end-of-term treats on the menu! It's a constant fight. Still, I think it’s important that we teach our children good habits now.      You're planting seeds, so to speak. Although, it's amazing how much the children pick up, even from conversations we don't mean them over-hear.

Rather skip ahead a bit here. So I've just poured us a glass of Malbec, real treat. I got it on special from Win Shop, you know the one by the gym.      A Malbec, nice choice, I prefer a good Pinot Noir myself, much more versatile on the palate. But I'll try a splash, just to be polite.      A wine tasting? I'm in! What's the deal, Miss Wine Expert?      Please! You're just saying that because you never had a decent Cabernet. You know what I like to pair with Malbec? Rich red meats, heavy stews, anything with a bit of umami going on.      Fun fact for you, most Malbecs from the Cellar at Mendoza and I think the ones in Europe are making inroads now, try to have enough acidity, but yeah, they do pair nicely with a good steak.      There we go, ordering steaks and wine in the house over dinner. Classy Waterfowl here, yes? Speaking of, I'd love to hear what your work week was like, Kris. You've been out in the cold on the slopes, haven't you?      Ha – no, not quite. I spent most of it buried behind paperwork, but the weather was perfect. We did have a team day out on the mountain toward the end of the week, which was a change.      Did you read about the new snowplow system at the resort? They're rolling it out in the next two weeks, supposed to clear the runs much faster, better for customers and about five percent more efficient for the company. Interesting talking points at the next team meeting.      Oh that was you! I read it in the news last night; the system, they said, was designed by Geo., right? Said it cut down the wait time by a third. That's got to be helpful with the peak seasons coming up.      Yeah, and that's what we did all week – flipped through data logs and tweaked the models. Not the most thrilling work, but it does something.      Yeah, go on then, tell me about your week, Leon – what have you been up to?      Not much, really. Just your standard secondary student routine. We've been learning about conservation and ecosystems, it was mildly interesting. I think we all agree the case study on the Amazon rainforest was a bit too ambitious, though.      Oh I got that topic for our project, kind of exciting, actually.

Rather annoying that the flash isn't working on my phone camera. I can't even get a decent shot of... What was it, some shot of the badger?      Oh, that's probably it in the box. The one from outside the children's hospital in Norfolk. Remember how we lay on the grass at dusk pretending we were both twitchers just to get the perfect shot?      I remember now. You swore the badger looked back at you, but I'm not sure if you were joking or not. You do tend to get a bit dramatic, don't you?      Dramatic? I prefer to say I'm passionate. And I'm still waiting for you to admit that the turkey on Japan's Mount Kazan was not the best photo of the trip.      Touché. I think the world might end if I actually admit that. But forget the turkey. What about the moment you said you'd "fallen in love with the sunrise at the foot of Mount Fuji"? Surely that's a bit of an over exaggeration too?      Haha, maybe a bit. But I can't help it! It was beautiful. And the real reason I still love taking photos is to capture those moments. Like when we found the hidden spring in Akita?      Right, the one with the waterfalls tumbling over mossy rocks. You got drenched, trying to capture the detail in the water.      I did not get drenched—just... splashed unfortunately. It's amazing how photography can make even the most mundane moments seem epic, don't you think?      Most certainly. And it's made about half the photos in this box gold standard. Speaking of which, I had a look at what you found at the back of the drawer and I'm fairly sure the one with my face reflected in a puddle is the most cringeworthy.      I have no idea why it's your least favorite. I thought it looked like something you might wear on a tour t-shirt to intimidate fans.      Next time we take a trip, I'm buying a better camera and you're not volunteering for candid photographer.      Don’t be so goody two-shoes. I promise I’ll get you one day.      I look forward to it with trepidation.      Great! I've made a special list—Japan, Norfolk, and anywhere with wildlife. Just like the old days.      Sounds ominous.

So, I heard you lot were up in Ireland last month. Any decent experiences out there, or just pints and pubs?      It was actually brilliant! We stayed in a tiny village near Kilkenny. The people were so friendly, and we even picked up some local recipes for Jewish food during our stay. Claudia Roden even recommended one!      Oh, Claudia Roden? I’ve only read a little of her work! I’m running a small café, so I love pulling together unique Jewish recipes to mix in with the classics. Didn’t you try the potje platter too?      Yeah! I can still taste it. What’s weird is that we found an amazing photo of our group skinny dipping in some hidden lake. I’m not sure how I’m going to explain that on LinkedIn...      Ah, don’t worry, storytelling is an art! Just say, “internationally experienced community pool manager with a passion for aqueous narrative construction.” Everyone loves a good anecdote.      Haha, classic Sam! By the way, tell me more about your café, Jess. I mean, with your background as a baker, I assume it's flour and love in equal doses?      Well, it’s more than that! My father’s side is fairly traditional, and I’ve tried to merge some of the old family recipes with modern twists. We do a Jewish deli board and some quirky cocktails that are inspired by poetry from the diaspora. It’s a vibe!      That sounds oddly therapeutic. You ever think about the apocalypse? Like, if the zombie apocalypse hits East London, where would your backup plans be?      I’ve already got gold-pressed lattes and a larder of bagels and lox. I’m ready! I mean, if the world goes to pot, I at least want to snack like a guest at a schlep.      Ha, I’d just surf the zombie apocalypse. I grew up in Australia, waiting for tsunamis to come and not end up being real. Zombified kangaroos would be the least of our worries if the dead started walking.      Pfft! I’d still snore so much I’d attract a horde of zombies before anyone else.      Sam, don’t go turning this into a snoring seminar. Focus on the food, focus on the stories!      Well, speaking of stories… I was just trying to recreate the Jewish joke from last weekend at the bar, and it went completely pear-shaped.

Rather annoying when a bar puts out peanuts in those little paper bags. I was just in Chester and it was all got and go, same with the peanuts.      Yeah, where we are in Birmingham we mostly get them in ceramic bowls and you serve yourself. Just like the ol' pubs of yesteryear, eh? Though I'm more used to the university refectory meals than most.      Fair dos. I'd rather have a cracking bowl of peanuts and some interesting company to pass the time. Hey, have you played that new sci-fi game? The one with the aliens and the futuristic theme park?  Variation Horizon  or something like that?       Variation Horizon ? I did play it last week, actually. Probably need to play it again, given the exam and viva prep I've got coming up in October. The game is better than breakfast, honestly.      Haha, yeah, it’s more addictive than a strong brew, even if it is a bit violent. I reckon it’d make a cracking movie, if someone had the sense to adapt it properly. You don’t think that Hollywood is going to touch it, do you?      Mate, it’s only a matter of time. They adapt anything with a sci-fi angle these days, even if it’s a load of old nonsense. It’s got aliens and all that, so what could go wrong? Still, the principles they’re using at that park in the game—placing sentient beings in an environment they aren’t equipped to survive—should really make the border security types red in the face.      Look, it’s not just theme parks with that kinda trouble. I was reading the other week about how secure the borders really are. There was some report done that showed that barely a quarter of the staff at one of the main border crossings had sufficient background checks.      That's grim. I remember a few years ago a lecturer was all fired up about it—the way people just slipped through the cracks. Not to mention the security footage being as dodgy as it is with some of those new AI systems. They're all supposed to spot weird things, but I bet they're missing a fair few folks cruising in with forged documents.      Just don't expect me to spend my holiday trying to get into a themed park that costs more than your average car.

Rather skip the mushy peas today, love. Just give me a sprig of it, if you like.      You're having more than a sprig, you old thing! Feast yer hols. Not every day we have a chance to catch up properly. And it was kind of you to meet me here — I do miss the atmosphere of a real fish and chip shop, not just a paper plate on a park bench.      Well, it’s been a while since you came down from West Yorkshire, has it not? Didn’t even get to visit you at your lovely home in Shipley last summer. Not when I was tackling learning to row out at the river. It was like climbing My turkey, I’m exhausted! The rowing’s a different game altogether, I was sweating buckets in a boat, and I hadn’t even screamed.      Catscratching it when you're old then? I happened to take a kayaking trip at the Yorkshire Dales not long ago, you'd love it. There was the wind, yes, and I nearly went into the river a couple of times, but the views — wow — quite a different way to experience the countryside.      Sounds like it would suit me. I did have a spot of good fortune at the weekend though: meeting my niece, Elsie, for the first time. She’s her mother’s daughter, right enough — bright red hair and all, and a proper talker, she is. They came down to Dorchester for the day. It was a rush, but oddly satisfying. You’d have had the giggles with her and my sister being their usual selves.      Oh, I do miss those times. My husband used to bring the whole lot down once a year. I suppose you've not gone back there since then? I mean, it does sound strange to talk of Dorchester like that. I’ve heard it’s quite passed on now. A few years ago, the whole family lost him.      Ah, yes. I went back once. It didn't feel the same as it did before. There were lunches, a couple of weddings, the various do's. My knees tell me I won't be doing that too often, but it's worth it on occasion. I do miss everyone.      I gather you had some news from the other side of the family, your cousin Mike’s latest sum-up about flu and all?

Rather annoying when the phone’s on 1%. Thought me Mam’s promising me her tablet ‘til tomorrow.      Aye, I remember when I first had a mobile, ‘ere, it’d last me all week with a bit o’ luck! These days they’re more than leccy guzzlin’ I reckon.      Nah, I’ve got me own aye. A Samsung, but me Vodafone’s all dodgy. Constantly on the blink, pulling me arse!      Funny you say that, I was sayin’ t’other day I’ve sorted unitedly to switch back t’O2, supply seems steady. Course, like that MyFone bloke told me.      Probably, but I reckon you D’you know what I think? They should bring back Morse code for textin’. ‘S been a proper mess of emojis lately.      Oh aye, you ever looked at that? They didn’t have no laptop in the house when I were lad—had t’write letters and hope the postman was up t’speed. Like a week to read back and forth off me old mate in Liverpool. These days, you've got it in a minute.      Real shame with the results, though, because they don’t come through the post no more. All online now. I were trying to remember what it was like when your whole future’s in a bit of paper in an envelope. Like a test readin' time, you know.      Aye, I can imagine. Anyroad, you're all set for uni, eh? Got yer about five offers off yer UCAS! Fit the right one’s for you. Not just a house full of books and lectures.      Aye, I think I have. But ‘course, I’ve got t’sort out me student loan. Bit worried me expenditure will go up a lot ‘fore I even get there.      A stick-likey good move. I’ll help you out if you need with that, aye. More importantly, you’re gonna need a fresh set of shoes for the shootin’!      Yeah, me nan had a pair of shoes for me in her Amazon line. Supposed t’be delivered today, bloomin’ usual what!?      Aye, they’re kina dodgy wi’ those last-minute orders. You might have to wait a week or two ‘fore they shuffle up. Or, if you’re game, I can take you to that eBay shop near the ring road next week, they’ve always got something interesting.      That’s not a bad plan. I’d rather wear me old pair than turn up in freshers week with my last years' boots still on.

Yo, mate, long time no see! You ain't been around much. How's uni been treating you, Jamie?      Man, I know, I've been buried with deadlines and exams. You don't even know the chaos. But at least I'll be out of it in a few weeks. You doing okay?      Honestly, I've been trying to keep up. A lot of group work and that this semester. Still, easier said than done. Hey, you gonna do anything after uni? I heard you might be working in Japan or something?      Yeah, I've got an offer for a junior software developer role in Tokyo. Just wrapped up my placement last term, and the company liked me enough to put in a contract. I’m kinda obsessed with the idea, but I’ve been stressing the little stuff—like actually moving halfway across the world.      Bro, that’s lit though! I’ve always wanted to travel and not just holiday, you know? I mean, working in Tokyo? That’s more like living the dream, if you ask me. Any place you fancy in London before you leave?      Nah, I’ve been thinking about saving up for a little trip first. Maybe hit up some of the sushi spots in Shoreditch, and actually take the time to explore the city like I’m supposed to. Speaking of which, you know what I could really do with? Some homework from the internet.      You lost internet again? When is that going to stop?      I swear, the ISP in my flat is a ghost town! It's so slow, it takes about five minutes to load a web page. I had to move to this place ’cause my old one was even worse. But I still barely get 20 Mbps up here.      Mate, you need to fight back. Write to the provider and all that. You can't expect any decent work speed on that. I had them install a new router, and the speed jumped up over 70Mbps. Game-changer.      I’ve been thinking about it, but you know, after uni with travel and everything, money is tight. But really need to invest if I'm going to work remotely pre-departure.      Hear hear. You're already one step ahead of the curve. I can't even picture writing code while in Japan. Sounds so cool though. You planning on learning any Japanese before you go?      Already started with Duolingo, so I know the basics.

Rather annoying Facebook keeps deleting my photos. You know when you do that thing where you post it public so they can be on the page? Just went to share more of my students with their certificates      Yes, it can do that, I had similar things happen with things on our recent visit to Buckfast Abbey. I had to do print screen and save them if possible      I've been meaning to ask if you wanted to go somewhere again, maybe easier somewhere accessible. I know there's that place in Exeter, the Castle for a short run when it's clear      That's a nice idea. Last time I had to drive the Citroen C15 and made that MyRoute on TomTom, you'd think left would take you back but I had to back around the A38 and I think the clutch screamed. I did get it fixed, eventually      Heh, I used to have a Leyland DAF Twin, you ever looked at one, you'd think it's a submarine. Good ones, built like bricks though. But tell you what, I can still get up and down in the morning without as much trouble as I did ten years ago.      Well, we should consider a cruise. You ever think about that Mate?      I had one once, long while ago, onboard staff had a heart attack and the whole Pacific was closed for a day. We sat in the harbor for eight hours.      And voting, unfortunately, is just one big game. You think you had the law changed with the Vote Leave and politicians will follow but I don't see it, Prime Minister remains in about five years.      Oh come on, Cameron had to leave over what, some tax avoidance scandal that was leaked? I mean it is unprofessional for both to have claimed rebates for their homes      Boy, when I was at the board the year before retirement, I insisted we had to report to taxmen about overtime claims. Didn't get to clear as much as they did though.      I think it's related to how we schedule our insurance, you remember, after the accident and diagnosis with the hip replacement, go for regular check-ups and if you don't get medical advice pre-trip you can claim for that.      Oh yes, your hip was fixed. I remember visiting you and you looked like you were in some steel sheep pen, all wrapped up in supports to keep you from moving      At least I didn't end up like your neighbor, I think her car ran out of oil

Rather annoying when the sat nav decides to mislead you, isn't it? I had such a miff when I was in Belgium last year—ended up in the countryside by mistake, sure I’d follow a wrong turn somewhere. Not quite what I'd call a holiday!      But it was all good fun, really. The markets were lovely. I reckon it's not all that different from a traditional British market, just with better waffles!      Oh, we had a reasonable time. We took to the bike occasionally and hit up a couple of the markets. Torey fetches up near enough spots, but when you're older, bicycling is a bit much. On the other hand, you'd be proud of Mummy though. She's got the hang of the sat nav now, at least, and I think she turned out alright with the new phone you got her.      The shops in Belgium are still alright for food, though. I had some of the best mussels in ages near the port town. Good to see they still serve strong coffee there, if a bit pricier than up here in London.      I tell you, it's quite a change from watching other people's trotters in a care home. The most energetic thing I do is walking fairly long distances and sometimes take the bus if the weather gets nippy. It's not as if you have to cycle when you're doing care work. Still, hearing all about your holidays reminds me how nice it is to not be stuck in the routine for once.      Well, mind, I can't be cycling much more—I'm not quite in the Prime of youth, about forty odd years off! But you picked the right season to take a holiday. Belgium in the spring and summer is quite gorgeous, you know. Doesn't hurt the trip when the weather's on your side for once.      I did manage that. I cycled a fair few miles. It's peaceful once you get out there, just waiting for the sat nav to come good again. I reckon being out there also meant trying the lunches on a couple of the roadside stalls—way cheaper, but far more exotic, than a nice British snack!      That sounds lovely. I do miss going somewhere different. But I'm just not in a position to go cycling in Belgium, let alone anything further afield.

Rather annoying that the oven’s on the blink again, isn't it?      Oh, come on, it's been fine this week, hasn't it? I've been using it for Sunday roasts. Not to worry, the microwave's as good for a quick supper.      Yeah, I suppose so. Not like I enjoy baking anyway. I've been making most of my meals on the stove.      Still, we should probably get it checked out soon. If it breaks down again, the timing on the roast won't be the only thing ruined.      I'd rather not talk about roasting the turkey at Christmas if we can help it. My turkey last year was more charcoal than meat.      We'll get you a good pastry chef for the day then.      Ha, very funny. Wait, I just thought of something clever—would you fancy trying out that new Indian cookery book I got from the library?      Oh, yes, that one with the bright green cover—personally I think spices are overrated, but your dishes usually turn out nicely.      Good, good—it says here it's quite a task, but I think we can manage it.      Let's just hope it doesn't attract any stray cats in the neighbourhood again like the curry last week.      That cat looked absolutely intrigued, someone should have given it a bowl. Anyway, while the curry's simmering, do you think you could fetch some more spices? I think the grocer round the corner does the best curry powder.      Sure. Just let me grab the car keys.      While you're out, are you going to check up on Anna? She hasn't mentioned much on Facebook, but she must be feeling rather low.      I will, I know it's been difficult for her lately.      You're a good friend. Speaking of friends and things—"do you think we've updated our 'About' section on Facebook lately? I feel like our work profiles are still in there.      Oh yes, that really does make it look like our social life revolves around transcription and administration.      Definitely needs a revamp—and while I'm at it, I could post a few photos from the garden. The hyacinths are looking really splendid.      Oh yes, they are—very pretty. They wouldn’t half brighten the place up if we ever had a dinner party.      And always a good cover for the poor fireplace.      It’s looking better than before, to be fair—I’ve had some fresh wood in there.

Rather lovely to meet you both. I do so enjoy a good chat about people's experiences abroad. Did you know, dear, I often taught English as a second language? Not a hint of negativity in me! But I must say, Australia has always fascinated me.      Aye, it's a grand place, I'll say that for 'er. I fancied a business trip down under a few years back. Everything feels so far away from here, don't you find? It was quite interesting, observing the men's fashion there. They seem to take more of an informal tack compared to the rather... crisp attire one finds around these parts.      Oh, I’d agree with you there, well spoken chap. I did my PhD in linguistics and have always had a soft spot for the spoken word. But let's say in the world of academia—my dear, aren't you from Bristol? I've heard that place has this lovely Anglo-Saxon twist in the lilt, you know?      Indeed I am from Bristol. Almondsbury, actually—just over the hill, if you will. Southerners are often short with their words, to be polite and all. But let me turn the conversation back to Australia, if you don’t mind. I read that most bank loans are rather generous with fairly simple interest rates, making it easier to start a business.      Aye, that’s a fair point. The cost of living isn't what it is here. Though, one must also consider the distances. Queensland, for example, is massive. You could fling a stone and hit a stretch of sugar cane fields. Not that I had to do the manual work, mind you. I ran a company in Manchester, far from the sun and surf.      Another person from Yorkshire would love to hear more about it. I was born in Sheffield, and our dialect has quite the character. To outsiders, it might sound a bit rough at first, but it's a badge of pride for many of us Northerners. You mustn't stick too much to queens and kings when talking to a Sheffie.      Oh, do go on! I've always found dialects fascinating. You're like a living library of human goings-on, dear. I do miss standing in front of a class, teaching grammar, making sense of complicated tenses, and inflections.      You were a teacher, then? I was a director in business.

Rather unusual to find such an excellent vegan restaurant in a place like Rzeszów, don't you think? It's rather heartening to see this side of Eastern Europe.      Yes, it is! I didn't expect such variety and quality—especially for a weekday. I was actually surprised on the way here, seeing more young people than older folks. Makes me think about all the social media trends that probably brought them.      Oh, absolutely. Social media has changed quite a bit since I was in my prime. I occasionally check Facebook for family updates, but the rest of it feels... like a different world. What do you think keeps people so glued to it?      Well, it’s a bit of everything—a combination of connection, entertainment, and validation, I suppose. You're on it, and you feel part of something. Plus, everyone now uses TikTok for short, catchy content—like dancing or recipes.      Oh, TikTok, yes, I've heard of it. My younger daughter showed me once. I still can't wrap my head around the way people create and share so quickly. I find it quite overwhelming. But I must say, it's impressive how people can draw such large audiences.      It really is. Though, for all the fun, I sometimes worry it promotes a very shallow view of the world. But on the flip side, it can also be a great educational tool—there are even teacher influencers now!      That’s interesting. I suppose it's a bit like TV was in the '70s—there was a golden age of documentaries and news, but now it's mostly soap operas and reality shows about people who don’t know how to act.      [Laughs] True! But there are also some great documentaries on streaming platforms these days. Have you ever seen that astronomy one,  Atom ? It’s quite well done.      I remember  Atom —that was on BBC! Very accessible, even for someone my age. I did enjoy the way it simplified such complex topics. Rather like your own English classes—you break a difficult idea into bite-sized chunks, and it makes it easier to digest.      Thank you! That's the idea. But enough about that. I must ask—have you ever tried a podcast? I’ve found them addictive, especially during my commutes.      I’ve heard bits and pieces, though I haven’t really dived into them. You know, I prefer a good book or a quiet morning with the crossword.

Rather than going out today, we might do a bit of swimming. The pool's closing time is in a couple of hours. What do you two think?      I've been waiting ages! Let me just fetch my togs and the pool hat—do you remember the one with the silly frog on it, Jack? I used to think it was   so   clever.      I remember that frog! I think it's more  weird  than clever but okay, Pippa, let’s go! Oh, wait—do we need to ask Anon the babysitter first?      Anon  promised  me she'd take the night off, but I'll check anyway. I still can’t believe she's nearly left her twenties—what  happened  to time?      Aunty Jess— Anon’s  old enough to remember when British people used to eat century eggs. They're supposed to be a delicacy, apparently, but we told you that already.      That is  boring . I want to see Anon's Travelling Circus next week! You said she said we can go, didn’t she?      Yes, we’ve got a rhythm going, don’t we. After the pool, we can visit the circus, and then take the photo you need for the Blue Peter Bronze Badge. You’re halfway through collecting already, Pippa.      There are people at that show with  wings ! That’s real? It just sounds like magic.  I  want to fly.      I want to be the lion-tamer. They wear make-up and flammable capes— so cool . But I still haven’t got my wings… or my photo for the badge.      I'll get a nice one in action. Maybe at the circus. I’ve got a couple of contacts there. Now, let’s not forget the most important thing before we all vanish.      Our little pockets need some loving. How about a  pound  each for swimming, two pounds for the photo and one from the circus? That's fair, isn't it Jack?      I say we add goody money on top—let’s say  another  two pounds.      I suppose we could go with four each—and Jack, your passport’s expiring at the end of the month. We need to sort that out soon so we don’t lose the holidays to bureaucratic nonsense.      Aunty, I  still  don’t get why we need to have a passport when we're in the UK. Am I always going to need one?

Rather than share a conversation about such personal matters, I prefer to talk about more general topics such as interests and hobbies. What are some things you're currently interested in or enjoying?      I see, that makes sense. I’ve actually been getting into photography recently—landscape shots mostly. It’s a nice way to unwind and spend time outdoors. Have you picked up any new hobbies lately?      That sounds lovely! I’ve been getting back into reading; it gives me a break from everything else. What’s the photographer's style like—do you prefer black and white or color?      I mostly shoot in color, but I sometimes play around with black and white for a more dramatic effect. It really depends on the scene and the mood I’m trying to capture.      I’d say black and white can make even an ordinary scene look incredible. Do you ever post your photos online or share them with friends?      I have an Instagram account dedicated to my photos, and a few friends check it out occasionally. It helps me get some feedback, which is always useful.      That’s great to hear. I think sharing your work is a nice way to connect with others. Let me know when you post something so I can see it!      Will do! It’s always good to hear what people think of your work. Have you considered starting a book club or anything like that for your reading?      Actually, I’ve thought about it a bit, but I haven’t got round to organizing it yet. It might be fun to gather a few friends and pick something to read together!      That does sound like a good idea! Maybe we could even mix in some photography-themed books and take photos of the places we read about.      That’s a brilliant idea! I’d love to get involved in something like that. It would be a great way to combine your hobby with mine!      Perfect! I’ll get some suggestions ready and we can discuss over coffee or something soon.      That would be amazing—coffee sounds perfect. Let’s set a date soon!      Definitely! Looking forward to it!      Me too—sounds like it’ll be a lot of fun!      It certainly will! So, have you made any other plans this week?      Not much else, just some more reading and some light shopping over the weekend.

: Right, I've just got my spice mix ready for the cauliflower cheese. Do you think it's worth buying those "Healthy Extra" packs from Slimming World?     : Honestly, I've got a half £20 voucher from somewhere, so maybe just pick up the essentials. They always have all the syns hidden in the free stuff, don’t they?     : Oh yes! A lot of those “free” things like the 0 calorie syrup are just as bad in the long run. I'm still trying to decide what to do when it comes to sweets. You know I like to have a treat once in a while.     : Treat days are the best! Saturday it’s on, right? I’m thinking leftfield—maybe just a walk to the shops and home-bake cookies. I’ll get the double peas from the freezer for later, and maybe a fresh breakfast, no frylight.     : That does sound good, thanks. I keep getting distracted, ordering online for veg boxes and then not using them all. Sometimes I feel like I should get back into it properly—there are so many things out of season now.     : Tell me about it! I had the same problem last month. Also got way too much Quorn from the supermarket, thinking I’d be smarter with the recipes this time. Instead, I’m faced with questionable amounts of it now.     : I might make a better calendar for this. I found an app—thought I’d sync it with Siri to remember when to do the exercises and check the scales.     : The scales at home are  definitely  not reliable. I did a little comparison walk to the local shops the other week and had a 2 kg differential. Maybe they're corroded with age.     : At least I still have the motivation. Work is so busy, constantly swapping shifts. I did manage to get some tax forms finished. It helps to have those small targets met.     : I could stick to my tax as well. Though being freelance, everything always comes with a cost. Rent and bills are the same, but with no guaranteed income, it’s a bit tense.     : At least I get a stable salary. If I work at the pharmacy, even in the evenings, it's always the same thing—counting what your actual body needs versus all the marketing gimmicks.     : From those “syn” foods to artificial flavour to everything on the shelves, it's exhausting.

Rather than going the usual route this year, I was thinking we could try somewhere completely different for our holiday. I got the travel allowance from work after all, so it would be a shame not to use it properly.      That does sound like a good idea. I'm getting a bit tired of the usual holidays, frankly. Where were you thinking about?      Hmm, I've been reading about a place in the south of France. They have these little villages with cobblestone streets and markets every Saturday. The description sounds like something out of a book I read last year. It’s like, very quiet and mostly locals—no crowds, no tourist traps.      Oh that does sound lovely. I’ve never been to the south of France. Most of my holidays involve airports, software demos, and sad in-flight meals. But if you're up for a bit of writing while I work remotely from a sunlit café, I'm definitely in.      Exactly that, you can do remote work and I’ll pack my journal and that new pen I got. Might get some proper writing done—perhaps I can even finish the draft I’ve been working on.      Make sure to write something decent. I remember when you got that tattoo. You said it would inspire you to become a writer, but all it did was inspire the dog to dance.      That was the plan, yes. Still, the principles remain the same. Who knows, maybe this holiday will trigger a second renaissance. Besides, I’d love to see you in the south of France in a café looking very ‘artsy’ while I sneak in a few romantic pastries about our trip.      Oh come on, I'm going for a business casual vibe not a cabaret manager. Speaking of, have you thought about the domestic situation? I mean, for the four weeks we’re out will someone feed the cat and water the dahlia I'm told is ‘important’?      You're getting distracted again. As for the dahlia, of course—Neville will come over and dote on the flowers while the cat gets free reign of the house. Now, back to the proposal: can go in late May before it gets too hot. Any chance of your manager letting you out of work that long?      I might have to pull a few strings, maybe flirt with the HR director a bit more than necessary.

Rather lovely to have you here again, David. That postcard from the Highlands was a nice touch — did you manage to visit some of those quaint little villages mentioned?      Oh, absolutely! There’s a village called Plockton, I believe—half cottage, half fishing boats, if you get my drift. I took plenty of photos for the family. They were fascinated.      Sounds charming. I’m still trying to get this year’s birthday plans sorted out. It was quite a success last year—remember the surprise at the pub? Didn’t even get the chance to complain.      Not when everyone was fawning over the fire, no. You know, they still talk about it. I’ve already sketched out a weekender plan over the East Midlands for this time. Rather more restful, mind you.      Restful? Good! I must say, I’m getting rather tired of the madhouse in London at this age. Speaking of which, have you given any more thought to that referendum? I still fail to see why one part of the UK should break away and start up on its own — quite a disorderly notion, if you ask me.      You always did have a traditionalist bent. Look, it's complicated – but it's mostly about self-determination, John. You can support the Union and still respect their wish to have a say. Besides, what do you foresee happening? A whole new set of politicians just starting at square one?      That's the trouble with politics, David – everyone flods off at half-cock and then cries foul when it doesn’t all line up in neat rows. Not nearly as tidy as university tutorials.      Fair point. I suppose you and I will know that better than most. Still, it does sound like we’re quite aligned on the weekend plan—y’expected to visit Harworth again with that niece of mine?      Oh yes, the little one—the one you always refer to as “young Casey.” She’s coming of age this year, and it’s about time we made the trip from Crickhowell. Nothing like freshening up a relationship with cake and a card, is there?      Nothing like it. If I can manage the train schedule and not miss any technical updates, we’ll box it off properly.      Splendid. I'll make sure the cake has a touch of Scottish flair—there’ll be shortbread included to commemorate your recent escapade.      I’m not entirely surprised—second to none, they say.

Rather than share a chair, Arabella wanted to draw a chair. I was her teacher, and when we discussed how to help people in need, she immediately thought of the Syrian refugees. It was such a sweet idea, really. She said that they would need a place to sit, something to make them feel at home, and she liked the idea of drawing one and sending it to them.      I remember that! I colored in red and blue because I like those colors. The chair was going to be for a boy and me to play with. But when the class talked about the kids in Syria not having toys like we do, I wanted to draw a chair for them too. I made it have little smiley faces on the legs, so it would make them feel happy.      I wanted my chair to have special chairs for sad people. I drew a cozy seat with a blanket and hot chocolate. Wait, does Syria even have hot chocolate? Mummy... I don’t know what’s cold and warm there?      That was a great question, Thomas. It’s actually quite cold there, especially at night, depending on the season. You did well to think about their comfort and even warmth, by adding a blanket. It shows how much you were thinking about making someone feel safe. And Arabella?      I still think it would help if we could send real chairs too. All of us in the class wrote a letter to the school, asking if we could make some for a group in our town to send. Miss said it was a good idea and we can do an art and design project at school. So I’m going to make a green and white rocking chair, and Thomas is making a bean bag with pictures of us all on it.      I’m going to make a chair that becomes a bed at night! I can handle it like a transformation in one of my games. That way the people can sleep well after sitting during the day. Miss will probably think it’s silly, but I think it’s very smart.      I don’t think Miss will think it's silly at all, Thomas. In fact, she loves the fact that you’re being imaginative and creative. The project is a learning opportunity too—you’ll be reading about Syrian culture, practicing geography on your maps, and even doing some work on materials and measurements in design.

Rather annoyingly, I haven't seen Sophie and Nathan in ages. I know her email address is out of date, and I've not managed to catch her at work. I need to call her over this weekend. I keep meaning to.      Yeah, wouldn't that be nice. She and Nathan are brilliant with the baby. It was lovely watching them at his first birthday – Nathan couldn't resist making a comment about how he would never have a child, and then there he was, clearly head over heels. Sophie just rolls with it, I suppose. Didn’t even blink when he said he'd forgotten to clean the nappies!      That's Sophie, always calm. I miss that. My lectures are fine, but I still get left with a lot of energy I need to burn off, and spending time with mates helps. Sometimes I just want an hour of laughter without having to explain differential calculus, or whatever it is I happened to be marking for the night.      Exactly, you deserve a break. And I know why you like Sophie so much – she’s just got this way of taking everything lightly. I mean, don’t get me wrong, she’s serious when she needs to be, but she doesn’t sweat the small stuff. It’s got to be so much better than being with people who take everything like it's the end of the world.      It really is. You know what I found interesting the other day? I was marking an essay someone wrote about language acquisition in infants. That made me think about how different we are as lecturers – you're more focused on cognitive theory, and I’m in more of a practical, educational context.      Ah yes, the "how the brain works" versus “what works in a classroom” approach! I know that well. I've actually been thinking about sending you that article I found, it gives a really interesting comparison between observational learning and formal instruction.      Oh, sent it over, I'd love to take a look. You know, speaking of babies, did you hear that Sophie’s doing a short course in infant development? I think it's related to her thinking about going back into psychology part-time after having this one.      Oh really? That's a bit of a switch – from full-on corporate line manager, to study-to-career change-in-the-middle-of-life!?

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? I needed this walk. The campus has been such a mire of last-minute essay submissions and end-of-term angst.      It does feel peaceful here. I always forget how quite rural Norfolk gets outside of those traditional busy days. And it’s strange how eeny weenys of dry earth on the walk look just like craters on the moon.      That's one way to put it. Oh, don’t forget, there's that spot just ahead where the old dry stone wall runs into the trees. Funny how some people swear by not walking under it. Mary at the admin office said her grandmother once told her only bad things happen if you do.      Oh, you mean the old "don’t walk under a wall at dusk" bit? I find it all rather charming, to be honest. Superstitions, myths—maybe they’re just stories with a bit too much emotional narrative attached. Still, I quite like thinking the old manor house a few miles over is haunted. Feels like it'd make a nice subplot in a comedy series I've been sketching.      It'd certainly add some spice. I mean, imagine the police trotting in, all humble and sarcastic at the same time: “Ah, another night, another suspicious ghost sighting,” while the locals treat it like routine.      Exactly! And then the universities bring in scholars, they start measuring things someone said in an old book. “This stone was laid by someone who oddly left a shoeprint in the mud,” they say, and then the headlines go mad with it all.      Not to mention how publicity loves these things. You can just see the local paper saying “Centuries-old Mystery Solved! Or is that Not?” and the national media picking it up for clickbaity nonsense.      It's funny how much of human life is just wrapped up in the need to explain something away, isn’t it? Whether it’s superstition or science. We just can't sit with the unknown.      And honestly, I think that's partly why I took the university job. Still trying to make sense of it all! But hey, as go the holidays, maybe we can both take a few weeks off and go somewhere even more far out, somewhere with less explaining, and more… just being?      That sounds like the best sort of plan. Just two lecturers with broken brains and wandering minds, trying to find some peace among the hills and hedges.

Rather annoying this new phone isn't it?      Aye, it's a bit too much for an old man like me, I'll tell you! Kept me up all last night trying to follow the messages.      Grandad, you can’t make a phone call without going through  at least  three different screens these days.      It's miraculous that I even remembered to set the alarm this morning, honestly. Oh but tell me what you know 'bout this Great Dorset Steam Fair. Is it the one in the summer?      Yeah, it runs mostly over the bank holidays, as far as I know. There's some steam-powered trains and agricultural shows. You liked that stuff though didn't you?      You're right, I used to love the rodeo pigs and the model railways at the old one. Wait, does it still run 'em?      Probably. I'll look it up and send you the details. You can have the instructions for getting there, like Mum said.      Oh, I might take the old landrover to go. I only took it out today for a spin anyway—it cleared the cobwebs off it, like. You want to come?      Maybe, I might need to help some friends move a flat though.      You're always helping people aren’t you? What's the daft name someone gave to one of those moving services again?      Hire a van—yes, the van hiring places. You can get a weekend rate if you book online.      I did that once—got the wrong van the first week and had to drive it back a second time. That nearly finished me.      You're not going to do that, I'll do the booking for you.      Aye, well the more the merrier. Do you fancy coming with us to the fair when it's on?      Maybe. Is there anything grandad? 'Cause I might have exams to do if I can’t book far in advance.      I'll make sure go anyway then. But tell me more about computer games—that one your brother played on the weekend.      It's something to do with medieval warfare and building bases. I can show you on my Xbox one night if you want.      Oh right, games like that sound very engrossing—just like fitting together string and nails for my shed.      Just without so many splinters, I hope. Right, I should get back now, I need to finish moving my last couple of boxes.

Rather annoying this, isn't it? The council wants to knock down the library. I would've thought they’d be more sensible with heritage sites.      I saw that in the newspaper this morning. Honestly, £2 million to knock it down and build a car park? Madness. They should restore it and make it more accessible. It was my first job, you know.      Oh, right, working behind the counter! I used to send books there for transcription as a student. That place was gold.      Yeah, it's full of history. I saw the plans online—it even keeps the original façade! All the marble and stone still intact. It's like they think people are blind.      Well, they might be dumb, but they're in charge. Have you been to the community meeting yet? I heard about 80 people turned up, all angry. I've been thinking of making some petitions.      You're not thinking of printing those out by hand, are you? Let me help you design it online, maybe we can get it shared across social media.      That would be brilliant, love. I’ve also got to choose some new fabric for the chair covers. You want to help? I'm torn between the velvet with chevrons and the plain cotton.      Go with the velvet! It adds a touch of elegance. We might as well keep the old charm here at home.      That's the second time today someone's mentioned keeping things charming—first about the library and now the fabric. I wonder if it's a new trend or just a feeling about preserving old things.      Maybe it's both. There’s a movement lately about maintaining old facades and renovating instead of knocking down. People are getting fed up with chain stores and soulless development.      Well, I say we'll do what we can. I'll set up a Facebook group, you can run with the petitions and the online stuff.      Sounds like a plan. And I'll definitely pick out the velvet fabric for you. Even if the library goes, we can still make the house a little gothic gem on the inside!      Perfect—no line in the sand is too small. Thanks, darling. You're the one to back me up at 10 p.m. when all I can think is tea and sofas.      And you're the one who still pronounces “library” like you’re reading Shakespeare!

Rather annoying this new Spotify algorithm, isn't it? Seems to think I like pop songs by some band I've never heard of, when all I really want is good old-fashioned jazz.      I know what you mean! It likes to play things you've never heard of, doesn't it? My playlist went  completely  bonkers the other day. I just wanted some good hairdresser playlist that I can play while styling, but now I've got weird indie electro stuff.      Oh, I was saying the same yesterday! It adds all these obscure songs under the guise of "discover more of what you like." I had a playlist of the 90s channels on the telly—MTV, TBS, you know the ones—and now it's filled with music I've never heard, and no idea who the artists are.      Honestly, it's a blessing and a curse. I mean, I did find a new band the other week from it—some blues outfit from Mississippi. But the problem is, I like real blues—vintage, slide guitar—personally, I don’t care much for the modern stuff.      That sounds amazing, though. I listen to playlists because I’m in such a rush during the day at the salon. I often just let the radio play because I don’t have time to pick out songs.      You know what I got for my birthday? A record player. Our daughter said I needed one to get back into vinyl. Surprisingly, it's been a bit of a hobby now—collecting records, sorting them out. There’s something so satisfying about it.      Oh, I'd love to try that! I still haven’t quite gotten into record collecting yet, but maybe I should. I know some people who have big vinyl collections, and it’s just a whole culture. Maybe you could recommend some vinyl artists to me.      Oh, I’d be happy to. I’ve got some Miles Davis and B.B. King. There's a real charm to being able to see the album artwork and hold a piece of history in your hands.      I got a nice travel journal for the holidays the other go-round. I usually travel about a bit, and so I thought it might help me jot down notes between jobs.      That sounds nice. I like scrapbooking sometimes, but I’ve never tried a travel journal. Maybe I should start doing that as well to keep track of where I’ve worked this year.

Rather annoying this new car tax eh, lad? I remember back in the day it was just a dicky-bird and a couple pound legal notice on the windscreen. Not like now, where ye gotta argue yer life with some £2k insurance bill and a brand new fancy motor.      Yeah, it  is  a bit sore, mate. My insurance just went up again. I mean, I only had a minor scrape earlier this year and I’m paying like a grand more now. It ain't fair!      That’s called a blackadder, lad. You gotta fetch the three-year no claim discount. People don’t seem to think the maths through before they jump on the road. My son had a bit of a skid last year on the A64 and had to cough up a shed load for the excess.      What about collisions? ‘Cause I’ve heard you can opt outta that. Less costy in the long run, even if it means paying a bit more if I have a shout.      Ah, clever lad, yes! Collision damage waiver—some people call it nil deductible. It’s like buying grief cover for yer car. If yer in a scrap, the insurance picks it up, but yes, it costs ye – about £500 a year extra, I reckon. Good if you’re a tight driver.      Should I get it then? I’m not the biggest banger in the world at the wheel. I’m not bad, but a rush here and there can do yer out.      What’s the marque ‘n model o’ the car then? Some make it more about the make than the driver. A banger such as a Fiesta is friendly on th’ wallet, but if you are driving a plug-in SuV it is a  right  step. My sister ‘ad to fork out twice as much after swapping to a Ford Kuga.      Nipper, it’s a Clio – fairly standard. I don't crack 100k on the motorway if I can help it.      Now that’s a smart way to think, laddie. Try and keep yer speed down goin’ on motorways if you can. Any extra over 100 is just ticking that “speeding nut box” on yer insurance. ‘Sides, the less you drive, the less likely ya are to shout yer napper off, right?      Yup. I ‘ope this lot’s not too bad this year. I’ll keep my fingers crossed I don’t get hit.

Rather than share a recording of this conversation, I'll provide a detailed written account for accuracy and comprehension. We sat in the dining room at home after a spicy chicken curry takeaway, with the hum of the windpipe outside doing its usual Cork moonlight routine.      That was a hell of a good Chinese, right? I mean, the chicken was spicy enough to make me think about converting to Buddhist for a week. A lot of people would think that this is a top-notch curry but personally, I'd dump it if it wasn't for the portion size and the chips served with it.      Get used to it, Seamus. In Cork, we've got the spiciest takeaway in the entire south of the island, if not the country. And if you're not careful with how you play the emotional card with these takeaways, you're going to end up needing a podcast about how to properly interpret facial expressions, no doubt.      Haha, yeah. When I hear the word "Cork", I think of the cork in the wine bottle, or that famous Waterford thing, you know? But I guess this takes the biscuit — quite literally as it is. I only started using words like "take the biscuit" during my work placement in London. Was that sarcastic or just?      Listen, sometimes it's easier to throw a bad joke out there than to deal with an awkward silence. If we all could just read facial expressions effortlessly, maybe the business world would make more sense to people. And regarding my accent? It's West Cork, through and through — something the kid here would have trouble pronouncing accurately through his premium frequency Google research.      I did listen to a podcast once about verbal expressions from different regions of the UK and Ireland. Honestly, you both make it sound like learning to ride a bicycle while juggling windpipes in Cork. My day job for the past few years has been expressing care — not for technology, but for a human. It's something else entirely.      That's the beauty of having a partner who's as expressive as they are academically grounded. Between lunches and bedtime stories, you learn the human equivalent of stress testing, you know? You find out how to calm the system down even in the most stressful of life environments.      I find it hard to separate out age eligibility for welfare in Ireland from the rest of what your lives look like.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh? You’d think for once we could have a decent day without it pissing down the whole time.      I know, I've been trying to take photos for this art project all afternoon and the cloud cover looks like a grey blanket. It’s proper dreich, if you ask me.      Ay, I wanted to cycle up to the old hilltop village by the lake, but this rain has me stuck in. The path gets all muddy and it’s a nightmare to cycle up.      Well, it's not too bad for someone your age. I used to walk mile and a half to school in all kinds of weather and made do with a plastic bag for my books.      That sounds brutal – I couldn’t even imagine doing that today. I’d be crying buckets faster than it’s raining.      Bucks or not, you’d still be getting in shape at the same time. I remember walking to college in the London rain so often that I actually became quite fond of it – it kept you alert.      I never did quite warm to it, but I did find something beautiful today – a pair of kingfishers by the river in the drizzle. Absolute miracle of colour.      Oh, that does sound magical. I’ve never seen one in the wild.      Bless you, you city kids. Kingfishers in the wild? Try looking for a suspiciously clean car in a rush hour car park. It’s all about observation, is it not?      Can we talk about something exciting, like Bear Grylls? I watched an episode where he survived the Andes by eating cacti and stuff.      Not that I’d recommend it, but survival skills are useful. My sister’s always reading up on law conversion courses in case she wants to branch out at some point.      Speaking of, I’ve been looking into one too – could see being a good move after I finish this degree.      Law and survival skills? Interesting combo if you're aiming for a career delivering babies around hostile environments.      Ha! I think I stopped sufficin’ for that in the midwifery course, between you and me.      Well, you two are both professionals in completely different fields, and roles we’d never consider ourselves in.      Just goes to show, over thirty and still adapting to the modern world. Weather’s bleak, legislation’s changing, and they’ve decided to ditch pints of milk for 200 grams of artificial butter.

So do you guys actually  like  the taste of that lab-made meat they've been testing? I mean... I don’t know, it just sounds like more science than food to me.      Honestly, I haven’t tried it, but I think it's brilliant. It could make vegetarianism a lot easier for people who miss the taste of meat. I reckon it's not as "creepy" as people think it is. Plus, it helps reduce animal cruelty and environmental damage. Imagine not having to send cows to slaughterhouses or rely on massive farming farms.      I agree with you, Alice. I mean, who  chooses  to eat something that’s been farmed in stressed and crowded conditions? It’s not just about ethics—you know what’s going on back there, right? I’ve seen some documentaries that are just brutal. They show pigs with broken legs, cows injured and neglected. It doesn’t sit right with me.      Yeah, and the environment angle is huge. I mean, even if you're not a vegetarian, reducing meat consumption helps—especially red meat. I’ve had some friends say they switched after reading up on land use, deforestation, and methane emissions. Honestly, it’s wild when you think how much goes into a single steak.      Exactly. Plus, I’ve been taking way more vitamin tablets since I went vegetarian. I’m trying not to miss anything the animal’s giving up. There’s a lot more to it than just salads and avocados. But also, I think it's a form of agency—small or not—resisting the mainstream.      For sure. That’s where  hunting  comes in as a weird alternative. I know a guy who hunts to eat, and he says it’s more "natural" and ethical than abattoirs. I find that argument weird. At least in slaughterhouses, there  should  be processing standards. But if you’re going to shoot something, you better know it's quick and painless.      I mean, I sort of see the ethics in that. But honestly, I’d rather not think about what I’m eating. At least with veggies, I don’t have to remember a face. Speaking of which—did you see that go in  Curb Your Enthusiasm  where Larry tried to eat bratwurst without knowing it was pork? That bloke lost his mind.      Oh God, that was so funny. I think it was also about cultural sensitivity and not respecting certain foods.

Rather annoying the queue was taking so long for coffee, wasn't it?      Oh, I was starting to think they'd forgotten how to make a cappuccino! Did you manage to hear the panel discussion before that?      Just about—Deirdre was on, and she mentioned something interesting about linguistic drift in rural communities. Made me think about home in Buckinghamshire.      That's a topic I'd be interested in seeing more data on. We did a small case study in Yorkshire a couple of years back when I was still at Lincoln University.      Lakelands? I studied there too for a term before moving up to Cambridge. Funny what you pick up when you're immersed in a new dialect. I can hear the difference between Lincolnshire and, say, Essex in a heartbeat now.      Catscratching, breakfast, and Buckshee... I mean, "cheep in," don't you?      Exactly! I say it a lot without thinking, and it always makes my parents chuckle—my nan can still say the occasional "good mornin’, innit?" like only real Bucks old-schoolers do.      I remember when I got home after my research trip to Cornwall last summer. I was still saying "innit" instead of the Cornish-like "ch,” as if it were a second language.      That’s the curse of someone who works in language—your own sounds like it's evolving weekly. I had a Japanese exchange student over the summer, and now I say "aru aru" all the time when I'm surprised. Driving my family mad.      Interesting! She must have been from Japan. I’ve always found the idea of pickups and phonology in cross-cultural exchanges fascinating. Maybe we could do something on that for the Gazette.      Absolutely. The Gazette always needs a bit more levity. I think it would be relatable, too. You know, people who study or work in languages end up being infected by them in their speech patterns. I once went on holiday with a Spanish intern, and now I say "alles klar?" by reflex!      That's brilliant! I've picked up French so effortlessly in the past six months, I only realised because I randomly said "ça va bien" one day without knowing. It just slips in!      We should start a blog or even a small column to track how we pick up and drop accents and phrases—maybe call it "Wittingly or Unwittingly."      I like that idea. Imagine tracing it over a year.

Rather annoying me a bit, eh? You know what me lectures are like this week, innit? All over the bleedin' place.      Yeah, I've heard ye going on 'bout it. Not to worry, love, I bet you’ll get through it. You’ve always een good at sortin' yerself out. Just make sure you're not workin' too hard. I don’t want me gal knackered all the time.      Aww, thanks! You always ken cheer me up. Didn’t even get round to studying for the uni test like I planned. Still, I’ll be knackered tomorrow and I’ve only got a few more days of it before it breaks up for Easter. Fun stuff.      Why don’t you chuck it all and I’ll give you a massage? It’d do you the world of good. I've been perfectin’ me skills. Not a professional in any way, but you’ll not tell anyone, will you?      That would be  so  good, yeah, luv. I’ve been knotted up since yesterday’s lecture. We were in that little library on Queen's Campus all day and I reckon I've got rhythm in me from just sitlin’ there – no good rhythm, just stiff, like, y'know? Could do with a proper rub-down.      If I donn't sort you out by the end of the evening, someone at uni ken get a go at me. Just a bit of peace and quiet, innit? Just the two of us in the flat and no exams. Can I make you a brew as well?      That’d be lovely, thanks! Just a green one for me. I’ve been trying to cut back on the caffeine. I’m up at ungodly hours to do bin, ‘cos lectures start so bleedin' early. I swear, if I have to leave the house before nine any bloody day I might have to start takin' overtime at the uni café.      Right, then we’ll make the best of it and have a mini break today, innit? You just veg out after the massage and I’ll sort dinner. Meat go or bin on toast? I’ve got both.      Meat go, yeah. Never could go with toast after a proper bit of pamperin’. Alright then, I’ll settle down and you take it easy with those thumbs, yeah?      Oh I will, over-qualified massage therapy at them doors. Just tell me if I’m knosherin' yer.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? That sun gracing the windows like it's easing through a typewriter ribbon. I've been meaning to get out more, but these rainy days sure tie you down.      Yes, finally feeling like spring is making an effort. We could make the most of it and plan a weekend trip to somewhere green and open. I’ve heard wonderful things about the Dartmoor National Park from a colleague.      Oh, now that does sound nice, pulling someone like you and me out of the house for once. We could take the kids with us too. Get the three of us out unitedly—our little family venture.      You know, that might just be the stimulation I need after this long winter. It'd be a change to hear the birds, rather than the microwave beeping every ten minutes. Living with two younger generations, you forget how loud breakfasts can get if you've happened to still be asleep in your recliner, you know?      Grandpa, you have the heart of springtime blooming in you, just don’t try to climb too many hills I don’t think your legs would like it. But serious note, let's book a small weekend—it would do us all good.      And while we're preparing for that sunny escape, I've been reading about this huge challenge the people in Calais are experiencing due to the migrant crisis. It's sad and worrying at the same time. I've just enrolled in a local initiative that supports volunteers trying to offer a helping hand.      Aye, that's a fair stretch from the sunny hilltops but all the more reason to appreciate what we have about us. I remember back in my days, such issues were foreign news—now they're on our doorstep.      Precisely, it does bring a lot to the surface, personally for me, being in education. I want to make sure that the next generation doesn't just hear about it but understands it.      So when are we making this crack to the hills and valleys beyond our mundane lives? Perhaps we take lunches to keep the energy high—my old management prowess is no match for a good sandwich around midday.      Let's plan on the following weekend. I can get the kids prepped, you can gather your hiking boots and we can box up some food from what your mother prepared—for the hills and maybe even for a few others less fortunate in Calais.

The plumber was hopeless, left things half done... like he was more interested in watching the football.
