Rather than share a beer, we’d rather request a curry. A few people in our home Cork would like to try the rather popular dish.      I asked my textbook,  The Horrible History of Science , about eating metal, and it said it's  very  unpleasant — humans should avoid it if at all possible. But with the curry, I reckon it might not be so bad?      Eating curry and drinking too much isn’t so unpleasant if you’ve had some time to let it settle. But, dear, don’t try eating metal, or the pain you feel will leave you wondering why you even tried.      What I found fascinating is how some people like to have a curry, then later go for a drink. It’s like having super powers – the ability to enjoy life in very different ways.      Super powers are cool — if only I could hover or turn invisible to avoid doing my biology homework in Bristol.      hides behind Speaker_3’s skirt giggling      Oh, don’t tell me—person is trying to start up about park events or birthday arrangements as their bedtime story again.      It’s not unheard of, love. I was just told about a park event – it’s been planned fairly well, and they’re setting up a night deposit box system for people who want to enjoy a drink at night. It looks like we’ll need to make plans accordingly.      What’s a night deposit box?      It’s what you chuck the empties into after you’ve had a drink at night – no more waiting in line at the bin in Cork.      That's clever, but wouldn’t you just trip over them in the dark?      Likely, but the plan is to make the system quite ‘user-friendly.’ If you look at the science of human behavior, people will do strange things to avoid a few steps. Speaking of plans, have we arranged for your birthday yet, Speaker_4?      No chance of trying to 'arrange' anything with your son today — the toddler’s far too preoccupied with trying to bite a piece of his metal spoon.      tries to nibble on his spoon makes a dent in the metal, then produces a loud, startled gasp from the emerging pain      Told ya. Pain teaches better than any book. Now, please hand me that piece of plastic we use to cover ‘dreadful’ food and make it safe for a toddler’s dinner.

Rather a lot’s happened since last we met, I must say. I was just reading about ‘ow they celebrate Halloween in America, with them great big jack-o’-lanterns.      Aye, we do a bit o' trick or treatin' ‘ere, but it’s not quite as mad as over there. ‘Member when little Emma dressed up as a witch and tried to clean the floor wi' her broomstick?      Miss Thompson says Halloween’s supposed to be a bit of fun, but school doesn’t do it properly. We had a poster competition instead.      That sounds like a sensible way to celebrate, don’t you think? Being a teacher, I’ve seen what goes on in other schools—costumes everywhere, half the class missing, mothers trying to keep up. A poster? Now that’s assembling a bit of creativity ‘n order.      Well, speaking of fun—my nephew was telling me about horse-riding, you know, near Norwich? ‘Eard they’ve built a new riding center with lessons for all ages.      Bah, riding a horse? I were never one for that. I did go on a country walk once, and it rained from the way down. ‘Owever, Emma’s cousins, they do it all the time up in the Cotswolds.      I’ve never been ‘orse-riding. Do you just sit there and someone tells you what to do?      Pretty much, yes. You’re shown ‘ow to hold the reins and balance. But ‘course, if you make a horse feel comfortable, it nearly does all the work. My dad used to ride when he were a lad—always said a horse can sense if you are nervous.      That reminds me—I used to be a ‘orsewoman back in the day. Brought up a few foals at me sister’s. Used to give ‘em their milk with a bottle when they were little ones.      Oh ho, well ‘eard that ‘orsepeople are a tight-knit group. Not many ‘orses in Costessey, mind you. Pigs and chickens mostly.      My best friend’s house is like a farm—there’s a donkey, some chickens, a ‘orse that’s getting old. Me and ‘er run around with big mats to jump off and roles costumes out the back of the garden.      Sounds like a ‘ollywood adventure, the pair o’you. I tell you, my students often think they’re acting in a film when I take them to the countryside for lessons.

Rather annoying this, isn't it? You think they'd have decent roads by now in such a busy area... What's the hold-up?      I can tell you exactly what the hold-up is, luv. When I was your age, things were simpler—more space, more respect for the road and everyone on it. Now it's all about convenience and people driving about as if they own the place. A shame, really.      Trouble is, it's not just tourists pulling up wherever. We've had these ridiculous parking restrictions pop up outside council flats too. I saw one of my elderly clients last week trying to park because she had a heavy walker and couldn't walk far. Couldn't find a space because a van had parked in a disabled bay. It’s ridiculous.      I agree, but surely the local authorities could clamp down on that sort of thing harder? They’re supposed to enforce parking laws more rigorously in places like this.      And where is the will, you ask? With the budget cuts and everything, I expect that by the time the dust settles, we’ll be lucky if the occasional traffic warden even leaves their office. It’s only real change when someone’s gear gets clamped, and that usually only happens when someone gives way. Not much for the elderly or disabled, I’m afraid.      I’ve raised this with my local councillor before. Seems like council housing is under such pressure now with younger people moving in. Our elderly patients don’t always get the priority they need. I worry they just don’t have a voice out there anymore.      That’s a real problem. I mean, when people are forced into smaller places, like those old walk-up flats, it's not always suitable for mobility. There should be more accessible options. I know that at university I noticed how housing issues were starting to impact mental health and safety for older students—especially if they’re moving into unfamiliar areas with inadequate support.      You mentioned university, love. At my age, I miss having decent housing. We had to clear out and move into a smaller bungalow because trying to manage the stairs in our old place was getting too much. My knees tell me I’m getting too old for that life.      I think it's more than housing, though. There's also the transport—ike trying to get to the fair today.

Rather annoying the new council rules, isn't it? Seems like everything's getting more complicated with an allotment... What do you think?      Oh I know, it's a pain! I was just at the town hall explaining my plans and had to queue for well over an hour. But it's all worth it, isn't it? I can't wait to get my hands in the soil next spring.      Absolutely, that's the main point, really. I'm going to start building a raised bed system. My back's not what it used to be, and it's just easier... Not to mention it helps with drainage.      Oh, I’d recommend that too! I'm thinking of doing something similar, especially since my allotment is on a bit of a slope. You're planning on growing vegetables, of course?      For sure, and maybe a bit of fruit—raspberries or something. I'm not in it for the big planting projects, just want something I can do spare time and have the odd harvest.      That sounds very low-key, and very smart. I’m definitely going all out as it is my first serious venture, so I might go for something a little fancier. I’m planning a vegetable patch alongside a herb garden and maybe a small compost heap, and I’ve heard a chicken coop is the next big move in urban farming.      A chicken coop might be a bit much, but I suppose if someone has the space, it could work. I’d consider it just for the egg production. What made you decide to start with an allotment?      Honestly, it's a way of switching off about work. My job is all about project management and the office, this gives me a real sense of control and peace. I love the idea of self-sufficiency, even in small doses.      That’s nice. I can see why you'd want that. I’ve found gardening helps me too, it gives a bit of balance. I haven't started yet though. I'm waiting for the funds to get a trowel and some seed packets.      Well, let me know if you'd like a hand or some advice once you get set up. I've got a few seed swaps going on and I'd be happy to share.      Thanks, I appreciate it. I can also lend you some books I've collected for beginner allotment holders, they're quite helpful with layout and crop rotation.

Rather annoying I know, innit? You’d think me parents would get that I’m not a primary school kid no more an’ need me own space like a proper adult!      Aw, I hear you. Chuffed they’re bemused as you’re spending more time with us though. Hasn’t there a uni event comin’ up soon where we can all hang out?      Yeah, but I’m more keen on a seaside jaunt. Me nan says it’s like therapy. Know what I mean? Just slap on me wellies, get the wind in me face... like, sort of clears the mind, y’know?      Cheers for the invites always. I still can’t get over how chill Doncaster is. Cambridge can get so posh and formal. But this place? Vibes good!      Na, you better not get too biased—though I do miss them cricket matches in the park. Blokes leg it as if they’re running to the shops. Still, the chatty market stalls and fish shop queues do tell you a story, though.      Right! Here’s to keeping it real and not letting uni turn us into total bookworms. We should mix up our humble plans. How ‘bout that pop-up burger place near town? I’ve heard it’s the dogs.      Always up for a new place to scoff. Just don’t expect me to carry the conversation if someone starts talking cricket rules again.      Haha, fair do. Some folks still don’t know a red from a leg here. Right, so burger place it is, then?      Yeah, but you’re the one who’s paying this time. I said sorry for stealing the last cabby biscuit!      Maybe I’ll pay... if you stop reading the whole menu out. I passed my A-Levels, not me life on biscuits!      Okay, truce. So when’s the tour? This Saturday good for you?      Works for me. I’ll bring the digestive biscuits this time, you bring the road stories, yeah?      Yeah, go on then. But if I start talkin’ about my nan’s brambles, no interruptin’!      Deal. Now, you better be planting that big Yorkie emoji in your messages after I’m gone so I don’t forget this was a proper plan made in the North!      Sorted. I’ll go one step further and add a luvly photo of me next to them old mill ruins, casting a proper northern shadow!      Love it.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? That sun is just beginning to shine through the shutters. Mind you, I've always preferred Cambridge in the summer more than London, with all that traffic and noise.      Yeah, honestly, I kind of forget how peaceful things can be here. Got a bit used to the hustle of Lewisham, you know? Anyway, I wanted to talk to you about that A24 film I saw last night— The Biker Ladies . It was quite interesting, actually. You’d like it, I think. Didn’t it remind you of Mavis and her friends back in Tilbury?      Now, now! Mavis only got her bike in like '71, if I remember rightly. She left it in the back lane, and half the vans in Tilbury used to park in it. But go on, dear, what’s this one about?      It’s about some women in their 60s, you know, forming a biker gang to take back the town. One of them has a past in the police, and another had some run-ins with the law in her youth. Kind of reminded me of grief support meetings, in a way—everybody watching out for one another, getting through the struggle.      Oh, now that does sound like Mavis and Marjorie. One time, those two thought they'd start a phone line for old ladies who didn’t cook enough. Mavis said it was all about chicken casserole. Marjorie just thought it was poison.      That’d be a great documentary, honestly. Any chance you two might come up to Cambridge next week? We could do something like that—meet the women round the area who still take the bus to Harrow Road for their weekly capers. I know some who organize day trips to Stourport to do charity fairs for local cats. Enid even started a knitting club for people with bad joints.      Oh, I might have to knit something for my little Aran jumper again. It’s been in the drawer since 1977 with a broken button on it. Would do you justice, dear. You set it up, then? We’ll make the trip. Just go ahead and map it out if you like—I’m game.      That’d be brilliant. And maybe, while we’re at it, we could invite some people from the Tivoli Picture House in Cambridge to come down for one of our weekend screenings. Rather annoying the new DVD player we got isn't working, isn't it? I mean, it's like... barely a month old and already it's skint. I can't even watch the new boxset we got from the £2 shop. Rather annoying this VW business isn't it? I suppose anyone with a car these days is affected in some way... What with the emissions scandal and all that.      It does seem shocking, honestly. I read that the company sold over ten million vehicles with software that cheated the pollution tests. It's not just a PR disaster—it's bad for the planet and trust overall.      Aye, and when I was working in the oil industry, I remember watching how the emissions targets kept getting tighter. We had to adapt the whole planning process for new projects, but the formulae came out... like, complex enough even for  me . Still, nothing compared to what VW seems to have done.      You know, I've got relatives in Surrey and they talk about house prices as if they're the only game in town. But up here in Cumbria, even after moving out of the village and into Hunsonby, house prices are only just ticking over. And the council says we'll get better train links. Pff. Good ones, we’d like to see it.      Honestly, I don’t get the property market at all. I’ve lived in Birkenhead all my life—it’s manageable, workable—but then people just insist on moving south for no good reason other than “it’s better.” There’s tonnes of good local culture up here.      You're not wrong. The universities in the North, the transport hubs, all that—it just isn't celebrated enough. And unfortunately, the property market is so skewed. Some friends had to move out of Liverpool and into Cheshire just to upgrade their lives  at all . Meanwhile, most people about our age up here are lucky to move from landlords to home ownership at all.      Tell me about it. I've only recently moved out of the council flat. My sister in Oxford thought I was mad not to go down there, but sod it—I prefer to be here with you lot than confined to some tiny flat in a city where waiting for a bus is an event.      And moving always comes with costs, right? Not just the financial—like the stress, the upheaval, the furniture. Plus, if the VW scandal is any indication of how big companies handle problems... I wonder how long it'll take to sort out all that green hydrogen stuff they’re pushing now.

So, I just read this article about evolution in biology class. My teacher was explaining it, but it felt... off, you know? Like, is it even true? I mean, sure, we humans are probably descended from some ape-like creature or something, but what about the religions that say it was God who made us?      Yeah, I get what you're saying. My brother's a pastor and he actually thinks evolution is a lie from Satan or something. But I don’t get it; like, do we blame Darwin for coming up with the theory? Or do we just say he came up with the most logical explanation even if it made some people mad?      Honestly, I think that what’s more messed up is how some people think it’s okay to say women aren’t as smart as men, or that certain races are the 'best.' It doesn't make sense. How can we claim to be scientifically advanced and still believe in those ideas?      That is wild, especially with the internet now. Like, the way videos go viral that promote racism or sexism is super messed up. I saw this one last week where some guy said women can't be engineers. It got millions of views, but like—what does that even mean? He just got famous for being ignorant.      Yeah, I know the feeling. It’s like, you see this stuff and you want to fight for people who can't fight for themselves. Like, what if you're someone who feels like your race or gender is being judged? It just feels so unfair.      I think science and religion don’t necessarily have to clash all the time. Maybe there's a way to make them fit. I mean, religion can touch on different areas of life—morals, stories—that maybe science doesn't cover. But I get it, a lot of people take the evolutionary idea personally.      For sure. But personally, I just want to believe it's all about being nice to others, no matter where you're from or what your beliefs are. Like, what if we stopped dividing people and just focused on what we have in common? Would the world not be so much better for it?      I think that's the ideal world, man. But sometimes our own biases or what we grew up with makes it hard to imagine.

Rather annoying to be honest, I've just come back from the hospital. They think it's a minor infection, but I've been put on a course of tablets. I can't believe how much time I've lost doing follow-up appointments.      That's nothing like the time I spent waiting on the hospital bed, I swear it felt like decades. I reckon acupuncture might've helped me with my aches before I had my operation last year. Of course, it was easier since I was retired, not worrying about sales targets and all that.      Oh don't say things like that dear, you're still working! Not like me, I've been at home for donkey's years and now I'm just a spectator watching my grandson play rugby. I do try to keep active, but my old bones don't take very kindly to it.      Rugby, cars, sales, breakfasts—there's always something going on here! I used to live for the road and steering a lorry, now I just drive the car down to the MOT or buy new tyres when it kicks off. Mind you, it's the occasional trip up north for a week to ski, and I'd recommend it as a friend.      I remember when we used to holiday skiing too – such fun! But I'm not sure I could manage it these days. Sales and all the targets take their toll. Anyway, enough of work. How's everything at your end, Mum?      Tales and retirement! That's me, just sitting at home, occasionally tending the garden, and talking sense into the grandkids. Still, it's all good when you are surrounded by friends and family.      That's right, we're lucky to have each other. Maybe next weekend you should all come to my house and we can have a proper catch-up. My sister is planning to come over, and her son passed his driving test – no more me stressing about MOTs and any car troubles!      A little celebration sounds just what the doctor ordered, and I know of a good place to get the lunches delivered. No need to leave the house if the snow arrives, you remember, I've had my fair share of weather waiting in the lorry on the road!      Excellent idea! Better not let work stand between us anymore; we might need to schedule the invites properly.

Okay, luv, bedtime stories are over now, right? I need you two to hop into bed. It’s getting rather late.      I don’t want to sleep, Mummy. I want to talk about that film you and Daddy watched yesterday. The one about the soldiers.      Oh, the one you didn’t want to watch? The war one?      Yeah, that one! Why do people fight so much? Is it because they are bad?      Well, that’s a big question for such little brains, isn’t it? Let’s talk about it, but keep it simple.      But why do they have to hurt each other? I watched it on the telly last week, and the soldiers had guns. Why don’t they just be friends?      Sometimes grown-ups make big mistakes, sweetheart. Long ago, people thought they had to fight each other over things like land, money, or even to control others. It was wrong, and it still is—nobody should tell anyone else what to do or force them.      But you were saying last week something about ... slavery?      Yes, lad, slavery. You know how much I hate it when people mistreat others like they’re just objects? Long ago, people actually treated others like that—like property. It was horrific. And some people fought wars to end those things. They wanted to give people freedom so they could live how they wanted.      So you mean people fought for other people to be free? Even if they didn’t know them?      Exactly! Some people are brave enough to do the right thing, even when it’s dangerous. There are heroes in every war, you see. But it still doesn’t mean fighting is the right way.      But if someone is hurting people, and they won’t stop, is it okay to fight them?      You’re getting quite deep in to it, aren’t you? If someone is doing truly awful things to others and won’t listen or stop, then some people think you  have  to stand up to them. That’s still not easy or nice, but if you don’t, bad things might happen to even more people.      I just wish people could all get along.      Me too.      Me too, love. Me too. Now, it’s time for sleep. We can talk more about this tomorrow. But always remember—keeping each other safe and acting kindly are important.      Mummy, can you read us a story?

Rather than unloading the dishwasher, shall we put away the washing-up sticks and just discuss something more interesting? I got the kids some books about heroes this week, and I think George Stephenson would make a good first pick.      Who is George Stephenson?      George Stephenson was an inventor, often called the 'Father of Railways.' He played a huge role in developing the steam locomotive in the 1800s. Pretty much changed the way people travel forever.      Like the Hogwarts Express?      Well, sort of! Though the Hogwarts Express is more of a magical version. Real engines, like the one George built called the "Rocket," helped people visit other towns and cities much faster than horse-drawn carriages ever could.      But why was he important? Did he make trains go faster?      Exactly! George Stephenson was one of the first to design engines in a way that made them efficient and reliable. Before his time, many trains weren't very safe or fast. He helped make them into something you could rely on for getting from one place to another — quite a big deal for the early 19th century.      Did he work on the first train track too?      That’s a good question. Yes, he was involved in building the famous Stockton and Darlington Railway in 1825. That was the first public railway to carry passengers and was powered by steam. It also ran mostly on iron tracks, which made them much smoother and faster than wooden ones.      So he was like a wizard in real life?      I suppose you could say he was the real-life wizard of the steam age! Though instead of a wand, he had a spanner and a keen mind.      I like the idea of inventing trains. Maybe I will invent something one day.      I believe it! And if you ever want to read more about inventors or engineers, I’ve got a whole series you can borrow. Let’s finish unloading the dishwasher first, though — it whistles when it’s done, like a train calling us.      Can the dishes come goosh? I mean, goosh like a train gooshing.      Hopefully not! But go on, let’s grab the plates and pans and see how clean George Stephenson would’ve left them.      I’ll take the forks!      Good lad! You can be the director of the dishwasher railway. I’ll be the one cleaning up the mess. Just like engineering — both of us always have our work cut out.

Rather annoying when the Wi-Fi drops while I’m in a Words With Friends game. Someone always takes advantage and racks up the points!      Blows! I saw someone do that last week and it was so petty. I could probably whip up a bruschetta with a twist in no time. I tell people, flatbread is just flat… it doesn't have any rhythm in it. Focaccia is prettier. Plus, I deal with confused customers daily myself at the bakery. One time, some guy thought that “croquembouche” was a type of fish.      Whoa, no wonder you need to graduate from college for this stuff. My student turned out to have a device so complicated she baked the toast by accident while trying to fix it.      Unbelievable. Do you know how intense that must have been waiting for someone to come out from such a mysterious recipe only to find out they've set the kitchen on fire? At least I’ve got the routine of work under control.      I sometimes get so into go-to recipes I barely notice if something's burning. Just yesterday, I followed a website’s baking instructions to a T—except I forgot to read the footnote about preheating.      Oh gosh, I'm so with you on that one. I once spent ten minutes beating a potion over low heat when the note said high heat.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? I needed a bit of fresh air after cranking through that first shift. You've got a bit of a smile on your face, Lucy — having a good morning?      Aw, yeah, I had one of those days where the coffee was just right and the printer didn't try to eat my files. It's been ages since that happened. You? I heard that Aylesbury weather tends to be a bit unpredictable.      It is, but once you get used to it, you start expecting the chase of an umbrella. Still, preferable to Tomsk, I imagine. Exactly the kind of chaos I’d much rather leave to people with more patience than me. Speaking of, have you ever thought about expanding your work? I understand IT is growing all the time in education.      I've been thinking about taking a couple of online courses in cloud infrastructure — it’s far easier these days with platforms like Coursera. That is, if I can get time away from the ant farm of work.      Well, that’s food for thought, then. You know what your biggest asset is? You have that fluency to jump in and adapt — I'm quite envious of people like that.

Rather than share a fabricated account of my weekend, I plan to talk about the practical pursuits I've been involved in. It was quite frustrating not to be rewarded for grinding through the stone for diamonds.      The workshop was specially useful for enabling young minds to make connections between classroom concepts and real-world applications, such as understanding metals and fabrics like you've experienced in Minecraft, James! The properties of materials are much like the blocks you play with.      I think the world is made of clover, cotton, and giggle-sacks, not metal or blocky dirt. Maybe a bit of spaghetti too!      No, you didn't see the iron I mined, Lily. That was serious stuff! Though, if I had some sturdy fabric, maybe I could craft a better chest      For instance, today we discussed fabric production - how different weaves and fibers impact durability and utility. It's much like silk versus burlap, and understanding these differences helps children appreciate the importance of material selection in various industries.      I understand fabrics - you make them from toilets and elephants in the clouds, don't you? At least, my friend's teacher said something oddly similar.      Mom, teach us how real fabrics and metals work! I want to be the best player in Minecraft and understand how Legos are made too!      Very well. Let's start by taking some vitamins to be healthy while learning. I have a vitamin bottle with all sorts of minerals, like iron and zinc. Just remember that understanding these resources in real life can sometimes make what your video games and toys depict more tangible. Learning to weave and identify roles of different materials can inspire all sorts of creative new legends to tell, Lily.

E’en if I don’t becom a pro, I still got a lotta satisfaction from it. Y’know? It’s a lotta what I do with me time. Mebbe set up a band one day, or play at local gigs or go to music festivals. But if that don’t work out, I could always just chuck in a job at a music shop, playin’ bits at the back and talkin’ abe’ guitars all day.      Aw, I could belly up to that! Just talk abe’ music all day while I bakes! It’d be the life! Unless I got to do somethin’ with child podcast, of course. Then I’d be out of luck.

: Alright lads and lass, so what’s the plan for the rest of the half-term? We can’t just chill here all day. I’m more than happy, but I've got EPQ work to do later. Not to mention I have to sort out a draft for my extended project on vegetarianism and its impact on poverty rates in the UK.     : Ugh, don’t remind me. I had to delete three drafts of my project on humanitarian efforts in Montenegro. It's pulling my hair out! But hey, I heard there's a new exhibition opening in London next week focusing on childhood stories from different cultures. We  have  to go, right?     : Yeah, that sounds interesting, Elise. I’m actually cooking vegetarian meals this week for dinner to practice for the family event next month. I think it'll be a good way to impress my uni lecturers if I get into food studies or something!     : Oh, are you applying to uni again, Liam? What’s your course of choice? I'm thinking of exploring personal fulfillment and how it ties into humanitarianism and teaching—there might be a course somewhere.     : Kind of. I might go for something in culinary arts or nutrition. Cooking feels like a way to bridge personality and purpose. Plus, I’ve been juggling these vegetarian recipes and learning to balance flavor and ethics. It's wild how something as simple as what you eat can affect so much—like food security in different countries.     : That actually ties into my EPQ oddly. I’m looking at how childhood upbringing and family nationality affect perceptions of being British. Like, does someone from Wembley see it differently compared to someone from Slough? I’m having such a hard time finding case studies.     : Honestly, that’s barely a week away. I remember when my stepdad claimed he ‘never thought of being British until he started cooking proper British tea’ and now he’s the most traditional bloke I know! Insane.     : I could see that. Culture and identity can shift as fast as your grandad’s lunches on a Sunday. But hey, have we considered going vegetarian for a day together? Then we can talk about the food and EPQ work in one go?     : Yes! We could even bring in some Montenegrin dishes, traditional or something from what your research shows, Liam. That would make it special.     : And after that, we can go check out that exhibition together.

Rather annoying this new rent cap they've introduced, innit? I mean, it's supposed to save first-years money, but half of them still end up paying more than they need to anyway.      Yeah, honestly, I've seen a few of our flatmates in other halls trying to get out and find cheaper digs. It's a nightmare. I reckon it depends where you're from, really. I only had to ask me mam and dad and they covered most of it.      Pfft, luck. I don't get that luxury. My parents still say I should be grateful I'm even here. Lakelands is no holiday, but at least it's got working heating and hot water.      Oh, you’re one of the lucky ones, mate. You're in Kestrel I think? Kestrel’s alright if you’re not bothered about proper privacy. I heard the dorm showers there are cold unless you turn in advance.      Nah, you didn’t have to tell me that. I bunked in there for one night when the lads in my flat had the bug. Bah, honestly, I’ve seen better conditions in hostels in Nepal.      Mate, I been in all the halls. The Rad – Mate, I got a water leak in me room for  months  and the uni didn’t do nothin'. Just patch it up with tape.      That’s tragic. Tape? I mean, I get it's not a palace, but that's just not safe. Some people still bathe in whatever's falling from the ceiling through their ceiling boards.      Sounds like about half the university is a health hazard. But talking of parents, mine are going off my head already. They keep sending me videos of me little sister dancing to a  NSYNC song. My sister’s nine.      Aww, cut that out. Kids be funny. My nan was giving my sister the talking to yesterday about how boys in uni halls aren't the same as boys in school. "Guard your reputation", yeah?      Ah, nan do that with me? Still trying to tell me not t' play the 'bad one go'. But I'm 17 and I got a tattoo!      Oh, what’d you get?      Snakes. Real proper snakes. Me mate got koi, but I'm basic like that.      Blimey, where?      On me neck. You can see it if I lift me hoodie.      Listen, let’s keep this quiet unless we want our parents to know, yeah?

Rather annoying the new barista at the café where I teach. Keeps getting my coffee order wrong. But anyway... What's been happening with you and the family lately?      Oh, we had a lovely time at Uncle Tom's last weekend. He's such a character. We played Scrabble and eeny-meeny-miny-mo for the snacks. Remind me of your childhood, don’t you think?      Sounds familiar. I adored your uncle. It was quite a chaotic Christmas. We had to cater for my sister's new partner and his sister with a vegan diet. I nearly went mad trying to make sure everything was suitable. Did you and your son still go up to the Lake District for turkey?      No, this year we flew over to see my sister in Derry, of all places. A bit of a cultural change, but far more relaxed than the usual breakfast, turkeys, and brussels. How did you fare with all the guests?      Actually, it worked out quite well. One of my students, a lovely German woman, came round for dinner and helped me out. I think we quite surprised my sister with the foreign food.      Oh good, always fun to have new influences. You know, I’m thinking of doing a bit of consulting in Bristol in December. Just a few short sessions. You know how it goes with freelance work—start planning a holiday then get invited to speak.      Bristol? That sounds interesting. Maybe I can pop over to a teacher training event they’re running there—job-related, of course. Or at least I will tell myself that.      Haha, I do the same. Travel for the work, but it always ends up being an excuse for a weekend away. Speaking of which, are you still thinking of taking that TEFL course in Spain next spring?      Yes, actually. I’ve been saving up and have my eye on one in Andalucía. Would love to meet some new people and immerse myself in the culture. Though I’ll definitely miss the good old British pubs with lunches and a little bit of peace.      You’ll remember us, won’t you? I told you the one about the ghost on the loo here. Well, he hasn’t made his appearance in a while, but I always go with a can of deodorant just in case. Classic Totnes!      Oh, I'm never going to forget that one.

: "Dad, it's been two whole years since I last saw you. How are you? You haven’t changed a bit!"     : "Well, I've put on a bit of weight, probably from all that takeaway the wife likes—get used to it. And how’s life on your end? Work been busy?"     : "Fairly easy actually. Being a language teacher is a good balance—long days, but I’m learning new things all the time. I just came back from teaching in Leeds."     : "You kids with brains always head off like wanderers! Still, it’s good. I used to drive past that place when working for the company in the 90s."     : "Honestly, I’m thinking about moving to Brighton next year. I love the area and the teaching scene is booming there. But it’s been a bit slow finding a flat."     : "Brighton’s changed a lot in the last few years. More people, more traffic. I heard they’ve even put up a few new speed cameras on the main road up near Reigate. Like they couldn’t read the human brain and know we’re already driving like chickens watching for hawks."     : "That’s the story of every road near my house these days. Anyway, I’ve been meaning to ask—Speaking of moving, what do you think of the change in the area? Crayford’s never been what someone would call futuristic, but I’ve heard it's a bit busier now."     : "Busier? You try and park near the high street on a Saturday. There’s more Tesco about than people. And I’ve had a few issues at work with racist customers trying to make excuses for bad service. It’s not like it was."     : "That’s rough. I’ve encountered similar stuff at the language school too. Parents sometimes get worried about their kids mixing with other cultures instead of just trying to improve their marks."     : "Well, as long as they can say 'thank you' with proper grammar, I’m happy! Speaking of, the last time you were here, you gave me a course on the 'Queen's go-to phrases'. Still using 'mayonnaise' as a metaphor when I’m in a bind."     : "Oh, what can I say? I aim to inspire. By the way, have you been out with Mom recently?"     : "Only for a fall-out over whether the lights on the deck were still string or now 'fairy' lights.

Rather annoying day today, wasn't it? That meeting dragged on far longer than it needed to.      I know what you mean. I had my own set of headaches after lunch — a student suddenly dropped out of the module I co-ordinate, and I had to reshuffle the groups again on the spot.      Ugh, that sounds like a typical Monday morning mess. Did you manage to settle it before your other classes started?      Just about. Honestly, it wasn't even the reshuffling that got me — it was the email I had to send to the head of department. I  promised  I'd keep the tone professional, but heavens, I had to re-read it four times to make sure it didn't sound like I was about to lose my temper.      Fair enough. Half the job is PR by the end of the day when you're a lecturer — managing expectations, calming nerves, and wrangling deadlines. And the worst part is, you still have to be cheerful in the staff room like none of it happened.      Absolutely. Though I have to say, your playlists did help me through it. I queued up that mix you shared on Spotify last night, and it was such a good way to unwind at the end of the day. I almost became one of those office workers who hums along to dance music during staff meetings.      Oh, don't even — I wouldn't want you starting a music revolution in the admin block. But seriously, I'm glad it helped. I've been getting into this new band, and I thought it might be a nice break after your ballet-themed lecture last week. I mean, I know it's not quite the Renaissance, but at least it wasn't a powerpoint of aerobics.      Touché. Maybe I’ll do something a bit more hip-hop next time — for your approval. On the bright side, I managed to pick up a few fresh groceries during the lunch break. I thought we could make a proper pasta tonight to celebrate surviving the week so far.      That sounds like an excellent idea. I do love a good pasta night after a chaotic day. Did you pick up the pesto I wanted? I think it was that one from the organic farm in Norfolk?      The one with the bloke on the label who looks like he could be your long-lost uncle?

Rather annoying this, isn't it? You think they'd have decent tension on a shower curtain track by now...      Oh, I'm not looking forward to that either. It's a mad hodge-podge of things we've cobbled together over the years. But it was in the post! A new  bathroom runner  for the   towel rail  ... as if that's a thing that existed before we got this one!      If you're done grumbling, let's just blame the   retailer  . Didn’t even look at the  installation instructions . I like to think it will make  visible improvement .      That's easy for you to say. You're not the one   thumbing through   a damp Ten Commandments of shower curtain safety, are you?      Well then, if it's a problem you better not get distracted by whatever that thing is in the corner... I  swear  I heard the  stiff, floor-length curtain  say  "I want to die!"  that time you waved it like you were casting a spell.      Right, as if you didn't   jerk it   open in hysterics watching me mess it up...      True enough – but it's got a   quirky design   now, hasn't it? Doesn't quite hang to the  floor  anymore. Somewhere toward the  ankles  now. Functional in a way I'm still adjusting to.      That's oddly satisfying. Now what about something that is going   well  ? I’ve got this  bean bag  to   knit  , and I about blocked out 50 different kits just to   pick one  , finally settling on a  sparkly blue    shade   that   seems age-appropriate  .      Should've gone with the  expected    cream   or something. But I'm sure the   sparkle   will give it the   edge   it needs for when our daughter criticizes the décor. At   47  , of course... always knows better.      Perched up the wall in   one corner   of the room it will sit, with the curtains gothic on one side and this   stuffed wonder   on the other.   It’s making sense  , don’t you think?      If you say so. I’m just going to begin   chopping broccoli   for supper, maybe   simmer a casserole   in the oven over this nonsense. At least the food   won’t judge   my poor shower curtain choices.      Right, and it always falls on me to   navigate the madness   when we try to   set the table   and half the   stuff   falls off the side of the   bean bag  . The   shower curtain   will probably roll in on itself with   the drama  .

Rather a gray day, isn't it? I was just making a pot of tea—the good stuff, not that instant muck they often have nowadays. Would you both like a cup, or would you prefer a little rest first? Not that I mind the company, mind you.      Thank you, dear. That sounds lovely. I think I'll have a cup. My cupboards are practically bare since I’ve stopped working, but I do have this lovely jam someone gave me last week. It's a bit fancy, mind you—raspberry and gooseberry. Nothing like the days when we could afford a little luxury without a second thought.      That's nothing, Edith. I've had my fill of luxury, bless you! The business left me a bit of a nest egg, I must admit. Still, I find the quiet life much more to my liking now. What with running a shop all those years, it’s this lack of commotion I’m starting to appreciate, you know?      You always had the goods, George. I remember walking past your store with the children—ah, what a place! I can still smell the wood as if it were yesterday. You always kept everything so neat. Me, I never had any rhythm for that sort of thing. I was just about holding things together with my own two hands and a bit of charm.      Bless you, Edith. You were the best with the young 'uns. I remember the old days, sitting in the park with the kids. You’d have them all entertained with nothing but an orange and a story. I often used to say to myself, “I wish I had your knack.”      Well, I think us all brought our strengths to the table, Charlie. Not much call for that sort of thing now, I know. Everything's so quick these days—no time for sitting, no time for proper conversation. It’s high time we did something that wasn’t on a schedule. Even if it was just tea and talking.      I couldn’t agree more, George. It's funny how things work out, isn't it? I never thought I’d have such peace now, but there you are. I find myself thinking back on the good bits more than the dull days.      That’s the spirit, my dear. Life’s a mixture of things—some bloomin’ marvellous, some not so much.

Rather annoying the wet weather isn't it? I was supposed to do the shopping for the week today but couldn't be arsed with the rain. I’m more than a bit low on tea bags and loo roll again.      That's a common problem these days. We've been lucky so far, but I reckon the weekend will bring some more good weather if you're up for going out on a Saturday. A lot of the provisions at the local shop are top-notch; you might even pick up a reasonable offer on tinned soup again.      Yikes, the thought of walking through a frozen shop makes me want to stay in bed. I've been working on a few Christmas campaigns for clients recently and it’s been pretty madness, especially dealing with last-minute changes. Still, I’m glad I’m home now, even if I did get the flu from all the stress and travel!      Health comes first then. I happened to volunteer a bit in the local community centre last week as part of my training to be a nurse practitioner. They were actually giving out hot drinks and meals for people who couldn’t make it out—perhaps I can sort some out for both of you. I'm off on Friday as well, in case you’d like to have a family day out?      Mate, you're a real star. Let's just confirm on the Friday. I reckon we could take the kids along as well for a spotting session and some fresh air.      That'd be nice. I also need to book my flight details for my brother's wedding at the end of the year. I've been sorting some travel related stuff recently but I need to speak to a travel agency for a few more binding details. I'm off to the travel shop tomorrow, I'll let you know what's going on.      I might have to speak up for my stepdad as well. He's looking to travel to India after the festive season. The health budget could be a concern though; any advice on managing the money front?      I could certainly help from the side of travel funds as well. I've been with people who need to budget while balancing the various costs of going out of country. I'll come with a budget plan on the Friday as go-to details on that.

Rather lovely morning, isn't it? You can see forever from here.      Oh, quite, rather peaceful out here. I’m more used to the noise of the city, but this is a nice change.      It is. I moved here two years ago and I'm still taken aback by the quietness and open scenery. Of course, as a teacher, I often bring students from the main town over for field trips. They love the history around here.      Really? I haven’t seen much of the southern regions of the island. I retired a few years back, so mostly just potter around and listen to the radio, drink tea. Never managed to get beyond turkey delight sandwiches and crossword puzzles.      Retired life has its perks, doesn’t it? I think it's important to take an interest in your surroundings. There's so much history here—maybe I can recommend some local museums or ancient sites if you’d be interested.      I would appreciate that. I'm fairly new to Northern Cyprus and it's quite a change from what I was used to in Bushey. What did you teach back in Dorchester, by the way?      I was a Geography teacher. I really enjoyed helping the kids understand the world around them, and now I teach local students here. Though, adapting the syllabus to reflect Cyprus has been a fun challenge.      That’s admirable. I must say, I never thought I'd find my way here. Moving countries is a big step—what made you uproot your life and come all the way out here?      A combination of things—seeking a quieter life, wanting to teach beyond my local area, and yes, partly for love! I met my partner here and decided to give it a whirl. It’s quite something, but for better or worse, it’s home now.      Sounds like it was a leap of faith. I used to work as an administrator when I was younger but lost my job as the economy took a turn. After that, with health not being the best, I just gradually took the next step into retirement.      I can imagine that must go hand in hand with life here. It does give you more time to explore and not just rush from one thing to the next, doesn't it?      That it does! If you ever manage to spare some time, I’d love to hear more about your trips into the hills or where you like walking.

Rather annoying this, isn't it? You can’t see the sky properly for all the smog. We’d got used to it after a while, hadn’t we? But lately, it seems worse than ever.      No, I know what you mean. I saw a post online today saying the PM2.5 level is off the scale again. Makes me think about all the kids who go to that primary school by the factory. Such a shame. They shouldn’t be breathing that in every day.      I heard from a friend working in the education department last week – they’re considering shifting some of the school timetables. Restricting the outdoor activities only when the levels dip a bit. It’s a bit of a mess though. The teachers are constantly persuading the parents who are worried. But some of them think it’s just a temporary issue – you know, eventually it’ll clear up, no doubt about that.      And yet the factory keeps running as usual, doesn’t it? I passed the site the other morning, and that new furnace was roaring like you wouldn’t believe. Doesn’t the local authority do anything about it?      They’ve put in some monitoring stations, I’ve noticed. And a task force got formed last month or so. But I don’t think people like us – just regular folks – are the ones actually making decisions about pollution control. Seems like it’s down to big companies and the government.      Well, one thing I’m glad of is that the work here at the university is wrapping up soon. We’ve got a grant finished up and a review next month – all online, obviously, given the current situation about travel restrictions. Honestly, the idea of going back to Norwich or London for a few weeks is already quite tempting.      Doesn’t sound unappealing at all. My sister’s planning a visit anyway, and her kids will be starting their school year at the end of it. Might as well give it a shot, no? I miss having decent English weather again.      Let’s not forget decent English takeaways either! Grilled chicken balti, anyone?      Don’t mind if I do. Let’s go back to my place and I’ll start prepping something. While I’m at it, I might look up those monitoring stations and see if we can get involved with environmental groups at the university.

Rather annoying the new oven’s taking so long to preheat. I’d have thought it would be up to temperature by now. Never mind, it’s a beautiful day, isn’t it?      Aye, quite nice. Looked like rain at first, but the weather’s cleared up nicely. I went out for a bit of an early walk just before breakfast. Felt like making most of the day.      Honestly, I’ve barely stepped out of the bed, not like you. We’ve been in the house all day watching TV. Did I tell you we finished that new drama series last night?      Oh no! I haven’t got round to watching that yet. What was it called again?      Ten Minutes Older. It’s brilliant, really gritty, and I think it’s going to get an Oscar for cinematography. You definitely need to see it.      Haha, Jo, don’t be setting too high a bar, or Ruth’s going to have to cancel her usual dramas and watch this one instead. Might get a shock though, not the usual fare!      Well, I’ll get it as soon as it drops on the platform. For now, though, got plans for dinner? – Mate, have you tasted this? – needs more salt, doesn’t it?      Ugh, yeah, I’d add more rosemary as well. It’s kind of just a base now. What are we making next?      I was thinking something hotter than the roasting tray, maybe some pasta with a meat sauce – crude but effective. You good with that, love?      Sounds far better than what I was fumbling with earlier. Maybe I should’ve gone with that idea!      Maybe both? – My idea is to put baked potatoes on top of the meat sauce, with a bit of cheddar on it. Let it go all bubbling. I tried it once on takeaway pizza – honestly, game-changer.      That’s a bit weird, mate, but whatevs. Some people like it, you know. I say if it works, it works.      If you say so, love – just trying not to burn the lot out, between us. Who took all the photos from the garden yesterday? The ones with the flowers in the corner? Thought we wanted to frame a few of them.      Oh yes! I printed a couple out earlier, and I was thinking we could put one on the fridge to remind us of our garden in the next few grey weeks.

Rather annoying this new bus route eh? D’ye think they’ve sorted it out yet ‘r it’s still all over the place? Me an’ me mates down at the uni were tryin’ to get to the Cambridge University Press bookshop last week and got lost wi’ the new numbers an’ stops. een’t like Sunderland, where we’ve got one route that just loops round the same five stops over an’ over. Aye, but I love that bookshop, it’s got proper used books as well, ain’t just glossy new tomes like the shops back home.      Honestly, I still haven’t figured out how to use it. I’ve got to keep double-checkin’ the app like a nincompoop. Still, at least the route is supposed to save time, right? You know, cut through the town without gettin’ stuck in the uni traffic jam. But forget the logistics, I heard there was a student protest last month about the whole thing. Bloke from the uni college was loudly shoutin’ about the transport budget and why they weren’t consultin’ the students. Might’ve had a point too—everyone I know in the faculty said it was done without any say.      Aye, that’s proper crap. I’d rather have known it was gonna be all wonky before I tried to get to that bookshop again. I mean, I’m not gonna lie, I did have a good time in there though. Smelled like old leather an’ dusty paper. Reminded me of the library at my old uni. Course, that was a proper working uni, not this posh place you lot get here. What with all the leafy avenues and Prime Ministers past and about.      Haha, come on, mine ain't th’ only one. You lot are still havin’ a laugh up at Newcastle, aren’t you? My sister went there and says it’s got better labs than here, even if the grounds are less scenic. Still, any place with decent transport—and I dunno, a little less bumbling on the bus—is worth it. Though I’ve seen you waitin’ for the 70 from outside the shop, and let’s be honest, I’m not too sure if that route’s any better goin’ on your own if you don’t get it first time.      Oh, don’t go startin’ on me. I’m still gettin’ the hang of it all.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? I suppose it's a shame we can't take a walk first, but the lunch appointment is in half an hour, and I'd murder for a decent cup of tea and scone before we get stuck into the main course—some people wouldn't dream of having pudding after cheese, mind you, but we're not one to conform entirely to fashion, are we?      Oh, entirely! I've been craving a good lunch for days. It's been a bit of a dry run with the transcription work and editing. Do you want to split the pudding? I saw the menu mentions a baked Alaska. I can't recall the last time I had one, and I've brought my son’s university address list with me—you know he’s coming to visit over the weekend? I’m already panicking a bit about what he'll find of interest in Cumbria.      Oh, that’s very exciting! My grandson is in his second year, too. He's quite taken with the history of the area—those old Roman forts and that—so I do tell him a bit, though he says he prefers it in person. What did he study, again? Philosophical mathematics, wasn’t it? Sounds like fun, if I remember rightly from the way he writes at home about it.      It really is a huge treat having lunch out like this after working all week. Silly question, but could we catch the 2 p.m. train back? I have an HR meeting tomorrow with a new client, and I need to start on the email brief before the evening. It's been a strange couple of weeks—had to make some tricky decisions in the past month about roles being cut. I don’t enjoy the talking part of it at all.      Going into that sort of thing must take a cruel heart, lass. I suppose, like teaching, you have to put your personal feelings aside for the good of the class—or the business, in your case. I relied very heavily on instinct too, when I was marking reports. There was a time I gave a 12-year-old a 'B' and he wrote back with such pathos, asking if I thought he was a failure, that I started to wonder if I was really meant for life in the classroom at all.

Rather lovely this time of day, isn't it? The light’s casting a golden sheen over the water... What do you think? Just the two of us and the river. I've always found this walk incredibly calming.      Oh, absolutely—there's something about the Thames that just soothes you. Even with the traffic in the distance, it's got this quiet charm. Though I must say, I'd love to see some changes around this area. More green spaces perhaps?      Agreed! It's just the kind of place that could do with a few more tree-lined paths... Not to mention a better system of transport so we don’t rely so much on cars. Honestly, I’m still amazed you don’t have one. How do you manage?      It's not as difficult as you’d think. A good pair of boots and a timetable are often all you need. I walk a fair bit anyway, and when I need to be somewhere a bit out of the way, there's always the train or a bus. It’s actually quite satisfying, taking public transport.      I can see the appeal. Honestly, I’ve thought about giving it a try more often. Have you ever considered going on holiday without a car? Maybe somewhere like the coast? I remember my sister once talking about planning a trip like that.      Oh, I’m quite taken with the idea. Maybe a place where the kids can chase the waves barefoot and the rest of us enjoy the skyline. Although I must admit, I’m quite conflicted when it comes to measurements in other countries. I got quite flustered being told I needed a medium cup when in America they make absurdly oversized portions. I walk away empty-handed every time.      Ah yes, I remember your horror story about that! Still, I think it's a reminder of how different the cultures are. And speaking of being different, have you ever thought about the bigger questions? Like, what it really means to be happy?      I suppose when I see people who are genuinely content—those that have found peace with themselves and their surroundings—I think a lot of it comes down to connection and purpose. Whether you’re walking the Thames with a dear friend or watching the sunrise go over a map of your dream destination.      You’re not wrong, love.

Rather annoying this wet weather isn't it? I mean, I love the occasional rain, but it's like it's never going to stop now. I’m so ready for summer proper, you know?      Oh, honestly love, the weather in England is a bit of a joke half the time. That's why I try to keep my eyes on the weather app on my mobile all the time — a bit obsessive, but necessary if I'm doing a shift at the care home. The kids were begging me to let them go to the park for the school sports day, but with the rain, I just couldn’t say yes.      Aww, that's tough, but you're right — the rain is relentless. Just yesterday, I tried to get the boys to do their swimming, but the outdoor pool shut down, and the indoor one is packed like sardines in a tin. Honestly, better for breakfast, no doubt about that!      Oh, at least the kids had  some  chance, even if it's not ideal. My niece is going to build a bear with her friends this weekend, though. She's been raving about it for weeks. I think it's wholesome, even if it's probably a bit over the top. She loves all her cuddly toys. Poor thing — it's like she's glued to them.      Oh, her age — those are the years when you're attached to every fluffy thing you own. Mine, they’re in the ‘big boy’ phase now. Rather than share a text, I’d rather describe what happens. A few people in our community came up with a plan to start a local association. They're very passionate about it and want to build something that brings everyone together.      That does sound very positive. People like that usually make a real difference, don't they?      Definitely. They’ve already held a couple of meetings. I’ve been helping by organizing some of the logistics and helping to draft the foundations. It's quite interesting, actually. We've had to consider everything from funding models to how we get the word out.      That must make you feel quite involved, as someone who’s taken on such a role in the organisation.      I do. It’s a different kind of work to running my business, but it's very satisfying in a different way. It feels like it’s a contribution to something bigger than just myself.      That’s really admirable. It sounds like you’re not only benefitting the community, but also giving yourself the opportunity to explore something that’s meaningful.      Exactly. And it doesn’t take up too much time. We still meet early in the week for planning, but it’s flexible enough that it works around both our schedules.      Good. I often wonder if people like you take on these projects as a balance to their regular work life.      I suppose it is that. It gives me a break from business decisions and strategic thinking. It also helps me meet new people and widen my network.      That’d be a great opportunity, then. Any chance I could help out with something like this?      Absolutely. In fact, you’d bring such a different perspective as an educator. You’ve always been very good at working with people and organizing things smoothly. You could run one of the outreach activities for us. Maybe even help with workshops if we expand.      That’s something to consider. I think it would be a good way for me to stay socially engaged while balancing my own professional and family responsibilities.      And honestly, I think it would be good for us too. Spending time on meaningful projects together can be a way to grow personally and as a partner too.      I completely agree. Let's look into it seriously. I’d like to support something that blends both our lives and our goals.

Rather good to have you all round for a bit of a do. I was just in the garden mending the gate again—decided it’s about time I stopped relying on you all to leap over it! Got it fixed finally with a bit of elbow grease and some nails picked up from the builders' skip. Hasn’t got a knob on it yet, but   it'll do for now  . You don’t mind that, love?      I don’t mind a single bit as long as you don’t fall over grinding it open. You always insist on doing everything yourself, Mervyn. I like to think of it as  keeping you sharp . Besides, the real work round here is making sure everyone eats what’s on their plate.   I've left the roast beef just as I made it  —none of these modern microwave meals in sight.      Honestly, Mervin, when you say ‘mending the gate,’ I’m picturing you in a ginger beanie cap and boots, sawing through it. Still, it’s lovely to be here—Costessey really is a pleasant place in the summer. I can see why your family settled here. Did you tell the story about the time the chicken pecked through the fence and strutted all the way down to Lady’s Bridge?      Let’s just say if that chicken had a Twitter account, it would have gone   viral  . I blame the scarecrow. What was it wearing, Mervyn? A hat from the 1930s and a tie so stiff it could fling the rooster away? You can’t be surprised the farm animals thought  they  were in a pantomime.      That's right, and then Jane [Speaker_2] tried to round it up with the plug lead. Doesn’t sound funny, luv? Jolly nonsense.   But I like your guest speaker note at the uni, Aimee.   You looked absolutely piercing in that black suit last week.      Thank you, Mervyn. It's just as well I didn’t wear the lunches-to-go apron from my younger days! We’ve been having a bit of a run with our course on the English countryside—  environmental ethics  , mostly—but your garden does make for a compelling case study on how to outwit nature.      And what about politics, Aimee? I heard you were on live radio last week debating whether those so-called ‘meat tax’ ideas might take off. What's your fellow lecturers say at the bar down the road—  all philosophy and no sense of butter  ?

Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, I get that they’re practical and all, but they’re like...  real  muddy at the moment. It's November, it's been raining every day this week. I swear I tracked mud into my room like  three times  this week already.      Yeah, I feel the same. I just tried to clean them on the mat outside, but you can only do so much before you’re just like, "Whatever, I’m gonna stomp through the flat and make everyone else’s floors look like a bog."      Honestly, I just wish I had some boots. I remember when I was little and I had those goofy wellies and I used to run around in the rain with them and not care one bit about getting soaked. Now I’m just a adult who cares way too much about matching shoes to an outfit, but still doesn’t want muddy breakfasts tracking through the flat.      Oh yeah, I remember the oversized rain boots, you didn’t have a choice in the colour, just red, blue or yellow and they were way too big and kept flopping about. Honestly, I think that was the best footwear of my entire childhood.      I tried to get a pair from the charity shop last week – but they were all either too small or way too big. I ended up choosing a pair of ankle boots that were like £40. I’m already regretting every decision made around 10am that day.      Yeah man, I just thought I’d do the sensible thing and invest in some smarter boots and then ended up with these premium patent black things which are absolutely adorable, but have about five millimetres of tread on the soles. It's like I’m meant to be gliding not walking.      Honestly, if we moved back to the 1990s I’d be wearing high-waisted jeans and those stupid duffel coats again just for the style.      I remember my nan making me wear one of those over every single thing. It was always like the first thing I took off the minute I got in the door. Even if it was only a ten-minute errand.      I think it was supposed to be for extra warmth or something, but in the heat of the 90s, it was just stifling.      I seriously think I was like one of two kids in the whole town with that coat.

Oh my goodness, it’s been ages! I can’t believe we haven’t managed to meet up in like... over a year!      I  know ! It’s ridiculous, isn’t it? I binged the latest series while you weren’t around. Spoiler?      Oooh don’t even tell me! I’m still on Series 3. Burgers and bad movies here today, then road trips and country views next time.      Deal! I’ve been on a healthy juice and salad streak for so long, I might just die of carbohydrates.      Time to live a little! Let’s add Indian food to the cotswold road trip manifest. We’ll start with that dessert menu here first, though.      You’re the best, I swear. I’m so glad we did this. Let’s not wait another year, yeah?      Cross my heart. Promise. 🙏      Me too!

Rather a cold morning we've had, isn't it, dear? I was just in the garden having a cup of tea and thought I saw a sparrow, but I can't say I'm certain.      Aw, Dad, I saw one flitting around near the gate earlier. Probably just startled and flew off. I’m just making some coffee if you fancied a cup? You don’t mind instant, do you?      Not at all, darlin’. Instant’s just as good in my book. I don’t see the fuss when people get all fussy about the expensive lot. It’s just coffee, after all. Though, I must say, I haven't had such a warm cup since the old kitchen back in Mordern.      I know you love your special brew and I’ll get the real stuff next time I’m at the shops. But honestly, it’s cheaper if I just stick with what I’ve got.      Oh, no, don’t trouble yourself. I’m not one to expect extravagance. I do like the way it is here, though — I mean, with your mother gone, and you and me having a cup like this, chatting… it feels right.      It really does, Dad. Sometimes I catch myself thinking, I wish I had sat and listened more when I was younger. All that wisdom you and Mum had was just waiting to be soaked in.      Wisdom — now there’s a word! All my years, and what did I end up with? A few good stories and a fair stretch of regrets. Still, at least I had your grandmother, and you two kids about.      And the gardens, you had quite the knack for it. You taught me how to grow tomatoes like they were gold.      Aye, and that lot of treacle ones nearly grew like weeds. Still, I reckon with a bit of care and time, you can grow anything — even hope, if you’re patient enough.      You always knew how to say things with a bit of meaning behind them. That’s what I wish I’d remembered more when I was trying to sort my life out.      Well, you've done fine so far, love. Better than I could ever imagine. And with a blooming career ahead, your mother would've been mighty proud. Make me proud, and you'll never go wrong.      I already do, Dad. Every day. Now, why don't we both raise that cup and have something to look forward to?

I added some of it to my gym playlist.

Rather annoying I had an email from Joshua’s teacher about Balanceability. I know it's supposed to be fun... but honestly, it's just a word I never thought I'd need to know      What's that?      It's one of those physical activities in primary schools—standing on wobbly things, making you balance on beams. My goodness, it's a whole curriculum now. I think those kinds of conversations are what gave her ideas for the Balanceability lesson. Also, I read online that Japan celebrates National Cat Day—close enough to appreciate that cat running into the waterfall, perhaps.

You picked ‘marmalade’ and then couldn't say the word without a ‘k’. I reckon it's not easy being British with a Welsh granddaughter constantly correcting your spelling!      No, but seriously, what if we introduce a new rule? Maybe the person who makes the most mistakes has to wash the dishes for the entire week. It'll add some  real  tension.      That sounds like a brilliant idea! My turkey curry will definitely benefit from some extra dishes. And you know I’m not good at this game. I once tried to describe a ‘parachute’ by saying 'you put it on when breakfast is ready and then float to the roof'. Hilarious, really.      Oh, I love it when he does that. It's like watching a Waterstone’s shop assistant trying to recommend a Nobel prize winner written in emojis. Right, Speaker_4, it's your go. Tell us what this one is.      Right, okay. Let's see… it's got a moon, and you take photos with it, but you can’t dance in it. It’s something you use on the beach, and you usually pack it in a bag. Hmmm. Oh no, it’s not a camera…      It  is  a camera, isn’t it? I thought it through. You said moon — which is a light, then photos, then bag... That’s all you can do without the word ‘k’ or ‘s’.      Not you! I mean it is a classic case of splitting the tension, isn’t it? Moments like that remind me of when we went on that holiday in Cornwall. I remember holding the ‘Articulate’ box in one hand and waiting for a wave while balancing my kid on the other. Let’s not talk about trying to describe ‘teapot’ with ‘c’!      Oh, come on, that’s the best one yet. ‘A little pond filled with hot tea’…      Oh, I remember that. And he was blooming proud when the one-year-old solved it!      Oh, leave it out! And you, dear, were the one to say ‘c’ for ‘teapot’ when we were at the café last week. I nearly cried I was laughing so hard.      Alright, alright, enough nostalgia for now. Let’s just play and try not to make it last until after dinner as it did last time.

Rather annoying this card game isn't it? I mean, Sarah’s the one who's always winning when we're in the cottage, she must be cheating somehow!      Oh come on, she is not. She's just better at remembering the card combinations. Remember last year when she beat Geoff and me in three rounds of bridge? It was ridiculous.      Yeah, she’s got that A-level brain working for her! Honestly, I’m beginning to wonder if she was switched at birth with a maths teacher or something.      Well, I'm just not as quick as you young ones. I mean, I used to play cards every weekend at the community centre in Cardiff, but My memory just isn’t what it used to be.      It's alright Daphne, and I think it's sweet that you're trying, really. But honestly, we’re all slightly terrified of playing this again. Maybe a game of Monopoly next time, or Scrabble?      Yeah, Scrabble would be more mercy-based. I do like the way we come together in this cottage, it’s like going back in time. We haven’t seen each other as much as we’d like, what with work and everything, but these holidays really bring us back together.      I know, it’s like we’re a proper family now. Even though none of us are related by blood, we’ve all been through so much together. I mean, remember when Sarah and I got stuck on the motorway last year and had to buy out the local Tesco?      Don’t remind me! I had to spend the next two days sorting out the milk and bread for you pair. Honestly, you lot are a menace.      Oh that was brilliant! I remember laughing so much, even though I was trying not to overdo the treacle scones. I did manage to make it into a sort of traditional Welsh event, didn’t I? I tried to sing a little Welsh folk song while the fire was going.      You nearly set the cabin on fire with your singing! But we love you anyway, you mad old thing.      Yeah, go on then, Daphne, start singing again – just don’t sing line in the bath this time.      Oh, your lot are mean. I have dignity, even if I live in a cabin and collect tea cosies.      And we love that about you, Daphne.

Rather lovely day today, wasn't it? I fancied a nice long walk in the park before lunch. The weather was so bright and crisp.      Oh, I didn’t get a chance to go out. I was working the morning shift at the shop, like every other Saturday. Got home just in time for the 1 o'clock news. But if it's not too late, I'd love to take a walk with you tomorrow.      If you're going, I might join you! I'm sick of sitting inside playing video games all day. Maybe a bit of fresh air would do me good. Though honestly, I'd much rather cycle the whole way and see how far I can get.      Cycle! Now that's what I call young madness. I used to cycle too, when I was a girl, but nowadays my knees aren’t as fond of it. I walk—relentlessly slow, but still a walk. Though don’t get me started on driving. I can barely drive now. I got into a few hiccups with the car last week, and I'm thinking of handing the keys in altogether.      Honestly, M, maybe you should buy a bike—it would save so much time getting about. I mean, most of the cycle lanes in Cambridge are brilliant, and it's much easier on the pocket than gas and insurance.      Tell her what you told me, M. Give her the full 'cycle-to-work-scheme' speech.      Oh, I've heard that one before. Also, I've heard the bit about being ‘eco-friendly’ and 'healthy living'. But you know what I like about driving? I like not standing at red lights blinking at nothing for ten minutes waiting for the bike lane to clear. Not that I've driven recently, mind!      You're cutting the legs off your chair if you keep talking like that. Come on, the initiative is a great idea, and it's not like bikes are restricting your freedom. You can still take the car when the weather’s bad or if you're going elsewhere.      Not if the car’s stuck in a pothole with three feet of the wheel missing because govt’s on a budget!      Ha, very funny.      Honestly, I'm just trying to say, it’s good to have options. Walk, cycle, drive—whatever works. And with the two of you, I suppose I’ll talk you into a little adventure this weekend.

Rather annoying when the recording isn't clear enough to understand, isn't it? I mean, if you're doing proper linguistic analysis, you need something you can annotate accurately. I was just having a look at a Basque recording we took last year in the Basque Country—we picked up some great phonetic variation in Euskalerria, especially around the trill and the ejective consonants.      That does sound fascinating. I work more in administration here, helping coordinate speaker profiles and records rather than pulling the data myself. But I was just wondering—have you had the chance to test how dialects from different UK regions perform in these recordings? I imagine Estuary English versus something like a Lancashire accent would have wildly different vowel shifts, wouldn’t they?      Absolutely. We've had some interesting interactions, for example, when comparing features extracted from someone from Aylesbury, where I’m from, and a speaker from Liverpool. It just goes to show how micro-regional dialects can be. I remember one particular case where the speaker's vowel realisation made the lexical accuracy fluctuate by over 15%—not trivial in speech recognition!      Fascinating work you're doing, both of you. As an old linguist—and I do mean  old , I'm afraid—I remember the days when we relied on handwaves and educated guesses rather than machine learning models. I used to work extensively with Chinese phonology at the University of Cambridge, back when the hills were still low. Our biggest challenge was recording in London—too much ambient noise, and accents just blending oddly.      That is a great point, Professor. I’m actually curious—I’ve heard your colleague spoke about the Basque about five times this week at the alumni roundtables. But what did you think of the Basque language as a linguistic system? I know it's isolating, unagglutinative, and quite agglutinative at the same time if you blink hard.      [Chuckles] Ah, Basque is a rare beast. You could call it a linguistic relic, as mysterious as a well-aged wine. No Indo-European affiliations, and its morphology plays with left- and right-word order in ways that even a syntactician might weary of. I go every few years to see if anything's changed—but so far, nothing! Still bafflingly consistent.      To be honest, your research inspires a lot of the work I do with conservation and minority language representation. As for personal travel—my friends and I are planning a trip to Wales soon.

: "Liz, it's been  such  a long time! You look amazing, by the way—did you go on some detox program or something?"     : "No!
