I spent a year swiping forms and scheduling appointments. You’d think it was enough to make you want to grin and bear it, but no. Give me CV screening any day. How about you, Jake? Still trying to teach a room full of oddly-talking Japanese students how to pronounce 'thee' and 'they' correctly?"     : "That remains a challenge. I’m now a fan of using the Facebook ice bucket challenge as an accent exercise. They try and fails—you know that ‘unexpected cold water’ bit is a classic for practicing vowel drops and consonant endings."     : "I remember that. I actually raised a bit of money for the ALS charity last year through that challenge. It was mad how many people just forgot about it and rushed to douse themselves before the clock ran out."     : "True. My students took it a bit more seriously, like it was their entrance into goth culture."     : "And what about college? Finally, did you finish your MA in something academic or something equally questionable?"     : "I did a MA in Applied Linguistics. It was intense—meant to better equip myself to talk about language change over time, especially online and dialect shifts like yours and Sian’s down here."     : "Oh, come on, it's not that different from the London slang we all grew up hearing."     : "Just say it—you think you've outgrown your Bedford twang ever since you went to uni."     : "No, I just realized that language evolves—end of.

Rather annoying this new coffee machine, isn't it? Seems like everything sticks and it's always coughing up bits of debris. Never had such luck as a teacher with my own espresso machine.      Honestly, I feel like we've already had half a removal job sorting out where it's going and then dealing with storage. I’m just twitching at the thought of all the costs. You don’t reckon we could swap it for something secondhand from a local ad, do you? It’d save a fortune.      Secondhand might be more of a mess in the long run. I’ve seen enough of these older appliances when I was working in the planning side of the oil industry — bits fall off at the most inconvenient times. Possibly best to pay the premium and be done with it.      Easier said by the man who’s never had to handwash his own morning coffee breakfast, no doubt. Look at us, still arguing over a machine at our age. I remember when we used to argue about idealism and political manifestos over tea and toast like proper young dreamers.      Don’t remind me — your Labour leadership debates still live in the house, by the way. Every portrait of Keir or Sir Keir feels like it’s judging my baking.      Compared to some of the other leaders we’ve had, he seems quite the dreamer. Not that it helps us much, mind you. Still, principles mean something in this world — even if they also cost a fortune to live by. Like this oddly priced drip machine with hotter than hell water.      Still, at least we had a plan when we started all those debates. Now it’s us trying to decide the best way to prop this coffee machine up so it doesn’t lurch sideways when we plug it in.      I do miss those days. When the biggest problems were votes and values, not whether our caffeine addiction could be sustained.      And yet, somehow, I think the two are related. If you had as strong a belief in equality as you do in your filter machine, the whole enterprise would’ve happened with far more precision.      Enough of that man. If you go on much longer, I might start trying to calculate the mean cost per cup just to shut you up.      Go ahead. Figure out how you could sum up the cost of disappointment and machine depreciation into one neat formula.

Rather annoying the new barista at the weekend, wasn't he? I had her get my usual — flat white with skim milk, one shot. But no, she kept staring at me like I’d asked for Martian juice or something. Do you think there’s still hope for me or should I just stick to my trusty handmade vouchers again this year?      I think it's probably the same with the barista, you know, learning the ropes and feeling a bit overwhelmed by the goings-on in the morning rush. It does get quite rammed in here on a weekend.

Rather annoying when John starts snoring through the whole of Happy Birthday. I swear, it’s like he’s doing it on purpose! And no one’s having the guts to tell him, either. It’s a proper laugh until you can’t hear a dicky-bird!      Aye een! I went to his place last weekend an’ it were like sleepin’ next to a freight train with a motorway under it! Got so infuriated I had to stick a couple of pillows in fron’ o’ me head. Still, he were apologizin’ when he come down with a right grizzle the next mornin’.      That’s harsh, though! You cannae tell someone they look like a bin liner in the left-hand side o’ the village, y’know what I mean? Snorin’s the least of it most of the time. Mummy once told Dave, “Davey, if you were any louder I’d throw a pan on you and not take it off for a week!” And he took it to heart, too!      Aah, Dave’s alright up t’ a point. What I do like is when the real deadly snorers go on a country walk an’ trot into a sleep on the way. I remember – Matey once got knocked out with a handkerchief in his face while the others were takin’ bets as he slept under a tree!      That’s right daft, someone actually using a handkerchief! All my lot use those blue wipes now. Funny thing was, Matey came out with a massive bruise and swore he’d been robbed!      I do like Waterfields though, the bakers. Got the best sausages in th’ house. Used to go there when I were younger. Still have the unopened Richmond sausages in the ‘fridge.      Aye mulher, them Richmond sausages are a proper treat. Do love the taste, but they do pack a bit o’ a crackle! Like when I were at Aunty Doris’s lunches, she always served them with the gravy and the mashed potato, you remember?      Aye, Doris were a one-off! I do miss those kinds of proper meals. I do not, however, miss her always goin’ on about her ‘snorein’s. She said it made her nose hurt and her heart weep!      It’s a right laugh talkin’ ‘bout this lot, honestly. I remember the last birthday do I had up near Motherwell and they were all about the soft furnishings, not the laughs!

Rather skip the new bar in town. You know what I mean. I was hoping it would be different.      Oh aye, more of the same, then.      Exactly. Not to worry—I went to that little bistro near the station instead. Had a lovely time.      Ah, good choice. That place's food has been on a roll. A lot better than some of the flashy new joints, if you ask me.      Definitely. Oh, I also met this new customer of mine there. He's one of those IT consultants.      Oi, someone who knows what they're doin' about that My turkey curry was brilliant, by the way. I've been back there a couple times since you told me about it.      Nice! I was about to try something new for breakfast, but then I thought, "Nah, I'll just stick with the café near my office."      Smart move. Good coffee, too, if I say so myself. Nothing like a sturdy pint of coffee in the morning.      I tell ya, it's been a tricky week managing the schedule. We've been scrambling from one project to the next – it's been madness.      You've been busy, eh? Still, you did good. You always do.      Thanks, Dad. That's what someone at my age needs—someone to say they're a bit of a maverick.      Aye, you've got the brain for it. I'm proud, love. Real proud about how far you've come.      I appreciate that. And I know you've been busy too. How's the farm?      Keepin' afloat for now. The new guest accommodation is ready, by the way. Just openin' it up for the summer season.      That's brilliant! You've outdone yourself as always. Maybe I should pop by for a weekend break. I could use the peace.      That's a grand idea. We'll have the good old family go-to-place on your own if you come.      Sounds perfect, really. I might just go with that then.      You do that, lass. You do that. We could do with a bit of peace ourselves, now that I come to think about it.      Well, I'll let you know when I'm coming. Maybe we can have a proper cookout, like always.      Oh, that'd be grand. It'll be like old times.      Just me, you, and a bit of countryside air. No rush, no city nonsense.

Rather annoyingly, I haven't had a request yet for that. But I think it would be so much more beneficial to learn it at home. Otherwise, your child could lose their accent or whatever.      Yeah, honestly, I would like to as well. The problem is timing, really. I'm working full-time and we're both very stressed about little Ayden at the moment.      A lot of people would love that too. I remember my friends said they watched quite a bit of Spanish television and taught their kids that way.     Oh, well, I'd already like to teach it even if it's just a couple of short words, like "hola" and "adios". Just something to start with.      Ten minutes, everyday – I think that would work, and I think he would pick up quite quickly actually, considering the way he's been learning with his speech therapy at this early age.     When I was five, my dad used to play flash cards and he got me to speak quite a lot of vocabulary over the summer, and it really helped.     Oh, brilliant! We might look into that for Ayden as well. Otherwise, watching shows with subtitles – it does help. I remember watching "Peppa Pig" with my younger sister and, because the words were shown on the screen, she picked up new words quite quickly.     That's a good idea, and he's just starting at full-time nursery so maybe they can read books or something like that as well.     Exactly. It's just starting and being consistent. If you speak the language in context, it makes it about daily routines rather than classroom type of learning.      It's much better doing things this way than forcing it to be academic. I think it should be integrated into their daily lives, like for little things like "Good morning" or "I love you".     Yeah, and being bilingual can help with their literacy as well, when they get older.     Oh definitely. Also, children always pick up faster when a new language is related to things they love, like characters in stories, songs, colours or numbers.     Mm, that's true. It does make it more natural and fun for them, rather than being a chore.     I can't wait to see how Ayden takes it all on, though I think I'm going to need to team up with my work to allow for some language breaks over the next few weeks at least.

Rather a lovely day for a walk through the garden, don't you think? I do enjoy a bit of fresh air and a spotter’s view for the birds. I’ve had a few robins visiting the feeder again today. Not quite as bold as they used to be — well, considering it was humans that chased them out of the warrens in the first place. Still, it's heartening to see them sticking around. A shame I haven’t got that stubby bird nest I found last week. It would’ve fetched a pretty penny at the antiques market for a curious customer.      You'd fetch the birds out of habit, mind, wouldn't you? That's the civil engineer in you — always needing to pin things down. I’ve been fixing my left leg a bit more these days, you know, what with the diabetes and all. Aches like a devil if I’m about to try something taller than breakfast, but I’m up to a half hour a day in the garden. I spotted the blue tit hides, you see, near the old patch of rhododendrons by the wall.      I’ve been up since six baking — quite a different kind of engineering, mind you, with more flour than formulas! Made a Victoria sponge with a few little surprises in it. Nothing too –  ha!  – heavy for the old crowd. Though I imagine some of the others might not quite take to the puppet décor I’s stuck on the side — don’t know what came over me, just someone at the craft shop said they looked whimsical.      Puppet décor? That’s something! Reminds me of the way the children crowded round Margery’s house when she used to make glove puppets with old socks. I don’t suppose the likes of us lot were allowed near her stuff. Maybe they thought us old people would try and take the handle. Still, I say to the puppet, ‘Pull the string and dance,’ and you might find it dancing on the plate with a teaspoon. Unlikely any puppet would survive the cake, though — too sweet for performance!      At this time of life, a bit of whimsy’s not a bad thing, I must admit. Was going to say you remember those afternoons by the feeders with the blue tit watching everything on your fence? It's not just the birds that made the garden tick, no, it's the company, blooming or not.

Rather skip the starter, I think. You know how my digestive system is these days—the doctor said it's all about portion sizes, not pepperoni. What shall we go for? I've been eyeing that souvlaki dish with the spiced lamb and feta.      Sounds excellent. I'm having that, too. The menu says 'served with fresh pita and tzatziki'—I bet it’s bursting with herbs. By the way, have you heard from Simon lately? He's been journeying around Northern Cyprus with his new collaborator. Apparently, the chap's into dowsing and shamanic healing! Sounds like a madhouse, doesn't it?      Oh yes, he told me. I met his eccentric mother last week—what a character. She still refers to his brother, who passed away a few years back, with affection, as if he's still waiting breakfast on a rainy morning. It's very touching.      Yes, the human heart hides many mysteries. You know, when I was younger, I used to visit a friend who believed firmly in reading tea leaves and destiny maps. I never quite grasped it, but she had a warmth and strength ... quite different from the others. I sometimes wonder where she is now.      Changes are often bittersweet, aren't they? Speaking of which, the weather here is quite hot—nothing like the mild days of Dorchester. You don’t seem bothered, though. Our dear someone at the table next door dropped a glass of ouzo and thanked the heavens it wasn’t wine. They’d been talking about cosmology and the stars through their lunch—an impressive anecdote in a small restaurant!      That table does have quite the spirit of adventure. I remember our trip a few years back—do you recall that innkeeper who insisted we light a fire for good fortune? My, I tried to count aloud in Turkish for weeks after that, with disastrous results at the bazaar. Still, it was all part of the charm.      I did stick out my hearing aid and speaker test to see what kind of English the lunches delivered. It was one of the more bizarre mornings. My grandchild is delivering a presentation this week on environmental policy—reminds me of your line of work, doesn’t it?      That is impressive. I suppose we could go further into the topics of what your grandchild’s latest spiritual inclinations might be, but this sounds like it could turn into a lecture.

Rather annoying the new kitchen isn't ready yet. Thought it'd be sorted by now, honestly.      Never mind love, the builders run late sometimes, you know how it is. At least it's finally getting done after all this time.      Yeah, but it's beginning to cost a fortune. I told you, I haven't even got the measurements confirmed yet for a table. Agh, this is so stressful!      You'll get through it. Oh, and we've invited your grandparents for Christmas. Do you want to start planning a present for them?      Oh, no pressure, then! I'm still thinking about what to get everyone else, honestly. I’ve already got my niece’s gift sorted, but I’m stuck for the others.      Aye, if you're stuck, just bring it up when I'm around. Me and this lot are still a bit in discussion about what’s happening with the farm next year, to be truthful. Should have been sorted weeks ago, but no!      Well, listen, the rugby match on Saturday is a go, is it not? You two remember the time we went to watch that local team? Absolutely chaotic, but brilliant fun.      True! I almost had to take cover from a thrown programme. You lot nearly caused a riot when the referee sent someone off!      And we didn't even like that team! That was pure mischief! Anyway, about the work – have you had a chance to think about the renovations?      Er, no – I told you, it’s all still in about five different stages. I don’t even know where the electrician is half the time!      Don’t you worry about everything yourself, love. Maybe your stepdad and I can give you a hand once it gets started.      Aye, it's a proper bloody mess at the moment, but once you've got it sorted, it's going to look beautiful. You've picked out some grand plans, by the way.      Thanks, but honestly, I'd rather just be tucking into the dinner you're making every night rather than stress about tiles or builders.      Then let's see if we can’t box this up properly soon. Pass the gravy, would you, David?      Passed it! And with extra thyme, as usual – you can’t say that's not proper British!      Haha, so over the top, Dad. But honestly, I wouldn’t want to be anywhere else right now.

Rather annoying when people just take things outta context, innit? I was watching the Jeremy Kyle show like... last weekend an' it was just one o' them whole wars going on.      Aye, them things are like a circus sometimes! I wouldn't be surprised if half o' it is rigged, honestly. I mean, 'ow do you even let people get that far? I reckon half the lot are catfishin'.      Catfishing? Like dump someone over the phone and never meet? That's what me cousin did, she said he was some hot bloke but turned out it was just 'is mums' laptop and a load o' photos from the net. My word, I felt for 'er!      I ain't saying Jeremy Kyle is all lies and no truth, but I mean—'ave you seen the drama they put out? I feel like if I walked in there with a story in me head, I'd come out with a whole new personality.      That's real, innit? An' if someone 'as gone catfishin', I reckon the best thing is to just cut and run real quick. I know a few peopl’ who've bin through it, an' it's no good for no one. Waste o' time and energy.      Yeah, an' sometimes these shows like the Jeremy Kyle one make it worse, don't they? Like they air it out for the world an' people judge you based on ten seconds o' bad camera angles.      Aye, and sometimes the people lookin’ like they're villains in it, when it might be daftness or a misunderstanding. I mean, the other lot on iPlayer th’ other day—he thought he was meetin’ some girl and it turns out she was in a relationship with a different bloke.      That sounds daft. I can’t believe it happened. But ‘at happens more than you think, I bet. I reckon some people just fancy the idea o’ being on telly more than they do 'aving a real conversation with someone.      Still, I think these things are like a reminder to be careful goin’ on them apps if you don’t know someone. I swear, me mate’s got a face like a goon, but on the app ‘e was ridin’ high with fluency and six-packs.      Nah kidding, innit? I had a bloke ‘ere once, said ‘e lived in London an’ worked in ‘is dad’s farm. Only when we met ‘e turned out to be 20 years older and from Blackpool.

Rather annoyingly, I've got to do a presentation in German tomorrow about bees. Do you think you could help me out a bit with some of the vocabulary, Nana?      Of course, dear. I used to do quite a bit of speaking at art exhibitions in Vienna, so if it's Italian and German, I'm not bad at either. But why on earth are you talking about bees?      It's part of this project I’m doing for my Classics degree. They want us to do a comparative study of mythologies and animal symbolism in different ancient civilisations. Bees show up in several—from the Romans who thought they were sacred, to the Greeks, who associated them with wisdom and prophecy.      Oh! The Italians left dozens of beehives hanging in the trees around the villa, and used to make the world's best honey. I remember my grandmother Mietz would breakfast on toast with walnuts and honey. She said the beehive was the symbol of diligence and harmony, you see. She had a very tidy mind, like your gran—set things in order, yes?      I can see that. What did they call the bee in German, by the way? I want to make sure I'm pronouncing it right.       Biene , fairly simple, and  Bienenstock  is the beehive. It's not as sweet as saying  ape  or  spider , but the principles carry through in many European languages. I noticed also in Paris: French people use the same root oddly. Funny thing— abeille  for a bee and  abeille royale  for royal jelly.      I did a little bit of travel in Paris a couple years ago. We were in Latin Quarter and I met this French student who was learning to code. She was trying to write a mobile app for beekeepers. Her German was rather basic, though.      A beekeeper app? Oh, I assume she was helping them with hive histories, you know, tracking nectar sources. It's a beautiful thing to think of, young people trying to help the bees survive.      Exactly. My computer keeps crashing, though, so it's hard sometimes to even keep up with my work. My professors are patient, thank goodness. But I'm really starting to think that I need to go back to the drawing board and re-build my entire system.      You know, I once had a computer technician fall asleep in the middle of a job on our estate, and woke him up with a cup of tea.

Rather annoying when people drive dangerously, isn't it? I mean, I was just trying to take the roundabout off the A35 and there was this guy in a van going at least七十 miles an hour and doing a full £200 worth of damage as well. Just like he's trying to rush and get somewhere before the world ends. It was ridiculous. I reckon his insurance's going to cost him a fortune. A lot worse than just having to do an MOT, right?      Oh, it's just the mentality these days. You can't chase speed, but the bloke looks like he needs to sort out his attitude. Last time I had to drive to Bournemouth, I almost got run over by one of those kids with a modified Ford Focus. I tell you, I was on the phone to the insurance company the very next day because the little inspector had an opinion, but the insurance would not cover anything, no doubt about that!      Honestly, driving nowadays, you ever looked at that? They don’t have the patience to stop and actually think. Last week I was getting out of a car, and a老爷车 I mean, a land-rover from the Seventies came speeding past with someone in the passenger seat watching TikTok videos. Absolutely no sense of control. I’m surprised the Sat Nav held out. I wouldn’t mind venting about this, but the weather is better in Dorset than what it's been in Harlow this week.      Honestly, I just don't get how people can multitask like that. It's bad enough doing a Windows 8 update, but trying to type and drive and be navigated at the same time? I spoke to my dad about about this last weekend. He's had a couple of bad experiences watching his job from a care home where they had to worry about people driving improperly. It's cruel, really, but that’s just a different story. I just wish people would take more notice.      Tell me about it. My mate Eddie was trying to get a solicitor for when he got hit by an uninsured driver, and that was as bad as getting hit by the car itself. It cost him more in legal fees than the damage. Still, I suppose it’s better than nothing, right? At least he’s on his own about it.

Rather chilly this morning, isn't it? I needed six cups of tea just to get out of bed.      Six cups? You're still on your tea kick, then? I told you, it's £2 a cup from the shop now! But yes, it is nippy. I saw the frost on the window last night, like a frosting on a cupcake.      Aye, just like that! I never thought I'd see frost again after all these years. My sister used to say I was born under the coldest star of the lot. Costessey frozen to the bone even in June—mind you, that's the only reason I left for London in the '70s.      London, you flew over to London from the sticks, didn’t you? I remember you turned up at my mother's for tea one day saying you were "going to chase opportunity and adventure". And here you are in your early seventies, still sipping tea, day after day.      Opportunity and adventure—ha! That city, though, loved it in its time. I never did land a proper job, mind you. Never got far with anything but odd jobs—paperboy, bin man, then nothing. You’re the one who actually made a living. I remember you, swanning around with the kids, telling them stories of black bears and white bears. You was quite the one back then!      Stories? I told them Tales of the King’s Baker, a man who made the sourdough with fluff from the queen's cat and worked magic with tea. Magic tea, mind you.      Magic tea indeed. I bet you had the little ones hooked. You had that look in you, always kind of knowin’ you were the only person in the world for them that day.      Well, I did what I could. The work was honest, the pay was small, but the love was big. Guess I did alright in the end. We both did, as far as these things go.      Aye, you did. Now if only the government’d set us both up with a proper pension! Still, we’ve go each other, haven’t we? Not everyone can say that at our age.      That’s the truth. You're the one person who’s still called me "Barbara" ever since we met in '72. I think even my new hearing aid calls me "love".      Then I suppose I better keep calling you "love" to make it fair!

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh? You’d think by June we’d have seen some proper sunshine in Cambridge yet.      Oh, I agree completely. I’ve been meaning to get out there and plant some sunflowers in the patch behind the house, but it’s like the forecast’s against it eeny time I plan!           Aye, well, if I were you I’d just get on with it! I mean, sunflowers don’t mind a bit of rain once they’re rooted in. I helped my nan grow them when I was a kid in Sunderland—we’d clear the whole back garden! Not as fancy as Cambridge, but the sunflowers still stood proud.      That does sound lovely! Gardening can be a tonic when you're stuck inside for weeks, especially with this thesis I’m working on. Half the time I’m at the library reading about something ancient, and then I need to feel some mud between my fingers just to stay sane.      You poor luv. I can't imagine sitting hunched over a pile of books like you do every day. Although—speaking of sanity—what’ve you been listening to to keep your spirits up while you're in the library? I've been rhythmically tapping out some Iron Maiden on the knife and fork at me desk trying not to go mad myself.           Iron Maiden? Now that’s a surprise. I’m more of a post-rock and chill-hop guy. Helps me focus. But I’ve been branching out a bit lately—my friend at the uni puts on these massive classical sets in the café and it’s surprising how much I’ve taken to it.      Oh right? I’ve not had the chance to pass by that place. Got a friend who plays some local gigs round Cambridge too—more of a folk/singer-songwriter kind of vibe, but she’s got a rather nice voice if I do say so me own self. I might try to introduce you two one night.      That'd be brilliant. We could make it a bit of a dinner date out of it—maybe catch the weather on our side this time.      Sounds like a plan. Just make sure you’ve got an umbrella goin’ on your back if you come though. You never know.      Hopefully by then we’ll have bloomin’ sunflowers and all. Deal?      Deal.

Rather annoying this new tuition fee policy, innit? Seems like everything's getting more expensive by the year. I got to pay off me uni loan now I'm earning properly, and it's nearly as bad as a second mortgage. £60k, I tell yer!      Aye, it is a right old mess. I was down at the uni library yesterday and all them kids on a work placement were groaning about how they’re gonna be stuck with debt for longer than most of us are supposed to be living!      Didn’t even get the full bursary as a postgrad because of some dodgy application deadlin’. All the hassle just to end up with a mountain of cash to pay back. You’ve still got yer PhD going on, haven't yer? Must be lucky not havin’ to shell out the whole nine yards.      Yeah, it doesn’t feel that lucky at this time of month though — in fact, more like being skint! No income, barely any spare time to do anything outside of research or that musical I went to last week. Mind, it was worth every penny. You should come round one night and I’ll tell ya all abou' it. It was  Les Mis , and it was like we were in the middle of Parisian revolt with the acoustics and all the drama!      It’s been a while since I’ve been to anything theatrical, to be fair. Most of the time I just come back here to Cambridge and catch up on me work. Besides, I had a proper laugh last week when this new intern in the office thought being ‘prioritised’ meant your colleague looked out for yeh about work! Midlands accent foolin’ the lot of us, I mind.      Going back to that debt thing, I heard yesterday a student moved back to Birmingham just to ‘avoid the cost of living here’. All that for rent. Can't imagine me leave’ Cambridge though — it's nice peaceful once yeh get outta the colleges.      Aye, but peaceful or not, it’s nowhere special to a lass from Sunderland if yeh can’t afford to be here, innit? Pity the man’s not got govt money on his own if he's not got work. Gotta wonder if it’s affecting the economy.      Aye, all them skilled grads can’t work in the city because there’s no jobs, and those jobs are being done by people from outside the country.

Rather than share a text-based conversation, I request that we do something different.      Okay... What did you have in mind?      I need something specific to your unique story and experiences.      That sounds kind of personal.      It is personal, and that’s the point. It will be more meaningful if it draws on your specific life choices and context.      I see your point, but I'm not used to talking about my personal history. What exactly are you proposing?      It's about learning more deeply about each of you—from your childhood, family, and personal experiences, through to your values and dreams. It will help me craft a tailored, meaningful dialogue.      So, you want to hear my story in detail, is that right?      Yes, and about the relationships you have with others, your life events, and any stories that matter to you.      I’m honored, but this is new territory for me. How do we start?      We can start with your earliest memories or your family of origin. What did you like to do when you were younger?      Hmm… Well, I grew up in humble beginnings. I remember helping my parents with chores and sneaking extra snacks because I was always hungry. Later, I got married and moved to another town, but things didn’t work out.      That's a starting point. Tell me more about your experiences after that.      I became a mother and focused on raising my children while dealing with being apart from their father. I did ballet as a hobby and made about forty birthday cards every year for my kids to touch base with them on special days.      Interesting. Any stories you particularly fond of or moments you’d like to highlight?      I treasured the time I passed on family recipes to them, taught them the importance of holding on to memories through cards, and tried to build a little bond with my stepsons from remarriage. I wanted to be a positive presence in their lives, even if it was hard at first.      These are rich details. This will make the context of the go-to-home conversations much deeper if you’re open to it. What else is important in your story that I should know?      I had some losses and loneliness at times, but I’ve also had moments of triumph and love. I never gave up on helping others, like mentoring kids in the community over the years.

Rather annoying this, innit? I’ve been tryin’ to get this leg hair ‘ere off and it’s decidin’ to play up now.      Ew, that's rough. Why d'you do it, though? It's summat like every two weeks or so een?      Yeah, 'bout that. I reckon it’s cos of the gym—ain’t gonna turn up lookin’ too much like a hedge, y’know? But my legs look all red and angry now.      Ooh, bloomin' hell, like you’ve been baked! Have you tried any razors lately? I found one that’s super gentle now that My nan recommended. You could give it a try.      Nah, still got them razors me mam bought me for my eighteenth. I was far too old for a body-shaving set then, I swear!      Aww, you poor thing! Maybe switch to shaving cream instead of gel? I found it makes all the difference. Less tugging, way less redness.      Right, I’ve read that somewhere. Gell tends to make it worse… I reckon I’m just slashin’ it off way too fast cos I’m in a rush. I should take me time, innit?      Mate, you ain’t at work yet! Slow ‘n’ steady shaves the better. Also, someone at sixth form said she uses a depilatory cream summat fierce. I haven’t tried it myself, but it’s a bit less scratchy ‘neath the skin.      Not sure about that—ain’t a fan of smellin’ like a chemist shop. But if you say it works, I might give it a shot.      Oh, and, ‘cos we’re being proper here, do you actually feel like you  have  to do it? I mean, you said it’s for the gym, but when I started doing it, my mate was like “Lad, nobody’s lookin’ that closely mate.”      Probably. I think it’s a bit of pressure from Instagram and the lot. Everyone goin’ on ‘about bein’ confident and real, but then posters of legs, no hair, and stuff. Y’know?      So summat about fluency and sums, eh? Like, you start and can’t stop now. Fair ’nuff. But if you overdo it, you’ll just end up        Red, raw, and a bit of an embarrassment, yeah. I see you’ve not got the same problem, though. You’ve got smooth legs like, always!      Thank you very much, I work on it babe. But look, honest, it’s all about what makes you feel good.

Rather annoying when a bar’s got decent whiskies, but they won’t pour ’em by the dram. I got to pick between a shot or a whole pint. I prefer a dram, thank ye.      Aye, seems like they fink you’re either here to get plastered or eeny weeny passive-aggressive drinks. Not like proper drinking’s possible. Where d’you get a clean Glencairn glass round here?      Probably don’t. Cam’s got more clued-up wine bars than pubs for that matter. But, come on, ’sjust a frozen pint o’ brand lager made by a multinational, ain’t it?      Correct on the turkey, definitely. Still, enough talk o’ liquor—what d’you think about the D word these days? I mean, the government’s spendin’ millions on a strategy to reduce it when, honestly, if I wanted a fag or a line, I could get it five minutes from here.      Yeah, it’s like they expect everyone to be angels with a bit o’ policy changes. Though I have to say, since the clubs’ve tightened things up, it’s less wild in there. Still, reckon the real work is in education from the get-go. Y’know, stop glamorisin’ it, because kids see it as “cooler” or somethin’?      Absolutely. And don’t even get me started on boxing. Fancies in Premier League—proper abuse. Ever seen a red card for racin’? Never hotter than the fury it generates in the stands and on online. Can’t even speak to people without they startin’ about how Arsenal’s walkin’ gold round the touchline.      To be fair, some o’ that is egged on by media. They’d run with that story for a whole week. Po-faced commentators callin’ it “rises in anti-social behaviour” as it they’re any bloody different themselves.      Aye, I could stick a finger up at some of these blokes. Y’know, proper nuanced analysis and whaddya do? Some lad with no voice experience calling a match as if it’s a bloody Netflix drama.      If I could pick one thing to ram down their throats in conversation, it’d be this—football blokes say “alright” and mean “move along, I’ve got sums to do” after twenty minutes. Talk about faux-friendly.      Same with that “dreadful weather we’re having” nonsense. It’s bleak as all heck out there and they’re still sayin’ “oh, it always passes.”

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? I suppose even with everything we've got on, it's hard to ignore the weather sometimes. Have you had a chance to look at the latest plans we discussed last week? I've been meaning to ask about the feasibility of extending the hall.      Yes, it is a delightful day. Made me sorely miss the gardens at my parents’ place in Buckingham. As for the plans, I did take a good look at them over the weekend. It's quite interesting you mentioned the hall—there was a crack forming under the eastern pillar, which suggests the underpinning might not be as robust as we'd like.      Oh, really? That's concerning. I'm loath to change course too much, especially with the Heritage Secretary pushing for the bid deadline. D'you think we could present a revised plan that takes that into account while still maintaining the aesthetic character? I'd hate to lose this project now.      Completely, I do. There was a similar issue back when I was working on a project in East Anglia. We managed to integrate a discreet reinforced frame inside the walls without altering the exterior. It did require some creative engineering, but it kept the building's character and met modern standards.      That does sound like a workable solution. I'd love to hear more about the funding side of things too. Any chance of securing that grant from the Historic England initiative? I remember we hit off quite well with one of their representatives at the symposium last spring.      Oh, absolutely. I've got some preliminary correspondence with the grant officer. What worked in that case was a clear timeline paired with a well-documented heritage value section. I'm compiling a dossier of historical references and nearby building comparisons to showcase our standing.      Excellent. I'll make sure the structural section is up to date to match your narrative. And do you think we should invite Historic England to a site visit before the final submission? I'm told it gives the project a very human touch, you know, makes them feel connected.      That’s a good idea. People do respond to a little bit of personal contact. I'll let the grant officer know and see if we can arrange something. Between us, I've always found that a bit of charm does wonders in these situations.

Rather than chuck a bar of chocolate in the bin, I tend to blame it on the North East dialect roots... got to keep it weird and local, innit?      Oh, that's probably it — probably £20 spread over ten words as well. Just like your research — if it's not clear,  innit ?      Naw, I've been making a bit of a point not to muddy things up in this project. Still, easier said than done when you're supposed to be comparing Received Pronunciation to the North East accent — it's like talking past each other in a tea shop.      A tea shop? That's quaint, don’t you think? Being surrounded by turkey sandwiches and "balance of payments" left and right. Ten more years and you’ll be writing a paper on how the Premier League turned into a cultural phenomenon in the North East.      Maybe I'll include this conversation. "Incorporating emotional narrative during tea consumption as a method of preserving dialectal authenticity." There we go, academic gold.      Only if we bookend it with some proper impacts — like, "tea as a social lubricant bridging generational and regional gaps in postgraduate linguistics." Make it sound like it cost a small fortune in grant money.      I think it's already got funding — the emotional support of my partner and my PhD student. You know what it is, don't you? It’s the coffee at work — full beans, full blaggers. At least with tea, we can do proper measurements and still sabotage ourselves.      Any tea scientist will tell you — over-boiled water is a sign of desperation. I think I burned off a language in the first 10 seconds of cooking this.      Not you! I mean it. You're the articulate one. My brain’s like a wet biscuit by now — passed its best before date and all.      Oh, I had a bit of a holiday idea waiting on a tour guide. France, as in somewhere beyond "nous" and "merci." I thought maybe a week in the South of France — far away from accents where I can't understand a man with a must go to bin on his own if he's not got glasses.      That's only brutal. I say, if you're going to your holiday with you in charge, bring fluency to the conference and leave it at that. “Je ne parle pas français suffisamment bien” or “Je suis prononciation faible” — tell the butcher you like lasagna, and they'll know where to hit you up.

Rather annoyingly, the children don't want to eat school dinners. I know it's not exactly up to me, but I've had them both saying they're not hungry at lunchtime.      Well, that's because they have no appetite! It's far too early after breakfast. They want to eat at Granny's again.      Yeah, I wanted to eat with Graham today. A big Sunday tea would be best!      I'm not sure that's feasible. We've had to buy the school dinner money for the term today. The parent pay thing hasn't stopped taking it out! It's so confusing, technology.      Oh, like that MyPayment thing? I had trouble with it last week. Try contacting the school to get the payments sorted. But, honestly, they should just have a proper tuck shop again like old times!      I know, but with the kitchen in the new building, they say it's too complicated, or something. Anyway, I suppose we can manage for now—after all, it's not like we can avoid it forever. I've also been meaning to speak to you about the tennis tournament. Have you entered yet?      Yeah, I got one of the forms – Mateo signed it. He helped me, because I don't really read the paper very well.      That was helpful. And the other thing – the circus is coming to town.      Oh, really? When is it? I remember when there was a clown walking around with a red nose in the park last week. The kids  loved  it!      That was the same one from the advert! We were allowed to throw stuff at them and make silly noises. I think I became the ringmaster for a while.      You just like shouting at random things.      Well, clowns are a bit silly, aren't they?      I suppose they are, but as long as they're doing something positive to engage the kids, I think it's good. Now, about the school dinners—should I speak to them and say that the kids would prefer go to Granny on certain days if that's possible? Maybe one day a week?      That would be lovely for them, and your mum would enjoy having them. Just make sure to let the school know in advance.      It's already been a week like that without much notice, but I'll see what I can do. I really miss the old ways, but I suppose this kind of thing is all part of it now.

Rather enjoyed the new biopic last night — what did you all think?      Oh, I liked it well enough. The direction was more than competent, though I've seen better performances from that actor in the 70s, I must say.      True, I'm not sure if the script gave them much to work with. Anyway, moving on… heard about the recent debate in Cambridge? Something serious about teaching history.      Yes, I read about it. Interesting time to be having the debate when the national curriculum is under such scrutiny. Politicians these days, they think education is just a box to tick, not the real world preparation it should be.      You're probably right, lad. When I was at school, history was storytelling, with some dates and facts in there. These days it's all too about political correctness and what not.      That’s something I find in teaching — the pressure to modernise while we’re still building foundations for the future. Young people need to understand context, not just pass exams.      Definitely. I think we should be linking higher education to real-world experience, like internships or industry-based projects. It's not just about degrees; it's about preparing graduates for the workforce.      I remember having to do a fair bit of hands-on learning when I was studying at Reading. It made a real difference in how we approached our degrees. They just don't do that so much anymore.      I agree. My students often finish their degrees with a fair bit of theory but not much practical experience. I try to bring in guest speakers and about half the time they're all about “How it worked when I was your age.”      Exactly that. We need more mentorship, less lecture theatres packed with 200 students. If you're lucky enough to attend a top university and have no idea what it is you're going to do once you graduate, something is seriously amiss.      All that to say, I worry about the next generation growing up in a world we’ve left them — with no real road maps, only a set curriculum.      It’s on us as educators and parents to make sure we’re helping shape active, critical thinkers, not just passive learners. I can see it already — some of my older classmates have grown into strong leaders, others seem adrift.      You have to start planning early. Education, from school through university, has to be a stepping stone.

Rather a damp day, isn't it? I was just dustin’ the attic, and it's like a proper nippy shower came in through the skylight. Not a bit like the sunshine we had last week.      Oh, George, you must take care in that attic. Got a bit of a wobbly ladder, if you ask me. I was watering the roses this mornin’, and even they looked damp and downhearted. Still, at least it’s not cold like last winter. We had to bundle up like forfendings when walking the dog.      You're right about the weather, but I was actually recalling the war stories you told me, George. My grandfather was a Signals officer in the North African campaign. He used to say the heat was the worst, even worse than the desert winds. They'd push forward with tanks, but the radios would pack up when it was 40 degrees in the shade.      Yes, the war! That's always brought back many memories. I was reading over my father's diaries the other day, and he wrote about rationing up near Harrow — quite a different world. Did you know that back then, we used to get three pints of milk a week, and you needed coupons for everything – even for tea leaves!      That’s not much, is it? Now don’t get me started on the tea. I still take mine with a spot of milk and two sugars, just like in the old days. And God help me, I’ve never been able to buy what you call the 'proper' type at the shops these days. Nothing like the leafy stuff we used to get in about 1950.      Oh, I remember that tea — what you could afford anyway. But let's not dwell on it. George, while you're up in that attic, do look for those guest books my gran had. They were filled with names from the 1920s and 30s — you know, people who stayed here while visiting family or just passing through. Rather a nice bit of local gossip, really.      Speaking of visitors, there was that time the police came by back in the '70s. They were investigating a break-in in the town, and they made me line up in the living room with half the box contents — it was the one time I was happy I had only made beds to show and not the furniture I was waiting to finish.

: You sure you don't mind us taking the scenic route? I need a bit of time to clear my head after the visit with Mum.     : Course I don't mind, mate. Gave me £20 to buy coffee and snacks at the motorway service station, didn’t I? That’s  not  a bad offer, considering I’m doing all the driving today. Though I reckon that coffee fund is starting to dwindle fast.     : It's worth every penny. Especially when we’re moving halfway across the country. Just want to make sure we don’t leave anything behind at Mum’s. Not like we had much, but the fridge full of left-over shepherd's pie is practically a keepsake by now.     : Ah, the good old Guardian of Leftovers, eh? She’s the only person I know who’d pack a Tupperware of breakfast, lunch and dinner for you in one visit. I swear she’s planning for the apocalypse.     : Yeah, I know. I reckon she thought I was moving into a cave and had to ration properly. Anyway, I’m seriously going to miss her and the grief when she tries to give me a hand towel to take with me.     : Oh, she  will  try. I almost had to take the bag back off her the last time she gave me that “I’m just trying to help” look. You’ll be fine, though. Our new flat in Plymouth has everything—fridge, kettle, a seat to sit on. Mod cons, you know!     : I’m not sure I’m  that  prepared for living in a flat with no garden. I’ve had a field practically the length of this car to myself my whole life.     : Well, it is a student flat, to be fair, but at least the rent’s less than your student loan. Parents were right to take on the mortgage again for it. At least it’s not another flat you’ll be passing on your way out to bigger and better things.     : I’m not the one with student debt, remember? And no, you  are  right. This is the best option. Just go easy on the snacks, Dad. I’m not walking two miles uphill into town in the rain just to save 50p on chips.     : Fat chance. You’ve been drinking her tea since you were knee-high, never had to worry about your dad on the road for snacks over tea.

Rather than share a text-based response, I am ready to have a natural and engaging conversation with you. Let’s begin and see how this goes. So, shall we start by going through the menu choices for your grandmother’s birthday? I quite like the sound of a traditional British roast dinner. What do you think?      I was actually just making some notes on that! A roast chicken would be lovely—it’s something she used to make herself before her dementia made it tricky to cook. I was going to add some scalloped potatoes and maybe Yorkshire pudding for a bit of a twist. Do you think your mother-in-law would mind a baked Alaska for dessert? I know she adores the Great British Bake Off.      Oh, I love that idea! A bit of indulgence never hurt anyone, right? Dementia makes some of the old school traditions harder for her, but it’s still nice to keep things familiar, like the roast and proper tea. I was wondering—should we ask the kids to bring candles and maybe some photos to put out so it feels more like a real celebration?      That’s a brilliant idea—mom always gets a bit lost in time, and seeing old photos triggers some beautiful memories. I was thinking of lighting some scented candles in the sitting room too. Maybe rose and lavender? Bring back a bit of old-timey comfort.      Definitely. It’ll make the place smell lovely. Oh, while we’re on the subject—do you fancy coming out with me to pick up the fish for the starter? I found a lovely local fishmonger with fresh lobster tails and some smoked haddock. It’s not too premium, but nothing too posh either because most people about our age don’t want the gold standard, right?      Sure, I can pop out with you. I’ll make a quick stop at the supermarket for some green beans and a lemon for the baked Alaska. Wait, do you know about the cupboard rearrangement in the kitchen? She told me she can’t find her teacups anymore!      Oh, good grief. I’ll have to sort that once we get back. I think it’s partly the dementia, but also maybe she just changes things after a nap and doesn’t remember. Don’t go wasting too much time on it today. Let’s focus on the meal plan and the seating.

Rather annoying me a bit, me wijsdom teeth. Cheek looks like it's been through a pinner, and I've bin putting it off because I don’t fancy going under the knocker with a buck tooth.      Oh no, sounds rough. I had mine out a couple of eeners and it  still  knocks me sore. At least if you're going under, they sort a few holes out at the same time, yeah? I got me fills done while I was there.      Naff idea, innit? Didn’t even get told about it. Just woke up like, "Oh, I've got fillin's now." Bloke, I can't even smile like normal 'cause I keep bitin' me cheek. I’m not sure I want to go back to uni with a mouth of stitches.      It is a bit of a gig. Wait, you're not actually thinking of bunkin’ off for a week, are you? Mega not on, especially with the move comin' up. My mam would  flip  if I even looked like a no-show this time—last year I missed a week.      It'd be easier, I tell ya that. But I've bin texting me flatmate. We’re movin' into this new place near campus, and I barely know the bloke. One time he left his socks to grow fungus in the bath. I’m already foreseein’ shenanigans.      Oh no, spare me! That's just a nightmare. I moved into a shared with a guy from Germany—only spoke three words and still filled the kettle with  oil . My flatmate and I nearly about lost it. Honestly, the move's the least of yer worries once you're back.      Definitely. I know me mam's been on at me for weeks to do somethin’ 'bout it. Says I can't keep borrowin' the DVD player to go round there. But I think I might have to meet up with them when I sort out me teeth, just to not end up as the lady who always comes with lunches to keep the peace.      Yeah, that sounds like a plan. Just make sure you're all patched up goin' in. If you're lucky, maybe you two can find some line in the sand that works. And if not, well… I’ve got some dodgy Wi-Fi and a big sofa if you ever need a bit of a break from the madness.

Rather than going out and doing something extravagant for Chinese New Year, I was thinking we could do a string of little random acts of kindness this week. Dress it up nicely and say it's our Chinese New Year contributions to the world. What do you two think?      What kind of acts of kindness? I like that idea. Maybe we could leave goodie bags on the doorstep for the nice lady next door? A little cake or something?      Oh, yes, and it’s fortuitous! I just bought some lactose-free cakes and cookies, so the nice lady won’t get the wrong sort of baked goods. I can throw a couple in the fridge, and you can make little cards that say, "In celebration of Chinese New Year!"      Can I help write the cards? I used the Draughts and Chess piece money last time to buy Mummy a chocolate breakfast, and I felt proud. Maybe I can help with the cards and the cakes too?      Of course, love! That’s actually a great thought—using the Chess and Draughts pieces as pretend money for special tasks. You did a beautiful thing with your chocolate breakfast idea, by the way.      What else can we do? Can we give toys to the homeless man at the bus stop?      That’s thoughtful, sweetheart. We could pack them in a gift bag and add one of the lactose-free cookies and a sweet note. Let’s make sure the note is in my hand because handwriting counts for oddly magic effects.      Mummy, can we also do something for the cleaners at your school? Maybe make a kind about-you book with nice things the kids can say in the hall?      That’s genius—you know that line you told me the other day about sending kindness in to the world, like a little wave? That's exactly what we are doing here. And if we leave the acts of kindness spread out all week, it’ll feel like little dragons waiting to be unleashed on the world!      Can we also colour with special glitter pens and maybe die my hair black?      Oh, come on, sweetheart! Maybe blue or even go for a rainbow day? I promise no one will laugh at your hair—if you promise not to throw your Draughts pieces in the air when you're excited. Deal?      Deal!      Deal, deal!      Alright then, let's get our kindness dragons and craft supplies together.

: Mummy, I just finished reading "Alice in Wonderland" again—it's still so weird and awesome. I got to the part where she keeps changing sizes, and I can't help but think about how much we've both changed over the years. Look at us—  Lol  !     : Aww, I remember the first time you read that to me when you were six. Your voice was so tiny and high. I love that this is a book we've both cherished.     . Speaking of changes, I heard from your teacher that your reading has really bloomed recently. You're choosing more complex texts! I'm so proud, love.     : Thanks, Mummy. I still get scared sometimes, like when I stumble over a word or I’m reading in front of people, but I’ve been trying to be brave. It reminds me about the car accident. Wait, you never really told me much about it. You have a scar on your arm, and I remember hides being on the back of the sofa that day. Did you read that night?     :      I don’t like to talk about it much, but I’ll tell you. I was on my way home from picking up something for you from the shop. The driver – he was talking on the phone, and he swerved into oncoming traffic. I hit the steering wheel and got this   scar  . I was shaken up, but your Nana looked after you both. As for reading, I   was   trying to read a music magazine that night. Music was my escape—still is. It calmed the panic down.     : Oh, Mummy, I didn’t know. I’m so sorry.     . I understand a little more about why you are so careful driving now. I like how you're so in control. My costume for the school theatre play is inspired by you—strong, with a bit of lace to show it's still soft inside. I watched a video online about how to make it, by the way—     : Is that right? What play are you doing?     : "The Little Mermaid"—I’m playing Ursula. I told my drama teacher I wanted to get your costume style across. And guess what? Dad gave me a present—ike a pair of sable box boots that match your old one from when you used to have that big garden!     :      I had forgotten about those boots! You really are your mother's daughter, always connected to the past   and   the internet!

Rather annoying, the entire planning process, isn't it, George? I was just reading through that letter from the Parish Council again, and it seems as though more than half their recommendations were ignored when they reviewed that latest wind turbine application. We gave those people in the village such good advice last week, I do hope it all pays off.      Yes, Margaret, it's not easy being heard these days with all the big energy firms behind the scenes. I've had a few cups of tea and some interesting chats with the director of the local group. You know, the one fighting the solar panel applications up north? Very thankful they were for our advice—though I suspect they’re still outgunned when it comes to funding and legal representation.      Funelling money into storage solutions would go a long way, if you ask me. I used to head up a firm that handled some infrastructure projects and saw first hand how difficult it was storing surplus energy in peak times. We need real R&D, not just subsidies for wind or solar to puff up the books and look environmentally conscious.      Absolutely, Leslie—there's a consistent mismatch between the development of technology and the focus from the government. It’s as if they're doubling down on subsidies for the generation methods without a thought for the utility side. I remember reading something last week about how, in the last year, wind energy subsidies were over £3 billion—yet less than £40 million went to energy storage research! It's madness.      Spoken like a seasoned director. And unfortunately, it's not just a technical issue—look at the politics involved. Whether it's the Development Control Committee pushing through plans for turbines in rural areas because it’s about appeasing corporate interests or the energy companies having such deep links with City financiers… it all feels pretty cosy.      I know! And the local protest groups are often just volunteers with limited resources. There’s not even a clear way to coordinate actions. I suggested to the one in Almondsbury that they might reach out to national groups for advice on legal challenges and regional funding streams—anything that might help them outmaneuver the 'system', as it were.      That's where strategy and networking come in, like any good business negotiations. There's room for innovation, if you ask me.

Rather annoying this, having to go through all that driving lot again. I was just starting to think I could stay off the roads, mind you.      Not a chance, Dad. Everyone's doing it now. Not only do they have to sit extra tests for motorbikes, but if they want to use a provisional license, even with an instructor, they reckon it's best to have that bit a bit fresh up before too long.      Still, easier said than done. I know someone who had to go back to the driving school when the insurance company asked for the license check-up. Only went three times a week, but still, it's a bother.      On the other hand, you know, I’ve met some people online who are learning to drive, and from what they're saying, the whole process of getting the insurance is even more of a farce. They have to get the no claims bonus agreement sorted early, and if you don’t have a clean driving record, you're looking at ludicrous prices for the first few years.      As if it wasn't challenging enough, what with all the roundabouts and the bloody roundabouts to contend with. And then, when you factor in the holidays—drive during August and it’s like being in Bedlam. I remember trying to get to the coast last summer, it took us three times as long as usual because of the congestion.      I understand completely, Dad. That's why I'm thinking this week I might just plan a staycation. You know, maybe just drive up to the Cotswolds for the weekend. It's less stressful and still gives us a break from the routine.      I like that idea. Just the three of us, no kids, just some peace and a nice walk around some rolling fields. Not to mention the savings it would give us on both gas and travel.      Yes, well if we are going to be driving at all, the most important thing is being sure I can still steer a straight line. You know, your mother would have had a fit if she were still with us if I've misjudged the distances while attempting the various turns and bends.      Then perhaps it's a good idea to set up that refresher course with Dad before our plans for the Cotswolds. Better safe than sorry, especially with insurance costs likely bloating up if there's an incident.

Rather annoying the new Facebook updates, isn't it? Every time I try to check my messages, it pings me again and again with notifications. I’m more than a bit fed up with it by now!      Yes, the technology nowadays—get used to things changing quick, my dear. When I was younger, we used to sit down at the kitchen table with a cup of tea and a paper. A lot less to worry about!      Haha, yeah, easy for you to say! You were never the one dragging me outside when it was still dark to feed the horses like Dad did! Still, I made sure I kept learning.      That's right, Myra, you did learn! Unlike me. I dropped out of secondary school to help my mother, and I haven't looked back. But now I spend most of my time watching old photos online and breakfast shows—relaxing this time of year after I used to live in Brighton.      Brighton’s always had so much going on. I remember walking around Waterfront with friends, and being so mad about not finding a decent parking spot! What did you do back then?      Oh, we used to circle the seafront for hours just to get a space – but it was worth it! Brighton was full of life back then. I remember betting on the horse racing with my mates and winning a few quid toward the week’s groceries.      I miss those pubs and the crowd. These days, it's all millennials and brunch! Some things don’t seem to change, though—like being able to find decent food!      I do miss the old markets where the vegetables were the freshest you could find. Not much like what you get at the supermarkets today. Speaking of which, have you managed to feed both children properly with all the healthy eating stuff you're always cooking up?      Honestly, it's a mission. They all love chips, but I try to sneak in beans or some vegetables. It's a tight line between being stubborn and getting them to eat lunches that keep them going all day.      Still, I remember bringing my three kids up the hard way— go out and get your own if you don’t like mine. But kids these days sure are spoiled, between food banks and benefits for disabilities.      You could say that. But at least there's support where it's needed now, even if not as easily to come by as some may think.

: You lot always exaggerate, mate. I mean, did you really try to hit a golf ball into a tree and then call it “straategic” just to make us laugh?     : Look, fair play to you, I respect what you’re saying. But let’s be real, when I went out last weekend and told the bloke I was “hitting the ball with precision and grace,” only to whack it into the next county, it was easier to call it a “tactical error” and blame the wind. Hence, “strategic.”     : Get out, I had no idea you made up golf terminology as you went along. That’s almost as bad as that one chap at uni who tried to play Shakespeare like it was GCSE lit, only to accidentally quote Oliver Twist and pick fights with everyone.     : Fair do’s. He honestly thought Falstaff was a surname, not some bloke in a funny tunic. And ever since he started being called “The Bard Bot,” he hasn’t lived it down. I mean, it’s not like being called “Spelling Sensitive Sean” or anything.     : That’s still better than my local nickname. My neighbour used to call me “The Man Who Can’t Find Mate,” because I mistook her cat for my phone charger and chased it into a hedge. It took me three mortal shames to get that one out of the village.     : Honestly, nicknames are the worst. At my uni, there was this lad called “The Spooner,” not because he used cutlery improperly, but because every time he spoke in a lecture, he made about five spoonerisms a sentence. “We should lit the fire this fag.” Honestly, you could write a cabaret routine off of that bloke.     : That’s brutal. I like yours better. Though I will say, if I ever open a café here in Wales, I’m calling it “The Cwtch Café.” See what your brain does with that pronunciation.     : Mate, that’s a death sentence with your sarcasm. Remember when you tried to fake a serious hobby so you could say you were “winning at life”? You ended up joining a model railway club and trying to look like it was deep, philosophical engineering.     : Okay, fair. But at least I made it to the conference seminar. Whereas you, you tried to teach someone belly dancing and ended up on the floor with a swirl of bed sheets and silence from the class.

Rather annoying I know, ain't it? That contractor lot down 'ead o' Doncaster they’re piling in heaps o' conferences on m’ desk at the minute! Got me head spinnin'.      Aw, seems like I got things turned on their head the other way. Got eeny plans at wok this week, an’ I haven't even got a dicky desk most a' the time! Just me hard knuckles an’ a shovel, innit?      Oh, cwazy! Me? I've been stuck chase of production lines like it's some meaty game of Russian roulette. One day everything is running smoothly, the next I'm on another mend job and needing a My turkey Diet, bless me! The new plan’s working okay, but I ain't shed as much as I’d hoped.      Blimey, at least you’re not stuck breakfast, no doubt about that! I’ve still got me inedible posh tray of ovo and feta to myself for the first time in three weeks since I joined Clean Water Quest.      Yikes, really? I thought Feta was as much as you could expect for something called fancy breakfast gear. Me on the My Turkey Diet, it feels like I'm living off dry turkey?      Listen, none of this means much if we’re all still flat out after work, innit?      Tellin’ the truth, I’m in this someone’s chicken and wine lifestyle. Just trying to keep a room to myself is a nightmare. Shared floring, and half my mates think I live here!      Look, as far as living in about nowhere, I’m not bad off living the touch-up life at this boarding house. At least you ain't got to be telling you’re a laying it out unival for gal to have your space ‘cos they need to hang guest.      Aint bad me, as it is. My mate Jess and me have a mini flat, just waiting till we get a crack to clear up and maybe sprite of doing a weekend space.      A whippit of doin' nothin' but a couple of drinks and some chats, innit? go out of my day life if you ask me.      Yeah, let's see if we could go further, maybe something weekend near your place Mike? So I don’t have to manage navigation and manage roles in Cambridge!      Wot's to say? I say, ‘cause this is the start o' a cracking string of conversations...

Rather a lot’s happened in the garden since I last gave you a tour, Peggy. What with the recent weather, the plants are growing like barmy things. I’ve had to cull a bit of bamboo near the fence—cut it back before it decided to move in next door again.      Oh, William, don’t be so negative. I reckon it just wanted to have a chat. You should’ve put a little sign on the bamboo: “Knock first!” I’ve had some interesting chats with plants myself when no one was looking. Funny how people these days get bent out of shape over a little fencing.      Aye, listen to the pair of you. You’re both like actors at a university play. Still, enough talk of greenery—what about the eclipse the other day, Vivian? Made quite the impression on me. Sat with a cup of tea and a bit of breakfast, blinking at that sun like a half-witted fool in a basewi’!      Oh, I had the television on for that, and goodness me, I do miss the days when we’d just enjoy the occasional bit of nature without a fuss. Now, it’s all politically correct and over-thought. You can't say a word in that house without someone springing up and adding three new words just to make sure you’re educated.      Truth be told, I preferred watching through the telescope Vivian borrowed from the Science Centre. Clever woman, she was. Always full of facts about the cosmos: black holes, the big bang, beginnings of space—piece of work, some of it.      Can’t say I fancied it all, but I did enjoy the programme about painting the other week. Got the urge to chuck some colours at a canvas myself. Sat there with that frosty egg sandwich and a cuppa, watching this man do something proper ‘cos he was alive rather than glued to the sofa.      I know it well. Proper uplifts the soul, doesn’t it? Not unlike looking at your garden, William. Those borders of yours are doing a right grand job with that new owl box up near the shed. Some lad next door put one up, too. Said it was for the kestrels.environment buzzword much?      Just don’t expect me to chuck in the telly licence any time soon, though. I’ve had some dodgy encounters with the man in the past.

Rather annoying this, innit? Stuck in the car with no signal and this GPS backtrackin' like it got a cow's brain. Y'know, down 'ere in Sunderland, we’d just ask someone for directions. Not like up North, I s’pose.      Oh come on, love, I used the sat-nav and it said we’d be here in ten minutes. I reckon that was before it worked out the best route. Harpenden ain’t exactly what I'd call 'easy to find'.      Didn’t even want to come 'ere. I said, “Are we really goin’ to this posh place to eat?” But you went on about needing posh turkey on Christmas Eve, did you not?      And I reckon you're grateful, ain't you? A good little local joint with proper meat and a nice sauce. Not breakfast at the chippy at half past ten like last time. Though at least we knew where that was — just follow the smell of battered potatoes!      Alright, alright, tell you what — we find a place up near that cathedral, innit? The one with the pointy spires. I’ve read something about it once, something about it being from the 1200s or sommat. I wouldn’t mind walkin’ there after a good dinner.      You mean St. Albans Cathedral? That’s not in Harpenden, that’s forty miles beyond. If we’re not even in the right town, we’re definitely not going forty miles further.      Oh, I didn’t even think about that, love. Not my fault I misread the bloody map! I swear it looked different on Google. Not like a house where your uncle lives is that hard to find. Doesn’t it even have a postcode?      It does, but the sat-nav insists it's 'Harpenden ', which is bloody vague. And there’s no bus stop for miles. I could’ve just run back and flagged one down if we’d taken the bus with lunches, innit? At least the bus driver knows where he's going.      Look, all I’m goin’ on is that if you'd left ten minutes earlier, we'd be in, out, and back with a box of brie and a bottle of red by now.      Oh, and you’d have driven, innit? You'd be lost by now and arguing with a lamppost.      Now that I’d be proud to admit, yeah! At least I wouldn’t take us two hours to get to a restaurant.

Rather annoying this newfit alarm clock o’ mine, is. Keeps goin’ off ‘fore I’m ready, and I’ll often jolt up like a startled bairn, sure I’d best be off to teach… when I’ve only ten minutes till breakfast!      Aye, I know exactly wot yeh mean. Me ‘ookeeper’s been givin’ me a right hard time too. I’ve set it so too early, an’ now I’m bless’d if I ain’t doin’ me exercises by the time I wake up properly, or still in me socks head-high like a fool!      That’s the problem wi’ ly’k us in our years—y’can’t rely on luck to left well enough alone. I’ve had me back playin’ up agin lately. Ate too many sour grapes in the garden, and ‘ave been breakfastin’ mostly on toast this past week! Havin’ me teeth checked’s becomin’ quite a regular affair, I must say.      Oh dear, do tell, is it bad? Lucy—my cousin—had a tooth removed as it were, and only ten days later, had a right good bleedin’ nose. She says it all got her so worked up – especiall’ with the chap, and now he won’t eat bananas because the sight of ‘em makes ‘im feel queasy.      That sounds most worrying! Now, what ‘ave we been up too lately? Ah, yes, the birds. I left a basin out in the garden this mornin' wi’ a ‘feeble’ mess o’ breadcrumbs, and it weren’t about five minutes ‘till the goldfinches were lit upon it like larks at a harvest ceilidh.      Aye, aye, I’ve quite the squirrel ‘problem’ now. Nutty little critters are, really. I have me feeder strung up where any ‘at all can reach it, and I’ve taken to sortin’ out my seeds as if I were at the market! Yellow ones for the canaries and whiffs o’ black ones for the sparrows.      A regular man of the house goin’ on! But if you ask me, real fun comes wi’ dentin’ out that bird’s song – ‘ave you heard the gray one singin’ in your backyard o’ late? It sounds like someone’s violin nappin’ off in the wind.      ‘Tis mighty hard to silence them! Occasionally I’ll go out ‘keeping an eye for the buttercups and daisies, and it always feels as if I'm in a whole concert of chattering-tongues.

Rather skip the starter and just go for the mushroom risotto. I haven’t had it in ages — and honestly, the thought of waiting another five minutes for more salad puts me in a right foul mood!      You do know the starter came as a side, don’t you? They sent it over because we  said we were sharing one . But I reckon it’s about as likely they’ll let you skip the starter as they would serve that risotto warm, so you’d best just grin and bear it.      Oh for goodness’ sake — can’t they even  properly  listen to a simple request these days? I mean, it’s the  second  time this week someone’s misheard me, and I’ve only been to the post office and back!      Aye, and I think it’s because we all talk in whispers now, don’t we? Too mindful of being overheard online these days, or some such nonsense. People’s minds are so loaded with doomscrolling, they can’t even hold a conversation properly. It’s exhausting.      I’ve had enough of it myself — quite honestly, if I hear another post about IVF, book parties, or passive lifestyles, I may scream. Be it humblebragging or just another person talking at me about their least exciting weekend,  honestly ...      Ugh, don’t even get me started on the passive lifestyle lot. There are people out there who think owning a plant is a hobby now. And they call themselves  influencers ? They’d better have a grant from the National Trust, I swear.      You know I did something far more interesting than all of that the other week — I finally sat down and wrote what I’ve been meaning to write for  ages . It’s not a novel, but it’s something, and for once, it’s not for someone else — it’s for  me .      Oh, I love that, Ellie. I’ve been thinking about doing something like that too, but I just feel like I’m always trying to catch up with the “hype” of the next best thing. Still, if you’re truly doing it for the joy of it, that’s the best thing about getting older — we finally give a toss about line approval, don’t we?      Aye — and we’ve learned how to take the seriously ridiculous with a pinch of salt and a tea bag soaked in dry shampoo.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? I needed a cup of tea after walking the kids back from the park. You've got a nice garden, by the way. Very well kept.      Aye, thanks! I like to sit outside on these days. It gets a bit quiet once you're retired, you understand. Light gardening keeps me on my toes. Yourself—still teaching? I remember you were at the primary school before.      Oh yes, I switched to teaching adults a few years ago. Mostly ESOL—people wanting to speak better English. You know how it is, more immigrants around these parts now. I do miss the children, though. There was something about that energy.      Aye, I know what you mean. Taught for thirty years, mostly secondary. I think the hardest part of teaching is watching the world move on while you're stuck with the same textbooks and budgets decreasing.      That’s awfully true! I mean, even in adult education, funding is tight. I’ve had to learn how to juggle—personally taking on extra hours sometimes. You don’t mention your family much. Do you live alone?      Aye, my wife passed a few years back. Only child’s settled down in Manchester. I’m still getting used to the quiet, but the community here helps. We’ve got a weekly phone call. Bit rushed, mind you! She always wants to know if I've got a new dating profile.      That's oddly endearing. My husband’s very into technology these days—keeps me on my toes trying to make sense of it all. He made me an online course to teach the basics of the English language. We chuckle most of the time.      That sounds lovely. Technology is a bit of a bridge, isn’t it? Keeps us connected no matter how far apart we live. Speaking of which, have you heard about the proposed new library down the road? They say it’ll have IT suites and adult education courses.      No, not yet. I suppose I haven't been out much these last few months. You think it'll help around here? More people coming into the area go straight online, but it's not always safe. Crime rates have been slipping up in Birmingham, haven’t they?      Yes, some of the older parts have been affected. Still, I'd rather live in a place with a little hassle than in a sterile, modern flat in the city where I don't know a soul.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh? You’d think in Cambridge we’d know if it’s ‘goin’ to pour or not by now. I’m more used to Leeds—always sure we’d have a grey sky followin’ us about like a bad smell!      Aye, it’s not nice at  all . Sunderland’s rain feels different—more like it's dancin’ on your face instead o’ flatlinin’ everythin’. Still, easier said than done to get out of it. We’ve got sommat cookin’ up for the weekend, anyway. You lot comin’ to the lakeland picnic?      Lakeland? In  this  weather? I’m more of a doorstep adventurer these days. Fun left the house when I moved to Londonish, you know. But I’d say yes if the forecast didn’t make everyone sound like a Chicken Little! Wait, is it even allowed to rain in Anglo-Saxon myth in Cambridge? Legend’s got to hold out, surely.
