Real cheek, Nick, real cheek—moving over to Kent, gettin’ all posh up in Pembury, and now you’ve got the  nerve  to mock Cambridge’s weather… You reckon you’re nearer to Kent then, or Saxons?      True, true, and none of us are  exactly  weather sommeliers. But hey, the whole point of the picnic is that Liam’s promised to teach us all how to make proper chicken Tikka masala. That stuff alone is worth dragging a tent across a soaked field for.      Now  that’s  music to my ears! Look, as someone who once nearly set off a fire while making risotto, the promise of a foreign taste lingers like a siren’s call. Just don’t let Liam cook the bread, will ya? He’s the type to ‘toast’ bread into toast that’s more like charcoal.      Ha! I remember that time he insisted he was ‘artistic’ with the toaster. Poor spoon stickin’ out as he rushed off to ‘get more butter’. Mark my words, the man’s got the charisma of an omelette set on a charcoal grill.      Yeah, go on then, James—let Liam take the reins. Show respect to the man in specs who’s had engineering behind him, not in front of him. And Mike, don’t you bring any of that North Yorkshire gravy, we’d miss the point entirely.      Fair enough. But if he over-seasons the food, I’m blaming  you , Liam. Unless I’m unconscious from the taste.

: Right lads and lasses, I've been thinking. I need to get back into the gym. I got a bit soft after lockdown. Anyone go to any good gyms in Cambridge lately?     : Honestly, I’ve been meaning to as well. The weather’s been so nice it’s easy to forget, but I’m told the new gym on Trumpington Road's actually really nice — a bit pricier, but they’ve got this amazing climbing wall. Oh, and they offer some interesting classes like aerial yoga and dance cardio. Bit girly for you blokes, but well worth it if you like to mix it up.     : That's the one I go to on and off. My friend Amber works there as a trainer and got me a discount. I go to the spin classes, they're absolutely brutal but fun. They screamed at me the first time — not nice at all, but it worked!     : Haha, yeah, I’d be the one screaming too, probably. Still, I think I’ll give it a go. I need something to motivate me.     : I can be your personal pain-free cheerleader. I’ll be on the treadmill next to you, watching Netflix while you work out. Be healthy, not pretentious.     : Haha, typical Lucy. You know, while you're all getting in shape, I’m thinking about trying a digital detox and going on a solo weekend trip up the coast. Brighton or somewhere. Maybe also check out a music festival? It's been oddly quiet on the music front recently.     : Oh, you should! I actually had a colleague at work who went to Brighton last week and came back with this story about finding the best chip shop in the whole of England. She even met her future manager or something. Doesn’t sound unromantic in that weird artsy way.     : Oh will you please cut that out? You'll scar the children. But yeah, Brighton sounds fun. I might even drag little Arlo out of the house for a few days. He’s at summer camp this week anyway, so I’ve got freedom.     : Still, I’m going with Gemma on the Brighton idea. I bet it's better than sweating your arse off at the gym.     : You might be right, Daniel. I’ll see your gym and raise you with a beach walk and a live kinaesthetic experience at a jazz club.     : Oh come on, that sounds amazing.

Rather annoying that the ref’s given us a red card, innit? That’ll make it real tough to stay in the game, especially with ten minutes left to go.      Aye, it were a harsh one. Should’ve given the striker a penalty at least. Look how he went een! That’s  not  fair play if I’ve ever seen it.      Aye, but I think he tacked too high. Still, we’ve got Premier League standards to live up to! You’d think referees were trained at the pub when it comes to decision-making some days...       laughs  I reckon they’re just out to make sure we’ve got a bit of turkey on our Easter dinner!      Ten o'clock on the telly, innit? We’ve got the world cup final to watch in the morning, and you better not breakfast on the sofa if I’ve happened to miss a goal in my sleep!      You can have the spare room laptop if it makes you feel better. I’ll give it a rest and watch some of those mid-90s sci-fi films as usual.  Men in Black  again today, innit?      Oh, don’t start that again! You know it’s got a load of sci-fi clichés in there, but the film were fun.      Aye, well, we’ve all got our guilty pleasures. Like this Sunderland team full of clichés.       laughs  Tell me about it! Though, at least they’re trying to get back into the top flight. I heard one of the researchers at work about to finish his PhD on motivation techniques for the club.      A PhD on  football motivation ? That’s barely a week away from a  PhD on the evolutionary chain of Burgers !      Aye, and I told him the most important motivation any player needs is the thought of a takeaway curry on a Saturday night. That’s real motivation, innit?       laughs  I think it works for the team, the PhD student, and us, honestly.      Yeah, go on then, get your curry and watch  Men in Black —I’ll be in the study figuring out why the boxset of films from the ‘90s all depict aliens as big, grey men with goggly eyes.      It’s to contrast humans—like, ‘look at us, we’re the natural ones’! Silliness all round, like football referees today.      And like half the Easter eggs you hide for the kids—they’re all in places you can’t remember and end up wondering if someone else placed them!

Rather skip to the front of the book, isn’t it? A few hurrahs for when the first one got the diploma, same with the second one more recently. Not a bad show himself, that boy. I was chuffed to bits when the photos came back from the graduation.      That was my  best day ever . I didn’t know if I was going to cry or whoop with joy. I still have that photo of me and my uncle Tim; he used to travel all the way to Cork just to give me advice before exams. Didn’t always want to listen, but looks like I should’ve.      Ah, Tim was the fire, always knew where to push you and what to leave be. Still, you turned out alright, didn’t you, laddie? D’you know, I think he saved your photo in an iCloud folder by the name of ‘ש breakfasts and Bucks’? I mean Brian, alright — in his own style, you know?      Grandpa, he called it 'Breakfasts and Bucks', not 'ש breakfasts'. You’d listen more if I put two words together.      And off we’ll go again — best not to provoke the IT men. Well, from what I’ve seen at the Baptism of his first-born, and now these photos, he’s a proper lad. Now don’t go making him embarrassed at his upcoming birthday. Last year you had that Pikachu banner and he was five.      That was just a rush order, we had a week’s notice. Also, he liked the marshmallows being shaped like Pikachu. That  was  a good idea. I did make the birthday cards for the kids, the red one’s his favorite. Not much else in the pipeline though — sorry, love.      You could plan something to do with a ‘marathon theme’ for guest entrance — like they all run into the house with a sponge. Or a cinema afternoon with all the movies they liked as a child. I saw somewhere they did that for a seven-year-old’s 7th.      Granda, I do like the cinema. My grandad used to take me to the one in the city when it go the 3D comeback. It cost a fortune but I think he just wanted popcorn, not that I was complaining.      Ah your grandad was the lilt — big-hearted to a fault and always after some excitement. Much like your Uncle Brian, now that I come to think of it.

Rather lovely to have you both over for dinner, Fran. I've been trying out this new lemon and herb recipe, and I thought it'd be nice to share it with family. I've found over the years that food brings people closer, wouldn’t you agree, Mabel?      Thank you, Deborah. I  am  partial to a well-seasoned roast chicken myself. It’s been a long week managing the admin team; just the thought of putting my feet up and not having to deal with disciplinary forms is a gift! Speaking of which, do you remember when your mum used to make those spiced applesauce to go with it?      Oh, the applesauce was always warm, and there was always a bit of cinnamon in it. Funnily enough, back in the Sixties, you couldn’t get cinnamon very easily in the shops round Peterborough. Had to write to Middlesbrough if you wanted a proper bit!      That does sound a world away from today! I mean, ordering cinnamon’s a click away these days. Speaking of which—did I tell you, Fran, I’ve started knitting up some jumpers for the children as their birthday gifts?      Oh, that’s brilliant. My neighbour used to knit when she got her diagnosis. It gave her something to focus on, helped her mind take a rest from the worry. I reckon it’s quite therapeutic.      Therapeutic, yes! I used to knit those little bears out of wool when I was a bit younger. You’d line the ears with red thread or black—looked very smart. It's amazing how the world moves on, really. I remember when the children would come home about five o'clock every day all excited to play marbles or hopscotch.      That brings back such fond memories! I grew up near Boston, so we'd have those big fields for playing Pooh sticks or chasing after hedgehogs. Nothing electronic at all—just the simple things. And those times are very relatable, you know, because today’s kids are always glued to some sort of screen.      It’s a real “it’s a small world” situation, isn't it? You come from different places and generations, but end up connected by the same life experiences—cooking, knitting, hopscotch. I was watching that programme about nostalgic British box sets the other night. ‘Bread’ and all that. I must’ve watched it a hundred times growing up.

Rather fine day today, isn't it? That sun's doin' me right good after that string of grey mornings. I've just boiled the kettle for more tea. You need a cup, love?      Aye, please, I'd love a spot of tea. Just put the last of the sandwiches on the table. Made them with the leftover ham and some of that lovely cheddar from the dairy. A shame we can’t get more of that sort of cheese these days, what?      Aye, was the best for a sarnie, that was. Tastes different these days, more like cardboard! Not like back when I were younger and real cheese still came in slabs like that. Remember when you’d get meltable stuff for bursts on pies?      Oh, I do, and I used to love bursting a flake in the pan, wait for it to get all melty then dunk a bit of bread in it. Oh, the dreams, the dreams! Used to make the lads laugh when I’d tell 'em I was taking a fry-up just for a snack!      Aye, well, as long as you weren’t off on the hop again, was it all good fun. But I suppose that sort of way is gone now – no one takes their time like that. Everything's slapdash these days. You couldn’t do that sort of thing without the phone buzzin’ or somethin’.      Oh, someone at the phone for ten minutes! That’s just a waste of time, if you ask me. Much better to have a proper chin-wag with tea and a decent sandwich! We’ve got us a right good chatter here, don’t we? Don’t know when the last time I had a decent chat like this was.      Aye, it is a proper bobble to have someone to talk to. I’ve been mighty lonesome since Mavis went up. Still leave the seat by the fire warm for her, mind.      I know how you feel, love. Sometimes I swear I’ve seen more of the birds outside than I have of the people in here! We should do this more often, you know.      Oh, go on then, come over more often. I’ll make more sandwiches.      With extra cheese this time, I hope!      Aye, and maybe I’ll manage a pie or two after that! We'll really make a belly of ourselves!      Perfection, Frank.

Rather annoying I had to take the bus in to work this morning. My car's decided it's not starting... again. I swear it's just doing it to wind me up.      Oh no, that sounds like a nightmare! I had a similar problem with mine last week — the battery just pack up. I had to leave it outside my mate’s house while I cycled back. It was a bit of a laugh. Not the best Monday morning, to be honest.      Oh, why don't you just take the train instead? I mean, with how often yours seems to break, it's not like it's saving you much time. I've taken the train almost every day now that MyUniCard's free until August.      Probably, but I like the drive. It's one of the few things I can spend an hour alone in peace. Though if it doesn't start again tomorrow I'll probably re-evaluate that outlook.      Honestly, I'd consider giving up the car altogether. I'm thinking of walking or using one of those bike hire schemes. I mean, the occasional falcon sprint through the park to work might do me the world of good.      You'd last a day. You'd be booking a limo by Tuesday with your backside in agony.      Yeah, she tries to be all healthy and then collapses on the sofa after half an hour. And let’s be honest, someone who eats four bags of chocolate digestives a week? Definitely not a cyclist.      Okay, okay, I accept the groans. But I'm  trying  to be fit. I did five burpees yesterday!      Ha, I'm going to take you up on that. Let's do a workout challenge next week.      My grandma does more burpees.      So funny. I have told her the same thing a few times. Speaking of, I tried to make her a cake for her birthday. It turned out like something off of  Phantom Planet  with layers of mud and chocolate glue.      Oh no, was it a fail or a disaster zone?      It wasn't edible or edible.      I think I might have genuinely burnt the box while I was trying to ‘add some warmth to the centre’. The smoke alarm really gave me a shout out.      It's alright, we can say it was overcooked in the middle and just needed extra marshmallows. You know I'm helping you get out of this.

Rather annoying this new bar across the road innit? Seems like everything sticks out in this ‘hood these days... got to be some sort of local investment scheme, eh? I mean, sure, where we are in L8 is £20 a pint and dodgy wi-fi, but now it’s turning into een kind of place  proper . Or so they want us to think.      Oh aye, I’ve noticed. Not that I go anywhere social, but.Gridlow used to be a dump, innit? Now it’s like the set of some BBC show, or somethink. I fetch the bins every Friday even, just because I like me peace. What I don’t lik e is the noise at the weekend, specially if they’re playing football left and right. Ten o'clock on a Saturday and the bin lorry and the Premier League blaring from every flat in the lane!      I heard the bar’s run by some returning HOSPITALITY lads from Leeds. Proper awards and fookin Michelin stars and all that. I dunno, I mean I do admin, not chef, but still—somebody in that bar probably wants to do their own grief. Anyway, what I asked earlier: did you read the new Harry Potter book then, Mr. Gripsby –?      Far from it! I’ve only read up to Book Three and haven’t finished Silmarillion yet. ‘Balances the narrative’ as they say in academia. Though, I did get invited to a read-through at the library for  The Return of the King —we got a grant and all. Anyhoo, I’m more into ballet and existentialism most nights about now.      Wait! So are there any ghosts in the houses around here? My grandad told me that house ‘cos of the treble guest entrance used to be a jail for something ‘esoteric’ or somethink. Not that I believe him—he told me the queens were holed up in a tower here trying to find the right Granger whiskee.      Oh, aye, that one. I told meself it go bad vibes on day one if you ask me. Just don’t go into the cellars. I had a job cleaning up there once—and I swear your legs start shaking. It was like I lost 3 kgs of confidence out the window just walking down them steps. True to life, innit?      Cursed houses tend to    vocal dissonance / interruption       And always, Mr. Philosopher. Just make sure when you’re writing that thesis, you don’t scribble in red ink in the library.

Rather exciting to be planning a trip to Nepal, isn't it, Ethel? I do think it's high time I saw some of the Himalayas properly.      Oh, absolutely! It is rather thrilling. When I was your age, I hitchhiked through India with a student backpack and practically no plan, but we do things very differently these days. Of course, all the comforts now. I’ve only done a little Ayurvedic retreat in Rajasthan, but I’d love to explore some monasteries and maybe go to the Ghandruk villages. Do you want to hire a guide?      I couldn’t imagine doing it without one. I mean, only two people in our village ever went to Nepal, bless them — an eccentric couple who lived off bottle gourds and lentils during their entire journey and said every single morsel had an adventure of its own.      Heh, I happened to visit a monastery in Bhutan once, thanks to an old school friend of mine who worked at the embassy. Goodness, those sausages they served me, wrapped in banana leaves and spiced I don’t know how! Still, I didn’t tell my doctor when I returned — he’d have had a proper fit.      Oh, my Richard would have laughed himself silly, and then made me a chicken and leek pasta dish because he thought that would be something resembling a British comfort. Actually, he’s our kitchen general now. Our food is far better since he retired.      That’s oddly enviable. My husband still insists on going to the Farm Shop and being ‘adventurous’. I had to stop him last week when he picked up ‘spicy bean medley’ without reading the ingredients. It was gluten-free, thanks be! Going gluten-free is madness now, isn’t it?      It certainly has made menu reading rather complicated. Though I suppose it's better than wartime meals — my mother-in-law was evacuated all the way from Siberia to Africa during the war, survived on boiled potatoes and lentils.      Oh, that’s a new one on me. I do love a good wartime story. But enough of that — back to the trip. Are we still hoping on the direct from Heathrow or are we taking the detour to Kathmandu via Kathiawar, as the travel agency suggested?      Detour it is. We might even bike out from Pokhara if we feel up to it. Just don’t fall and sprain your ankle like at the last Iron Man.

Rather annoying this new event planning software, innit? Seems easier talkin’ to me nan ‘n typin’ on it!      Blows me mind, actually. I mean, where I am at work we do use the same kind of things — project management tools — but if it een’t clear, just shout at the team an’ they’ll come runnin’!      Aww, but serious tho — this stuff isn’t so bad if you’ve had some time to get clued in. Leeds University did give us a run through, but still… brains not wires, like.      Aye, that’s the real debate now, innit? Man versus machine? Just wish I had someone who’d left themselves a note back in 2019, telling me this was comin’ up!      Honestly? I think we’re all just trying to survive this week. My last week in production at the factory, and it’s like, you didn’t see the mess I had to sort out before I even sat down for coffee, luv.      Bah — well, as long as you’re takin’ it as a chance to move on, right? Ya know, when the old way is no good anymore… it’s got to be better elsewhere, yeah?      Truth — don’t get me wrong, I like the work. ‘Balances out’, as we say. Like this work — full on, but I’ve got my own flair for it. I mean, plannin’s all about meetin’ folk, and being ‘prioritised’.      Sounds glam about it! I’m stuck in admin hell, touch wood — cups of coffee and document stuff. But I dunno, I’m thinkin’ of upping sticks up North in a bit. Fresh ‘start’ and all that clap.      Aye, well, it’d be something fresh, at least. I dunno how long I’ll last here stickin’ to queens and copying papers. But I’m waitin’ for the right role to whack up online, innit?      Just make sure you lot don’t end goin’ on your own about it. If we go one by one, who’ll gather for that brutal weekend trip in a bloomin’ van to your nan’s?      Haha, sounds like we’d need a roadmap, not just friends! True to say, though — that trip over this summer’s promised to be a belter. S’all go down in history, luv.      Listen, let’s get that sorted out. Just make a group and tag each other in it — like you would plan an event!

Rather annoying this, isn't it? The council wants to knock the old library down. They've got to be joking, I mean, it's got history, don't they? I've been in that library since I was a kid.      It's ridiculous. We've put in so many letters and emails, but no one seems to take notice. Someone needs to start a proper petition, a paper one, not just online—get that stubby pen and send it into the records office, you know?      That's what I've been thinking too. I reckon if we get a decent number of local signatures, maybe hand it in with some photos of the place, people might have to listen. I know you work early mornings—you might not get a look in by the time you’re done, but maybe pick it up in the evening?      Yeah, I can manage breakfast, but I tend to just drop everyone off and drive in. Maybe I can pick it up on the way, or even take a break and grab a few details directly from the shop floor. My shifts are always shifting, aren’t they? I never bloody know where I am half the time.      It’s funny, isn’t it? The council all got their little meetings and –  ha!  – their experts, and none of them seem to know what the people actually need. All that brain training and their use of mnemonics fails them every bloody time, huh? Like, someone said ‘policies should reflect the people’—well, not in Plumstead.      I know, and I swear it’s all top-down nonsense. Look, as long as we have about forty or so signatures by the end of the week, we’ll show them. Maybe even get some media attention. Have you got that pen I lent you?      That green one with the leopard print? No, you passed it to me once and I lent it on. But I’ve got my own. I’ll start collecting them tomorrow when I’m out on the run. Just hand them over to the lady at the front with a nice word and maybe a digestive.      That’s a good idea. Popping into the library is one go-to-place on your own map. It’s got so much in it, even in the back, between the shelves—papers, old films, whatnot. It’s like a time capsule in there.

Rather fine day today, isn't it? That sun's doin' me right good after that mizzle yest'day. Bet them Jehovah’s lot will be about, knockin' on doors agin. I always tell me missus they’re like the pest on a well-worn gate — can’t eeny harm ye, but they’re a pest all the same.      Oh aye, I remember one time they came t’ this old biddy down the road, bless her, who ain't clued in to the modern ways and nearly gave chase when they told her 'nothing’s too trivial f'r the truth'. Mary used to laugh like mad, but the poor soul still lets 'em in like they’re visitin’ royalty!      Well, I can't see the point in arguein’ with ‘em. A body might just say "Oh, aren’t you very polite," and leave it at that. Now, Brian, did I tell you about the cookout the Smiths had? They brought puffin pie from the coast. I reckon we should go out one of these days—personally, I’d take a bit of puffin over that tarted-up grief of ham and eggs any day.      Aye, been a few good meals out since the new parkin’ orders. I almost lost me vent to a lime suit last week causin’ me car to clock up £40 in fines. ‘Balances the budget for toilets and bins in this here village,’ one of ‘em said. Pah! It just goes to some fancy accountant’s hotter chuck!      I’d be givin’ ‘em a clip round the ear if I did. Not that I’d have bin round the area, mind. I had me dentistry fixed thanks to the cap, so I shouldn’t be worrying about parkin’ tickets.      Oh, Brian, if you start shoutin’ at sundry strangers, me grandkids would laugh their heads off. Speaking of, I hear there’s a little one getting wed in the spring. Those young things these days, they’re always popping the question when I’m not watching! They're such a good bunch, you remember Jack? He’s head of some group—environment or goenvironment or one of them names that sounds like a real ramble.      Oh, Jack? The one bloke who’s always ‘pro-something’ and ‘against-other-things’ and still finds time to collect those plastic bottles by the river bend. He’s a wonder in that ‘eco hippy’ lot o’ his.

Rather annoying the new restaurant’s smoke finds its way into the back garden, isn’t it, Peter? We’d got used to the quiet evenings after dining at home. I can’t say I miss the smell much, though.      That and the children at the end of the street — if they’re not vocalising, they’re drilling somewhere. Having your parents-in-law over for tea doesn’t help a bit. A lot of shouting tends to happen from their back garden. Oh, and what was it, Jane? You mentioned you had to buy a new log burner?      Yes, specially because the prior one had malfunctioned. I can no longer rely on the fire supply only, especially with the winter biting at our heels. You must remember, though, Peter darling, back in the days I used to withstand even the coldest Scottish winds without the help of artificial warmth.      The logistics of it all are more modern than they were when I was in teaching. Today’s children deal with desktops, not even looking up. We had coal once, yes, and I used to do the rounds of the school academy with a small stove in hand — quite a different world altogether.      I might go on a walk for the fresh air, it feels like the only chance to breathe – unless it's raining. I saw a new antique store opened on the high street, supposedly with quite a few homely things. You know what it is, don’t you — fudge, old furnishing — but it could also be boring. Ever been a fan of fudge, mother-in-law?      Oh, delicious and very nostalgic. Reminded me of when I used to make it in about five variations for the school carnivals. One had orange zest, another had nuts. The children would circle round like bees to honey.      You could run your own celebration with that. Meanwhile, the budget for guestrooms will have to be cut somewhere. I suggested to the higher ups a few months ago that some of the tasks could be done by people in India who are already good at what they do. Rather than getting it done with lunches and a new sofa from the upholder, the money could be set aside for something more pressing.      That go-to-place on your own street is always there for you. But I agree with Peter, we must assess what we can loosen in the budget.

Rather annoying this new tax they’ve brought in, isn’t it? I was just reading the  Norwich Evening News  and it says they're now charging more on second homes. I've been thinking about buying a flat in Norwich for the winter months, but this tax might put a stop to it.      Aye, I heard about that as well. Costessey's all agog with it. I don’t know where they get the money from, to be honest. The council was already pulling in more than a few quid from us for refuse collection. And yet the bins still don’t get emptied properly. I had lettuce growing in the back garden last week from the rotting veg!      My Harry, bless him, he still uses a Sat Nav like it’s the only way to survive, even though he used to drive blindfold round Harrow with his eyes closed. Now he won’t get in the car if he hasn’t got a blue light in his hand! I pity the poor man — he’s even looking for the motorway slip roads like he’s walking around Watergate.      I’ve noticed the same with people — even round here in Norfolk. I tell you, when I was a civil engineer on the A11, I’d put the signs in, and now no one even looks at them, least of all the younger ones. All the time pressing buttons and looking at their phones instead of the road.      And the recycling’s getting more confusing by the day. They keep changing the rules. First it was just glass, then it was paper and cans, and now they want you to separate fruit skins from meat bones —  what  are they doing with it, I ask you? I reckon they just throw it all in the bin again.      That’s another thing that grates — the TV. These new channels are full of jungle nonsense and overpaid footballers. There used to be proper dramas with plots and characters, not the same faces just arguing on different decks.      Aye, I agree with you there. At least the pension’s doing alright for now. I’ve got a little bit from the civil service, but it’s far from luxury. Mind you, it’s better than watching the bank go broke every year.      That’s one thing I don’t understand, the politics. It always seems to be the same arguing, one lot promising you the moon and the next promising to build a wall across it.

Rather annoying this, the laptop's playin’ up again. I've had it fixed twice since we first brought it home.      Are you going to take it back to where you bought it, Dad? Maybe they'll give you a new one if it's still under warranty.      That's the plan, if the warranty covers it. But I wanted to see if a local lad I know, Davy, could have a look at it first. He runs a tech shop in Ballincollig.      If it's still under warranty, isn’t it risky to let a local fix it? What if it voids the warranty, and you end up paying twice? My brother had that with his phone.      Probably, but if I tell Darcy, he might say it’s the same brand. It's just about the software at the moment. No harm in letting him take a quick look, I reckon.      What’s he charge to look at it?      It's only €20 if he can't fix it—nothing if it’s under warranty. If he can fix it, then maybe €40 max. It's not bad for peace of mind, really.      Well, at least it's cheep.      Yeah, better than waiting to see if the phone’s place sends it out for a month while we pay extra for expedited.      Mmmya?      That’s my cue—go weigh your muddy boots into the kitchen, Seamus.      Should we have about the rugby game after dinner? I’m thinking touch rugby at the park—Tom and a few others said they’d come.      Sounds a plan, but if the computer takes time to fix, I’ll tell Darcy to drop it here on the weekend.      What about supper? We haven't eaten yet. You mad or just stickin’ to fajita sauce again, Niall?      More likely the chicken took the sauce than the other way around. I had it in the slow cooker by mistake go bad. I’ll see if the fishmonger still has barrack ready to cook.      That’d be nicer than what your computer’s dispensin’.      Can we eat after I go for a swim at the pool? I promised to meet Kyle.      Go ahead, laddie. You’ll get refreshed and back for supper. Make sure you tell Seamus he's not to copy your flippy swimming move.      He’s just like you before he talks, always sticking his ears out like he’s trying to hear his reflection.

Rather than share a lengthy account, let me describe what occurred. A promising meeting was arranged, only to be abruptly called off at the eleventh hour. It was expected to bring together several key individuals, yet there was suddenly a complete change of plans. No one had been informed in advance. It was quite confusing and left many in disarray.        Alright, so basically, all the excitement disappeared in an instant. It’s like someone reached in and just pulled the plug on a big, hopeful moment. That sounds pretty frustrating. Did it hit everyone like a slap in the face or was it more of a... like, a quiet letdown?          Wow, only to have it cancelled like that at the last moment. It must have felt like someone hit you with a brick wall from nowhere. D’you think it was just a fluke or was there actually a reason for it? Because honestly, it sounds like total chaos to me.          Just imagine the look on everyone's faces when the meeting got the axe. One minute, they were all geared up and ready, and the next, everything was up in the air. Like a storm swept in and knocked everything off its axis. You’ve got to be kidding me, right?          O – Mate, talking about a let down like that is just bonkers. You imagine all the time and effort that must have gone into setting the meeting up, and then—poof, gone. Like a balloon being popped in your face. Just because it was a rush call-off doesn’t mean it’s not ridiculous, is it?          Honestly, it’s like someone pressed the emergency stop button about five minutes before the big setup was due to go live. One second you're standing there with sandwiches and notepads, and then—wham! The whole plan went out the window. Makes you wonder if someone just got cold feet last minute.          Just the timing of it was all kinds of messed up. It’s not like anyone saw it coming. It was as mysterious as a disappearing cat or a lost sock in the machine. No one gets to have a say, it just happens. Genuinely wild.          Can you really get your head around that? If it was at the last minute like that, no one had a chance to box punches or even catch their breath. It’s like someone said, “Okay, let’s cancel the team bonding trip hours after the venue was booked."

Rather annoying the queue at immigration eh? You’d think they’d have more people on in peak season.      Aye, I’m more used to Heathrow, sure we’d queue there but it was always faster. Still, the view from our table is well worth the wait.       Looks around the restaurant  Yes, I reckon this is the best choice of all the places we looked at when we got here. The view, the friendly staff, and bless me, the portions are generous!      Oh the chase when it comes to decision-making isn’t it? We’ve been spoilt with places so far, but this has a lovely ambiance. You can almost hear the waves from here.      Can we go back to the beach later? You promised we’d pick up a seashell for mummy and I’d like a nice one!      Of course love. After this I reckon we’ll lounge by the pool for a bit, you can gather some shells while I soak up the sun. It’s warm enough for that, don’t you think?      Aye, it is. I’ve been reading up on some gear for underwater filming, fancied capturing some of the sea life. Think I might try it out here while I’m on school holidays.      That sounds fun. Technology these days is brilliant, isn’t it? When I was at your age, we never dreamed of someone being able to film so easily underwater. Steve Jobs changed the game for sure.      Speaking of which, I wonder if they teach much about using all that tech in schools there? I recall about how excited Steve was about the technology being the means for education and creativity.      Yeah, it’s pretty cool. We’re even doing a project on how to record and enhance sounds for marine animals. It’s part of our science work. A bit more interesting than the usual stuff.      I dunno, I like school but I like being here even more. I wish every day was like this!      Aye lass, but let’s hope you remember a bit of this by the time the exam season comes goin’. You’ll see if you miss it or not.      I reckon it's always good to have an adventure now and then. It’s funny how something as big as Brexit or concerns like immigration officers don’t matter so much when you’re here, sipping on wine and enjoying the sun.

Rather annoying this new debt collector phoning every so often, do you not think? Frightfully intrusive if you ask me.      It is, I can't say I like it either. One chap phoned me last week claiming I owed £200 for some PPI compensation. Got eeny weeny passive-aggressive about it, 'course I didn’t buy any P.P.I., I didn’t even have a loan policy before that! I reported it to the police, bless me, but you know what they say to you? "We can't chase it, but keep a record just in case." Pah! Still, at least I don't get chased every day, only when they know someone’s well-meaning like me and might believe them.      I hear you both, yes, it is a right sad situation. They seem to take advantage of the vulnerable, and sometimes it’s breakfast, no doubt. I've been lucky so far — only once did a sales charlatan call me, thinking I might have had a car loan once. I told him I was over 60 and had never owned a car — I mean, seriously, who would expect that from a woman in her early 60s?      Absolutely ridiculous, all these calls. I remember my father used to complain about them, and now it's my turn. I had a funny experience last week when one chap phoned me pretending to be a mail-order company that had missed a delivery in 1998. He said they were trying to track it down and oddly had a picture with my name and address. It was vile. I told him I was a university education reviewer and, "If you have about five minutes to walk to the nearest bobby van, you're welcome to come and collect what you found." Let me tell you, I've never felt more unashamed in my entire life.      Oh, well said! I did once tell them I was a retired childminder and was quite famous for talking to witches — you know, ones that could stick out their tongues as long as a bus. It shut them up rather quickly.      That’s the spirit, no need for sugarcoating these days. While we're on the subject, have you read that article about the antiques market in today's magazine? Thought it was interesting, especially about the new box plants that could be worth your house in ten years.

Rather a long day in the court today, wasn’t it? I could tell it was taking a toll on everyone.      Oh, you're not wrong! These cases can run over, especially when it's full with new clerks trying to sort things out. How about you, love? Got a good handle on everything?      I did, overall. I’ve been trying to adapt my teaching methods online too. With the way this world is heading, you can't just keep teaching in the traditional way. It's important to keep up with the times when it comes to education. You'd probably like to hear about it, wouldn't you?      Aye, do tell! Being older, you know, I rely more on others to help me navigate things like this. I still use the same methods I used as a schoolgirl in Insch, if you can believe it!      I actually find this fascinating. Technology can drive in so many ways, even the justice system we work in today is changing. There was talk about reducing paperwork and more e-filing.      That sounds promising. I can see the appeal of that. But what worries me more is the issue we’ve got on the roads—and it’s not just about getting here. The transport networks – buses, trains, everything—it seems like it's all falling apart these days. I’ve been quite taken back by how poorly the government spends the budget toward infrastructure.      Yes, I couldn’t agree more. It’s frustrating. And unfortunately, it contributes to the cycle of poor socio-economic mobility—especially for semi-routine workers and people like you and I. I speak from experience as a teacher in about how important mobility is for students to travel to better opportunities.      You’ve put your finger right on it. Money barely stretches these days. I remember when my children were younger, they used to dream about travel. Now, I can barely afford a train to Scotland to visit my family. But I do love the idea of travel, you know. I always did enjoy the culture and climate over there. Even though it’s always been a bit of a struggle to survive in the cold!      I know exactly what you mean. I sometimes dream of visiting gothic cities on the coast, maybe even Insch or other parts of Scotland. I’ve read that it's beautiful in the summer—nice and warm due to the Gulf stream.

Rather than money, I often say to the children at school that happiness is like a pocket—it can be filled with all sorts of things, not just coins! What makes  you  happy today, sweetheart?      £100, I want £100!      een! That’s  not  a rhyme, Georgina. Try again. What makes you happy? I said that money can buy things, but it doesn’t always bring happiness. If you have a hundred pounds, it might go away in a day. But what you do when you don’t have things can make you happy for a long time.      Having toy cars, and then going to the park like that one turkey on Christmas Day!      Well, Harry! I see you’re working on your rhymes. I think he meant “turkey trotting” at a brisk pace! But I see what you mean. The park  does  bring joy, and it’s free!      No, it's not! They charge for the ice cream stand!      Only a little, Georgina. But if we spread a blanket under the tree and tell jokes, that still costs us nothing and can bring us all extra happiness. Would you like to hear a real rhyme?      Yeah!      Yeah! Let’s have fun!      Silly Goose! Let me try this one:  When the moon feels someone sleepy, And the stars wink shut upon thy eye, Then we dream a dream so deep, And find a golden secret heap… Happiness is all around! No need for coins or gold about!  How does that rhyme?      It’s not brilliant. I made one:  Lots of toys, and chocolate treats, Climbing up to secret seats, But if the treacle oozes slow, Then that’s the time to go below!       I don’t get it!      Ha! Well, Georgina, as long as you’re trying, that’s a kind of happiness—being creative! And let’s face it, a houseful of rhymers is a happy one. Even if my pond life improvements cost a fortune!      What is a pond life?      Time to head to your bed. It’s getting late, and I’ve been writing a poem about pond life for your mother. Just not as fun to say on the way to sleep!      Can I sleep in a pond?      No! At least, not tonight. But promises, promises, Georgina. Tomorrow we’ll make a happiness and rhime blanket fort. Deal?      Deal! I want some chocolate in it!      And a ‘treacle oozing machine’!

So, I heard you mentioned last week you want to be an inventor when you grow up. That’s like... proper cool, innit? I mean, like, I can’t even fix a toast properly!      Haha, I mean, it's not like I'm gonna invent WiFi or anything like that, but I do think it'd be sick if I could create something that makes life a bit easier.      Why not? Look at China, they’ve done some crazy stuff in the last ten years. I read once that they're literally building cities from nothing. You'd think like, how is even possible?      Yeah, I’d heard that too. And that’s just one example. I’m really fascinated by how they prioritise tech inventions and investing in big future ideas, like AI and renewable energy.      Wait, wait — what’s "investment" even mean? I mean, like... I invest in snacks and fortnite skins, but that's probably not what you're talking about.      Haha, yeah, maybe not. I mean, like, when people or companies put money into something to get more money back later. Like, if I invent a machine that washes clothes, and I get funding from someone – that’s investment.      Oh, okay, I sort of get it. But why would someone give you money to make a washing machine? Isn’t that like... kind of obvious someone already did?      Well, maybe not. What if I made it hotter? Or more efficient? Or if I patented it, so no one else could copy it? Then it becomes a product people actually want to buy.      Oh, right! So a patent is like a special copy that no one else can take?      Yeah, kind of. If someone patents an invention, they legally own it for a while. Like, the inventor can sell it or give it to someone, but no one else can just copy it without permission.      That’s kind of like with lunches, innit? If I have chocolate cake and you want it you can't just take it, you have to ask first or go buy your own.      Haha, yeah, kind of, but that’s food. But with big inventions, it can really affect whole countries. I’m planning to look into starting a business one day, using those kinds of ideas.      Man, that sounds amazing. I wish I was more into that. I'd probably go all in to invest in your machine.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? That sun is making everything look so bright—the snow's glittering like diamonds. I could really get used to this sort of weather!      Aw, it's gorgeous, honestly! I've not had as good a holiday like this in years. Got a bit of a cold last week while out on the slopes and had to cancel our plans, but now I feel so much better. Much better! Such a shame, though.      Oh, it must have been frustrating. I hope you're feeling completely back to normal now. You know what I like about this place? The people—everyone’s so helpful. The staff at the resort have been brilliant about sorting bookings and answering all my silly questions.      Yes, they’ve been brilliant, haven’t they? I think the world of this place. I was speaking to Mandy yesterday, when she dropped by for a coffee while she was here for work. She said she’s planning to come back with her kids next year.      Oh, I adored Mandy, didn’t we both? She takes such good care of them. I do hope she and Tom are well. Have you heard from Tom lately?      No, not really. We spoke at Easter but that’s it, and I know they were busy after. Tom’s working on this big new project, something to do with the building firm he’s with. He said they’re in Bulgaria again—but in one of the coastal towns. Not this one, obviously.      Oh, is he working in Bulgaria as well? That’s curious—I thought he was in London most of the time about now. Anyway, back to you. Have you thought about what we’re going to do tomorrow? We could meet Sarah and Andy at the bottom of the slopes after lunch?      That’d be great. I was thinking about it earlier. They mentioned they wanted to go to that new après-ski bar near the lift—the one with the little performance area. We could join them for a couple of drinks. And also, by the way, I think I told Mandy we’re doing a night out for New Year’s Eve with the rest of the bunch. She said she’d get Tom to come along.      Oh, that’s smashing! I was just thinking how lovely it would be to have all of us together at the end of the holiday.

Rather annoying this, isn't it, love? That third string’s snapped again. I swear they’re like spaghetti in the wind sometimes—just can't hold up. I’ve had this same racket over ten years, it's practically part of me now.       Pause.  Aye, it’s beginning to cost a fortune to keep it twitching. I reckon cable ties are as good as most replacements these days. I've been thinking, if we'd got a few spares and started fixing rackets for local schools and clubs, it could turn into something. The way things are with education these days, they’re thankful for a working broomstick and a flexible rulebook.      That's an idea worth turkey twizzlers, love. Though I’m no expert on materials, I’ve watched enough D.I.Y. shows I think I could fashion a method with cable, some clamps, maybe even a bit of old-fashioned wax to keep it snug.      Yes, and as for dimensions, you'd need to be careful—those racquet frames are mercyless on over-zealous hands. Too tight and you’ll crack it short, too loose and it might as well be a fishing net. As for positioning… well, the tension point is everything, like the way spring looses work?      Right you are. And weight—it’s got to be balanced otherwise you’ll be slicing shots through the air like a butter knife through a loaf.      You know, in primary schools they’re more forgiving. Children are chaotic, but oddly so. Secondary— chuckling —well, let’s say their sense of propriety kicks in mid-match and you can nearly hear the violin strings snap.       Snipping quietly for a moment.  I wish they had you in that ‘Dragons’ Den’ lot. No disrespect, but the idea, the confidence—it’s all rather marketable if you know what I mean.       Damage is being inflicted to the left ear lobe.  Oh bless, I hope you weren’t hearing that.      No, truly, I wasn't. A bit of lopsidedness is no disgrace for a woman of my age.      Then go ahead and get rid of that stripe of black hair—that one has been bricking it up for years between us.      Aye, well, you could at least take the pressure off the strings and the hair alike. And speak of ‘fleet’ as well, like we talk about the ‘fleet’ of thoughts or ideas shooting off like string-ended arrows.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? That sun in through the window does cheer the place up. Mind you, I've always preferred sitting in the garden more than indoors, but these days I find myself a little more cautious. Not quite as sprightly as I once was.      Yes, it's a pleasant weather, George. Light and warm enough to sit by the window without feeling like you're missing out on the sun. I do so love a spot of art; it gives you a moment to think without the noise of the world pressing in. Funny how things can capture the imagination so easily.      That reminds me of when I was much younger. I used to sit for hours trying to draw that old turkey on the mantelpiece. Funniest thing is, I never thought I'd become a lecturer on art, and I certainly didn't imagine I'd be giving it to a room full of students. But here I am.      I remember you talking about that, Clara. You always had such a way of seeing the ordinary in a new light. It's something I strive to communicate in my lectures as well—how art can be a lens through which to view the human experience.      Sounds like both of you are trotting out all the big words. Let's see if we can't simplify it, like I do with my watercolors. A bit of this here, a splash of that there. Doesn't have to be a meaning behind everything, just the joy of creation.      And there's the truth of it, George. It doesn't all have to be about meaning or messages. It's also about the experience, the act itself, the colors mixing and about how it makes you feel in that very moment.      I completely agree. There's a lot of that in the younger generation's work, too—more about expression and less about ‘say this or that'. It's quite refreshing.      Well, as long as we're on the subject, have I shown you how my little ones reacted when I hung my first exhibition in the school hall? It was pure chaos with lunches and a couple of whistles. But their pride, oh, you should have seen it.      Oh, go on then, James, if you've not broken out the drawings and posters yet, perhaps we could have a little show of our own.

:  [currently scrubbing the baseboards]  Ugh, I literally just cleaned this kitchen  last week , and it’s like someone shot a paintball gun of flour, tea, and negativity in here! Why is cleaning always left to Friday night, huh?     :  [sitting on a barstool, scrolling on her phone]  Because we’re basically vampires—only come out on the weekends, and when we do, we swoop in, destroy the fridge, and expect it to be clean the next time we appear? Hence why this place looks like a warzone. You know what I like to call it?  The ghosthouse method of cleaning .     : You made that up, didn’t you? Typical. You’re so weird. Ten more minutes and I’ll be done. But I swear I’ll collapse the second I finish. I’m about 80% procrastination, 15% rage, and 5% actual productivity at the moment.     : You're not the only one. I spent all yesterday trying to get into this super challenging patients’ progress system—somebody coded it with enthusiasm and zero usability—and I finally got it, only to find out I’d been typing GIRL crap into a PATIENT ID field. I looked at it for  five minutes  before I noticed it.     : Oh my god, you what? Silly British spelling or is that a typo that made you cringe in public?     : God, unfortunately? It counts as  both . I was flapping like a peacock in a tea shop being accused of typing nonsense.  “No, Laura, it’s about the patient’s mood patterns not their bimbo status.”  Very professional vibes.     :  [laughs]  You’re so cruel. At least you’re not the one dealing with the baked-on toast incidents. My kitchen counter is probably holding onto at least three toaster-related crimes.     : Honestly, I miss when we had a schedule. Back when we had that cute little chalkboard we always updated with lunches and tasks and stuff. Now it just says "Congratulations, you lost your mojo".     : That was a goody of my uni life, that board. But real talk, I miss the system, not the art. I think we might need to schedule a proper clean and maybe some self-care planning. Maybe even a conference call with my therapist?     : True to life? I say, schedule over self-care. We can do both. I’m not entirely sure if I'm paying for my therapist to say "clean your kitchen, it reflects your inner being" or to actually make progress, but either way, she’s worth it.     :

Rather annoying when the barista at my local café misses my name. I know it's spelled ‘Eloise’ and not ‘Elise’ now, yet somehow I still end up with a ‘love you’ personalised cup. Not quite the professional image I was aiming for in front of the director.      That happens more than it should, doesn’t it? I reckon it’s because they don’t care enough to listen properly. Not that I’m one to talk—I once spelled ‘Anthony’ as ‘Antony’ and ended up in the wrong queue at the airport. Mistakes.      Right, but it’s mostly just because people don’t listen. It’s a small point, but it’s that sort of detail that shows respect or lack of it. It makes me wonder, do you think common sense is something that lacks correlation to intelligence?      Hmm, possibly. I think smart doesn’t always mean sensible. I mean, take my mate in IT at the office. Mega smart when it comes to servers, but can’t remember the time to take out the trash himself.      Exactly what I mean! I mean, we all make mistakes, but ignoring basic things like manners or respecting someone’s name… it shows a lack of empathy in most cases.      Mate, I often wonder if people still value that sort of thing these days. I mean, don’t get me started on phone use at the table. No, I’m not suggesting they should be banned—but at least one meal a week with no screens, a bit of eye contact, preferably not with a cigarette in your hand.      Cigarettes and alcohol make your daily routine look like a war about self-control. I remember the days when the cigarettes lit my mood more than my health.      Oh that was you? I didn’t know. No wonder I always thought your chain smoking was part of some kind of performance art.      Come on, don’t start. But being serious, it does feel like there’s a balance to strike. We discuss feminism and cultural expectations sometimes. In some countries, smoking by women can still be stigmatised. It’s an interesting contrast when you think of how casual smoking by men can sometimes be considered ‘job-related stress’.      And yet, here we are, smoking in separate rooms, between jobs. Who lives in the 21st century?      The same question I ask myself every morning when I consider drinking wine while doing the crossword puzzle to fuel my intellect.

Rather exciting day today, isn't it? That farm trip. I've been meaning to take the children somewhere a bit more open, out of the classroom for a bit. Just need something to break the cycle a little, don't you think?      It's been great! We saw rabbits and eeny weeny chickens. Mummy, one of them tried to nibble my finger. Wasn’t funny. A lot of muddy puddles too! I got my wellies all soggy.      We saw a pig! It was big! The cows, too. Mummy came too close and it sort of snorted at her. I thought it was laughing, but only a little.      Oh, did you? The cows can be a bit aloof, to be honest. Darcy, I thought I told you to stay back—Don't worry about the mud; it'll wash out. But if you've been messing with the animals in class again, I might have to take that toy you brought back from the farm and hide it away.      Nuh, I didn't mess with nothing! I left it with the other cows to play. I only took photos with the book bag on my head. Mr. Franklin said it was silly.      Matey's got a point, and I take photos all the time. Mr. Franklin said I was moving too fast and couldn't even hold the book still. I showed him, huh!      That’s enough. Just because you like a rush doesn’t mean it's appropriate—especially not in the library. Speaking of which, here’s an idea: after supper, we can pop on a DVD about animals. Something educational for the both of you. Maybe even something on the farm. I’ve got a few good ones that are age-appropriate and have helped a few of my students quite a bit.      Can we watch the one about the ducks and the daffodils? That was funny when it drowned out the farm song.      We’ll see about that. I’ll pick one out tonight. Now, lunches to be eaten before the digestive larder calls. That's you, Jack.      I'll eat it gookly, mummy! It's not as gooky as the sludge in the pond, anyway. Although the ducks ate that up.      So could have you, if you opened your gob a bit more. But you just sat there like a grumpy toad.      That’s quite enough of that.

Rather annoying I can't get this bobble to come out. I've been knitting this jumper since before Christmas... got to finish it by Easter. Otherwise poor Jonny'll be stuck in the same one as last year again.      That's not what you were saying about the footy kits when I saw him at Newton Park last week. You didn't seem to mind him running all over that!      Oh, he's got too much kit already. Not that I'm not proud, mind. Today was gold in the Olympics for him. Didn’t even blink when the bloke came out of the penalty area like it was  Obi-Wan  or something.      You mean that Mycroft lookalike? I watched it last night on the laptop. I had the commentary on in the background while I was trying to draft my thesis. It actually helped me concentrate somehow.      He doesn’t much look like Mycroft, in my opinion. I reckon the real stars of the tournament are the spare players warming up. One of them has that same curly hair as that artist—person—what's-his-face that does the land art in the Wolds.      You mean Andy…?      Yeah, that’s him. I remember my nan had one of those calendars with his stuff in the living room. All the sheep and those long black lines in fields. Silly really, but it looked gorgeous at Christmas with the lights.      That’s a good way of describing it. It just goes to show, innit? Art is wherever it's seen and enjoyed. Any tea yet?      Just done it. Apple cinnamon with a splash of milk for you? I’m still clinging to mine—cardamom. My flatmate says it smells like someone boiled up some old spices after a curry night.      Then I’m definitely not taking you to Manchester for tea. I’d spend all the time coughing. What about you? You fancy a trip down to Birmingham?      Only if we can stop at the market and pick up some lunches to bring back. I hear the deli section is doing this Moroccan chicken shawarma with tamarind. That would go goon with my knitting and a film of  I Dream of Jeannie . Still in the spirit of Easter, really.      Go on then. Shawarma at 10 am, jumpers and  I Dream of Jeannie  by 1. True to life, innit?      We are the very picture of modern Britain, my friend.

Rather lovely day today, ain't it love? Thought we could do a bit of a jaunt up to Bethnal Green and see what’s happening at that museum down there.      Aye, it’s sunn’in alright. Looked up what you fancy—there’s a new exhibition on 19th century London. Sounds fascinating if you ask me. Bet they’ve got them big 3D screens like in them IMAX places.      Oh aye, I’ve always admired them. Know me, was teachin’ foreign lads when them 3D films came out, like, ten years back!  laughs  They used to think the popcorn was still likker, and they kept squintin’ at the floor like it’d jump out at ’em.      Aye, and I’ll be the first to say, them films aren’t for me! Too loud, too flashy. But this museum’s exhibit... I reckon it’s more me cup of tea. Show us what life was like back when me dad were a kid.      Yeah, and we can take the Overground, it’s a proper pain-free way to get there. No need for fancy trips on the Tube—it’s Sunday, we don’t want to rush.      Should have got the off-peak Oyster cards months ago! I’ve a cousin in Greenwich who did, and she always raves about the ‘fix’! Though, let’s be fair, someone at the ticket office should sort out the queues—half the time you can’t get on cos you’re waiting to weigh your luggage and buy a bottle of water at the same time.      Aye, I agree. I’ve had a man in the queue once who had to choose between his sandwiches and the cap for his squash bottle! I mean, it’s  meant to be  a ‘green’ transport system, not a fancy fruit juice bar with a side of dithering!       chuckling  Ah, but when you’re out on a Saturday or Sunday and them trains are runnin’ late, with people shouting up and down the platform like it’s the 5 o’clock news—telling you, it’s a laugh!      Well if we miss the 11:15 to Bethnal Green, I’m soddin’ well not getting the one after cause you’ll be missing the big 3D show and I won’t forgive you! I’ve had bellyful of your dad stories for one day.      Fair enough! I’ll grab the tickets now—second to none, they said.

Rather annoying, though—Santa costumes. You know, in China they still give me the squint when I try to explain it's not about the man in red. I ended up dressing up himself last year, and it was… chaotic to say the least.      Ha, I can imagine. My friend Andy, he’s a primary school teacher over here, tried the same thing last year with a paper crown and a cardboard box “sleigh.” The kids adored him but then started asking questions about “wife-beaters” and “coal.” You can never win when it comes to Christmas in China.      Tell me about it. I've got the turkey taken care of this year though. It's turkey, Christmas crackers, and enough Brandy Alexanders to last well into the New Year. D’you fancy coming round tomorrow night?      Yeah, sounds great. Domino breakfast, no doubt? I've been meaning to ask—what are we planning for the non-turkey contingent, then? I told the in-laws I would bring that Chinese chicken with the subtle soy and ginger, you know, the one that never puts anyone off.      That’ll do. Good on you—it shows you’re making an effort, and the way to most Chinese – and British – hearts is through the stomach, I reckon. Oh, while we're on the subject—what’s your postcode at home? I’m picking up a few DVDs for the night. Our usual someone-from-Manchester-year-in-London-relearns-cycling routine sounds oddly therapeutic at this time of year.      Chained hill in Margate, but don't hold me to it—I about blocked the main road once trying to round the corner on my bike. It was a whole police drama and not because of that frost you get in the mornings.      My, my. You really have been enjoying your British winters here, haven't you? Well, the film selection is sorted—I’ve got the Criterion Foundation DVD collection you schemed about getting your hands on two years ago. Perfect for a cold night and a warm beer.      That’s the spot. Classy set-up, mate. Just make sure you’ve got the popcorn goin’. I’ll see if I can procure some real Marmite—if you can call it that by now.      Lift your glass, you fool—it's Christmas in the East. Here’s to questionable costume choices and questionable cycling skills.      Cheers to that!

Rather annoying when people just take a photo of your food and give you a one star review for no reason. I got one the other day from a group at my café saying it was "overpriced". I mean, we use £6 pastries, and they expect us to charge £2?      That’s  not  fair. I get that all the time at the bakery. You spend a fortune on A2 ethics and Fairtrade, and all you get is a cup of tea and some criticism. I had one customer last week who said my sourdough was "bland". Told her I like to keep it simple!  laughs       Honestly, I can't stand bad reviews on MyTable. I opened my café in Margate last year, and there was this guy who wrote, "the décor was sad". Fair enough? But then he added, "you should be better at breakfast, or whatever it is you do." Ugh.      And the worst part is, you can’t always report the people. Rather annoying when the supermarket’s out of stock, isn’t it? I was just trying to get some pears for the crumble this evening. I’m hoping it’s not going to rain again, or I'll be stuck inside with no one to speak to. By the way, Martha, how was your day?      Oh, it was all right. I had a few easy jobs today, nothing too tiring. I actually stopped off in the town center to pick up a few things for Mrs. Taylor next door—she’s not doing too well at the moment. Did get the pears in the end, but I had to go to the store down near the roundabout. Still, easier than trying to get a taxi, I suppose. I did get to have a bit of a chat with the shop assistant as well. Rather nice place.      Blimey, you’ve been working hard, Martha, dear. You always do look out for the neighbors in a kind way, you do. I was shopping earlier today myself before the rain came down. I fancied a nice chicken casserole, and I found a rather good one in the frozen section. What did you say you were making for your crumble, dear?      Apple and pear, with custard. It’s my especial favorite. I do love getting together with the family for something like that. I was saying to Martha that if the weather improves tomorrow afternoon, I could take you both to the café up the road. Fancies a change of scenery?      Oh, that'd be lovely. Some fresh air’d do me good. I do get a bit cooped up all week. Though, there is one thing about the café... they always have that rather sticky toffee pudding, and I’m not a fan of that! Going to be telling you now I’m not having it, so you won’t be able to persuade me otherwise.      Tut, tut, and I do so like it myself. But no, I won’t argue with you, my dear. I could stick to my good old scones and cream instead. What about the lunches we keep meaning to do together, dear? We haven’t managed it yet, have we? I was thinking the other day how goody it would be to just sit down and catch up.      Oh, that’d be brilliant. Maybe we can combine it with your regular haircut, Mother.

Rather than chuck a full-fat bottle at him straight away, I think weaning him off slowly would be kinder. You start with a mix of full-fat and semi-skimmed, sure? That’s what my sister-in-law did with her lass, and it worked a treat.      Right, so like, we do one night with the semi-skimmed and full-fat mixed? I’ve been panicking a bit because I don’t want him to hate milk or think it’s some sort of punishment. We’ve been feeding him full-fat every evening for the last few days.      That’s fine! Take it easy. I’d start the mix at only 10 or 20% semi-skimmed, just to tide him over. Ten per cent works if you’re nervous. He might not even notice the difference at first. It’s all about the transition, not the breakfast, innit?      That makes sense. Thanks, Muv. I thought I’d have to jump into the thick of it, but this feels less stressful. By the way—my nan and grandad are coming over on Saturday morning. Want to bring the kids over for lunch?      Course I do. I’ve missed the little one. Let them come over. Bring buns, though, mind. That’s what we’ve done every time. It’s their tradition, and Sil’s always thrilled. What about you? Any weekend plans?      Yeah, actually. I’m meeting some of the other teachers from school on Saturday—job-related, but it’s a nice way to unwind. And then I’ve got a sign language class on Wednesday evening about babies. I’m not the best at the basics, and it’s for our son as much as for me.      That sounds brilliant. Signing with him early on is a good move. I’ve always thought it helps passed on down the line. Just remember to take it slow. You don’t want to get disappointed if he’s not picking it up quick.      I won’t. I always try with him, keep the big whinge in check if the translations aren’t flowing. But serious, this class is a proper good chance to go over common words for life, like "hungry," "sleep," "wet." It’s practical. And he deserves all the help we can give him.      You’ve been doing a great job, love. It all gets easier as he gets to know you better.

Rather lovely to be out here today, isn't it? The countryside looks so peaceful in the morning light. I feel like I could walk for hours and not run out of interesting sights.      It is beautiful. I can see why you wanted to come to Norfolk. The hills aren’t too dramatic, but they give a nice sense of rolling space, don’t they?      Oh yes, that's one of the things I love about this place. No high-rise buildings, no traffic noise—just quiet and green. The villages are so charming too. I remember when we went to Little Walsingham, the old cottages with their thatched roofs, the village green, and that little church in the middle of it all. It felt like a page from a storybook.      You're right, and it's not just the aesthetics. Living in London for so long, it's almost shocking how much space there is here. I still can't believe how far the horizon seems to stretch. No, you don’t have the skyscrapers, but you’ve got something more enduring.      Absolutely. And the people in the villages—they’re so friendly and open. It’s not that Londoners aren’t, but it's busier, and people are often more reserved. Here, it’s like everyone knows each other and actually does wave when you pass by the pub.      True. I find it quite comforting, honestly. We could walk around town for ages just saying hello to people. Although I do miss the variety of places to eat out. I wonder what you had for dinner last night in the village tavern.       laughs  Oh, it was a proper English roast—tough but scrumptious lamb, Yorkshire pudding, and all the rest. There was even a jug of gravy you barely need to handle. And we had to step over the dogs at the bar just to get to the table.      Classic village tavern. I'm guessing it was quite atmospheric once we finished eating, too?      Definitely. The fire was going strong, the old photos of bygone lunches on the walls, and the mismatched chairs and tables—it's like stepping back in time.      Yeah, I love it here. This place has a soul. Just one question—do you think we could ever actually live in a small village like this? I can picture it, but I’m not sure if I could live without the occasional takeaway!

Rather lovely to be out here today, isn't it? The spring has been so kind with colour this year.      Oh, I’m with you on that. I've been walking this path since we moved to Norfolk two years ago, and it never fails to take my breath away — the wildflowers, the way the light changes everything.      Yes, I’ve been thinking a lot lately about how communities like this depend on more than just tourism, though. I was reading a paper the other day about small landowners and the economics of cash crops — it made me wonder how we could support these fields to thrive without spoiling their character.      That’s an interesting point. From what I remember of university economics, land use is a balancing act. But I suppose if the right crops are chosen — maybe even something like lavender or medicinal herbs — it could actually complement the landscape and bring better long-term value.      Exactly! I was in discussion at a conference last week with a few agronomists looking into the feasibility of small-scale agro-tourism. It’s not about replacing tourism, but augmenting it. I think we even had one from Manchester advocating for the idea as a way to revitalise local economies.      Speaking of Manchester, I’m surprised – weren’t you at a lecture last night? Any interesting insights on language evolution or something?      Oh yes! A fascinating talk on how language evolves in regional dialects and the role of geographical isolation. It made me reflect on how even in a place like this, so peaceful and out-of-the-way, our own speech and way of being is influenced by so many things – history, trade, migration.      I love that. Interesting how the same sun that warms these wildflower beds and the same fields that feed us and draw visitors have also helped shape the way we talk and think. And speaking of being shaped — how did that Manchester United game go last weekend?      A disaster, as always. I tried to follow from here, but honestly, the only good thing was that our player of the season got a yellow card and a new nickname from the referee.      Still, I’m happy with our local team's performance so far. It’s not as glamorous, but there’s a real sense of community at the matches, don't you think?      Definitely. Though I’m not sure I’d call flukey 3–2 wins in mid-week hours “glamorous”!

Rather annoying the new developments in Peterborough aren't they, Sarah? I was just reading about that case on mute, and I thought she'd be let off more leniently. Rather annoying this new bank’s gettin’ so much in tha papers, innit? They’ve been poked for money laundering, same as half the banks up and down the country these days. Rather chilly this morning, isn't it? I needed three cups of coffee just to get out of bed. I swear the weather's out to get us this time of year!      Aw, it's only November, love. Don’t worry, I’ll get the day go-kart on stand-by if you need it.      Oh, no, I’ll be in town anyway—should be easy to swing by. So all sorted! Rather lovely day today, isn't it? I mean, for Cambridge – you’d think it'd be pissing down, but it's been almost dry all morning. I’ve had trouble getting into the rhythm of this publishing gig. Not quite as glamorous as I imagined being a language co-ordinator would be.      I understand the sentiment – I started here as a publishing assistant just last month, and I’ve only now figured out which drawers in this filing cabinet are important. Prior to this, I was in marketing. We had wine tastings instead of proofreading.      You’re both like gilded onions. I grew up in Malaysia, so when I tell people I work in "publishing" they think I must be living some jet-setting life. But honestly, I’m just here five days a week, getting used to the A4 filing system. It's far from the Thailand weekends I had when I was in university.      Oh, don’t get me wrong, I quite like the ordering of things. There's something oddly calming about checking that every comma is in the correct place. But I still miss the occasional PhD colloquium. Here, I spend my days reading and re-reading the same page three times without getting any closer to understanding it.      I get that. I, um, I just started as a temporary assistant a couple of weeks ago and already feel like I've accidentally removed the Oxford comma once too often. I mean, in Sweden, we don’t use it quite the same way, and now here I am, trying not to flinch every time I see it.      That’s fascinating – I’ve done some research on Scandinavian language influence in the UK. I’m from Buckinghamshire originally, but I've always been keen on accents and linguistic patterns. Do you feel more British now, or do you still identify strongly with Sweden?      Honestly, I'm a bit of both. I was born in Sweden but was mainly raised in the UK, so I feel like I'm sort of a linguistic compromise. Like Swedish yellow sprite being gently diluted by British English.      I’ve had similar experiences. My parents are both British, but I grew up in the tropics. I still say my ‘r’s like a Malayan monsoon, and I struggle in the British winter without a sari.      It’s like we all have these tiny linguistic contradictions.

Rather annoying when the traffic’s stuck, innit? I do love the coast, though. Cornwall’s like... far away enough to feel like a proper holiday, don’t you think?      Aye, it can do. That’s why we start early, love. And I’ve always een fookin’ fond of the sea an’ all. Grew up near Bolton, not too far from that, but never had much chance to go anywhere fancy like Cornwall.      You should’ve! It’s proper bonkers once you get further down, like the past has just disappeared... like, literally, even the  traffic  slows down as we near Plymouth, don’t it? That job was like working at Jurasssic Park with all them deliveries.      I know! I tried to read some Latvian or Hungarian while waiting for a lift. Though I think I ended up trying to read the  back  of the box for some reason.      Then again, if you started watching the Northern Lights in Norway on your phone, you'd be doing real Latin next.      You might be on to somethin’, innit. Now that I’d pay to see. Always fancied a bit of weird history mixed with some magic, really.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh? You’d think by June we’d have seen some proper sunshine by now.      You’re not wrong. I’ve had trouble getting much done with the garden, let alone with the clerical side of things as it is.      I always say the more passive the weather the more twitchy people become. Of course, as a headmistress you’ve probably had your fair share of that too, Louise.      Oh, there's truth in that! It was the same for me when I was running the transcription service. You'd get tense, thinking it will rain  this  week,  this  day, only to find it holds like that for weeks on end.      I can imagine. As if everyday office tasks weren't enough, the thought of being cooped up for even longer is enough to wear anyone down.      You need to take it with a bit of grace though. I've learned not to get fussed by the weather. Out in the woods, you don’t argue with the weather, you get on with it.
