Establishes a sense of order in the world and shows people how to carry on through it all, good or bad.      Absolutely. I try to do the same with the administration. It might not be as dramatic as running a school, but I take it as seriously as anyone else.      And I take it as seriously as building a house. The way I see it, it's all about giving people stability and structure, no matter what trade or job you're in.      Well said, David. Even in the smallest of tasks and settings, we must show respect and dedication. Whether you're delivering a lesson, tending a garden, or even goading a map of life from woodland.      You’re all in separate fields, but it always ends up coming back to the same thing – keeping going. It's about respecting the craft and the commitment one has to give.

Rather than Mother’s Day itself, I wanted to get ahead of everything and start planning it out with you two mince pies. What do you both fancy doing to make it special this year?      Can we have pancakes and make the cards in Art club style with glitter and feathers? Please, please, please!      Me too! And then mummy can have a cupcake with a ‘best mummy in the galaxy’ message on top. Oh, and she can wear a cape to be a superhero!      Oh, look at the two of you — you’re full of good ideas! Art club is a great idea, and I do love pancakes. But we’ll have to visit the shops for some extra supplies though. I’m not sure we’ve got glitter for two card projects!      What’s an idiom, by the way? Chloe’s breakfast club teacher said something about ‘butterflies in the stomach’ and being ‘beneath the weather’. They didn’t make sense to me.      Ah, idioms, yes! Those are funny phrases that people use in English quite a lot to mean things that aren’t exactly what they say. For instance, if someone says they’ve got ‘butterflies in their stomach’, it doesn’t actually mean they’re full of flying insects — it means they’re feeling nervous or excited about something.      Ooh! Like when mummy told me I was going to Forest School and my tummy went all wobbly? That’s when I definitely had butterflies in my tummy!      Exactly! And as for  beneath the weather  — I’m not quite sure where the teacher picked that one up from, but it doesn’t sound like an authentic English idiom. Maybe you heard ‘over the weather’ or ‘below par’ instead, like for when someone isn’t quite well?      I remember one the year before last was ‘raining cats and dogs’. That meant it was very rainy. We had to draw queens and yellow sprite-like things out of the rain with felt pens!      That’s a good one! Okay, after the cards are made and the pancake mountain gothic is on the table, maybe after breakfast we can give your cards to me in front of the group at Forest School, and then we’ll read your letters and you’ll all have a big celebration together?      And then can we visit the park nearby to feed the ducks in the ‘butterflies in our stomach’?

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? You know, ever since my sister was diagnosed with breast cancer, it's got me rather paranoid about my own health.      Yeah, I mean, it is tough. Not only for her, but for the family too. My brother-in-law’s had a bit of a rough year with his heart—and between that and the stress of looking after their kids, I’ve been constantly worrying about them.      Heart issues? Is he getting any support? That must be so stressful, especially for his wife. She’s only in her thirties too, needs to look after three kids.      Oh, she's doing her best, but you could tell she's under pressure. The kids are starting school this September, so the worry for their future is piling on top of the whole health thing. It's too much for anyone to cope with.      That’s so true. My sister’s kids are about the same age as ours, and it’s scaring me that they could lose their mum—especially when they’re so young. I can’t imagine the impacts that sort of trauma leaves.      You’ve still got time on your side, though. But it does make you think more about your own family. Have you got your checkup booked? It really is wise these days.      I’ve got one scheduled for next month, and I’m even thinking about doing some blood tests just to be safe. Honestly, I’d rather be a bit paranoid than miss something.      I think that’s sensible. Mental health is part of all this too, isn't it? I’ve been feeling quite down lately with everything going on in the family. I had to take a week off work not long ago—I needed to sort my head out.      That’s understandable. You can’t always put your head down and ignore it. I’ve been trying to go for a run every morning to clear my mind. It’s not much, but it helps.      That’s a good idea. I’ve started a new regime with mindfulness and tea instead of coffee—it's not much, but it’s something. I think the main thing is that we need to look after each other, wherever we can.      Absolutely. It’s the small things that sometimes make the biggest difference. Look after your own health, and help others when you can.

Rather nippy today, isn't it? That wind's nippin' right through me coat. Mind you, I've always preferred a bitta sunshine, don’t you think, Alice?      Oh, honestly, Herbert, I'd kill for a bit of sunshine after all this rain. My dear legs  ache , it’s that 'wet weather' business again. And don’t let me start on my back — I swear it's like a damp sock in there.      You’re lucky to still be mobile, Mum. I’ve been meaning to take you up to Norwich for that physio appointment, but I’ve been buried with work at the uni. Still, I managed to get the turkey on the table last Sunday.      Ah, well, I've been meaning to pick up a new pair of boots. These old ones, they’ve got more holes than a colander. Winnie, you remember when I used to walk across the Norfolk fields barefoot in the summer, didn’t I have the strongest knees?      That’s because you didn’t have a care in the world! You don’t stay in the garden for grief nowadays.      Speaking of gardens, I remember pacing it when I was younger — playing football for Mateha's team. I wouldn’t mind getting back into it, but the aches set in after ten minutes. Seems like me body's not got the legs it used to, huh?      You should try swimming. I’ve seen it work wonders for some of my students’ dads. Swimming's a gentler way to stay active. Not like chasing after a ballet ball in the middle of a muddy pitch.      Oh, Herbert, I remember when he used to walk all the way into Dereham to get the Saturday paper. These days, he'd rather sit here with his tea and the telly. All passed his prime.      I'm not that old, love. I still meet up with Bert and Charlie on a Thursday. We had a bit of a joke the other day — trying to find the right buttons on that new remote. Some of them are far too small for these old fingers.      Technology's a beast, isn't it? If it wasn’t for the college providing us with IT classes, I’d go mad trying to figure out what your Sky box is doing at 1 in the morning.      And let’s not even mention the hearing aids I had to start using two years ago.

: Right, so am I still up for helping you plan Sarah’s wedding this weekend, Jess? I just need to confirm my diary—new system is being so glitchy!     : Oh, thank you, Georgia! I’ve already got the venue picked out near Peterborough, but it’s all about the  details , you know? Having your Postgrad brain on this will be brilliant. I’ve been panicking a bit—she’s my sister, after all.     : Oh, and we’ll be there too, obviously! We’ve been meaning to catch up anyway—we saw the three of you at Mary’s dinner last week and didn’t even get to say hi. It was like that MySpace era all over again!     :  haha  I nearly sent a text saying, “Is it me? Or is Georgia in the room and we’re just not acknowledging it?” Remember when we used to all meet after college in Cambridge and talk about  nothing  for hours?     : Ugh, yes! It’s so easy to lose touch—personally, I’ve been swamped with the new property launch. But this is perfect timing, with the wedding stuff. Speaking of… how are things with  anyone ?     : Honestly, I broke up with Tom three months ago. We were drifting apart. It was nice while it lasted, but I’m not ready for marriage and kids yet, and he was just starting to mention it.     : Oh, Georgia, so sorry! That’s tough—especially with your job and admin and being split between Germany and here! Look on the bright side, we’ve got the weekend to us girls!     : Both my and Jess’s stories are not too exciting—I’m still single but dating this guy who  definitely  has a dog. And Jess, you’re still happily engaged?     :  grins  Yes, Billy and I are very much still on. We’ve been talking about kids too, but as long as we’ve got a stable space financially, I figure  why rush ?     : That’s so true. You’ve got that sales manager income cruising goin’ on! Georgia, you’re not going to give us cold shoulder just because you’re an artworker with a boxset binging problem, are you?     : Haha, Georgia’s been blaming her Netflix addiction for never answering texts, but to be fair, she’s been overworking at the new company.     : Fair enough! But if we’re planning a weekend of wedding planning, wine, and nostalgia, we need to guarantee no slipping into the void of administrative doom or TV oblivion!

Rather a dreary day outside, isn't it? Seems like we've had nothing but rain since the first of the year. Never mind—tea is comforting enough. I can't say I much fancy this new business with them tablets and computers. No, I prefer my crossword in the paper and a decent bit of eeny-meeny-miny on the telly.      Oh come on, Cliff. A lot of things have changed since your day, love. You know, even me, who's never had a regular job, I got one of those mobile phones—you know the sort with the pictures and everything. My granddaughter even helped me send a few messages to the children out in Manchester.      Aye, I’ve seen enough of those flashy things. Ten minutes, and you’re lost in them, I’d say. A world of nonsense if you ask me. Back in Costessey when I was a lad, we used to pass the time in the fields with a bit of horse racing and a few games of skittles. No need for all this blooming technology.      I hear what you're saying, Cliff, but as a teacher, I’ve seen how it all works in education now—everything's digital. The kids, from the way they bounce at the keyboard, you'd think they were born with it in their hands. Some of my students set up entire web pages for their projects.      That sounds positively modern, Alan. You must enjoy working with them—what with all that energy and rush of ideas. I always said children are something special, even if they can be a mite exhausting at times. I used to look after a few in about five different homes while I was still living the area.      Aye, and not a bad life that is. I've no issues with sending the kids to the fields, but for goodness' sake, education should happen more outside, not slumped at a screen. I used to pass a nice day watching my brother's racehorse gallop across the county one day to compete in the Norfolk races.      Family stories add the spice of life. I do miss working in the classroom sometimes, even though teaching pays a fair bit better than some goings-on I've known about. Not everyone has work these days—still, I suppose it's better than being in a long line of queues at your local job centre.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? I needed a walk after marking so many essays. Retrieves a mug from the kitchen and fills it with tea. Would you like a bit of cake with that?      Aye, that seems like a plan—get the sugar to help me make it through the rest of the afternoon. I’ve been twitching about on the settee all morning, trying to resist the urge to hibernate. Do you ever find yourself doing that?      Oh, absolutely. Today wasn't even the worst. I've had days when I've buried myself under a blanket and not moved for hours. laughs Not terribly professional for a language teacher to be too lazy, though.      Ha! You’ve got enough to keep you on your feet between prep and the students. Distant memory of work I think. I managed a firm most of my life, and sometimes it felt like I couldn’t sit still even if I wanted to.      And how is that now, Ken? Still working the old brain into overtime?      Retired, thank goodness! Well, technically—there are still a few things I consult on for old colleagues. Nothing too stressful, thank heavens. These days, I’m mostly into birdwatching. You ever try that? Baptism of sorts into nature, and it does the soul good, I imagine.      A bit, yeah. I've watched a few things at our local park—Blue Tits, Robins, and Magpies. But not professionally, like you. What made you get into it?      Well, I thought being stationary once in a while might be alright, and it brought me about five minutes of quiet a day! But the birds lit my curiosity up—each one a little story. Makes you wonder how varied life is even in our own backyards.      That’s beautiful. I always tell my students that language is the same way: open your ears and you’ll find stories all around.      Aye, I could see that from hearing you talk. You've got a real gift passing it on to students.      Thanks, Ken. That means a lot coming from someone who's led the charge somewhere himself. So, aside from your birdwatching, got any other hobbies lately?      Some. I’ve dabbled in photography—mainly of the birds, but sometimes I get lucky with the odd sunset or two. And I've never had children, so I’ve been helping my niece with stuff—teenage girl, mind!

So did you go out for Valentine’s weekend? I couldn't decide what to do, and it just felt...  weird , you know?      Honestly, I didn't do anything! It felt like everyone was out and about, and I just wanted to stay in and watch a film. I'm not really a romantic event person, you know?      Same here! Though I did treat myself to a takeaway from that new Thai place near campus. Oh my gosh, it’s amazing. Have you tried it yet?      No, but I’ve heard good things! I’ve been more into Lakelands lately. Bit basic, but it’s only a few quid and you get a full meal for dinner.      Honestly, I miss the good old days of stealing chips from the chippy before the parents came to check in for the night. Remember how we used to do that when we were kids?      Aww, yeah! I remember hides, you ordering the spare rib and me taking a few mouthfuls— ew , it was way too greasy, but I always said it was the best. We still had to tell our mums we washed our hands!      Haha, yeah! So what about the weekend?      I went to watch the new  Deadpool  film. It was hilarious and ridiculous in the best way. I highly recommend it if you liked the first one.      Oh, I saw that too! I thought it was amazing. I definitely need to go back to the cinema more. I've been being bad recently—DVDs  every  night! Blameshame!      Don’t worry, I’m the same. I did a little bit of shopping yesterday though—I got this new coat and it is killing me for my £40.      Envy. All I managed was some leggings and a top. You know how I always go all  budget student  on shopping days!      Join the club! I end up being  so  tempted by the '2 for £10' t-shirts and then going home with a bag of junk I don't like.      Ugh, yes! I think our accents must have something to do with our shopping habits. I swear, we were born with the "cheap and cheerful" gene.      Hah, totally! Must be that Midlands-London mix—me belly-laughing over a cheap t-shirt and you dramatically pronouncing food at the canteen. You really go all over the place with those "arthritic salmon".       Oh God , don't remind me.

Rather annoying the new tax policy, isn't it? Seems like everything's getting more expensive, especially when you're trying to save up for a place of your own. I can't even afford a deposit with a mortgage broker thrown into the process.      It's ridiculous. We've talked about it before, and nothing really changes. The government says 'we want to improve social mobility,' but they don’t even let students buy a flat or rent without being priced out. And don’t even get me started on the private landlords—predatory and lazy. You're lucky working in an office.      Right, but it's mostly because I can afford flexible work hours and a decent deadline schedule. On the other hand, you're freelancing, you get to choose your projects. Still, I see you working late, even on the weekends.      It's either that or not earn at all. I've been trying to land this article about housing developments for The Times. People usually avoid the subject unless there's some scandal involved. But the truth is, the divide between the haves and the have-nots is getting harder to overlook every day.      It is. And when you start reading articles like yours, pointing out how the government refuses to fund affordable housing properly, it's clear who's really in charge. I mean, who benefits from having a huge percentage of people living in overcrowded, questionable housing situations?      Capitalism at its finest, huh? Our elected officials don't seem to care. And regarding racism—well, just look at the racial disparities in renting and homeownership. It's as real and as systemic as it gets.      Exactly. I did an architecture project last year involving social housing, and the challenges we faced—mainly from local councils and funding bodies—were obstacles you barely find in housing developments for wealthier families.      Unbelievable. To sit in here, eating our noodles and philosophising over the state of the world, when it's very different worlds we're from.      It's as close as we can get, right? At least lunches like this allow us to talk about things we can’t usually voice in public, where it matters.      Agreed. But I'm still curious—what did you end up ordering? I just picked the pad see ew because I'm a traditionalist.      Shawerma pesto pasta for me. Thought I'd be adventurous.

Rather annoying this new routine of getting up at the crack of dawn. I know it's only temporary, but it feels like I’ll never get a full night's sleep again! How's the nursery settling in for little Emily?      Oh, it’s going alright, actually. A few tears at first, but now she seems to love it. Mrs. Dunne says she's really taken to the playgroup. A lot better than me, that's for sure.      That's lovely to hear. We've been thinking of starting to wean her properly, but I'm a bit worried I'll mess it up. I mean, I read a lot online and it all seems conflicting. Any tips from your end?      Honestly, the most important thing is to go at her pace. Darcy, the nursery nurse, gave me some really good advice – watch for the signs she's ready. She said that if she starts trying to grab food off your plate or visually focuses on what you're eating, that’s a good time to start. And just begin with simple things like mashed banana or apple.      Mmm, that sounds quite reassuring. We might give it a go next week. Thanks, love.      Absolutely, it all just takes time. Looking back at it all, I feel like I worried far too much about everything. You're doing an amazing job, as always.      Well, thank you. What about you? How’s uni going? I feel like I haven’t heard about it properly in ages.      To be honest, it's been a bit of a rollercoaster. I'm in the middle of a big project for my design course, but I’m loving it. It's chaotic but exciting. I’ve already started planning a little trip to Barcelona for the spring break. You up for coming with me?      Barcelona? That sounds absolutely wonderful! A bit of culture and sun to soothe these tired bones. Do I need to pack a sunhat or am I getting too old for such things?      No chance, you’ll be the envy of the whole place with your timeless style. I'll set the date after I pass this course presentation. That is, go out with my best friend if you'd like.      Is that a complement, a proposal, or a threat?      All three. Now, eat up! You’ve had a long morning, and those babies are going to take a bit out of you.

Rather annoying day today, isn't it? That phone bill from EE came through again—their charges just don’t make any sense sometimes. Have you all received your bills yet?      Yes, dear, mine came through this afternoon too. I had to ring them up about the usage charge. Got on to the customer service, and the chap was quite helpful. Said it might be something to do with a data spike last Sunday when they hosted that streaming event. Rather odd, if you ask me.      Ugh, mine hit me for triple the usual. I don't even know how that happened. I was just scrolling through social media and shopping apps, that's it. I haven't even left the house all week, really. I’m going to have to switch back to Three, to be honest.      I think Three has worse coverage here in Lichfield, actually. I had breakfast with a mate of mine this morning, and she was in the café next door using five different networks to get a decent signal. EE was the best one for her.      Well, maybe we can all shop around next week instead of panicking now. We still need to think about sorting out the situation with the police statement. They asked me to give a written account of what I saw at the estate agents on Thursday. Bit stressful, but they seem to be treating the case quite seriously.      Yes, I gave mine already last week after that visit to the station. They wanted confirmation about which car you saw pulling out from the alleyway just before the break-in. Bit strange, the way it all went down.      I thought the same. Did they make it clear about how long this is going to take? I’m still waiting to hear back from my solicitor.      Not really. They just said it’s up for review soon. My, I do hope someone gets caught for it.      I’m dreading the meeting tomorrow afternoon. I’ve got to present the new store layout to the team, and I’m not good at public speaking. Let’s not talk about work after dinner, right?      I can let you borrow notes from my presentation last week. I’m the director of a chain store too, remember? I’ve had plenty of practice. Let me know if you’d like that.      Oh, thank God. That would be really helpful.

: Hey Mark! Mate, how’s the new life in Luton treating you? I’ve been dying to ask—after the wedding, you disappeared off the face of the earth for like a month!     : Haha, I know, bad timing, eh? We went on this dodgy holiday to Cyprus, and then got hit with   sealice   on the last day. I came back with a rash and swore off the sea for a decade. But yeah, how's it all going with you and teaching in Bedford?     : Busy as hell. I swear I spend three-quarters of my time watching re-runs of   Spartacus   only to jump on the PC and mark essays on   Romans  . Fun stuff.     : I still love Spartacus, and I think the   Brits   did a far better job with it than the Americans, no doubt. But this happened to me last week—my sister ordered me a   mortar and pestle   online for some   herbs and spices   she thought I’d enjoy. I haven’t had one of those since I last made   ras el hanout   with my dad when I was 14. Smells brilliant, tastes better.     : Oh, that stuff is amazing with grilled   chickpeas   and flatbread. You know, the kind you slap out like it’s a   Chinese   tea press. Smashing the nuts and spices in a mortar gives it an extra kick.     : Definitely. I do buy fresh nut mix from this market in Bedford and grind them up myself. Can’t beat the texture. Oh, by the way, did I tell you I’ve started trying to   dress nicer   this year? Got a new pair of chinos and that.     : No way, that’s impressive! You used to look like you got dressed in the dark. Hey, speaking of dressing up, I had a funny moment with my sister last week. She sent me a photo of her   new outfit   and wrote, “This is what you always wear with lunches, right?” She clearly thought I wore sweatpants 24/7.     : That’s classic. You really need to invest in more   souvenirs  —even just a fake Italian hat will do. But, bloke, I’ve been meaning to ask. You said you fluished to North Africa a while back, was it with the language team or as a holiday?     : Um, actually, I went with a group—got my chance to practice French and get hit with   malaria   once, which always makes for a good dinner story.

: "Hey, Jess! You're just in time! I was just trying to get my chemistry homework done... but honestly, I’m stuck. Have you done it yet?"     : "Nah, not yet! I’ve been stressing about the English test we had today. Honestly, I think I bombed it. I blanked on the poem analysis totally. Did you get that one with the metaphor about the storm?"     : "Oh, yeah,  The Storm’s Second Thought ! Ugh, I got so confused. The teacher, Miss Lane, always asks the trickiest questions. But I mostly just made sure I talked about the tone and mood. Still, I managed like three paragraphs, which is better than I expected!"     : "Lucky you! I, like, panicked and just turned in a mess. I’m definitely going to fail. Wait, you said chemistry homework? What happened in that lesson today?"     : "Okay, so Mr. Franklin is so grumpy he actually yelled at Charlie—again—about not wearing goggles. But then Lucy raised her hand calmly and pointed out a mistake in his example and he actually  apologised . It was brilliant. I wish we had a teacher like her in English. Miss Lane just…  huffs ."     : "You and her. It’s not just you—French’s even worse. Madame Véronique gives homework every lesson, and someone said she failed half the class last year. I’m already worried for next term. Oh— wait—  have you heard about the new wind band replying to the orchestra?"     : "Oh yeah! My dad brought it up at the dinner table last night. He said they’re going to start giving pickups to school choirs and orchestras. Isn’t that cool? My sister’s in the choir and she was screaming when she heard about it. I wish we had a fundraiser like that for art too—Mr. Baker always complains about not having enough canvases!"     : "I know! He’s been using the same sketchbooks from the 1990s. Still, I’m amazing with recycled materials! I made an entire gothic cathedral out of toilet paper rolls and matchsticks for our art project. Miss Hart was blown away!"     : "No way! That’s so creative. I made a 3D map of London out of those plastic bottles—my friends gave me a right laugh for doing that. But hey, we’ve got the art fair next month—remember? Maybe we can make exhibits together?"     : "Absolutely! I’ll bring the glue gun. Now, quick, want help with chemistry yet, or are we just bragging about artsy stuff all night?"     : "Alright, alright.

Rather skip the newfit lattes innit, ‘ow’s the hurty today, ‘enry?      Y’know, still a bit sore after the football match last week. But it were worth it! We played against a team from Scarborough, near the coast.      Oi, Scarborough’s ‘ood enough fer some people. I’ve been up there a few times with my pals. Got a laugh every time, even if we’d nae a chance!      Leeds United were on TV last night when I come ‘ome. Had to fetch the remot’. Result of united is still dead popular round here.      Yeah, like everyone else’s dad, I guess!      Ten to one your old man’s a Leeds fan, and I’ll be the third ‘Ole in the room’ if ‘e’s breakfastin’ with us at this time.      Blooming cold it is today, though, even for this time of year. Good job we sat near the window with the sun, otherwise we’d be properly nippin’.      I were outside last week, walking to school in this weather—it were ice! Had to put on all me clothes.      Schools these days, still opening when they should be shut. ‘Old somethin’ to say ‘bout that to the head. ‘Balances education with the principles of health’ what someone said in one of them reports!      That’s sour language talk outta ‘er mouth. Don’t think I’d be ‘feein’ that if I were a teacher, eh? I mean, I were a teacher!      Aye, and a good one too! Still know that ‘three rhoas and it were a ‘oliday’ policy. My kids ‘ad to learn that by rote if they wanted to stay active.      That was ‘fore I relied solely on ‘ole ‘ad waiting till I could stick the key in the door. Now’t of me brain space’s with 'im anymore.      Was it really that hard rememberin’ rules? I like rules, personally.      If you like rules, maybe you’ll end up in line in the future, boy.      Aye, nae like teachers all have it made! Me? I’ve been in and out of jobs, never had the stability of a classroom.      That’s sad to ‘ear. I tell you, my lot appreciate the security of knowing somethin’.      Yeah, I dunno what I’d do if I suddenly had to support me own family and ‘alf me school needs help, just like me grandma says.      Well ‘enry, on that note, best be off.

Rather annoying driving today, wasn't it? That Christopher in town’s practically had her car permanently booked in. I got stuck behind her at the supermarket this morning, and I swear she stared at the road for a full ten seconds before deciding to do a U-turn in the middle of the car park.      Aye, I understand the frustration, but I haven't driven for about five years now. Had a few health issues, and besides, that woman’s got every right to be careful. It takes time as you get older.      Oh, don't get me started on older drivers. I had to go to the doctor last week and was delayed because someone at the junction near the surgery decided to contemplate life at a red light for ten minutes. I left fuming. Ten minutes, mind you, and I was late for my appointment.      It must be about muscle mass and hormones, doesn’t it? You know, people are so much bigger in general these days, thanks to genetics and bad diets, and driving requires a bit of sensitivity to environment, too.      Might have something to do with genes, I reckon. My cousin drives as if he's in a competition, and I've never known anyone so tense at the wheel. I was like that too in my twenties – all elbows and heels. He even still needs an operation for his back from the time he nearly flipped the van going around a tight corner.      Interesting observation. I’ve read in journals that there are correlations between lifestyle choices and driving patterns. Urban rush contributes to stress, which can affect decision-making—especially for those in urban areas and being overweight. Not that all overweight drivers are bad, of course.      I don’t doubt the research, but watching this man from the corner shop try and parallel park is like waiting for a jigsaw to finish unassisted. I do feel sorry for him. Maybe it’s not even ability at this point. The anxiety shows on his face. He told me he's allergic to stress, but I don't understand how that could be.      He’s probably lying. He probably just lunches on a couple of whiskeys and took the wrong medication. Still, I wouldn't dream of stopping him. That's one go-round he doesn’t need if he's not feeling settled.

Rather annoyingly, I've got to update the Moodle course for my computer software class this week. The university is pushing for a more interactive format. I’m dreading it, honestly.      Oh, don’t be too dramatic. Look, we’ve both used Moodle for years now — we know the drill. What exactly do they want you to add?      They want me to incorporate more hands-on activities, like simulators and quizzes that give instant feedback. And they’ve mentioned some sort of peer review section. It’s like they expect us to run a gaming site.      Right, but it could make the learning experience a lot more engaging. I had to add a forum for my students last term, and I was surprised how much they actually interacted. Maybe consider a discussion thread around case studies, or something?      Hmm, I was thinking of embedding software tutorials. I could use those interactive Python modules again. They worked for last year’s GCSE group. But I'm not sure how to fit that in with the current syllabus.      Have you spoken to the educational technologists up at the university? A few colleagues suggested their support is surprisingly helpful, for once.      I considered it, but then I got distracted by that email about the new AI ethics committee I’m being drafted into. You know how these things go.      Very true. You know what I found useful when I redesigned my principles of software course last year? Spreading the interactive elements over the term rather than cramming them in. It helped with engagement without overwhelming the students.      That’s a decent idea — spread it out, make it a drip-feed of interactivity. And you’re right, the students did better when things weren’t too concentrated. Maybe I’ll split the course into three parts: setup, analysis, and application. That could help structure the content.      Exactly. And maybe throw in some peer evaluation. It helps build technical communication skills.      I’ll add that. We could even cross-link some of our topics. Websites and data structures with your machine learning examples. More integration between our modules could help the students see the bigger picture.      That would be good. Work on your own improvements and help each other out at the same time.      Cheers. You’re a lifesaver when it comes to Moodle madness. I owe you a coffee.      Or a tea, considering we’re both British.

Rather annoying this, having just got back from New York, do you think the baby will be okay when we head off to the theatre this evening?      Honestly, I've been over this a thousand times in my head. Yes, the baby should be fine — we'll have a night nanny again and all the feeds are scheduled. It's you I'm worried about.      Oh please, I taught a full seminar this morning and hardly felt a thing. It's only four hours, not like it was one of those transatlantic jaunts.      Still, you did get in three hours after I did. I imagine it's worse when the baby’s still wide awake while you contemplate that one turkey sandwich you had on the plane.      Yes, well, I’m thankful for the company and I think it turned out worth it — assembling that cluster of alumni at the university breakfast, tracking down that elusive museum director. They're definitely in discussion about the partnership.      And the drama group is so impressed. Good for you.      Thanks, yes, we must make more time for culture like this. What did you think of  The Hound  last time? It was brilliant, though I'd love to see it again.      I did, the performance last night, it really was something. I imagine it'll be quite different with the new lighting and set. I understand the team has been working on a new kind of ambient visual scheme — quite avant-garde.      That's oddly precise. You've been talking to the designers again, haven’t you?       Shameful grin  Not in so many words... though I might have picked the director's brain a little during our tea.      Oh that was you! I was puzzled by the slightly strange pauses in the scenes, like someone was re-directing them in real time.      Well, the technical preview was something else. I watched it through a lens once — waiting for a friend who lost their hearing aid.      Next time you do that, keep me in the loop. I do love a good mystery set behind a veil of fog and strobes.      Then I shall see if I can procure a side seat for you at the next preview. Hopefully between 8:30 and 9:00 — you'll be alert enough then.      Perfect, and you'll be regenerated by then as well. Do we need to bring anything over?      Wine perhaps — and the baby’s been asleep for the past hour, so I’m sure by the time the overtures start, we’ll be safely gone.

Rather annoying this, having to get my visa sorted when my parents are moving house. You would think the Home Office got the memo it's 2021 and we can digitize such things by now!      Yes, the process is as bad as ever. But it was even worse during the war when I had to leave Iraq for the first time. I had to get every document notarized by thirteen different offices.      Still, easier than having to deal with pulling up stakes and moving to a new country. My sister just called me, she said she's thinking of emigrating because of the cost of living. She's looking at the Netherlands, actually. Have you ever considered that?      The Netherlands is good, especially for people with Muslim backgrounds who are not into the more extreme Wahabi school of thought. It's actually one of the more liberal places for that, and the prime minister keeps a firm grip on religion in public life.      You mean to say it's less restrictive than, I don't know—Libya or something, maybe?      Exactly! Libya is a different world entirely. I tell you, since the war there in 2011, it's gone from chaos to relative control, but it's been mostly controlled by people with oil money and tribal allegiances. The politics of oil don't just end at the border for places like Iraq or Libya. It affects the whole region.      That also explains why young people in the Middle East are looking to move out—job markets are either tied to the oil sector and being unstable or underfunded altogether. My students in Liverpool talk about about how even university is a type of “visa problem” now, depending on where they're from.      Speaking of which, have you managed to tie in any of your friends in Germany for the new academic guest speaker series at Manchester? I’m just curious, since a lot of them have got visas through the E.U.—      Honestly? Not really. Those lectures I’m being asked to coordinate always end with someone explaining how the whole process of getting someone from the Global South into the Western academic world is undermined by these silly procedural points. Rather annoying day today, innit? The till at the shop’s been playing up again, an' I had to argue with some customer who went on like he owned the place. I've had enough of this job for today. Rather annoying, though, isn't it? That whole lot of talk about progress an' peace, but first thing they do is send lads off to die in Iraq. I mean, sure, where d'y' think we were with the world before '03?      Aye, it een't like there wus no prior warnings, 'course. Ay me pa's all "They're a-liar, Tony Blair's a-liar" and I thought 'Oh, na, he wus reasonable'. But now me daugher's schoolfri'y in Salford's pa came back... not the same, even if he made it. Got one lad in me cab said he’s read Churchill and Wolsey, and still remembers the quotes… but says "He'd never been taught how the government really works." – Mate, I said, “Welcome to democracy, eh?”      Now don’t get me wrong, I still fancy a decent game o’ football now and again. Liverpool's still got a bit o' soul. Just wish they’d stop signing those foreign blokes wot can’t speak the language. It's like watching a play through a glass – all motion, na feeling.      Yeah, but hear this—I picked up a German bloke once, mate. Chats me up in Swabian, then shifts to English like it’s na effir to him. Says ‘Yup, treble European cups under Rafa, innit?’ I told him, "You a Liverpool ‘ulie now, ain't ya?" Bloke laughs, says he's from Frankfurt, and that "even though they lost to us, 'e aint na English ‘ulie". Was a good chat.      Pah! Still, I reckon goin' on aboot football and politics w’en you're in Finland is like chuckin' confetti into a snowstorm—no one cares what your team is. So how have things been for ya down in Liverpool?      Fair ’n’ middlin’. Still on the road, ‘cause what else’s there to do? Occasionally I tell the tourists ‘You know, Tony Blair once sat in this very seat’. Only they’re always like 'Who?' Then I say 'Oh alright, he was a Prime Minister—" and you’d think I told ‘em I used to be Elvis, the looks on their faces!

Rather annoying to be honest. I’d love to get more people into the BNC recordings, especially in East London. You know, capturing how local dialects influence language research these days. That’s the dream. I go every Sunday on a morning chat like this, and still feel like I’m just in my head, figuring out what the next big post should be.      Well, I for one am obsessed with the idea of language as a journey.

Rather annoying to be honest. I’d rather be hanging out with you both anyway. How’s the renovation coming along, by the way? Have you sorted out the contractor yet? Rather annoying isn't it, how even simple things like coffee have to be hurled into the public eye like it's the next James Bond movie. Rather than going the usual route, Dad, I’ve heard that the A303 is real busy at this time o’ year. Have you ever taken the coastal route before? I've heard it’s a proper sight to see with all them vi’lets and things by the motorway.      Aye, I took it one summer with your mum when you were about five. You were a bit too young to remember. The views down this way are top-notch; you can see quite a way ahead o’ the car.      Do you want me to read you some directions? I’ve got a map open on my phone. I don’t like getting lost, especially with no signal like up here. Just in case, I’ve written down the main turns and stuff.      That’d be great love. I might be able to drive, but a bit o’ back-up doesn’t go amiss. Like when I was trying to read telegrams back in the day for work, you didn’t always have the time to double-check. That’s the one, pull in up there. Looks like there’s a nice little place for a tea stop soon. Thought it was daft as a box of spanners, mind — all them talking mushrooms and the Queen o’ Hearts. Though I’ve seen worse tales than the old fables and Sherlock Holmes stories.      Oh, I love Sherlock Holmes! Dad, the tearoom even has a room with bookshelves and antiques — like one of those country mansions in the stories. It’s called ‘Jamaica Inn’ — sounds romantic, don’t you think?      Sounds like a startin’ point for a new adventure to me. I saw a wind turbine over yon hill, them modern things do take some getting used to.

Rather annoying when the petrol’s run out on a Sunday, innit? Me an’ ‘im had to traipse all the way outta Wincanton to find a garage with cash left      Aye, we had a bit o' bother wi’ our car last week — sensor went eeny and we ended up stuck on a roundabout by Watchet!      Roundabouts. A lot o' folk still get lost on em, especially if it’s a new one. When I was a youngster, the roads were simpler. Didn’t even need indicators, most ’a the time!      Oh, I reckon, but the roads are only getting more stressed by the minutes.      The new left-hand loop near Tenbury was a proper trial for me. Knew I’d make a muddle of it an’ was far too nervous to use it when it first opened.      I used to live in Timperley, near Manchester, back in the war. We didn't 'ave no fancy roundabouts — just dirt roads, and if you missed a turn, you had to legislate your way back!      Blimey, did you live through it? The actual war, I mean.      Aye, I was drafted in ‘43. We were stationed up in Carlisle, guarding munitions. Lot of snow, no ‘eaters — made for a fair old hardship.      I bet my gran told tales of ration books and sleeping on floors hotter than the bed.      Still, at least she had a bed, eh? Not many about then. My granda talked about living the war in a trench on the Home Front — no thanks!      Aye, it were a tough time, that. My sister ‘ad to work at the Manchester docks — passed out from exhaustion once. Signals me Ma to collect ‘er. ‘Ere, talking of worlds, how about your job, lass?      Oh, I’m a Corpus Administrator. Bits a new one, I know.      What does that entail? Sounds like you're cataloguing books goin' on holiday!      Not quite, but sort of. I study language use in different contexts, particularly dialects. ‘As to make sense o’ it all for academia.      Och, I always liked languages. Never got far wi’ it ‘cause I left school at sixteen, but I dabbled in Russian when I worked at BT.      That's an area where I don't fancy plungein’ in — I barely keep up wi’ Latin at uni!      Ah, well, them young ones now’ve got it far too easy. I didn’t get a chance to study much.

Rather annoying to be honest, I’d rather be at my flat. But anyway, it’s good to visit... What's on the agenda today?      Not much, love. Aye, I agree. We were lucky in our day—had more coursework, more time. Not like these kids now, stuck with all exams. I’ve been thinking of volunteering for a while.      That’s noble of ye. Yer a proper heart, Rob. It’s just one of those big issues we can’t ignore. Got Izzie with a cough that’s dragging on and the GPs can’t book no appointments…      That’s rough. You should try one of those online ones, the NHS 111 site or something. I’ve heard somethin’ about them being quicker.      I will. Thanks, love. Oh, someone at work gave me this cutting—d’ye reckon it’ll root? I’ve got it in a jar at the mo. I’m not being very green-fingered today.      I reckon it’ll grow if ye give it the right lovin’. I had a plant a few years back that refused to die. Water it once a week, give it light, and it just kept going. Then I left for a holiday and passed it to my sister and it shrivelled up in a week.      Ah, typical. I sort of stick to my routine, and that’s what they need—routine! Do ye think I should tie my hair back today? It’s all over the place, even with this headscarf on.      Aye, tie it back. Just don’t go for the full pirate queen look. We’ve seen ‘un enough on campus already.      Ha, seriously, that lad with the dreadlocks and those silver hoop earrings… bit much. But I do wonder if that ‘dreadlock craze’ will catch on up north. I’ve been curious to experiment a bit, but I’m not brave enough to go full Tamil brow or nothin’.

Rather annoying me a bit, eh? You know what me mam’s like—she’s always on about university and all that. But she don’t seem to get it’s not a given you can just rock up and suddenly be cleverer.      Yeah, well, my gran was the same een Cambridge. Thought I’d just glide on in 'cos I got decent A-levels. Nonsense. You’ve gotta actually  want  t’dig yourself outta debt for a few years. Honestly, ain't it just mad how expensive it is for what you get?      Oh hell, talkin’ finances already? I can barely afford me bus fare outta Newcastle, let alone paying for halls 'n lectures. You’d think after the plague bursts, they’d sort their priorities out an’ stop chuckin’ money at blokes in suits.      Cats, it’s a proper scam. Me older sister went to UCL and came back with more student loans than opinions. No, rea’lly. And don’t even get me started on the work ethics of the lot of 'em.      Funnily enough, I were readin’ something ‘bout the Black Death on the train the other day. Dunno why, but it got me thinking about how people back then were, like, barely educated at all, but the world didn’t end. You know what I mean?      Smashing topic, huh? Like, someone back in the 1300s’d have none of our hangups about school—job’s done, they’re farming and prayin’. Anyway, sol’r topic. Why are there so many people about daft about feminism now?      Oh, luv, it’s chaos. My sister’s been telling me I’m not a real feminist ‘til I stop doin’ eyeliner 'n burn my heels. Madness. I just want t’work without bein’ ogled. ‘Course I want equality, but some people take it too far. We’re not in a  revolution , we’re out here waitin’ 'n a bus stop whippin’ up the kettle.      Rea’lly, it’s exhausting goin’ on about it if you don’t even fight for it in real life. Like, if you don’t support your bloke takin’ your shift cause you’ve got tutorials, you’re not really a feminist, are yer?      It’s suffocatin’ sometimes, ‘spose. But I dunno, like I’m allowed t’like make-up and still think it’s important women can choose what they do. You gotta be realistic, y’know?      True enough, but at least it’s better than the alternative.

Rather annoying this, isn't it? You know, how people think they know you just because they passed you in the office once or twice. I was at that café in Santa Barbara today, and someone I used to work with spotted me. I haven't seen her in at least three years. She was trying to chat, and I just wanted to say, “Look, I really don't want to hang around with a fading memory of my life,” but I managed a smile instead.      Oh, I know that. We've all been there. It's never easy when friends become just… inconvenient. I had the same sort of thing happen at the end of last year. I just… don't have the time or the mental space for certain people anymore. The problem is phasing them out without being rude.      Exactly. I think honesty is important. Or at least, being honest with yourself first. I've started distancing more and more people. Not because I hate them necessarily, but because the effort required to keep up the pretense is so exhausting. One time, I actually told a friend, "I don't need this in my life anymore," and we haven't spoken much since. I think she understood.      That's brave. I’m not sure I’d have the guts to just say it straight out. I tend to fake it for a while until I just fade out of their life somehow. But it always feels a bit sneaky, you know? Like, they never quite know what hit them.      Yeah, but maybe that's just because we're all flitting from one phase of life to another and being dragged along with social ties that don't fit us anymore. I did this one time—started not responding to the group chat messages, then gradually removed myself from social media and even changed my number. It was gradual and painful, but kinder in a way.      That’s actually smart. I wish I'd thought of that. I sort of just told people I was moving on with my life, you know, “I’m focusing on my career,” and that was as much as I would say. It wasn't really the whole truth, but it kept the peace.      You're not alone, really. It's part of maintaining your own peace of mind. Life is too full of demands as it is without trying to keep up with everyone who once mattered.

Rather skip a meal just incase I'm working out later. I've had coffee though, that's something... What about yourself, hun?      I grabbed a few crisps and a chocolate bar earlier. Not really proper food, but I didn't want to stop. We haven't been on the road that long, I don't think.      You know, I used to be quite athletic back in my day. Got fit from all the walking in Cambridge. Now it's just pulling weeds in the garden and nothing else. I do miss the chase of feeling strong.      That's easy enough to fix. I can show you a few exercises once we get to where we're staying. My lectures on fitness are only rivaled by my lessons on English grammar! I’m half-joking, obviously, but I do think it's important for health and mental clarity.      I appreciate the thought, love. It’s not that I don’t want to, it’s just... Well, you know how it is when you're not driving, or walking around, and it just becomes easier to forget about it all. I mean, we're not as bound by time and schedules as we used to be.      You'd be surprised, being English and all, how much structure we have in our daily lives still, even if it's not as strict. Rise and shine, tea at seven, phone calls with the family, and don't even get me started on the obsession with the weather forecast. It's a tradition, unfortunately.      Funny you mention that. Also, have you noticed the way people here look at you – all the time, as if you're made about something. I know I'm not a man talking here, but I have to say it's different for you. You don’t see me getting the same amount of attention for being English.      There's that. I passed off a few stares as just me being a westerner, but being a woman does get intense. It’s not all bad – some people are genuinely curious and kind. Though being asked out by men who've never met a British woman is... odd to say the least. Even more odd when it's not by a local man, but some guy from overseas on holiday.      Just don't flirt back and it’ll all go away. And if it doesn’t, I'm your backup.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? That sun's doin' me garden the world o' good.      Oh, I couldn’t agree more, love. I’d a proper pot o’ sun tea brewin’ this mornin’. Gave me a right warm feel inside eenough.      Light one o' them if yer still havin’ sun tea. I’ve only just started me gardenin’ this year, an’ bleedin’ hells, there's more spiders in me plot than me actual veg!      Oh well now, I saw one o’ them big ones in me greenhouse last night, lookin’ like it could’ve swallowed a bird if it wanted! Still, they’re best left alone. One day last month, I had the worst mishap, slipped and磕 in me head on the kettle!      Blimey! Are yer alright then? I mean, ye alright for yer age and all, but bleedin’ hides, that kettle’s near deadlier than the garden spiders!      N’all, luv, I’m as right as rain now. A bit o’ bruisin’ only. But that reminds me, we did have a bit o’ a power cut the other day. I was just about to decorate me cloakroom, and now it's all on hold while the electrics dance their way back to normality.      Oh aye? That’d ruin the decorations just before the festival. We weren’t invited to the local one this year, oddly. Funny that—everyone’s been talkin’ about the delicious looking mugs they were using, but we were too far away to have been considered at all.      Oh the mugs were a hit. I made some myself! Hand-thrown, you see. Doesn’t it feel better to drink out of something you’ve made yer own?      Aye, that’s true. I’ve never had a go at it meself, but I reckon I’d appreciate it more if I did. Speaking o’ that, have ye seen young Pete from next door? He and his lot were doin’ the rounds again, you remember, the ones with the dog that's always sniffin’ every bin on the road?      Oh yes, I do! Poor lad, I think he’s a bloke who’s been tryin’ to find summat steady to fill up his day. Must be tough when you're never worked and all that.      Aye, poorer still when yer used to teach like yer. S’all so different now, isn’t it?      That's one way o’ puttin' it!

So do we get to take our bikes on the train, Nan? I was hoping to hop on when we stop in Brighton.      Oh, I don’t think you can take bikes on regular services, love. You’d have to take the cycle train — you know the one — or maybe ride all the way there from the station. Not sure about the rules this year.      Aye, I think they’ve got a rack at the end of most services now. But not sure it’s one we’ll be using. You’d need to check, but the main thing is — what’s the plan again?      We’re going to Brighton for two nights, and then camping at Eastbourne. Mum said something about a farmstay on the last day, but I haven’t seen them yet.      That’s right, darling — the Catsfield Farm. I called earlier and they said to bring our own sleeping bags in case they don’t have enough. You’ll sleep on the straw bale area again. Good for photographs, that farm!      Aye, place takes you back in time. Got cows, pigs, and the real deal shepherd. Reminded me of watching  Wuthering Heights  when I was young — dramatic skies and all.      So does that mean I can meet the animals?      You’ll get to feed the lambs, at least. Maybe even help gather the eggs — but no promises about the rooster.      Roosters are hotter than the summer sun! Nan wants to sing with their music group at the farmer’s market, don’t you, Nan?      That’s right, lass. Gonna be a little ceilidh caper with the folk band I met up with a few weeks back. Going on a ‘heritage music’ stall — playin’ the fiddle, and they do a bit of traditional tunes.      That’ll be lovely. You always play so beautifully, Ian.      Ah, it’s just a bit of fun with the lads and lasses. Reminisces, you know. Paves the way for the younger generations to learn the stuff their grandparents used to sing about work and war and love.      Will you teach me any tunes? I can strum a bit — just not fluently yet.      Aye, maybe we can have a session by the campfire, sound over the waves. We’ll see if you can tell the difference between a reel and a jig!      That would be magic, love. Now, let’s make a list of what we’re bringing.

So did you watch  10 Things I Hate About You  last night? I just finished it, like... ten minutes ago! I love that film—it's so  classic .      Yeah, I did! We watched it together, kind of! I texted you halfway through but you didn’t reply.  Such  a bad move, by the way.      Oh my god, sorry! My phone just died. Honestly, I felt so bad watching it alone. But anyway, did you like how Patrick was so swoony? Didn’t even want to act in the play at first, but then of course,  Katarina .      Haha, yeah! But what’s up with Kat? She was so serious and prim. I mean, I get the whole Oliver situation, but was I the only one who felt like Joey was the cooler sister? Like better character? More fun?      Honestly? I agree! Joey was the real star of the film, you know? She had so much energy. I would’ve loved to see more of her, maybe even a spin-off— 9 Things I Love About Her  or something. Anyway, moving on... today in school was  horrendous . We had a pop quiz in history. How are we supposed to remember all the Tudor dates? It's  insane .      Ugh, same! I was sure I got a C at least, but now I’m just panicking. Miss Patel also gave me a detention for doodling in my notes. I  should  have known better.      Doodling? I did  literally  the same thing in about five subjects this week! I used a highlighter, though, so it stands out a  bit  more. Definitely not smooth.      You're so bad at subtlety. But hey, you got away with it more than me. I just have terrible luck. Oh! Speaking of school, I heard there’s a field trip planned to London next term. Do you think we’ll get to go?      I overheard the geography teacher talking about it last lesson. Something about visiting the British Museum and trying real scones with clotted cream. I need to see if my parents will pay extra. I’d kill to spend a day in London. We could maybe team up and convince the class to vote for us to have the best trip!      We  could , but I doubt we’ll be the only ones lobbying. Still, imagine walking around the city, tourists! It would be so  epic . I already feel nostalgic just thinking about it.

Rather annoying this new Facebook isn't it? I used to get proper messages before, but now they just plop all them pictures and videos in the middle o' the feed! Mind, I think I might’ve lost me login… Not quite sure if the bird or the hand picked them!      I'm with you there, George. It's all too flashy if you ask me. Though I don’t use it much now, to be honest. My孙辈 keeps telling me it’s alright as long as you don’t let me get sidetracked for hours! But when he messes with my photos, I like to sort of organise them  just so . I get cross otherwise, poor thing!      My lectures are full of students who swear by Facebook. It’s their main form of contact, you know. But I used to think it turned people a bit obsessive – always checking notifications and liking things. I even had a student once who refused to attend a class in person because he’d posted about it and thought he'd already showed up. Madness!      It’s all over the shop, luv. I’ve got the occasional rattle with OCD myself. If I flick a drawer shut and it doesn’t go properly… I have to do it again. Be like the way I used to –  ha!  – clean my boots in the old days. Not that I had many, but cleanliness was part o’ the whole charade when I was younger.      Honestly, George, I think it’s more than just a bit of a habit – OCD is a proper thing with a name, you know. I had to give a lecture on it last term! It’s not just about liking things about yourself or needing to organise the photos. It’s the severity and the time it takes over. My sister had it bad with washing her hands. She couldn't even touch a doorknob without a whole complicated ritual!      Oh Lord, I remember when I used to wash my hands after any contact with  anything  I didn’t trust. You know, when I was still working as a childminder. Even if it was just a child’s face or a toy. Now I can’t even bear to touch a spoon around here if it’s not spotlessly clean!      I think our generation grew up with much less of an obsession, but that might be because of the differences in societal pressures.

Rather annoying when the oven’s on the blink, Christopher grumbled. I was just trying to rustle up a proper Sunday lunch, but no luck. It switched off on me mid-roast      Aye, we've had the same sort of dramas over here. We've been using the eeny weeny toaster oven more times than I'd care to reckon. Not much call for that sort a thing day to day, but emergency's got a way a funny ways of happening      Oh, Christopher, you’re so lucky you're never called in to be the glorified kitchen repairman like I am. One wrong fuse and I'd be chucking the whole supply board out the window in frustration      Honestly, who even left themselves in charge of replacing the oven? I mean, can they pick and choose what electrical appliances they want to take apart for fun? Cats would have been breakfast, no doubt      Haha, Joanne, I pity the poor sod that's going to deal with that mess. They might as well expect mercy from a grumpy puddle of water, sturdy and soaked up in riddles      Did I tell you, by the way, that I managed to mess up the rhythm of our services just last week. Made a cheeky error with the calendars, and suddenly it was all jumbled up into a somersault of wrong appointments      Ooh, Liam! That's a prime candidate for a funny story in one of my ads. All it needs is a bit more oddly-timed chaos with hotter cups of tea going astray and customers looking bewildered as heck      Haha, I about did fall off my barstool when the talking wall clock had finally had enough and just stopped working altogether. Time is such a fickle companion these days, unfaithful in its most basic form      To be fair, I did manage to get the oven to work again by holding it tightly with my bare hands and whispering calm words into its wires. We had to trust in mysterious things sometimes to coax out the right spark of faith      That sounds like the perfect advice for Christopher's next relationship. Just tuck it close and coo goody words into its life if you ever meet another one of those mismatches      Honestly, the box might as well be what your cat left you with at 1 in the morning. Thought it was a present, hours after the incident had gone cold      Lisa, you're so right.

So, I heard you've been up to gigs a lot lately. Any good bands jumping out at you? I got to see some local lads the other week down in Notting Hill, decent tunes, a little flat on the drums, though. Was I the only one thinking that?      Notting Hill now, huh? Sounds fancy for a drummer. Yeah, I try to hit up most gigs in the area now I'm back in Devon. Last week, I saw a trio down by the docks—acoustic, mainly. The guy on drums used just brushes and his fingers—it was wild how different it felt compared to a full band. I've been practicing with sticks and skins again, thinking of trying something like that one day, maybe for outdoor events. Fun stuff. How about you? Still tapping around the house or have you picked up a set again?      Nah, still just the old snare, no room for a proper kit. But I’ve been thinking about applying for an internship at a production company, maybe get some hands-on experience. One of my mates from uni is over there, and he said there's a place for dab hands if you're willing to do the early grief. Kind of like digging in gear, setting up for the bands. Still, feels like a step toward something real – even though I know I'm not Mozart, but hey, every bit helps.      That’s sweet. Maybe you could work some of that into your uni portfolio, huh? Our cousin Georgia got in doing something similar. Just a tip—when they ask for skills, definitely put out you had the patience of a cat and can survive being told to set up again  every time . Haha. I about lost it doing catering once when they wanted the layout changed five times in an hour. Anyway, you going to that gig at the school Friday night? Some of the lads mentioned it. My sister’s on bass, playing for guest band.      Oh, you mean the one with your cousin Billy on vocals again? I tried to get a spot on drums but he said you had to have a signed player from a regional band or some weird rule. Sounds like a laugh. I do miss going out like that—fresh air, nice tannoy, heaps of dodgy drinks. I might see if your cousin needs another shout at the door.

Rather than going straight home, thought we'd pop in for a coffee – nice and quiet, ‘ow. I got us seats over by the window, saved a couple of tables back, so we’ll have a little peace before the rush starts in. Look like it’s going to be a cheerful place for a chat eenyhow.      Yeah, I reckon this is a good shout. The queue at that coffee shop by the library was ages this morning, and I swear it took five forever to get my barista to remember to not put sugar in mine. Here it’s calm, blokes not yelling at the football match on the TV.      What’s that now, football? You like that?      Nah, not really, I just overheard the guy at the counter saying, “Blimey, the Blue ‘uns gonna lose again!” and I figured better not get involved. He looked like he’d be returning a match in his head the whole time.      Ha! Well, I’ll tell you, I’d rather stay over here, looking at the river and listenin’ to that classical station on the radio. So, how’s your week lookin’?      Eh, same old. got a test on Thursday – physics. Don't fancy it, but I'll slap in a few revision hours over the weekend.      You know what, if you don’t fancy the homework, then you just work at the pace you can. Just don’t fall behind. Besides, we can do some revision while we're out tomorrow. I’ve got a domino drive at the church, which is a good few miles out about Durham way. Couple of stalls, bangers and chips, cups of luke-warm tea, and some folks are doing toys for younger ones.      Oi, that sounds like the kind of stuff that’s right up my street. Can I have me a go at the stalls?      Of course you can. I expect you’ll crack it too, like that lad at the youth group always wins with his speed shots on the whack-a-mole.      You saying I’m like him?      I'm sayin’ you're about as likely to win as him in the raffle.      Fair point. Pass the sugar, innit.      You sure about that?      Nah, just wanted to wind you up ‘cause I remembered the barista guy this morning swore up and down my order was to have sugar.      You cheeky sod, I swear.

: Hey Mark! Mate, it’s been ages — how have you been? I haven’t seen you since... What, our final university fresher’s party? Blows my mind how long ago that was!     : No way, that must’ve been four years ago now — or is it five? Either way, I’m still sore about that kebab mishap involving your flatmate’s dog.     : Oh God, don’t remind me. The pup was fine, but it took three months to regain the full use of my voice when he leapt up at me. Still, seems like it did you good — I read you moved to the West Midlands?     : Yeah, I did, settled down in Bromsgrove. Ten minutes from the city, easy commute, and the place is blooming. You? Living in Sussex now — heard it’s better for breakfasts and considerably worse for budgets these days. Haha.     : You know, you didn’t spare a single colloquialism, and that’s exactly why I asked you round for tea — listen, I’m working on a linguistics project to record accents and regional idioms. I want to launch something to help my students grasp rhythm and regional speech. You’re from the West Midlands; I want to capture some of that rich lilt and slang while the memories are fresh.     : Oh sure, no problem. We say things like “well, what someone said,” which is also “well said,” or “barnet” for a hairstyle — you know, plenty of quirks and delicious lexicon down here. I’ll make a chart for you when I get about to transcribe conversation patterns.     : That’d be brilliant — what about your job? You mentioned becoming an assurance analyst? Sounds fancy.     : Yeah, it’s like risk mitigation for high-profile projects. Cool work and surprising earning potential. I’m holding off on marriage and joint bank accounts for now, though. After seeing your sister get pregnant last year and how funds disappeared from her budget, I've got no trust in big financial commitments.     : Fair point. Then again, if you started with a Spanish go-to-place on your own, you'd be free to trade your salary into cigarettes and quality TV, without a partner breathing down your neck about chore splits and childbirth timelines.     : Exactly, and I’ve seen your hours with the budget and cost of living analysis you did for your flat. Sounds like you’ve become a bit of a money expert.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? You know, how they talk about people as if they're not even... real. I mean, look at the way they portray my mam in their programmes. It's not even anything close to how she was. That film they made about her, well—it's just... it's all wrong.      I know what you mean. I've only seen a bit of it, but I could tell right away from the tone. She wasn't like that at all. Always said what was on her mind, but she also had a soft spot for the grandkids. That’s not to say she wasn’t brutally honest—ask me about the time I accidentally left my hair in the pasta sauce.      Ha! Yeah, she'd have had a right old go at you for that, and I think she would have appreciated the fact that it was a laugh at first. I still miss her, you know. She was... I don’t know. I think part of being a matriarch is always being the rock. And now, with Dad—after the cancer, you know—it's like everything's uprooted.      It is. For all of you. For me too—it always hits close. I remember when Nan got hers. It was a long time ago, but I still remember how it felt—like the ground had moved out from under you and you didn’t have a way to catch yourself back. I suppose we just carry the weight of someone being in one part of our lives and knowing they might not be there the next.      I suppose. I try and be there as much as I can for him, but it's not about trying. I know he's proud, but talking to him, I can see he just wants things to make sense. Doesn’t matter if they do—he just needs to be able to talk.      That's part of being there, isn't it? Letting the words come where they will. I mean, I tried to do some little things—some reading about how to support people. You know, Websites and stuff. But honestly, sometimes the best thing to do is just be there. Even if you don't say much. Sometimes it's the silence that's the best map.      You're right about that. I think I learned that with Sue—my sister—after Tom left.

I'm trying to figure out how I could get into a robotics apprenticeship after school. I don't really know where to start. Can you tell me what steps I might need to take?      Oh, Lucas, that's a brilliant area to be interested in! I absolutely love how it combines engineering and creativity. Let me break it down for you. First things first, I’d highly recommend focusing on your science and maths GCSEs this year — they're your building blocks. Next, once you finish your exams, start looking into what you specifically want to do: hardware, software, or both? But you can also look at apprenticeship schemes from engineering-based companies or even tech startups who are beginning to move into that space. I’d also suggest trying to network with people in the field—maybe join some online forums or even set up a LinkedIn profile with a bit of professionalism. Don’t go overboard on the formatting if you’re new to it.

Rather annoying when the book club meeting finds its way into a discussion about tax returns, isn't it? Mind you, I rather liked discussing Anna’s poetry last time. Here in Peterborough, I actually had an old bookcase in which I would hide stickers and little trinkets. It's funny how some memories pop up seemingly out of nowhere and remind us just how much our homes shaped us.      Very true. You know what struck me about our current job roles, though? I think that’s what truly makes the book club function as well—it's not just about the books or even work. It's about the shared language of connection between us.
