Used to run a childminder service, but that’s long gone. I did all right while it lasted, but when the numbers dropped and the hours were too long, I just gave it up. Some people call it retirement — I call it runnin’ out o’ steam.      That about sums it up.      Still, I reckon between us we can manage a bit o’ what we need. A cup o’ tea, a few sums, and a bit o’ mindin’ our garden — as long as we can talk and reminisce over this, we’ll be all right.

Rather annoying this new train station delay, isn't it? I've been trying to get down to Exeter for some time now, and with the delays, it's been impossible. I've heard they might open by the end of the summer, though.      Yes, Andrew, it's awful. My friend at the local school even got stuck in Bridgwater last week on her way back from a training day. It really does make the village too cut off, especially for young people. It would be great to have a regular train again.      I agree, Jan. And not just for the kids. My parents who live in neighboring town can’t easily pop out for day trips or even visit us without driving. With the current bus schedule, it's unreliable. But back to the dinner – I followed the lemon and thyme chicken recipe you gave me last week, Jan, and it was amazing! Your breakfast recipe is next on the list.      Oh, the lemon and thyme recipe – sounds mouth-watering. I was thinking the other day, we should all try one of those meal prepping apps I heard about. I mean, with your recipes as the base, it could be perfect for the week ahead. It's supposed to help track portions and suggest ingredients you already have at home – saves time and money.      That does sound useful. I’m quite health-conscious these days, what with the new year and all. I’ve been focusing on adding more lean proteins and superfoods to my meals. Let me download it this evening and see what it's like. Andrew, did you ever weigh in again after retiring? I’m guessing fitness is still something you keep up with?      Ah yes, the "retirement shape-up," as I call it. I’ve switched from golf to daily walks and occasional swimming. Doesn't sound too glamorous, but it's better for the joints. I've been tracking it all on my phone – active minutes, steps, the whole nine yards. It's surprising how easy it is to lose momentum when you’re out of the daily rush, really.      That’s great to hear, Andrew. I’ve been trying the 5km walks on weekends with a few friends. It's good to keep goin' on your own, but even better with company. And speaking of company – anyone fancy trying the local scones this weekend?

So did you watch The Lie last night? That Shakespeare remake they put on TV was wild, right? I mean, I respect Shakespeare, but casting a 16-year-old in a lead role where he's whispering lines… honestly, I was half asleep by the end.      Yeah, I saw that too, and honestly? It was ridiculous. I reckon his character's motivations were completely lost. I’ve only read Julius Caesar twice before in English class, and even I could tell what was going on. This version just… didn’t hit the right notes.      Tell me about it! I was thinking of how brilliant  Romeo and Juliet  the 1996 Baz Luhrmann one was, you know? There was so much ambition in this new one, but it just felt like they lost the essence of the story. I mean, did everyone watch it?      I don’t know about everyone else, but my mate in my university seminar was ranting about it this morning, even showed up late to class. One guy said it was like watching a dream, if the dream was about a bad idea written in iambic pentameter and scored with a synthwave track.      Haha, classic seminar banter. So is your session actually about Shakespeare next week? I remember you mentioned it was a module thing. Let me know if you want to team up for the reading. I could probably foresee you wanting to swap homework again.      Oh yeah, it's a seminar on Early Modern Drama. I've got to give a presentation on Hamlet. So if you want to split the workload, I’m your man. Although, I might flake out and go to the pub instead the night before.      You always say that! Going to the pub shouldn’t be an option if you're giving a presentation. My sister had to do one about  Macbeth  and she actually based her presentation on her stag weekend. She told the professor all about the anal probe question, you know the one…      Oh God, I remember that joke! He nearly flipped his lid. I can't imagine the seminar leader reacting like that. Still, maybe something wild would make your presentation interesting. I can go out of my way to be wild.      You’re just in denial about study. Honestly, go to the library, read the texts properly, and don’t play FIFA in the corner of the seminar room after falling asleep.

: Hey Meg! I haven't seen you in what feels like ages!     : I know, Claire! I've been so swamped at work, and then my break got pushed back again. How are you?     : I'm good, busy as ever with the project coordination at Newton Ltd. It's one thing after another. Have you had your coffee yet?     : Not yet! I just got here. Oh my god, what is that smell? Is this the new coffee machine? It's amazing.     : Yes, the new one! I've been here so much lately, I'm practically part of the staff now. So tell me, how's Manchester treating you?     : It's good, busy, but I absolutely love the marketing executive job at Pearson. It's a far cry from working in Oxford.     : Oxford! Haha, I remember the days you and I were both felling in love with the first-years. Good times, right?     : Oh, I still joke about that! Anyway, what about you? Still seeing that guy from your old uni?     : No, we broke up just after Christmas. It just wasn't working out. He was still living in the dream world of his final year!     : Ugh, I understand completely! Liam and I ended around the same time too.     : That's unfortunately a bonding point for us, then! So, what are your plans for the summer?     : I'm heading back to my parents in about a week. They want the "usual." You know: watching football, going for a walk, and not doing much else.     : At least it's the peace you need! I'm hiding out at my flat. I actually need a health check-up next month.     : That’s a good idea. You must take care of yourself, Claire.     : Thanks! And what about your new role? Any exciting projects?     : You bet! We're rolling out a new campaign in July. I'm leading a small team now, so it's been very exciting.     : That's amazing, Meg. I’m proud of you!     : Thanks, it's been a bit of a whirlwind, but I love it. I have to get back to the office at 3. I’m so glad we caught up like this.     : Me too, always a pleasure, friend. Let's make more of these catch-ups soon, yes?     : Definitely, we can go for a walk in the park next time.     : Great! I’ll bring my camera, it's been far too long since we snapped something fun.     : Can't wait!

Rather annoying the new herb’s not grown in yet, ain't it? That thyme I put in first... got nigh on no leaves left now.      Yeah, I mean, it is a sun spot we gave it, but maybe we overwatered. Or maybe it’s that eeny weeny pot, don’t think it’s enough room for it.      Aye, I dinnae ken. I just got it off this market stall down by the dump, it looked nice and bushy. Bit like when me n’ ya first moved in ’ere—we bought like three miniature ferns and  promised  we’d look after ’em.      My turkey pot fern died first, then the spider’s one. Ten minutes after the water came out, them leaves started drooping. Fair turned brown an’ fell off, like a dodgy Christmas tree.      Fair daft... I reckon if we’d got planting books from the library, or even showed up at the gardening society once, we’d be like terracotta lords by now.      Aye, well, as it is, I only took on that PhD in botany so I’d know proper. Still, first project got rejected. Not enough – what’s the word – empirical, they said.      Blimey. All that scribbling down about photosynthesis and ‘Balloon plant propagation’ principles and all. They wanted more ‘peer-reviewed data’.      Aye, so I’m out in the greenhouse at dawn, cataloguing these strange ivy-looking microbes I found slipping along the balcony wall. Not nearly about to make sense of it all yet.      Well, whatever happens, you’ll not need research to learn to make a proper cup of tea, eh? Got the herbs, got the mugs. Got that nutty Virginia Boy Blend.      Oh, aye, give me that. I tried making them matcha ones once. We ended up with a green yellow sprite of lukewarm earth.      More importantly, have we got biscuits? The scones I made this morning. Still warm, an’ go straight with the tea. Got a recipe from me aunt. Gave her line in the baking classes at Darlington—bit blokey, but what can you do?      Biscuits and blokes, eh? Sounds like a team-up. True to say, we’re not ‘bakers’ per se, but this lot tastes a fair bit like what I got at Nana’s.      And always remember, tea first, biscuit second. Or we’ll lose all our good work, and before we ken it we’ll be off herb-taxonomy again.

Rather a wet weekend, wasn't it? I spent most of mine pottering in the garden — finally got round to pruning the roses before they went to sleep for winter. Not a bad way to spend a rainy Sunday, in my opinion.      Aye, we had a few showers up in Tredegar, but I managed a few snooker games at the club — always nice on a wet day. Mind you, I’ve got this backlog of marking to catch up on. It seems my students are as keen to forget the essay guidelines as I am to mark them!      Ha, I know the feeling. I’ve been grading law essays and I swear half my students think the Napoleonic Code still applies to British highways. Fun stuff.      I heard you're from Cairo, and I was just curious — did your childhood in Egypt at all influence your views on institutions, like the police or the military? They're taken in completely different ways there, from what I gather, compared to the UK.      Oh, absolutely. I suppose growing up in a place where those forces aren't always seen with quite the respect they might be in the UK, it made me appreciate how much domestic stability we take for granted here. Of course, it's complicated – but it's often the same, isn't it?      Truth be told, I've been thinking about it a fair bit myself, what with our student recruitment committee looking into how someone with a criminal record might stand a chance to join the police force or the army. Strange times, eh?      It is, and it's not always a bad thing — as long as we make sure people are suitable for the roles, right? Although, I have to say — what's this I hear about that young football player who treats his toddler like a trophy in social media selfies, like it's some kind of performance for the masses?      Aye, it's something, isn't it? I tried to explain to my niece that pro-players live such strange lives that they've probably forgotten what ordinary life with kids is like. At least the snooker players play it cool — you know, they’ve got that calm, composed image even in the world championships.      True. I find watching snooker quite refreshing between marking sprints — all that quiet concentration. Passes the time. I have to get back to grading soon though, before I'm hours behind again.

Rather annoying the new barista at my office isn’t turning up. I was hoping she would’ve handled the coffee rush on Thursday, but no luck yet.      That does sound a bit awkward, doesn’t it? I’ve seen her a couple of times at uni events, so if it’s the same one, I’ll try to give her a nudge about it. Is she not responding to emails?      Nope, just radio silent. Oh, and by the way, someone mentioned you’re coming to the christening for Elise?      Yeah, I just confirmed with Mum. I’m still bringing Harrison, as we said, and we’re working on the nursery arrangement for Saturday. Elise must be enormous now.      Yes, I’m Oliver. He is very sad in the world now.      Mummy! Wait, I meant Elise, not Oliver. Elise is getting ever huger, isn’t she!      Hugier. And I like Oliver.      Of course, of course—Oliver is a delight. Now, to go back—Elise, yes. I’ve got a plus one going for work on Friday, but I’ll be here at the Baptistry for the christening, and I’ve just organised a huge cake.      A huge cake! You know what that means—Mum and Nana will be in their element. Oh, and also, I might not be able to work at the café on the Saturday morning anymore, at least until October. I want to be at home with Harrison more.      I daresay. You’re doing a mammoth job as it is. Work can take what it wants! Though are you telling me you’re resigning?      Not quite. Just cutting back to part-time. I passed my exams with exceptional results, by the way.      Oh, I am so pleased for you! I told you being a good student and a good mother is not impossible.      I told Mummy I’m the best mummy in the whole world.      Oh, go on then, you are!      Well, I do love a confident daughter. Alright, let’s not bicker today. Pass the strawberries, would someone please? I am famished and we’ve still got the tea to prepare.      Just made some, Mummy—lemon and green mint. It’s supposed to be sooo healthy.      I like mint!      Then you’ll enjoy this, alrightOliver-takes-a-strololo.      I want some biscuits.      You’ll have biscuits. After a bit of tea and some healthy stuff.      Well then—family, strong and chaotic, as expected.

Rather annoying the wet weather isn't it? I was looking forward to getting the garden in order over the weekend... What d'you think Anna?      Honestly, I've been over that! It's thrown my plans all over the place. We'd decided to take Martha to that new soft play centre down the road, but with the rain it's just been too bleak.      Mama, can we go into town?      Maybe tomorrow, love. But what about you Sophie, have you done anything planned?      Still mostly just rewatching some old films and thinking about New York. We've made that reservation yet, haven't we? The tickets left so quickly this year! I do hope the kids are on board with it.      Martha's actually really excited. She keeps asking when we're going to 'go to the big house with all the lights'. And I'm ever so grateful we talked you into looking after the bookings, Sophie. That website was more confusing than I could manage!      Well, I can be quite tenacious as you know. And I'd rather deal with that than watch another rainy afternoon passing by. I remember when we got married it was much the same—fine one moment, downpours the next. But Anna, the weather wasn't quite the problem as what you did with the wedding cake!      Oh God, you still bring that up? I remember slipping on a puddle and crashing into one of the waiters—piece of the cake flew across the table into the vicar's wine!           It was a disaster, but good fun in the end. Speaking of which, have you managed to sort out that schedule with work for the week of the trip? You do have that time off?      I'm holding on tightly, I've arranged it with the new team waiting till I get back. It's been tight this month being both a manager and trying to find time for the big trip! But it's worth it. Six months of saving for a New York holiday! Martha’s practically got go bags ready with snacks and 'NY' stickers.      She is a clever one. Well we’ll need to start checking out what your schedule is like. I have a few ideas about where to stay and where to go. Grand Central, the museums, a walk around Central Park. Anything sound good?      Anything sounds amazing.

: Right, so I've got this load of paperwork from my thesis advisor that I'm trying to get through... got to submit it by Friday. Otherwise, I’ll miss the submission window.     : Oh no, do you have a plan yet? I remember my thesis advisor was pretty strict on deadlines.     : Yeah, I reckon I just need to break it down a bit. A lot of this is just forms—like the ethics declaration, funding paperwork, and some data analysis protocols. You’ve been through the same for your psychology thesis, right?     : Yeah, it was mostly bureaucracy, honestly. I filled in the ethics form only to find out I needed a separate one for each dataset I used. Fun stuff.     : Oh great, I feel like I’ve avoided the worst of it so far, but this is starting to catch up. Let me explain what I’ve got. First, I need to input my topic into the university portal, then get the supervisor’s approval—and that’s not optional, I’ve seen people get pushed back because of it.     : Oh definitely, I had to chase my advisor for two days just to get an approval note. They’re usually quite busy, especially this time of term.     : Right, so that’s one thing. Then there’s the consent forms for participants—this one’s for the interviews I held back in Manchester. And, uh, there’s someone who hasn’t returned their filled-out copy yet… a bit of a blocker.     : Oof, I had the same problem. Had to send  multiple  reminders. You might have to make a note to chase them up properly.     : I will. There’s also this research methodology form that I need to submit. It asks for my hypothesis, the sample size, the techniques I’ve used. All quite detailed.     : Yeah, I assume you’ve already got most of that typed up for your thesis, so it should be straightforward to extract. You can cut out the fluff and just include the essentials.     : Exactly, I’m going to run through it like a checklist—tick each part off as I go. I’ll start with the portal first, then the signatures. Once I’ve got those sorted, the big one is the literature review section of the proposal—it needs to be verified by the academic committee.     : Sounds like a solid to-do list. I’d get the easy stuff out the way first so you can focus on the meaty bits later.

Rather annoying to wake up in the middle of the night grinning like a fool, then spend ten minutes trying to remember what the dream was about. I’m more than a bit confused by this one. It was something to do with £20 million, I think?      Oh, don’t get your hopes up, Nick. You told me the same thing last week. I’ve given up on believing you’ve won the lottery. If you had, I’d expect you to actually tell me rather than pulling these little stunts at midnight. I nearly kicked you out of bed, I was so bewildered.      I’m  this close  to actually winning the lottery, Karen. You know I’ve always said if I did, first thing I’d do is adopt two dogs. I’m not obsessed or anything. But imagine having the freedom to look after a labrador and a German shepherd? They’re both such noble creatures.      A labrador and a German shepherd, you say?      Woof woof?      That’s right, Zoe! And this one— as enthusiastic as ever. But real, proper dogs. Ones that live in the house, trot around in little harnesses, and generally make us all feel like we’re part of something important.      Let’s not forget the part where they chew through the furniture, bark at everything that moves, and make a mess of the garden. I’m just saying—before you audition dogs on a daily basis, we should at least consider our ability to keep a clean home and let the politicians look after the world’s problems.      I do clean up after myself! And you’re the one who said watching kids grow up and watching old things break down is alike. So shouldn’t I get to break a few things in my own way, like owning a dog?      That’s true, I did say something like that. Okay, fine. I’ll consider it. You can dream your dream. As long as we’re clear:  you’re  buying the lunches,  you’re  walking the dogs, and  you’re  washing the bedding. Deal?      Deal. And when I win the lottery, I’ll commission a building in your name. Finally, a legacy to be proud of.      Maybe we’ll all live in the house made of £20 million’s worth of money.      It’ll be like Hogwarts!      Precisely, my young dreamer. Hogwarts, with dogs and oatcakes on tap.

Rather annoying I had to go to A&E last nigh', love.      Oh no, what happened then? You're not poorly, are y'?      Noo, it were me foot. Stepped off the garden wi’ a stone in me shoe. Got eenywee out of me runner.      Oi! Sounds like a job fer the A&E, but serious?      Oh aye, me foot’s like it’s on fie. They did an x-ray, said it’s no broken, but I’ve got a sprain. Still, I’ll be randy as a rat in a week, innit?      That’s a relief though. I’d be rallyrified if y’d had a break, specially now I’m stuck lookin’ after you fer a while.      Aye, I know. I’m a bit in pain at the momeh, but I manged to drive myself. Should’ve thought to call you instead, though.      Well, listen—stick t’ the ice an’ asprin fer now. If it ain’t better in a coupla days, we’ll take a trip to the physio.      I’m not looking forwards to that, mind. I hate all that rubbin’ and stretchin’. Silly if I’m already in enough pain.      Nah, but it’s the sort o’ stuff that’ll help you run up i’ the garden without a stone in your foot again. Just give it a shot, love.      Alright, I’ll try. What I don’t get though is the queue at A&E. Sat there for three hours! An’ that was on a Monday nigh', unbelivable.      Unforty, that’s happenin’ more n’ more at them places. I’d imagine it was all sorts of folk, from heart attacks to little ones with scraped knees.      Right enough. Next time, I’ll just keep the whinge to meself an’ let it sort itself.      Don’t be a m goon then. It wasn’t that bad, was it?      It were alright. Bit of a bloke on the telly all the time. I watched half The Great British Bake Off while I waited.      Oh, well that’s worth it alone, ‘preciate the pasty silence of A&E.      Aye, they gave me a plaster an’ all, an’ a leaflet on recovery. Just didn’t mention the bakery-telly combo.      Aye, but now you’ve got a story t’ tell, don't y’? A&E on a Monday nigh’ with a dodgy foot and half of Bake Off—end of the world, innit?      Typical Del!

Rather unusual day today, isn't it? That news about the new tax laws in France—they've been talking about it on the telly all morning. It's going to have a few ripples over here, probably.      Aye, heard about it over the wireless on my way in. I'm telling you, I don't think they've thought this out properly. Costs will only go up again—already affects my suppliers. Not that I'm complaining, mind you; but times are getting tighter.      It was the same for us last week when the school had to cancel the international trip due to currency restrictions. Mary was terribly cross. She wanted the children to learn about another culture, and now that's off the table for another year.      Tenacity, isn't she? D'you know, I remember her coming round for tea with a plan about a pen-pal scheme when she was younger. I said, “Why not get in touch with a teacher in the States?” That's where the idea for the first store came from, actually.      Oh, yes! That was a clever idea. I never thought about it as a business idea at the time, but now that you mention it—it shows how far we've both come from humble beginnings. How's the new branch in Brighton coming along, by the way?      Well, it's not moving as fast as I'd like, to be honest. Still finding the right space. Our usual contractor said there are too many restrictions with the old buildings. It's a bit of a tangle, but the dream's still in the air. Any word from Margot about the future ballet competition?      Not yet. I think she's having problems getting the foreign talents to commit. Expenses are too high, or it's the school holidays. Doesn't matter—the youngster's got spirit. My, they've made me proud over the years.      Aye, well, it's folks like you, bringing the next generation up, that makes all the difference. We may run our own businesses, but it's people like Mary who've shaped the community.      That's very kind of you, Jack. Then again, you've brought a bit of go-get-it spirit to life about here. If it weren’t for you, we’d probably all still be sitting in the garden, knocking the ball about and calling it a day.

Rather skip the chips and meat pies tonight, to be honest. I've had enough crumbly sausages to last a lifetime this week. Have you tried the salmon on toast by the window? It's been doing rather well with the locals.      Oh, the salmon was alright last time, mind you, I think the one they bring out is always slightly overcooked. Though they don’t serve that bad a gammon or the sticky toffee pudding, so we're not complaining terribly.      Oh, I'll pass on the gammon, but the sticky pudding is too tempting not to try again. Though honestly, I keep hoping for someone to rediscover the apple crumble and custard.      Ha! Yeah, we tried that once, and the custard was more pastry than milk I think. But I did watch Happy Valley again while we waited for the last breakfast, and that lady inspector is just brilliant with a gun in every episode.      Oh, didn’t you say the costume designer once worked in your university office? I do like the way the series changes location from the moors to the landfills as if they’re choosing the prettiest possible hideouts for villains.      Oh right, she was here at the old estate office before they let her go, but they say she went on to film somethings quite notable later. Anyway, speaking of the university, didn’t you say the toilets looked exactly like this someone at the Guardhouse?      Oh, absolutely, it's got the same paint-chipped urinals, and I swear it’s repainted using university wall colours from the 1970s. I walk in sometimes and feel like I've stepped into the loo at my old halls.      I noticed the handle is the same one in my old office, too. Though I rather miss that ugly light fitting they used here. It’s been there as long as I can remember, and it used to flicker exactly on your passing.      Oh that one’s constant now! Used to take a week for the maintenance guy to come and do the light, but you remember, after the fire alarm incident in the admin buildings, goings on were quickened up a bit.      Yeah, that must’ve been it. Incident, bloke on the coat peg, and you could've sworn it was swinging to the tune of one of our old hours of lecture halls.      Oh yes, and over by the bar, that cat they keep stringing up in the net near the cold lagers, do you still think it’s remotely real?

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh, lad? Thought we’d get a bit of a break by now. I got nay pictures out the other day because o’ the sodden clouds.      Aye, cannae argue wi' yer on that one. But it’s no’ een time to be out takin’ photos anyway, really. Ay, I had a break in the rain last Friday, though, and I got out tae the top o’ Arthur’s Seat. Got a reasonable panorama. Manage tae get decent shots?      Nae really – too many drops to see through. I’m still practisin’. Got me the new camera only a few weeks ago. It’s a bit fancy for me standards. Och, but I dinnae ken if I’m gettin’ the knack o’ it yet.      Aye, it takes a bit o’ time. I used tae take photos in my gap year, wanderin’ aboot Spain, France, Italy. Still got the memories.      Nae, tell me aboot it. I’ve been thinkin’ o’ doin’ a wee trip, maybe. A gear change from trainin’ folks in warehouses.      Ha – that’s a new one! Gear change, eh?      Aye, just to dinnae be cooped up all the time. I might head doon tae the Lake District in May. Maybe get me camera out there a bit moor.      That'd be a good stretch. It’s hillier than I’d expected when I went there, but I did dae a wee trip wi’ a couple o’ friends. Camped out threet nights, and the photos are still better than some I've seen.      That does soond like the ticket. Geo., do ye think a basic camera would be alright for landscapes? Or shood I splash out on something a bit moor advanced?      Well, depends ho wee professional ye want tae get with it. If it’s just for the joy o’ it, like you said, the one ye’ve got will do. No’ goin’ tae see improvements unless ye're takin' classes or readin’ up on the art.      Aye, well, maybe I could have a look at a class, then. I’d like tae get better.      That’s the spirit. Tell ye what, if ye're headin’ doon tae the Lakes, maybe we could do a wee trip together. Get the limbs movin’ and the camera roll growin’!      That’d be noo bad at aw, Geo. Och, I’d be muckle grateful for the tips. It’d be good tae stretch a bit.

Rather annoying the new layout in the living room, isn't it love? That coffee table squinting like it got the hiccups from the dining room. But I suppose it gives the place a bit o’ character, don’tcha think?      Character, yes—Deer in headlights during a thunderstorm, more like. It was all   Vicky  ’s idea, trying to tie in that awful yellow curtain. Honestly, I don’t see how she can breathe around so much fluff.      Well, she’s young. Looks like she’s still learning what “style” even is. But don’t frown so much, love. You’ll get lines around your eyes and you’ll look like a grumpy old   Margery   from the bingo hall! I’m far more worried about your brother,   Tim  —remember? Drunk at the pub again last night, trying to plant hypothetical tomato plants in the community centre’s budget.      Ugh, yes! That’s what I get for inviting the whole family to Christmas dinner. Last year was better, at least—  Aunt Lucy   showed up in Wellington boots and a banana tart. Did I tell you, by the way? I’m watching that new documentary on BBC about nurseries. So fascinating. They showed this one in Sweden where they let babies sleep in the Hayek, but the nappies don’t count as mortal sin?      The what? The Hayek? Now you’ve gone and put an idea in my head. You’d better not let them try that on  our  grandbaby, I’ll have you know. Anyhow, speaking of plans for the week, there’s a school about forty minutes up the M6 you mentioned the other week. We were thinking of a visit on Thursday—heaven knows it’ll be less dramatic than staying around   Vicky  .      Oh, I’ve got guest speaker Friday morning too, some chap called   Tomlinson  —sounding extremely pompous. I haven’t met him yet, but I hope he doesn’t start tutting at the kids. And also, by the by, I think I told your mother I’d be going over there for Sunday lunch.      Oh good Lord, go over  there  again? Don’t forget to ask her for those brussels sprouts she freezes between layers of guilt. I swear, if I had to eat another one at her house I might grow stalks and move into the garden.      It’s alright, we can complain about her over tea and biscuits on Sunday.

Rather annoying day today, innit? Conference request came in last minute and had to sort it real quick. I got nuffin’ done after that.      Yeah, sounds hectic! Me day was… well, me and the lads were layin’ floorboards at a new site een Mesty. Hard work, but got the job done.      That’s a relief. A lot worse than me day. I’ve got a meeting with a supplier tomorrow and I couldn’t find a decent pair of trousers to wear. Found me one when I gave up and went out to fetch chips.      Aww, don’t worry love, you always look smart. Though if it’s a proper meeting, you best make sure your blazer’s clean, ain’t right to turn up lookin’ sad.      Sounds posh, all that! Why’re you havin’ supplier meetings anyway? Sounds a bit in me opinion more like bosses and spreadsheets to muck about with.      Nah, it’s more practical than that, luv. I’m controlling the production flow in a warehouse. If the shipments don’t arrive on time, everything gets held up and folks get annoyed.      Sounds complex. I just have to book meeting rooms, make sure delegates know where to go, and sort out tea and scones.      Bless, that don’t seem too bad. Least you don’t have to wrestle with nails and splinters like me.      Some folks would’d think it’s a stretch to call being tea steward a proper job! But it’s all logistics at the end of the day. Just different levels of the scale, innit?      At least you know that your work makes a difference. Me job feels like organisin’ bin collections ‘cos everyone hates it.      Hey, no meself to knock it. You probably got all them fancy folk eating outta you hand when you sort out all the event stuff.      That’s probably the dream, innit? More importantly, have you seen Johnny? We set him a task earlier this week to feed the cat while away goin’ on his holiday.      Nah, I haven’t, but I will. He’s likely bloomin’ forgot already.      Typical. Me feels we should’ve just left the cat in a kennel.      Nah, that ‘d be mean. We trust them!      Unless we got a cat that’s a bit of a menace, in which case, I don’t think we made the best choice of pet-taker.      Aye, better get Johnny sorted out first thing tomorrow.

Rather a cold day, isn't it? I’ve just boiled the kettle and made us a pot of tea. What do you fancy—milk or no, and how many sugars, if any?      Oh, a nice cup of tea is just the ticket, isn't it? Thank you, dear. I'll take mine with one sugar and just a touch of milk. It’s not often I get a proper sit-down with a brew in this weather, honestly.      To be fair, you can blame the weather for everything these days! Here in the North, we’d have grudgingly accepted this as mild! I reckon it's the government supply of tea that's turned everyone posh since I retired. Still, best to not argue with what we’ve got.      Roast and I in mine, please. Living in Newport, you’ve got to have something breakfast-y to get through the morning! And no shortage of tea, if you ask me. I remember when I was still teaching—it was the only thing to keep you going between classes.      Aye, listen to the one who’s had a proper job to work for it. Us two old lads just sat around watching the telly and wondered what was for dinner.      Ha! True enough. Though I reckon retirement suits me best now. Not that I was ever the best at keeping a job—never could be bothered with someone bossing me about!      And I’ve had my fair share of children floring themselves at some point or another as a childminder! A good cup of tea and a sympathetic ear have about the same effect now as a gold star did in the past, I’d say.      You know, I used to take the children out for a picnic in the school garden, and we’d always have a nice thermos ready for lunch. Nothing brings people together like a bit of food and friendship, I think.      You're getting all deep on us now, aren't you? But I agree. Tea with company is a proper luxury these days. Not many people about who’d care to sit down for half an hour and talk about nothing in particular.      It's not about the conversation, really. It's just being together. It always lifts the day up.      Indeed. It's the little things, really, isn't it? Like tea with friends.

Rather skip the new bar in Norwich. You know what a nightmare the CRB checks can be if you’re serving or taking kids around afterwards. Remember the last time?      Oh, absolutely! It took ages before we could even entertain the idea of being at a restaurant with a kid’s section again. That and my passive-aggressive sister-in-law didn’t make things any easier.      Aww, now I feel sorry for you! Coming from Wales, we don’t even think about that as much. We’ve got our own kind of chaotic vibe, but nothing like the English CRB tsunami.      Ha! Welcome to our chaos, then. I had to go through one for my job at the university. Honestly, I swear my childhood photo is still haunting the system.      But let's not make it all about administrative nightmares. I was thinking we try something new for breakfast, maybe even go out to a cafe with a drive in morning. Nothing’s more English than a decent scone and a croissant side by side!      As long as it's not one of those places that takes three hours to make your latte. I've had enough of London delays as it is. Speaking of, how are things over in the Capital?      Mate, it’s fairly nuts, still. The protests are getting huge. One time last week, I got stuck in the middle trying to get to a lecture. I might as well have been in a geographical seminar in real life!      That does sound dramatic. Nothing like an impromptu walking tour of a protest while sipping takeaway tea. Can I come next time?      I don’t think your constitution would handle standing on the spot all day like mine. But if you're into art, there’s that small new gallery near King's Cross. Maybe we could do something less ‘Revolution’ and more ‘Impressionist’?      Sounds like a plan. But before all that, how about someone drinks their water instead of getting distracted by the lure of pubs and art?      What? Pubs are the soul of England! Now if you're not having a drink, where's the Britishness in the dinner?      Fair enough, Professor. If it's one thing I've learned in my Welsh upbringing, it's that a bloke without a drink can get a bit… dry.      Romans, we're Romans. Always something to toast to, even if it is our endless British bureaucracy over tea and biscuits.

Rather annoying that the new planning application for the old manor house was rejected, really. They'd been talking about selling it for years, and it would have sorted out that awkward path by the field where we walk.      Hmm, I heard as well — wouldn't have been much in it for the owners anyway, considering the cost of the necessary works. They probably just wanted to hang on for a bit. A shame, but I suppose that's just how it goes.      Yes, and now we might end up with another developer coming in with yet another proposal. You know how these things go — it will mostly mean more dead ends and double yellow lines, no doubt. Have you managed to get Myra on the phone at all? I left her a message about calling her back from the hospital, but I haven't heard anything.      No, not yet — it's breakfast, and I'm working this week. Honestly, I only just spoke to Peter, and he says that she's still looking quite weak after the latest chemo, but that the consultant is optimistic. Might get her some more time at home now that the next round is over.      That would be nice. I dread to think of her pacing in that bland hospital room. I remember the last time I saw her, her hands were shaking quite a bit, but she still found time to ask about the sale of the manor and the village plans. Still that much energy, even in her state — full of determination.      It's amazing, really. You think you know the limits of someone, and then they still manage surprising you. I had a colleague at work last week who about lost his voice after a bad cold, but talking to him, I had to wonder — what's really stopping us is that we let ourselves slow down.      That's a good way of looking at it. Although I can't imagine managing that while fighting for your life. She told me once that it wasn't about being strong, but waiting for the right moment. As if you had control over it. Even if it's just a fraction of the truth, I do like thinking about it like that.      Sometimes that's all we can go on really — the bits of truth or hope that work. I made her some soup the other day, and she asked me to bring it again.

Rather annoying when afit of kids play music at nigh on. I’m on the job ‘n all, got to keep it quiet in the block.      Yeah, I knoowww. I’m only doin the rounds in me capacity as well. But it’s like they een don’t care if I’m tryin to get rounds done peaceably. I’ve had kids who think they’ve got all the rights just ‘cause they’ve got Bluetooth speakers.      Aye, and some of the lads from the ground floor even chuck mess about in the common rooms. Not bothered about takin it out when I knock. Got tired the other night and grabbed a broom like I’m a cleaner.      Oh no, did you get into trouble for that?      A bit of a chat with the manager, yeah. ‘He’s a security officer, not a cleaner’ he goes. Likes to throw that line around. But I tell you, some of them take the freedom too far.      I know what you mean. I was speaking to one of the residents yesterday about a student who left electricals plugged in and cluttered in the corridors like it was a car boot sale. Be a fire risk if I’ve ever seen one. But he just laughed and said it was “harmless fun”.      That’s the problem innit. ‘Harmless fun’ till they cause a bleedin’ incident.      Tell me about it. I had a girl cryin’ the other day because someone trashed the communal fridge and threw all her milk over. Stuffed because it was about five days milk. Just frustrating.      Aye. And it’s not even like you know who to tell. I mean, if a student says something to the bin, they just ignore you like you’re part of the walls.      You sayin’ it’s all hearsay? I tried once to report a complaint, but they told me “no evidence”, so what do I do? Go with a camera?      Some days, I think you do. You runnin t’em the same report cycle goin round on report forms?      Gomen, yeah. It’s like I’m sittin’ in a loop. Pass it on, no action, repeat.      That’s where you and I should team up, eh? Do a joint complain or summat. Might give the head office a headache that they can’t ignore.      Now you’re talkin my language. Imagine, two departments gangin up on the management.

Rather annoying when you've got aching feet and nowhere to perch. But you know, it's not like it used to be, is it? I mean, when I first came to Brighton after uni, there was nowhere decent to eat or drink without the place being jammed.      Oh, it's always been like that in Brighton, love. I remember taking my lass on her first day here. A Sunday, if I recall correctly—such a crowd, we had to go as far as Hove to find a seat.      But, Jerry, you know what else hasn’t changed is the charm! The character of this place, the seafront, the independent shops on the Lanes—y’know, I still get a thrill when I smell the salt air and hear the kids running on the sand. I think it's why we all come back, isn’t it?      You’re right about that, Hattie. And the people, the locals! No matter where you go in England—and I’ve been to my fair share—there's something very English about being abroad and bumping into people you know. Like a week ago, I was in Antwerp with my book club, and there was a bus load of West Country people just wandering around. Made us all feel at home.      That’s something I’ve noticed too. It’s not just the language, it’s the shared quirks—like our English rhyming in songs. I was in Paris last summer with my university cohort, and we ended up doing a  lesley/geordie  kind of song in the café. Made a few French tourists laugh, as well as most of us.      Oh, I still remember watching you lads at university doing those silly limericks. Not that I mind, it helped keep up the spirit! Jerry, you had us all in fits once with your "There once was a lad from Herne Bay..." it was a classic.      Ah, I haven’t done that one in years! Those were the days.      Family, I think it's funny how things do come full circle. Still remember when you lost Grandma and how we all met by the gothic cathedral on the seafront? It was a real emotional day, but even in the sad moments, Brighton always feels like home.      It really is something, isn't it? Even though I live out in Harlow, I always make it back to Brighton on the weekends or holidays—whether it’s for a craft fair, a birthday celebration, or just to be near the sea.

So do you think the equality vote in Ireland last year was a big deal? Our teacher said it passed like... surprisingly fast.      It was  huge , love. I think over 60% of people voted to change the law. Some places even had over 80% in favour. That kind of support doesn’t happen every day, especially on something as important as marriage equality.      Yeah, but I heard some people were really against it. Like,  really  against it. My sister’s friend was saying her grandad called it a “sin” or something.      Oh, you mean like the religious protests? That’s sad, really. Some people just like to think they know best for everyone else. Fun fact—I went to rally in Dublin the day before the vote. Hundreds of people just in rainbow colours and smiling. It felt like hope, you know?      Wow, I would’ve wanted to go. But don’t people have to vote when they’re, like, older?      You’re right—voters had to be 18 or over. But I remember talking with your nan about it and she said the real battle for rights is often in changing minds, not just laws. And then people got to vote. Pretty amazing?      Yeah, kind of makes me wish I was old enough. Oh wait—what’s next? Do you think Ireland will do anything about education or the pay gap for women?      Honestly, I hope so. But it’s one step at a time, pet. Also, it’s funny how some of these things make headlines and remind  your grandmother  how embarrassing it was about her birthday speeches. I swear, she doesn’t know what a “quiet” celebration means.      Don’t you mean  your  embarrassing stories? She mentioned that time she wore  all  the socks twice at her 50th. Classic.      Okay, okay, you win. But I tried to make her understand that getting your socks mixed up is as cute as a toddler doing a handstand. And honestly, a little less annoying.      That's not true, you looked terrified.      Fair go. But on the serious side again—do you think your generation will push even more for equality? Or do we just box ourselves in with arguing?      I don’t know, but I think we want to stand up for stuff, like in school, or on social media. But maybe not over birthday socks.       Exactly , unless they’re rainbow ones.

Rather fine lunch, don't you think? That shepherd's pie of yours, Peggy, it's just like when we used to go to auntie's for Sunday tea. Not a hint of the microwaved variety, mind. Not like that hamster I saw being frightened half to death in a microwave the other day—mind you, I don't think it was      properly.      Ha! A hamster in a microwave? Why on earth would someone stick a hamster in a microwave, Tom? We've had our fair share of animal anecdotes, but that's the most peculiar one I've heard. I had a guinea pig once. Now, he preferred apples, not surprises in metal boxes.      You must have watched the wrong bit on the telly, Tom. I saw a documentary about microwaves in the Netherlands last week—something about heating cottage cheese and boilies for breakfast, no hamsters involved. Though, speaking of kitchen appliances, Tom, I hear you used to tinker with lathes. Still got the old ones in your shed?      Aye, I still tinker about in there, mind you. The old tools are getting on, like me, but they're not dead yet. Got a few little jobs on—I made a wooden knife block for Peggy last week, with a bit of carving on the end. Nothing like the days in the shops, mind you. Nowadays, everything's got plastic handles and comes in a packet.      That’s a shame. I always liked a bit of hand-wrought wood. Some things just don’t have      in them anymore. I used to do crafts when I was about forty—trying to make money off bangle holders and whatnots. Not much call for them these days, are there?      The market's moved on to electric juicers and voice-activated toasters, Peggy. But I think nostalgia still has its place. You know, I was thinking the other day about how lathes work when I was doing some curriculum reviews for a design project. They asked me whether to include traditional lathe usage in the syllabus. I said "absolutely"—useful for learning      and an appreciation for the past.      Well, you're in good company, David. I reckon it's always good to know how something’s made. Makes you appreciate the mess you can make if you don’t mind the speed on the tool bit, or     .      True that. You know, when I first met Tom, he was drilling a hole in the kitchen table to see if it would fit the clock.

Rather unusual day today, haven't you noticed? I saw a story about a cat in the news that typewrites and another about some child writing poetry in reverse. I can't say I found either particularly surprising. I've seen plenty of people left-handed and mirror-writing seems almost charming now.      That cat sounds like something out of a very strange fantasy novel. As for mirror-writing, I don’t suppose that transcription job you have would ever involve anything like that, would it? I'm rather curious how you deal with such oddities anyway.      Oh, don't worry. My work is usually far more sedate! Mostly legal documents and some old medical files. Still, I do get the occasional handwriting that’s a bit of a puzzle. Fun to decode, really. Probably more interesting than the average administrative drivel I used to do before transcription.      You’ve both managed better than I, I must say. I used to transcribe for the school board back in the 60s, and even back then the documents could be a challenge. But that reminds me—have either of you had trouble with the banks lately? I’m seeing quite a few people struggling with early retirement savings and debt as property prices in cities are becoming less affordable. I worry about the cost of living these days – it’s been rising fairly dramatically, and savings barely cover a down payment these days.      It’s all very worrying. I understand the banks are trying to make sense of the current climate. The interest rates are so suspiciously low, it's like they expect people to do risky things with their savings. I've considered investing in something more solid recently—possibly property, but I can't see most people about to buy unless they want to be living the landlords' dream.      I think property fails to account for the debt crisis we’re seeing. There's also this whole bag charge nonsense. Plastic is being taxed, but no one's actually solving the bigger issues at hand. Makes me wonder if any of this was thought through.      You’re not wrong. It’s as mysterious as a cryptic crossword—only without the satisfaction of a solution. At least the crossword clues make some kind of sense sometimes, even if they're maddening.      I usually solve about three or four of mine at a push!

Rather than spending ages glued to the screen, I think it's time we had a read together. The boys have got to learn some balance with their electronics.      But Mummy, the Ninjago world is SO exciting! Look at this—  Lori   is saving the   Spinjitzu Temple   from   Lord Garmadon   again!      I built a   super-cool castle   in   Minecraft   last night. It even had a   dragon trap  !      Oh, did it, Tom? That's brilliant! But listen, I’ve even got  this  book—  Lego: Journey to Nindroid X  . My colleague lent it to me, and it’s actually a really cool story about the ninjas and what they go through. I think you'll like it. It even lets you build your own missions while you read. You don’t even know what’s coming in this book—but I promise, it’s got dragons, traps, and action.      Hmm, is it   Ninja vs. Robo-Ninja  ? I saw that Lego set in the shop about them.      No, but it’s just as exciting. The mission starts in the   Isle of Ninjara  , and the ninjas have to stop the   Nindroid X   from destroying the city. They even fight with   cyber-legos  . Mummy’s got a ring of lightning in her hand, ready to zap the screen out of us.      Fine, fine, let’s read. But only if I can read out the   dragon lines  . The ones with   咆哮   included.      Of course, love. The book’s got a bit of that in it, too—because let’s be honest, every adventure needs a bit of magic.

Rather lovely to have you both over, love. That coffee’s just the ticket after the mad morning I've had. You've both had a cup, I hope?      Thanks, Mams. I've chucked two sugars in, like always—get me one with a splash of milk when y'have a minute, will y?      I'm good as well, thanks. Just one coffee for me. Not done so well last night, so I'm keeping it simple.      You poor thing. What mischief were you up to, then? Still working on that art project, is it?      Yeah, more or less. Got another deadline coming up like next week, so I've bin burning the midnight oil. It’s just a plaster cast sculpture, but Oliver thinks it's very sad in the head.      You’ve got to make it breakfast, then—maybe I'll drop some pastries on the way back from the shop. Proper breakfast hides a multitude of sins, if you ask me.      Brilliant idea, dear, and well said. Anyways, I wanted to chat about your holidays. Young one, tell Mams what you did in Cornwall.      Oh, it was brilliant. Stayed at this little cottage with view of the sea and, yeah, just relaxed. Went into Falmouth quite a lot, done a whole heap of painting. Oh, and I found the cutest little coffee shop that made the best scones!      Sounds divine. I do miss going out there—had a family holiday there when I was your age. The beaches were so wild, but we had a whale of a time.      And how were the kids during the trip? Hope you weren't rolling your eyes at school photos or worrying about muddy socks up the side of the wall.      Oh, well, they are growing up so fast now. I remember it like yesterday. Some of the food there—makes a mockery of Burton-On-Trent's best!      Well, if you've had a good time, then bravo. Right, now, what about the day ahead? You both staying for lunch?      I am, yeah—got a bit of shopping to do, maybe visit the new mural outside the town hall. Know where they've put up that graffiti guy from Manchester?      I do indeed. Bring some paints and spray it red, would y? Makes it look a dash more alive.

Here in Australia, we only tend to get fancy festivals in Byron Bay—it's basically stickers and rhythm and then sea. So yeah, Ed – Baptism of Royal mist, Cathedrals and all? Bet you’ll be somin’ about that later like you always are after spotting some haunted vibes.      Honestly, just someone needing to read a book or two first. I’m already half-decent with vampire myths—don’t need to meet a real one in the fog!      Look, it’s romantic at least, right? I hear the architecture there is to die for. Oh, and I'm cooking for you all weekend—you know that, right? I've been baking a new loaf all week. My sourdough is baked like lava rock. Super crusty, soft on the inside. Just the right amount of tang.      Ed, you know your sourdough is crack to us... and that’s being polite. Jake always comes with lunches ready for the whole team—my customers do love a good scone or a buttery croissant.      Actually, speaking on that—fine, I’m going to be preoccupied this weekend. Just got offered to do a gig with a band on Saturday at your mate Mike’s latest party. I’m seriously toasting this one, after two months of heckling from him.

Rather than a new album, we're going to have a little fiesta with her songs, aren't we, luv?      It will be so much fun, Mummy. I want to hear “Alice in Wonderland”.      Yeah, and can we take photos in the een? Like when we had the photoshoot for the family album?      You bet. I’ve got some amazing props from the last photoshoot, including that Alice costume. Imagine what photographs we could get. We can even do the aerial hoop this time for some magical shots.      Mummy, what if it’s like that party last year when the fire alarm went off? It was like that My Chemical Romance song, but you made it okay.      We’ll avoid fire, I promise. We’ve learned our lesson there. This party is all about the music and photos. I've invited a few friends to come and lend a hand in setting up the fairy lights and getting everything ready.      And can we do the muddy obstacle course like Granddad’s birthday, but smaller?      I suppose we could make a mini version in the garden for you two. As long as you don’t mess up the lawn too much. I’ve already planned the menu – we’ll have some nibbles and snacks because no one wants to be hungry and grumpy in the photos.      I’m already hungry. Can we have some snacks now?      Not right now, but after we've cleared up the kitchen. I need to make sure the photoshoot setup area is all ready and look at the outfits we might need to borrow or make. I’ve got some ideas from Pinterest about using storybook themes for different areas of the kitchen.      Like “Alice in Wonderland” in the living room?      Precisely! And the kitchen can be “The Mad Hatter's Tea Party”. We'll need some hats and probably a wooden tea set. I wonder if I can raid my nan’s storage. She had a few things from Auntie’s children when they were little.      Can I do the omelette for the Mad Hatter’s tea like in the story?      Only if you promise to not throw it at your brother. We’ll go for a nice presentation this time, not an obstacle course. Okay?      Okay, if I don’t manage to throw it high enough to fall into the river of pans!      That was a one-time experiment and not fitting for a photoshoot, so let’s keep it simple for now.

Rather a lot of excitement in the house today, what with the pizza and that. Don’t ‘member the last time I ‘ad a pepperoni, but more than I can count on one ‘and with chocolate roulade. Not quite my usual, but I’ve a fancy for something cheerful after hearing the lass’s exam results.      Yes, dear, it  is  rather nice to mark a day like this, isn’t it? The girls did themselves proud, mind. Imagine what it’s like to be a youngster and have to sit for all those tests when your world feels so big and you’re still finding your way. I used to give little ones a sense of security, now I do it for my granddaughters, if only in my own eccentric ways.      And I for one am proud too, having gone in for the parents’ evening and given it my all. Made sure they understood the pressure points of learning this early. Not a bit like when I was at school, not enough support, you see. But the girls? They’ve got a real headstart.      We were both in the top tier for two core subjects! I’ve still got grief over the English exam, though. Tore my essay apart in my head a hundred times. You’d think after – what is it, five edits, I would’ve nailed it…      Oh don’t be so hard on yourself. If I could blame the calculator for that science test and still managed a ‘good pass’, then so can you. Besides, Dad’s just been oddly proud bragging about our ‘academic sparkle’.      Now, now, don’t make your grandmother blush! You two have about five decades of conversation to catch up on, talking of sparkle and calculators.      Speaking of sparkle, I shouldn’t be worrying about it too much, but that girl of yours ‘as been taking driving lessons. Don’t like the idea of her driving at night on the A11 any bloody hour it takes her fancy.      I told her the same when she passed. You can’t outdrive the clock with lunches and a new football team to pick from, but let’s face it, a lass with a bit of the mettle can go far. I remember your Dad being just like her – always full of brimstone, but that was a long time ago.      Yeah, but I’ve been planning to tweet a picture of us with pizza and the roulade.

Rather lovely morning, isn't it? Perfect for a bit of garden work before it gets too hot. Mind you, the weather's been so changeable recently, it's like living in Wales!      Yeah, honestly, I've had to layer up and take things off three times in one day! I was just thinking we should start some beans in the greenhouse. My students all love making a fuss about how to plant them. Got one in class who insisted seeds needed to listen to records while they sprout to grow faster!      Didn’t your mum always play Chopin while she did the housework, Dad? Not sure that works with beans, but I'm not arguing. On the topic of records, by the way, you still got that old player you brought over from London? I found a few Kinks and Deep Purple vinyls in the loft last week, about 20 years out of date but still prime listening material!      That sounds like gold dust to me! I remember ordering some records from Korea a while back for my own collection—vastly different, but always interesting.      Korea, now that’s a bit of a mystery to me. I’ve read a couple of books about their traditional legends, but I find it all rather exotic! Mind you, I’m not sure I could cope with the climate. One time I nearly passed out in 40-degree heat in New Zealand, and that’s not exactly the Arctic!      New Zealand! I’d read about the agriculture there—bits of it reminded me of our very own beans and kiwi fruit. Anyhow, speaking of university education, I spoke to my cousin in Scotland last week about tuition fees. She’s having such a different experience over there. And with what's going on about Scottish independence, you barely know where you are politically!      Yeah, the debates about independence always remind me of discussions about the weather. They never end. I remember a time when my students relied solely on witches and willow trees for contraception. We’ve come such a long way!      Oh, we’ve certainly moved on! My own path through university was far more chaotic, mind you. I had a mania for English literature—especially the Brontës. If I was at it now, I’d probably spend all day reading and explaining the blooming rules of Chinese chess to my pupils.

Rather annoying the new testing regime they've introduced at the school. My students are just children, they don’t need to咄咄逼人的 standardized exam every term.      I know what you mean, Lucy. I feel the same about the way things are going with student loans now — it’s just not sustainable. I remember when I got mine, it felt like a lifeline, but now? I reckon half the students I've taught over the last year don’t even see it as a loan, more like a tax!      Oh亲爱的, it’s worse than that. You know my brother, he’s retired now. Last month he got a letter about his pension being cut because of some new policy the government pushed through. I’m just so fed up with this back-and-forth from the politicians, it’s like they’ve forgotten there are real people with real problems out there.      Absolutely. And I've been thinking about this drive in the car next week. We need to make sure we don’t have any problems with the MOT. I don’t want to get stuck here, and it is quite a drive up from Kraków — quite a few winding roads and no Polish for me!      You're not the only one, love. I still remember the first time I came to Poland, I was terrified because I thought I wouldn’t understand a word. It took me weeks just to realize that the Polish “dziękuję” sounds exactly like the English “thank you”, but slower. Honestly, I think my accent helps me here more than it lets me down.      You have a very calm and clear way of speaking, it’s good for your teaching, isn’t it? I sometimes wonder if the English we grew up with is going to be what the next generation needs. I mean, barely a week goes by without a new abbreviation or slang on Netflix.      Don’t get me started on that. I remember when the whole consent culture was being pushed through the schools I tried to teach at. I think it’s a good thing, but I just feel like a lot of people take it the wrong way. It’s about being respectful, not creating paranoia.      I think the points are good, it’s just communication is key. It’s similar to what we were saying about the language — if you don’t talk, nobody will understand anything.

So, I heard you got an offer for Human Sciences at Oxford. That's massive, mate. Well done! What made you go for that over, like, Physics or Maths?      Cheers, it was pretty hectic to get in, I'll admit! But I like the idea of studying how humans work from loads of angles — psychology, biology, anthropology. It feels more... all-encompassing. Maths is cool, but I just needed more from my course, you know? What about you? Still going for Economics and Maths at Leeds?      Yeah, but honestly, I'm not sure if I want to even go. My A-level results were okay but not amazing, and my dad's like "You don't get scholarships unless you get A s." It’s just more pressure than I wanted.      I get it. But you’re thinking of uni while we’re still drinking beer? What are we drinking anyway? That’s like... wheat beer or lager?      Haha, lager. Pretty standard for a bar like this, right? I do like the vibe of Westfield, though — I mean, we’re not in some dodgy back alley for once. Have you tried their fish and chips? Mate, it’s legend. I swear it's better than most pubs.      Yeah, the food’s decent. Though I reckon the apple pie and custard is their saving grace. I could eat that every week. Anyway, what's this about not going to uni? Let me guess, your mates already have parties booked for the summer?      Don’t even start. My weekend plans were all about house parties in Staines, but I did make a pact with a few of us to touch base over rugby this summer. I might actually try and make it into that club you told me about — the one near Slough? West Berkshire, I think it was?      Slough Rugby Club. Yeah, they’ve got a solid youth team. I might come down for a training session or two. My cousin plays there too, and he reckons they’re getting good at the lunches after a match. More importantly, it’s the perfect excuse to avoid washing my hair for weeks.      Classic. Look, I get it if you don’t get into Human Sciences next year. I’ll still see you at the rugby, bloke. And what your dad’s saying about scholarships — maybe you can focus on writing impressive personal statements next year.

Rather annoying this new tax, eh, love? I’ve been looking over the statements, and they’re taking a bit more out than they used to now.      I know, Dad! I was doing some cash flow calculations for my own budget and noticed it too. They say it’s for public services, but it doesn't feel like it's helping much where we need it.      Aye, it’s all policy and promises from those lot in Parliament. They tell you one thing, but it’s always the working folk like us who end up paying the price. Let me explain how it works, just so you’re not fazed by it all.      That'd be brilliant, thank you. I’ve only studied it academically so far, and I want to understand the real-life impact too.      Right. See, tax is split into percentages — corporation tax, income tax, then there’s national insurance, which I used to pay a shed-load of as an accountant, mind you. With the new budget, they’ve hiked the income tax rates for folks earning a bit more, and raised the national insurance cap. That leaves less in your pocket and more for the government to spend on education, health, what have you.      Hmm. So does that mean people with fairly high earnings like me — just scraping above the higher rate — are paying quite a lot more than average?      You hit the nail on the head. And what’s more, they're also putting more pressure on self-employed folks like teachers oddly, or people with freelance work, who have to calculate and declare profits accurately. Made it a bit more complex in the system, but I suppose it's meant to be fairer.      I had no idea it was so much more than just that line you see in the wage slip. It’s quite complex. But, honestly, do you think it will actually help the NHS or cut the health budget into something useful?      I suspect there’s a mix of both. The problem is who the money is going to. If it’s not managed well by the people in charge, it just ends up being squandered. The money’s there, but not necessarily where it's needed the most. It’s a juggling act.      True. I just hope, when I’m earning more in a few years, I’m not paying for someone else’s mistakes.

Rather annoying to be honest. I've barely had a weekend to myself since September. We're managing a university infrastructure update and it's just non-stop organisation.      That does sound exhausting! You’re thrown into it quite early in the project, aren’t you? I can’t imagine what it’s like dealing with deadlines and paperwork while coordinating teams and suppliers.      Yeah, a bit. A lot of it’s learning as I go, to be honest. The upside is it’s given me a lot of experience, though. But when you're in it, the pressure is hard to ignore. It's like being juggling everything and worrying you might drop the whole load at any second.      I get that! When I left school, I was working directly on the administration and logistics for school exam trials. The school turned over a huge number of exams every year and you better make sure each student gets the right materials in the right place on the right day. It’s the same in a way, even if it's not a university.      I bet it is—personally I can’t even imagine how you did your job as an exam manager and only having a secondary-school education.      Well, it was all about detail. And communication – that’s been one of my strongest points, I think. There’s a fair amount of staff and students to coordinate and you have to know what each one needs and when. And, let’s be honest, sometimes people aren’t great with instructions. You just have to stay calm and push through.      It's amazing how much being calm under pressure matters in both your roles and mine. I have about five people asking me for different deadlines every day and the stress is real. I'm starting to think about maybe taking some kind of training course or something to help manage the workload more efficiently.      That’s not a bad idea at all. A bit of training might go a long way. And don’t forget to look after yourself too. You can't be good at work if you’re completely run down. Even if it’s just a short holiday or speaking with friends more often, it helps.      You're right. I owe it to go out with my parents this weekend and take a proper rest. I could really do with a day that doesn’t involve spreadsheets and emails.      Exactly!

Rather annoying this new recycling schedule eh, love? Thought me and mine could just chuck it all in the bin... got to sort it out now. Otherwise they'll fine yer!      Aw, Grandpa, it's not that bad! We’ve got these bright red bins for paper and plastic and all the rest can go in the black one. Just make sure yer not mixing in food waste with the paper. A lot of people do that by accident and it gets contaminated.      Aye, and me bin was full the other night! Tosh, come and help me sort it... like to bin a baked potato in the red one mebbe. What’s the point if we can’t put anything in?      Fun fact—recycling just one tonne of paper saves about 17 trees. If everyone chipped in, you’d be planting a forest by the end of the year.      Haha, yeah Tosh, thanks for the stats but, Grandpa’s just trying to get the knack of it. It helps though—less landfill, cleaner air, and it looks better round here if we all keep it tidy.      Blimey, I didn’t know it worked like that then. Mind you, most of the stuff we chuck out could be reused. My old boots are still in good nick, but no one wants to wear them after I've been tramping ‘em round the hills.      Well, there’s also the community swap shop on a Tuesday, run by some local volunteers—garden sheds, tool boxes, even some old games boxes. If you fancy getting your boots up there, it might do someone good.      Oh, that’s a great idea. I’ve seen some proper bargains there. Got me a second-hand IPod classic for ten quid last month.      Aye, I did see that. Just mebbe a bit too techy for my liking. I still use me Nokia from 2005. It works as it should.      Vintage tech, mate. They told me the same thing when I brought up my first-generation Galaxy phone.      Anyway, shall we get some of this sorted or not?      Lead the way, love. And Tosh, can we grab a bottle of that Shaw Wood red you’ve been saving?      Only if you promise not to belly up to the table with it. Knows how I get when I drink and discuss the finer points of concrete reinforcement.      Again, with the concrete talk, Grandpa, I swear you never shut up.
