Rather annoying this, having to pull over every so often for directions. I thought internet would solve  everything , yet here I am, maps on both phones having more or less given up on us!      Yeah, honestly, sometimes the Polish road system is a bit like a puzzle — if it’s missing the solution  and  the pieces. But look on the bright side — all this stopping is a bit of a stretch break. Not that I do much exercise, but at least I’m not sitting there like a lump!      Oh亲爱的, when was the last time you  did  exercise, apart from sprinting to catch a bus? Look at the state of you, you’re beginning to resemble Mycroft Holmes! You really should get back into it. I’ve taken up some yoga, you know. It's very zen in the mornings before coffee.      Oh come on, I haven’t gone that soft! And besides, I teach TEFL! I’m on my feet all day, ordering flash cards and giving shouty instructions over noisy classrooms. You try doing 8 hours of that, and we’ll see about the yoga!      Touché, touché. You’ve got a proper job, proper work rhythm — which is more than I can say for me. I often wonder if I still  count  as a teacher if the only students I've taught in the last year have been a rather grumpy Italian man at EFL Central and two confused tourists.      No, no, of course you do. TEFL isn’t all about the number of students — it’s the  quality , right? Look at your experience, how you talk about about literature! I’ve read all your blog posts — the one where you critiqued "Brave New World" is still one of my favourites. People out there  definitely  learn something from you.      Aww, thank you. I used to be a voracious reader — mainly all those classics. I tried to read some modern ones, but they just didn't  jar  with me. Websites and screen reading take the soul right out of it!      I think you're stuck in the 90s with the books. Look, I get it, but some new stuff hits harder, makes you question more, you know? It’s different, but it works for what it does.      Maybe I shall begin reading one after I find those directions, and we find that campsite we were meant to have stayed over yesterday.

Rather than share a text-based article, I request a more detailed video explanation.      Okay... What's the video topic you're interested in? I can help by providing a description or title first.      No topic is stated as such. Just provide the video link if it's available and relevant.      Which   specific   site or platform do you want? I need that to look it up or search for a suitable video.      It doesn't matter to me. Just give the best one for this issue.      But how else can I share the right one without knowing the topic or a basic description to search for?      It's a   thread   I sent you about DNA and telomeres relating to anti-ageing and what we can influence and what not. A   video format  , if it's there.      Ahh, I see. Let me check for a relevant video summary, or maybe replay the core ideas you remember from the text so I can present it differently.      Yeah, maybe reading aloud or summarising the written article instead — no video as such is necessary if only text is available.      Okay, I'll read it out from the original text. –  Okay, so the article begins by talking about telomeres as these protective caps on the end of chromosomes...       Right, and what about mitochondria? There was also something about cellular energy and how lifestyle choices affect that. That's the key part I remember.      Yes, later in the text it mentions mitochondrial function and energy metabolism — calorie restriction, exercise, and NAD+ as a key enzyme type you can supplement. Also, this whole part about "metabolic flexibility" becomes important for longevity.      And the part about chronic stress and how it suppresses mitochondrial response. That’s crucial. So ultimately, the article ties telomeres, mitochondria, and general lifestyle to the question of how long we live or could live.      Exactly. And also, it mentions that we can't control all of the genetic risks but there are specific things we  can  do by way of diet, exercise, and possibly even novel supplements.      Right. And I think it also touches upon the technical stuff like tectonic shifts and what emerging research is coming up with. The Vikings' navigation and Romans' hygienic knowledge were historical parallels too.      Oh yes, and there was even a mention of the pyramids and how the ancients were fascinated with longevity and immortality — in kind of a symbolic, mythic way.

Rather annoying I could've got a latte at the café down the road but instead, I've been poked with the idea of using the new coffee maker yet agin! Works fine, though. Beans are getting me down, though. Need to buy some decent ones at the shops.      Right, well, I’ll pick some up on the way if you tell me your preference. Cappuccino, latte, or just regular? I got a voucher for a couple of pounds, which should help. We can use it to save for when the baby chair comes in.      Right, I’ve sorted the baby chair. Got it delivered today and it’s only another few quid now that the turkey voucher helped. Still, enough to pay for a few coffees, ain't it? D’you think we should think about the referendum? Living in St Annes, we’re better off if we stay in Europe 'cos of all the imports for the garden centre and the planting season is coming up.      Yeah, the EU ones, I mean—plants and stuff. We get nice fruit trees too, and I don’t wanna be stuck paying more for plants and food for the chickens. Plus, if we leave, what happens to Mr West, from the customer service office—he’s Polish. Don't seem fair, like, making life harder on him.      Mate, you ain't wrong. If we go out, don’t see the sense in chasing supermarkets out. We need 'em here. And not to mention the sunglasses shop down the prom. They give us a good rate for family, and I’d be gutted if they all had to shut up shop because of some flamin’ vote.      I agree. We can’t let the whole house vote without knowing what it’ll do to the little things we rely on. Maybe we should have a proper ‘chat’ with the family about it before the referendum. Parents, grandparents, cousins—get it sorted properly. And as for the money, if we can reduce little expenses, like not buying coffee every day and using the coffee maker instead, it might help elsewhere.      That’s doable. I’d be happy to brew around once or twice a week. Yeah, go on then, make it a savings plan or whatever you lot wanna call it. I’ll do that. And we can use the vouchers on anything else your lot need—for plants or something else.

Rather annoying the new neighbours, eh, love? That grumpy old thing next door—the one with the poodle—shouted at me again about the decorations. Blows me away, really. It’s a Christmas tree, not a moon rocket. Look at it—get a bit of joy out of it for once!      It was ridiculous, honestly. You just ignore her, Nana. She probably only moved here to find someone to boss about. Still, your tree is  brilliant . That bauble you put on the top from when me and Jack went to Germany last year looks lovely.      Aye, I thought so. It’s taken me two hours to get that thing looking decent, mind. Still, you get left with a qualified nurse! I’m good at organisation, even if I’m not in the NHS now. Living with you lot’s harder than working a 12-hour shift. Look at these nails, though—can’t live with the state of them! You told me to do some filing and I thought,  Oh, that’ll be simple . Next thing I know, I’ve filed one side smooth and the other one as if I’ve tried to murder something with emery boards.      Oh Nana, just take it easy! My Mate Laura showed me this chap in Horsham who’s got a little shop and he does quite a nice line in gel polish for a fiver a go. Smashing finish, and he even does someone’s full eyebrows for free if they book a mani. He’s oddly sour about the Third Reich, though. I think his grandfather worked in a concentration camp. I don’t know, it’s a bit sad about how people don’t remember the past properly.      Honestly, I’ve never been good at remembering facts and figures. I mean, I’m up for history if it’s a good story. Like that time you told me about the Bauhaus people and how they used the minimal style for something bloody logical— adaptable, practical, waiting for the future . Not sure how that relates to putting glitter on a nail, mind.      Well, I do love a bit of irony. Jack’s bringing me birthday present next weekend— a gothic room on the lake , as he puts it. Not that I’m going in, but I suppose it’s the thought that counts. You’ve met him before, remember? Fat lad in the pastel trousers?

Rather annoying that the internet isn't working yet. Thought it would be sorted by now. I've been living here in the flat for a day and I’m already ready to lose my mind.      I know what you mean! No Netflix and no emails is a bit like a parallel universe. Got a pack of cigarettes in the bag if you fancy some company while we wait for it all to come on. Maybe we can swap notes on how to best infuriate the internet provider while we smoke.      Please! Put the cigarettes down quickly and pass me one. It's the only thing getting me through the stress of sorting out who is responsible for the rubbish collection round here. Still don’t know whether it’s the council or the building management.      Oh, I think I heard from the nursery next door, the one I passed on the way up. They mentioned it’s the council — better make a note of that before I forget again. They’ve got a couple of kids running around non-stop in there, you can hear them from the stairs!      I need one of those, maybe for some company. Though I might settle for a takeaway instead. We still haven't bought anything to cook. You buy, I’ll pay tomorrow.      That’s the most generous offer I’ve been given all week, and I barely paid for dinner last night. I’ll pick up some fried chicken and maybe some seasonal vegetables if I can find any at the store. There’s also this funny looking chicken curry for a suspiciously low price.      Now that sounds promising. Just don’t forget to check the ingredients and be sure it’s safe to eat with those chickens! We can have about five minutes of conversation before the curry takes the talking over.      I’ll take your word for it. I know barely enough to handle the basics, so I’ll do what I can for the chicken. Speaking of basics — passed by a bank on the way here. You need to set something up before it becomes impossible.      Argh, yes. Banking is as mysterious as rural internet. I’ll go later with your plan. It can't be that hard if the chicken curry survives you trying to cook it.      Don’t go there. I’ll pray if necessary. If it survives, it's yours.

Rather do share a drink, eh, love? That post-1960s upheaval in-colocation got us rather well fixed with local dining and more than a glass of something.      Aye, quite right. After all, there’s no harm in tea and a proper chat now and then to keep the spirit alive, is there?

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know what grannies are like with her rules and stuff. But I got the gist of it. You know, more or less, how it goes      Aww, honestly, I would not even mind! Rather skip the new house in Oxford. You know I'd rather stay in Cambridge for my thesis work. There’s far too much rewriting to do after this road trip. I can’t say I fancy moving yet. I never really thought of translation as a job, but I suppose it could work. It’s something I enjoy, and it’s not as if I’m tied down to anything else. He’s all  “proper career, son,”  about this sort of thing.      I’m sure I'll find something eventually. Maybe even write a proper book one day. Rather exciting to be here at Cambridge Law Faculty for Alumni Day 2, isn’t it? I work on language research and documentation, so it’s fascinating to run into people from all sorts of fields. Are you involved in this sort of event often?      Hi, yes—it’s actually my second Alumni Day event now, and I’m a research administrator for a language institute. I’ve been making sure a few of our lecturers have provisions in place this week. What brought you into language research?      Well, I was doing a postgrad in applied linguistics and thought it made sense to get involved in projects that document endangered languages—especially with how much globalization is threatening them. I’ve even managed to assist in a small project with some Chinese language documentation last year. I suppose you must see quite a bit of linguistic work through your role?      Oh, absolutely. We coordinate various projects, including some with universities in the Middle East. They’ve been looking into language contact, especially the impact of Arab dialects on regional tongues. I was just reading up on how that kind of exchange has subtle, deep consequences for cultural identity—particularly in areas with a strong archaeological history.      Ah, archaeology—now  there’s  a field I’ve dabbled in. I used to lecture part-time at a university, and I worked on a few excavation sites in my youth. It fascinates me how language and history are so intertwined. When you unearth the remains of an old village, sometimes the language patterns of the surviving population can tell a story just as vivid as the architecture.      That’s really interesting. I hadn’t thought of it that way. Did you come across any particularly tangible examples of language evolving as you excavated these sites?      Indeed. There was one site in Shropshire—my birthplace, actually—where we found evidence of a once-thriving Roman-influenced settlement. The local dialect there reflects layers of language influenced by Latin, Celtic, and even some Norman elements. It’s a little like a linguistic palimpsest. Those words that survive in the local speech always make me curious—like the word  crog  in the old Welsh, which meant a hill, but it’s still sometimes used by farmers in the region today.      That’s beautiful—and makes me think of language documentation as almost a form of archaeology in itself.

So, I just saw this video of a guy doing a dance outside the Tube station in London — it's gone completely viral. Someone must have filmed him because he looked like he was auditioning for  Strictly Come Dancing … but honestly, he nailed it. It's picked up like a million views in two days!      Oh yeah, I saw that! My bakery actually had a queue a mile long that day because people just  had  to see it. And believe it or not, a few came in and asked for cupcakes shaped like his shoes! It reminds me of the TikTok dances too... like, young people are united by these little viral moments, whether you like them or not.      Honestly, I’ve never watched it. I run this café in the morning and then try to sleep in the afternoon. If it turned your place into an assembling for dancers, I’d better not get involved. But yeah, I mean, isn’t that the point? People needing something to share and talk about, even if it's just a dance?      I suppose so, but it does make you think — I mean, we all work different kinds of jobs and have different education levels, but there's something watching that video that brings it all together. Like, it's absurd – but it's also kind of beautiful in its own way.      Now don’t get me started on the idea of work. When I was at uni, I was chasing film producing. Everyone in my class had these ideas: they’d be the next Spielberg, or preferably the next hotter Hollywood A-lister. Meanwhile, I thought being able to greenlight a  documentary  about village life in Devon would make me the happiest man on Earth.      Honestly, I used to feel kind of sorry for people like me who didn’t go the classic academic route. I left school earlier for apprenticeships and ended up in catering. But now I’m running my own bakery. I think a lot of people don’t get it — there are so many ways to be good at something. Like, I’m not academically gifted by any means, I’m actually dyslexic, but I can work out complex pricing models in my head by 9 AM.      That’s true. I left school at 18, just started my café, and it wasn’t planned, but it’s what I’m best at.

Rather annoying isn't it, how NHS waiting lists just keep going up and up. We had that letter from James last week saying it's another three months before he sees a specialist. I've nearly had enough.      You're not the only one—half our friends are in the same boat. If they spent as much time listening to their constituents as they do arguing in Parliament, maybe things would get done.      Don’t even get me started. Last week’s budget proposal—tax giveaways for the wealthy and a token 0.5% increase for schools? The Prime Minister’s on autopilot by now.      I know. I’ve been turned down for grant funding again for my research. They’re waiting "for priorities to be realigned," whatever that means.      And the worst part is, you didn’t even say the budget was unfair. You sat there like you accepted it.      Because I’ve written it off, honestly. It’s like trying to tell the tide when to turn in. At least we can pay our bills on time. That’s more than can be said for half our students.      You mean the ones who work part-time shifts just to cover their tuition?      Exactly. I keep telling them they should take out someone’s eyes in protest—just kidding. But seriously, it’s unsustainable.      Just don’t let me catch you watching  Line of Duty  again. I’ve had enough Prime Suspect dramas about corruption in government to last a decade.      You’re worse. You rewatch  Doctor Who  like it's some kind of therapeutic routine. Now  that’s  a solution I could get behind. At least the Daleks aren’t in it for the money.      Maybe we should set up our own political party—the Whovians for Public Health. I could see you in a regeneration suit leading a protest.      Just promise me we’ll still come to the Swan for a quiet evening like this after all that.      Deal. But only if you promise not to overorder the calamari again.

Rather lovely lunch, don't you think? That shepherd's pie was practically childhood in a dish.      Honestly, I could eat this every day. My mum's tries to make it, but it always ends up a bit soggy underneath.      Aha, it's all in the layering, love. You want thick layers of mince and just the right amount of onion. A lot of people just chuck in too much water, I've noticed. It's a common mistake among the younger generation.      If it's any consolation, I've only ever frozen shop-bought. I've never fancied tackling it from scratch. Still, I'd give it a go one of these days if you're offering to guide me, Margaret.      Darcy, if you say the word, I'll spend an afternoon with you. It's better than breakfast, honestly.      Haha, I don't think you ever looked at breakfast fondly to begin with. Still, the memories over shepherd's pie—vastly preferable, yes. Speaking of,老爷爷 I've never really quite understood why people still spend weekends baking for something when they can buy it so cheaply now.      You’re missing out – it’s not just about the food, it's the act of making something with your hands. It's part of what gets lost in the digital world we're drifting into.      True, but I think also part of tradition. Like the time your brother tried to do an open fire for the first time and nearly set the curtains on fire. Margie had to douse it with her best jug about five times.      Oh, typical David. Still, he learned his lesson and now leaves it to the professionals!      Maybe I’ll do something like that for the family. Enlists Dad to make proper Welsh rarebits and shows me how. I’d like something to pass down.      You're getting your stick out already, Elise. You've got a young grandkid with lunches to keep up with one day.      Still, I'd rather pass it on than the notion of ordering gochujang pancakes from Thai Express.      I do love the Internet, I genuinely do – but I can't tell what your actual meals will be at the end of it all. Thought we wanted to avoid that for our birthdays.      Born into the digital age over this, why not? At least it's a modern problem. The holidays are so much better now.

Rather annoying to be honest. It’s not like they’re even that hard.      Okay... Well, I’ll let you sort this out with Dada! I’m sure he’d love a little help.      Look, lads! C’mon now, it’s not eenad to be passive aggressive with the lassie. She’s only trying to help.      Aww, but serious, that was a bit funny. Oh, don’t look at me like that. We can laugh about it.      It’s not funny. You don’t even know how it plays! It’s so confusing and it doesn’t make any sense.      My turkey, ye have to give it a wee bit of time. Most games take a back seat if you don’t give them the attention they need.      Yeah, but if we’re all playing together then I just want everyone to enjoy it. And at the minute, it’s not quite fair, is it?      That would be ideal—settle into a game and everyone is on the same page. I’m not saying it’s impossible...      Exactly. Listen, if ye want, tomorrow we can walk in the park again and let the wee one have a bit of a chance, and then we can all gather up and give that game another go.      Tig!      Yes, yes! That way, the little one can have some fresh air out and about, and it’ll give you some more time to sort this out.      That actually sounds about right. I’m not the best at the touchy-feely stuff, but I can manage.      Not to worry, lad. The most important thing is that the wee fella has a good time. And if you can help, all the better.      And if he gets tired, we’ll curl up with some stories or a movie while the game is put to one side again.      Yeah, I think that would work. I do love a good cuddle-up, after all.      Oh come goon, ye softie! It's not every day ye see lad at your age admitting to that.      Well, when the little one is asleep in your lap, I suppose all bets are off.      Fair point. But as long as we can talk about the game over tea and biscuits, that's fine by me. S’all part of the team effort, yeah?      That's the spirit, lads. Now let's make a plan and then we can get on with our evening before it's too late.

Rather a lot of excitement in the house today, what with the two lasses here and all that mucking about with the Christmas decorations. You're not skint of mince pies, are you, Anon? I've spotted £2 quid worth of crumbs outside the hall.      Oh, don’t be worryin’ about that, dear. I reckon it was the cat, not the missus. A lot of excitement tends to bring a lot of crumbs, don’t you think?      Well, nothing was ever quite so chaotic as setting up the Christmas table with these two around. I swear they’ve even tried to hang fairy lights on the cat. Still, it’s Christmas, and they well mean well, don’t they?      Honestly, I told him if I had to wrap another sock and say "Merry Christmas" to an inanimate object, I’d have been breakfast, no doubt about it!      Ha! Me and me best mate looked at one another, and said “Well, that sock’s Christmas is ruined, innit?”      Well, listen—there I was in the garden yesterday, brushin' up the leaves, when I remembers there was something I had to say. I saw a boy walkin' his lovely pony by the road, fairly proud, and I thought to myself: that’s the spirit of Christmas in a sense, ain’t it? Still beautiful, no matter what the world throws at it.      That’s a touching way of looking at it. As a teacher, I tend to think about the kids—how many of them don’t get that kind of joy walking a horse, or even a dog about the village. That sense of wonder doesn’t touch the ground very often for most.      Aye, and you’re right. But it does touch the ground if you take a moment for it. I always tell meself that.      Speaking of the ground—did any of you know the car’s in for a service? I sort of told the bloke at the garage to "give it a bit of a special Christmas treatment," and told him the car had "lived far too long for a runabout and needed a man’s hand."      And if you ask me, he appreciated it.      Oh, don’t go getting blokey about it, lass. The only thing that needs a man's hand this Christmas is the Christmas pudding.      Haha, now that’s a hearty sound over this cold Norfolk air, innit?

Rather annoying I had to take the day off work, but Sarah’s birthday was her big one — sixty. I got her a lovely candlestick set, you know the one we saw by the river? Thought she'd appreciate it. Though I still can't get over how the frame accidentally had another picture in it at first — you'd have cracked up.      Honestly, you're the one who needs the rest, dear. I think the world of framing accidents you've made by now. How’re things at work, by the way? That’s been a bit in the lurch, hasn’t it?      Managing. We got the new grant funding through, which was monumental. My team’s got some changes in place too. Been keeping me quite busy. But still, I tell you, nothing as fulfilling as going out on a Sunday for a walk in the woods. You should join us – Mateo brought his dog along, and it's quite the riot.      Mateo? That's Silvia's brother, right? I heard he's got a new business going. Pretty cool one, too. Just trying to keep afloat, like most folks. Anyway, you were saying about going for a walk? Maybe I'll tag along – need something to get away from my laptop for about five minutes. That marketing ad I’m working on is giving me the jitters.      Going for that Sunday walk sounds lovely. Sarah is doing up her garden to match the woods, for heaven's sake. Geo., you might find a friend there. She could do with someone who knows something about wooden decks and flowerbeds — you know your way around those, being from Kent and all.      Garden? Please, I once planted a tomato in a pot and forgot it there for six months. Then had it back in the spring looking like gothic art on the steps. It's not gardening – it's camping out with rumors of dirt and green. But go on, Sarah could use the help.

Rather annoying this, having the power off for so long. I do miss the radio in the morning. Mind you, the weather’s been so mellow I’ve actually been enjoying a few long walks over by Costessey Park. Not quite as lively as I used to be, but keeps the blood moving.      That does sound nice, dear. I haven’t been out much—been trying to keep clean water stored up, but I must admit this has got me feeling quite domestic. Imagine me, pulling out that old shelf we had in the cupboard and dragging it outside when the pipes froze last week.      Oh, you mean when I had to come round and help you lift it? That was quite a comedy of errors. You’ve still got my left earring from back then, didn’t you? D’you know, I think the world might be coming to an end if we can’t even manage breakfast with no kettle or toaster!      Ha! Well, I for one have been quite content, to be truthful. Cooking a bit more over the camp stove—set one up outside, and it’s oddly therapeutic. Got the dog keeping me company, as usual. Did I tell you, old Max has taken on a watching brief during all this? Suddenly feels like he’s staffing a checkpoint – no one gets in unless I shout!      Honestly, the animals adapt better than we do. I’ve been trying to fill the silence with a bit of BBC Radio 4 in the old wind-up one. Honestly, they still read books like they’ve never been written. You’d think something’d be about a cat and a washing machine!      Well, as long as it’s about something! I was listening the other day to a talk about how people used to cope without power. Used to be quite the art. Rolling out the carpets, killing the lice—didn’t sound like much fun, mind you!      Speaking of fun, d’you fancy a small event when the power comes back? Proper evening, some wine, a bit of crackling in the hearth. Let’s not go full party with lunches and all that, just a small gathering? We could even invite Tom and his wife around.      Oh, go on then! But let’s promise no Big Brother or politics, nor even the in-laws, will you?      A promise can be made—for now at least!

Some say it’s democratic, others say it’s a shackle on the past. I've been in education for a bluddy long time, and I’ve seen how folks can get all flustered by politics. So, let me be plain. Back in 2014 there was a big vote—most people said "No!" to independence. But now, with the Tories and stuff what's going on in Westminster, the SNP think they might have another chance.      But why now though? If the first vote was passed by such a big margin? Seems a bit pointless to me. What's changed?      Aye, that’s a fair question. Politics moves. Some of the old guard always fancied their own shots and maybe with the UK being such an awkward place at the moment, they think people are feeling left out. Don’t go getting too excited though—the system is pretty tight. They'd have to get the approval of the Queen, and then the box-ticking in Parliament.

Rather annoying this Jeremy Kyle luv. You can tell ‘e’s tryin’ to ‘eap p’dith on the bloke with the tattoo.      Yeah, ‘e’s always doing that. Not like we’ve all got perfect lives! Yeah like that one turkey from Essex who c’n barely talk left or r’ght! I ain’t seen ‘er since, but ‘er twat of a ‘usband looked like he’d sooner died than admit ‘e was wrong. That’s because goon really on! If I see one more person go on about "fish an’ chips innit" like we go t’ the chippy every ‘our of the day summat! I lives 300 yards from one!      Haha, fair enough! But that sound stuff is so interesting though, innit? I’m doin’ a project on it and they said elision is when y’leave words out, right? So like we say "c’mon" instead of “come on”?      Yeah, an’ like we shorten words, or jut don’t say ‘tha’ as much.

Rather annoying this half-time’s longest than the whole match, innit?      Oh aye, I’ll not lie—half these ads are longer than a pre-season game. Still, at least we’re not watching it in silence. We’re thinking of something simple. George? Maybe Harrison?      Naa, get serious—George sounds like one of them politicians. Like a Prime Minister. You want the lad to be as powerful as that?      Well, it got a good sound to it. Or maybe Leo. I quite like that one.      Leo’s cool. Bit Roman-y for Silly Billy down the road, but y’know, up to you. Who’s in the lead anyway?      Man City, by a point—look at the screen. Don’t you ever pause it to make a brew?      Not I, doll. I like to watch it properly. Got the remote, I mind my own stuff.      Not you! You're missing the point—archery goonies on the telly is better than another monochrome pre-season match line-up, innit?      Fair point. Pass the Snickers. I’m planning to make 300 more stiches before the next half anyway.      Why not get over this one’s half and see if the lad scores? I reckons he’s got a shout today.      If he does, I'll make him a whole extra woolen bobble hat for Christmas.      You better make one for me too—just in case I want a bobbly one for a laugh.      Aye, once you finish helping me pick out this lad’s name, I’ll see you right.

Rather annoyingly, The Bee Movie is on request again. Lucas, I know you love it, but let’s be honest, it's starting to get a bit of a loop going on.      But Mummy, Barry B. Benson is my hero. Now, only if you two managed to stop giggling during the serious bits!      What’s a "royal fruit"?      A royal fruit? Only if your Grandma’s old house doesn’t take over!      We’ll see about that. Just like your Grandma promised more fruit crumble than ever over the weekend. Rather a lot of dust got stirred up on the way back. That lorry was full of old muck from the weekend clear-out at the bungalow.      It does make me feel old to be talking about dust and lorry loads, mind you. But I suppose it was necessary. I'm just glad we didn't leave that lot to rot longer.      Was it your old house? I remember hearing you talk about it a bit.      Aye, dear. It was the family place for generations. We had to get rid of some of the old bits to sort it out, but still, it's heavy lifting and harsh winds now.      I still can’t believe you kept the horse rug in the attic! I’m half tempted to take it, but then I think—why?      Oh, forget the rug. What really struck me was this photo of Mum when she was young at the social club in Thirsk, you remember? She looked so different.      Ah yes, Thirsk! That was a place back in the day. A proper heart to the community and all that. Bit more orderly than some of these modern places, if I’m honest.      Mate, I don’t even know where Thirsk is on the map.      It’s in the north of Yorkshire. Not far from the hills. Beautiful spot. Our parents always said there was a time when you could read the newspaper by the firelight because the air was so still and smokeless.      I still miss that sort of thing, really. Not that I’m old-fashioned—well, maybe a little—but the pace of life now is just so much different.      Aye, it is. Technology moved in like the tide, and for every new development, something gets lost. I miss the way people used to talk about the weather and the crops instead of the last stag do gone wrong on telly.      What's a "stag do" then?      It’s like a birthday party, but far more chaotic, with a lot of drinking and sometimes— laughs —a little pond life if you know what I mean.      It really was a different time, wasn’t it?      It was. The lives we live now seem quite far removed from those days, don’t they? True to say, we can’t turn back time, but we can at least raise a cup to it.      Cheers to that. I’ll take another one of those coffees.

Rather annoying the new museum’s parking’s all walled in. I nearly had a crick in m’neck parkin’ round back there. Otherwise it were good, eh? An’ maybe when I sort out me finances, we could do something proper.      Yeah, I s’pose. Me interview last week, Manchester hospital too — I got a buzz from them! Maybe we could even go together? You get your interview, I meet them for my pre-start, an’ we could see the sights.      Proper proper holiday? With us at the same time? Mate, you’re genjutsu. I never thought I’d be hearing that from you talkin’ ‘bout proper holidays.      Oh yeah, an’ I got us Christmas sorted, too — bought you a suit, an’ me? Right, you get us somethin’ nice back. No more last-minute Amazon-ian slippers for me, yeah?

So did you watch The Crown last night? That episode was mental. I was just gobsmacked when they showed the Queen's face-off with Harold Wilson.      Yeah, I binged it over the weekend. Rather annoying this, really. Sorting through all these old things. I didn’t think it would take so much... What was it, a box of old cards, or something else?      Oh, it was that cupboard with the toys and trinkets — you know the one — in that corner by the window? I was just rummaging about and came across something quite nostalgic. An old gardening set. A plastic one — red and green! I used to play with it all the time in the back garden.      Oh! Didn’t we get that with a big green trowel, remember? I mostly used to pretend I was clearing the weeds out of the pond. It wasn’t that Mycroft, was it?      [laughs] I think you were the one who made the pond idea — or the bog. You were always making things up. Made it almost breakfast, really.      Haha, well at least I didn’t claim to have found a cave back there. Also, the Bako set we had— you remember the one, yes? That sturdy wooden one — I built a garage out of it.      Oh, we were in awe watching you build it. I remember when it got left out in the rain — it looked like a water wheel and you had to pull it back in. You were quite cross about that.      I was! It took hours. Lost those tiny green wheels someone gave us.      That wasn’t just gardening we had a knack for — had the creativity going on in the kitchen and garden, I suppose. Still, it’s strange how these little things about our childhood resurface now.      Strange but comforting. It’s like you stumble across part of yourself that you barely noticed was missing.      That’s quite poetic of you.      Well, maybe I should stick to the minimal gardening these days instead of pottery.      You mustn’t stick to anything too elaborate. I know tidying out is always a bit of a task, but it’s the same with the weather — you think you’ll get around to it, and the sun leaves you go.      Precisely. But at least we have the company of old green trowels to keep us going through the storm.      The gardeners of the future, we two.      It’s a pity we can’t have a little plot in the middle of Leeds!      Unless we build it from memory, brick by brick. With Bako, always.      Oh, alright, then — let’s find that Bako before it disappears into the long grass of this room.

Rather annoying this newfit in the boiler innit? Seems like everything sticks on an’ it’s makin’ a right racket!      Blimey, I've heard about that! Got to call someone in to look at it before it winds us all up. We can’t be havin’ the place freeze up again.      Aye, an’ not with a cold snap coming in too. I remember when this house got stuck in a frost last winter. To be fair, it were me and the auntie and this old gas fire, messin’ ’bout with a frozen pipe.      Oh, goodness, the fire supply only lasted a few hours an’ Myra still talks about that!      Ten o'clock on a Wednesday and the place feelin' like a freezer. Me and your mother in the kitchen, tryin’ to get the kettle boiled an’ this happened. "Look Jack, there’s icin’ on the window!"      An’ the hot water, gone! I nearly boiled the kettle, didn’t I? Thought I’d be puttin’ the kettle on to wash my hair. Hilarious.      Well, we sorted it out. Dug out the bottle – Mate’s of mine fairly laughed, but, it worked!      Now don’t go temptin’ the council to shut us out o’ the mains again, huh? Our gas someone said might be faulty too.      So what we doing then? Some hotter something, is it? Or just call the plumber an’ see if they can sort it out properly?      Call a proper man, the lot of you lot! Both our thins be sorted and not gone another winter frost.      Aye, that’s the idea. Burgundy and treacle waters for Friday passed are not cuttin’ it no more.      I’ll get the phone an’ ring that Archee who did my kid’s bathroom. He’s from out o’ Malton but knows a thing or two!      Thanks for coming, gran an’ grandad! The house is brighter goin’ on your visits anyway.      You’re a good lot, that boy. And the box room, tidy as a button! Reckon I’ve never seen it so spick and span in all my hours!      Oh right, we saw that ‘bath pron’s on the telly the other night. I reckoned I could’ve done better, but then I remembered I once accidentally poured vinegar in the bath.      It’s not a good look when you’re 10, left in the bath sour as vinegar, an’ the whole street can smell it.

Rather than share a text-based response, I request that you frame a suitable question for me, enabling a typable text-based interaction. I shall facilitate this by generating questions related to Peter Pan or the films we’ve discussed, ensuring they can be answered via text and are consistent with our conversation. Please proceed.       Okay, then—what do you enjoy most about the character of Tinker Bell in the original Peter Pan story?       She’s really brave, and she’s like a proper sister to Peter. I like how she helps chase Captain Hook but also how she looks after the fairies.      That’s a lovely understanding of her character. Do you think she changed at all when you watched the new film about her?      I think she got a bit more of a story—like how she felt about being Peter’s helper and how she almost doesn’t shine no more when he forgets to say “Tink.”      Yeah, she didn’t have any sparkle in the woods.      Exactly, and it’s a really beautiful message about friendship and kindness. Was it sad to see her like that?      Yes—it wasn't proper happy time in that part. But it was good for Peter to learn to say it, and then it all turned back to proper fair and square fun.      You know what? That’s a very grown-up way to look at it.      I think my favorite movie is the one where Peter first comes to Neverland—there are pirates, and he doesn’t look like a regular boy!      I do like that version too—it shows you just the right amount of magic and danger. And it ends with him not growing old. Do you think Peter should have gone back to London in the end, like in the story?      No, he should stay at Neverland. Who wants to grow up when you can have adventures every day?      Not me! I like Neverland better. Even if there are crocodiles and pirates.      And it's for that reason that I love talking to you two—your insight go straight to the heart of the story. If you could write your own Peter Pan story, what would it be about?      Maybe about a new fairy who just moves to Neverland and how she finds her way to be part of Peter’s group.      Or maybe adventurers from other places—like from Captain Hook’s past—come to Neverland to make peace.

Rather annoying this, having to get up so early on a Saturday. I was just starting to get some decent sleep after the kids were out late again last night.      It does seem a bit unreasonable to be heading to the airport this early, especially as you picked them up the night before. But I'm assuming there’s no changing the flight time?      No, no point. I’ve been through all that. The tickets were too good to refuse. And besides, she was insistent—she’s always been impulsive like that. Always wanted to go, always.      I still remember when we lived in Taunton, she'd drive out at the first sign of blue skies and say, "Come on, I’m taking the kids to the seaside." I used to think she'd never live this down.      Living in Taunton was nice, better for breakfasts—there was always proper tea. Not this drive in the dark routine, you ever notice how we never seem to leave before the cockerels cluck?      At least you get the drive in daylight now. I remember Wellington was quite a different pace. Everything seemed calmer, even the traffic moved in something reminiscent of a circle. Still, moving from there to Devon was a good move for us, the opportunities, and with the kids in school here.      All that’s done and dusted now. I suppose we don’t talk about it because the old house is just full of memories—memories of my bad haircuts, bad management decisions, and what I now call 'the adventure of the lost key'. Still, at least the house sold alright, better than most in about half the time.      Speaking of which, I had a great chat with your sister yesterday about her house-warming party. She mentioned it should be a Christmas to remember with a ‘very special someone’ in guest list.      Oh? Who’s the lucky one this time?      Guess!      Honestly? Not sure whether to chuckle or feel sorry for the poor soul.      At least the party will be good no matter who pops along.      I think the actual go-to event on your life map is our house-warming. But I digress. Flying out early will be a shock, but let's make the most of it—for the warmth, the fluency, and the champagne, metaphorically speaking.      It's early, but it’s going to be a good one—just like everything else we've managed to go through over the years.

Rather a lot of folk taking a rest in these seats, do you not think? Felt like a panto last weekend, with all them local volunteers skidding about on their tea breaks.      Aye, quite right. Look like they’ve frightened half the townsfolk with all the clattering and the diggers. I’m told they’re doing something to the track near the bridge. Though I’ve no idea what, to be fair.      Oh, it was some sort of road journey project—think the council got grant funding for it. But don't ask me what they're doing to it, I couldn’t tell you. I've got the patience of a wet cat when it comes to all this building nonsense. Still, best to have bursts of fresh air between the works, I daresay. Always thought I'd be the type for green gardens and sunloungers.      Aye, but here we are in these concrete seats, planting our bottoms in hides, day after day. Have you got the knack for Swedish massage, by the way? My Florence—passed on a few years back—used to swear by it as the best way to keep circulation, especially as we get on a bit.      No indeed—I’ve no idea about massage. But I do deal with antiques, and I'd say you could call somethin' that's done wrong as badly as a bad massage! When I owned the gallery in Bath, I had a full-time masseuse. Woman had a real eye for tension, oddly. Funny thing—job had her at a hospice too. Chained through some awful things, but she taught me how precious it is about helping people feel at ease.      Oh, now that’s a good outlook. My sister is working at the hospice down the road. She says it’s the most humane job she's ever had. To sit with someone knowing they're at the end of their journey. It's something bloody sacred, if you ask me.      We should talk about that over a cup of tea. Next to me, lunches cost a pretty penny these days. Not that I mind—it's for a good cause. You know, I sometimes think the ME event next year could do well if more women were involved. Not just as performers, but in making the rules. After all, blokes like myself might overlook some of the finer details.

Rather than going somewhere extravagant this year, do you think we could do something more low-key, like a staycation in the countryside? I remember one summer we went on holiday to the coast as a family, and you were only about six. Do you remember that?      I do! It’s one of my earliest memories. We went to Bournemouth, and I was so fascinated with the waves crashing into the sand. It really does mean a lot to me to preserve the memory of going on holidays with the family.      I agree. I think having a staycation might be the perfect way to do that, especially now I’m getting a little older. It might be easier on me than ferrying breakfasts and luggage around at this stage. What areas in the UK would you suggest for hiking?      There’s the South West, of course, and that’s not far from here, so we can take a trip up into the Dartmoors or Exmoor. It gives me confidence knowing that whomever I’m with can also be there for me in a practical way.      That's very kind of you to say. I think it's one of the reasons our relationship is so special — we always support each other in different ways.

That might be something we should pay attention to—for the future. I might suggest to my students to think about investing in cheap index funds or even ISAs if they can afford it.

Rather annoying I couldfit in the summer holidays to go anywhere. My mam was on at me ‘owt I got to visit Gran in Carlisle, like as not I’d rather sneak off to the coast! Got me a sunhat to wear or the like, mind you.      A een, I went up north to Bishop Auckland for a few days at the start of August. Wandered round the old town a bit, got me some fudge, an’ chilled out by the riverside. Gran said she wasn’t impressed with me sunburn! Didn’t even get to the coast.      Oh, I  managed  to go to the south of Ireland for a few weeks in July. My uncle lives near Cork, so I spent most of the time pottering about the countryside, exploring Dingle, and eating way too much seafood. Locals were lovely, by the way — better than breakfast, no doubt about that!      I stayed in Wales, actually. Me nan’s got this little cottage in the Brecon Beacons, and I spent a week there just walking round the hills and cooking up a storm in the evenings. Got to see loads of birds and wild creatures — like, there was this owl that used to call at night, it got to me in the end!      I ended up just staying local, to be honest. Woss the point of wasting money on a holiday when I could save up for that weekend trip up to Morecambe? Spent a day in the sun, went for a walk down the prom, an’ had a massive fish and chip lunch at some old-fashioned tea room. Still a right treat in me books!      That all does sound quite the touch, but I’d have gone for a wilder sort of holiday. Proper hike or something. Know it sounds a bit strange, but I just like ‘aring out the trekkiness in me. Although, I’m not sure me legs could handle it after sitting ‘ere all semester!      Aww, come on, we could do that wee weekend trip out to the Lake District proper. I’ve got a cousin in Keswick an’ he’d be chuffed to come with us. Might even get to see goosanders on the lake if we’re lucky.      I’d be in, but only if we stop off on the way for some of that proper northern tea — I lost me taste for the Greek coffee I forced down last year!

Rather annoying this new speaker’s consent form innit? Seems like we need to list our qualifications  twice  in the bloody thing. Just went through it yet agin, and I've a right proper headache. I’ve only done it once yet tho.      Oh, you lot, I ain't touched it me own self yet. Still busy looking at the seminar content. I reckon the international business comms module needs more emphasis on digital platforms. These days, half the world don’t do meetings in person anymore.      Aye, good point Sally. We need to show the students how cultural nuance and technology interact. Think about how different the rules for email etiquette can be across Europe. Or the way Chinese and Japanese businesses approach negotiations via micro-expressions and indirect communication.      Exactly, and that’s a great way to divide the seminar—into verbal and non-verbal components, then add the digital side in there. We could structure it with case studies. For instance, use a German firm and a Brazilian company as contrasting examples in our workshop.      Or even better, let’s add some live exercises. Get the students into groups and set up role-plays where they have to negotiate a deal in Italian, with subtitles if they need ‘em. That’d help them get a feel for the pressure of a real professional exchange.      That'd be a right stretch for some of ‘em, but I’m up for it. We can have about five minutes of conversation, then show a video of the same negotiation in Italian and let ‘em compare. That’d highlight the cultural differences and the linguistic subtleties together.      And we need to stress that even if you know the language, communication isn't guaranteed. I remember a time when my Italian counterparts used formal Italian, but their tone was off, and the whole meeting almost collapsed. Language isn’t just words, innit.      So true, Angela. That's where body language comes in. We could split the session into three go-rounds: verbal, non-verbal, and then digital. Each section with a separate activity and some food for thought.      Yeah, and we could have a short Q&A after each part, just to make sure folk are engaged.

I’m so ready to get home by the time I remember I haven't even bought ingredients to cook dinner.      Ugh, it was pretty awful on my end too, honestly. I got an email from one of the undergrads—apparently, I didn’t clearly explain a reading policy in one of my lectures, so now I’m being asked to re-address it. You’d think by the third year they'd chase it up before the coursework is due.      Still, at least we're not alone in the chaos, right? You know, like that one student who wrote "Thanks for today!" in their email this morning. I’m half convinced their brain doesn’t pick and choose what it processes properly. Or maybe I’m just a bad lecturer.      You’re not a bad lecturer; I’m just betting they were distracted by their 4,000 group presentation meetings and the three exams creeping up in different modules. At least you're being loved in class—everyone I ask says you’re a gem to teach. I only wish I could say the same for myself sometimes.      Be nice. You’re okay too – just… occasionally cursed by students with chequered comprehension levels and huge expectations. I reckon it’s part of the job when you work in the UK higher ed system at the moment, huh? Our students work forty hours in part-time shifts while trying to keep a grip on their oddly-timed semesters.      Absolutely. I feel it’s part of the charm  and  the curse of our jobs. The funny thing is, the other day the landlords of our flat finally called me back about what's going on with the water pipes. Supposedly it's a classic "Chinese plumbing," and there’s a series of "poor decisions" passed down through generations that no one expected to become a problem for any of us.      Oh for goodness’ sake. We just need good water pressure. Is it  that  rare here? I’m starting to wonder if we should have just lived with the landlord who let us believe the fridge was working.      Look on the bright side, at least there are no mice in the walls this time, right? Or maybe we were just too busy to notice them?

Rather than share a meal and discuss various topics, I prefer to talk about one specific subject. Let's first discuss food and cooking, shall we?      I think talking about one specific subject is a good idea. So, do you have any specific dish you'd like to talk about?      Food wastage has always been an issue that has concerned me. I've been trying to reduce the amount of food I throw away, but it’s difficult to be consistent. Do you have any ideas or methods you use to minimize food waste at home?      That's a really important issue. I’ve been trying to meal plan and use up leftovers creatively. For instance, if we have leftover chicken, I’ll use it for chicken pie or soup the next day. What about you?      I try to do the same, but I must admit I’m not as systematic as I’d like to be. Sometimes I just forget about things in the back of the fridge, and they go off. I wonder how our grandparents managed so effectively. They had to stretch resources so much further.      I think they really had to be careful with every ingredient. I remember my grandpa always reusing vegetable peelings to make stock. That’s something I’d like to start doing more of – it’s a shame I’ve not gotten into it yet.      Yes, I wish I could be as practical about food as they were. It’s not just about saving money, although that helps, but also about reducing waste. I was reading the other day that food waste contributes significantly to methane emissions, which is a major climate problem.      I hadn't thought about it in those terms. I’m more interested in the practical side, but it's reassuring to know that reducing waste can help the environment too. I know some people are even starting to grow their own vegetables. My sister tried that on the balcony, and she said it was surprisingly rewarding.      Oh, I’d love to try that. I tried growing herbs on the kitchen windowsill once, but they died after a week. I'm not very green-fingered! It’s one of the things I envy about young people like you – you’re so into these environmental and self-sufficient projects.      It's not about being young, though. It’s just that I grew up with the idea of sustainability being more mainstream these days.

Rather annoying to be honest. I’d rather be at the lab. But this Sunday roast is a family tradition... got to keep it alive somehow.      Well, you didn’t have to wait for me. I only took 15 minutes to get over. No need to make mince and two different types of pies before I got here!      But seriously, it smells amazing. You’ve outdone yourself.      Oh, don’t think you're off the hook that easily! You said you’d come and help me chase the kids out the garden. You disappeared with the dog for half an hour!      What? I only grabbed him for a quick bit of turkey on the grass! I swear it left the house like that! I didn’t know you wanted them all herded into the sitting room like a farmer with sheep!      I just wanted a moment’s peace while everyone goes mad playing in there. And honestly, ever since we started felling the old tree in the back, they won’t stop asking about it. "Is the tree dead, Mum?" "Is it sad if we cut it down?"      Honestly, we’ve got to be more considered with our answers. They think we’re removing national monuments – not a dodgy old oak with a dead branch on it! But while we're on the subject of worries... how's the work going? I haven’t seen you properly in weeks.      It’s been brutal. All my focus is on publishing one of the papers. Some nutty editor is flagging every bloody statistic and being an absolute sod about the  literature review . You know I did all that years ago!      Well, I had to deal with my own nonsense at work today. One school barely informed me about the unannounced Ofsted inspection. Had to reschedule four assessments within an hour. I swear, some people just have no idea what it's like any more.      I know what you mean. We’re all good at planning until something goes off the rails. At least lunches ready. Gravy? Would you like some extra Yorkshire?      You're like a man with a griddle in a crisis. But if you've made it – yes, I’ll take it. Just promise me we'll go out for pizza on Friday. No research, no marking. Just us.      Deal. As long as I don’t have to do the washing up either.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? I was just thinking 'ow nice it'd be t' get down t' sea 'fore it turns cold proper. D'you ever miss the feel of sand under yer feet, Elise?      Oh, I do, Andrew. I haven’t een been since my William was a baby. I 'member 'e loved collectin all them shiny rocks. A bit like yer baby blue tits, that swoopin down 'pon 'em. Makes me miss 'im. We 'ad somethin once. Didn’t we, Jerry?      Yeah, I 'ear you. Those little birds are quite clever. I found one tryin to feed its 'atch turkey bits oncet, of all things. Makes sense though, natur’ selects whot works, innit? Now I think 'bout it, I 'ave been helpin at the community centre when I can—maybe 'elpin out with a garden in exchange for a shed, ever considered that?      A bit too much for me, I'm afraid. I do like the company 'ere though. Yer always askin me t'house-sit fer yer son, Jerry. Tellin me 'e's got problems, workin too much. Tell him t'see a professional. Don't let it linger like mine did.      You 'ad depression? Oh, Andrew...      Aye, 'forty odd years ago 'n all. Spent m' retirement tryin to sort it out, thought I 'ad t'earn back the lost time. Never worked real and still got no money. Family 'elps, but it's not about money. It's about the ties, the talking.      I see what you mean. Going into that silence can be a real trap. I remember one of my students, a bright lad 'bout sixteen, got real down. Said 'e 'ad no future. You know, I mentioned volunteering as an option. Not just for them, but for me too. Gave me a bit of purpose again.      'Ow d'y do that with such cheer, Johnny? Even after all those years runnin t'ground?      It's the kids, Elise. They're resilient, innit? Always smiling, always full of ideas. Y'know, I might give some of that to someone like Andrew. Maybe help out with a bit of gardenin or somethin?      Sounds nice. Anything ‘as a bit of routine and them blue tits round. Specially if I get to watch telly while doin it.      Oh 'e'll be on telly for 'ours, 'and flaked wallpaper and all before realizin 'e's on mute again.       laughing  Same every time. House matters a lot, doesn't it?

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? You know, how they glue the cuticles in those nail bars. I got them done last Thursday and it was like my fingers were trapped in something sticky after. I had to wash them straight away.      Oh, I hate that too! I had mine done the same, and I felt like they didn't explain what it was properly. It just sort of came out of nowhere when they handed me the hand towel. They gave me a few blocks to put my hands under as well—must be heat or something. Didn’t even get told the name of the product.      Yeah, I don't get why the people who do these things can't just explain what’s going on. I’m not asking for a chemistry lesson, but I do like to know what goes on my body. The lights are blinding too, by the way. All that blue light when you're drying your polish—it’s messing with my eyes in the car the next day.      You're not the only one. I reckon it's like that with most beauty treatments—personally, I'd rather have someone explain things properly. I’ve asked my hairdresser once what the difference is between a keratin treatment and a deep conditioning mask. She looked at me like I was mad. But I’m not mad, I just don’t like to be in the dark.      Honestly, I understand. You don’t have to be a scientist, just someone who knows what they're talking about. I went into this shop down the high street the other day and the woman there told me I had "intrinsically reactive pores." I hadn't even mentioned my face in about five minutes.      Oh come on, that’s brilliant. "Intrinsically reactive pores," that's barely a real phrase. I mean, I'd pay just for her confidence. Maybe she thinks it’s high-fashion jargon.      Oh absolutely. But you know what? I don't mind them giving advice, I just want the truth. Like when I bought this new serum—looked amazing online, right? They told me "it regulate the skin’s natural hydration barrier," whatever that means. But it started causing acne breakouts. So I'm back to basics now.      Yeah, I’m with you. I tried a new face mask from the beauty shop at the mall—it said it was for all skin types and pH balanced.

Rather annoying isn't it, how grown-ups think they have to glue sticks and glitter in order to know anything about children?      I’m more than a bit tired of having to justify my lifestyle to people who probably don’t even know the rules of being a good parent yet.      Right? I met my friend Ruth today, and she just looked at me like I was completely clueless because I don’t have a policy document in place for social media use for a three-year-old.      You know what's the most ridiculous? The way people think kids should be walking around with clear plans for independence even before they've mastered potty training.      Honestly, I’m doing what’s right for my child, not what the next-door neighbor says. I’m not obsessed with Dora, and I don’t let the little one watch an hour of Barney every day.      Exactly. I've been home with Hattie ever since she was born and I plan to keep it that way for a bit. It's important to give her the time and space she truly needs.      I think people struggle with the idea that you can choose to be a stay-at-home parent without needing to have a five-year strategy in place from the start. It's just about being present with your child, and sometimes that means having to rethink your old ideas.      And it's hard enough when you already feel you're not matching the expectations of people you've known for years. Let alone trying to read books and rush your toddler to start school early.      It's like people want these miniature adults now – all analysing ballet as if it's a career move. I just want the child to know that the sun is shiny and that they can be silly and not worry about that.      And the truth is, step parenting is a whole other world. There are no playbooks passed out at the starting line.      You mentioned being quite close to my brother, and I know your situation with your stepdaughter has had its challenges. You've always taken it in your stride but I can tell it's been tough.      Thank you for saying that. It's a relationship that's still in the testing stages for both of us. I think real relationships, step or otherwise, are built upon daily decisions and the small things that say “I care about you”.

Rather annoying this new box set eh? You've only just started watching it and it's already addictive. We're all on the same wavelength with it, me, Claire, and Steph, anyway. They said it's got a twist in the third episode, but I bet you've worked it out already.      Yeah, I reckon so. Not like I haven't watched enough of them to know most twists these days. What I don’t get is this obsession with participating in friends’ birthdays. Last week, someone said they were spending £40 on a cake for their sister, and the rest of us were just like, "Okay?"      That’s Claire for you, always thinking of the next big gesture. Honestly, I’m lucky I remembered my niece’s birthday this year. I had to pin reminders on my phone, and I think I turned Pinterest into my secondary homepage for about a month.      Bucksy? I mean, I suppose for little ones it adds up, but I remember once, you didn’t have a laptop and still came up with the best damn Waterstones gift voucher, wrapped it in a cereal box and written in crayon. She couldn’t read it and only realISED it was for a shop when she opened the wrapping. Absolutely cracked up.      Oh Mate, I got a sneaking suspicion that it was Haylie who told the others. Now they're expecting me to do something grand. I’m already foreseeing a Pinterest disaster, and I might just have to give in to the birthday crowd. You’d have thought being a research manager would make me hotter stuff than this.      Any day. You're all right when it comes to actual research, about half as useful when it comes to gift finding. But you're not the first one in the family to have gone overboard. My cousin once spent a fortune on a superhero-themed party. My sister had to put the kibosh on it at the last minute 'cause it was way over the budget.      At least someone knows how to rein it in. We should talk about that over a pint of something stronger than the usual. 'Cause I think it's been a while since the last time we set Pinterest aside for a nice, long chat without the pressure of goin' on some wild mission to impress everyone else.      Lead the way, I need a respite from the "Hashtag Exceptional Birthday Vibe" for a minute or two.

Rather annoying that the chandelier we liked on eBay is now sold. I was hoping it would work in the dining room and give it a bit of elegance.      Yeah, I remember you saying it was quite fetching. I'll have another search later—there are always more out there. Got a preference on style? I seem to recall you didn’t want anything too ornate.      Aye, less is more in this case. Maybe something clean but with a decent weight to it. You know me and clutter. I like when the light adds to the space instead of overwhelming it.      Noted. I’ll keep an eye out, then.      Thanks love. On another note, I left the browser open on Rightmove. I reckon the two-bedder in Ealing might be the one. It's in a decent spot and the photos look breakfast-y enough for us.      Which one? The one with the oversized kitchen? I saw the views near the back—those gardens are fairly sizable. Could be a dream, if it’s available.      That’s the one. I flicked through the floor plan as well—it’s got a decent room for extra storage and then the space left is usable for a study. Imagine having a real corner of our own for work again instead of the kitchen table. It would be like luxury.      You're not wrong. It’s the little things that make life easier. Let’s see: can we arrange a viewing week? I preferably don’t want to juggle a meeting in the evenings and being back at home trying to make dinner.      I'll check the calendar. I can manage the week of the 22nd if you can. That leaves us with the school week out the way.      That should do for me. Let’s put in an expression of interest. The more shows of interest the higher the chance something stays open for us. I’ll keep you posted when I sort out the light fittings too—don't know what we'd do without you with your eagle eye on spots of dust.      And you'd be lost trying to sort any man-sized task away go it on my own. I'll keep the responses on Rightmove open—if they tick, I'll let you know quickly.      Good plan. So we're planning for the 22nd, we're watching those listings, and we're hopeful.

Rather annoying the new cleaner at the nursing home, Fran. She’s promising one thing then forgets it. I got to my car this morning and discovered she’d left my keys in the canteen!      Aw, that’s not good—get her sorted yet?Deirdre      I gave her a friendly shout about it at break time. Proper upset me, I’ve been working all day with just the one pair and I’m not about to let her keep costing me time.      Bit of a drama for a cleaner, isn’t it? Care workers like me seem more reliable! Not that I’m saying she’s the only one, mind.      Yeah, I’ve met enough new staff who forget this and that, to be honest. Darcy, the one I work with, once came to an appointment for a home visit and forgot her breakfast, no wonder she was late!      That sounds like you, not her!      Well, it might’ve been me, but I was the one who told her, “Oh, I’ll put two slices in the toaster for you, and tell me when it’s done,” then… well, you can guess where I was.      Mate, you got a job, and now it’s serious! Bet your boss raised her eyebrow quite a few times already.      You don’t know the half of it. Last week I turned up to a retirement home and my clipboard wasn’t there. I had a map with me, the key for a padlock, and no clipboard. Can you imagine? Looked like I’d just dropped about five eggs on the floor trying to gather the pieces of my brain.      At least you know that better now!      Maybe she’ll do better, time for her to grow up a bit. As for me, I just handed her a piece of paper where I’ve written all the basics I expect from her. You know, “arrive on time,” and “clean as you go.” Nothing fancy, but it seems like it helps!      That sounds like a good idea. I like that you’re not giving goody-two-shoes lectures about being professional, just real expectations in black and white.      Yeah, blokes like Fran might zip off with you ranting at them, but if you say it’s in writing, you’ve got solid ground to stand on.      Exactly, and when I’m not even near her, the team can just point to that piece of paper.

Rather annoying when a new study comes through and messes up all your old routines, isn’t it? I saw this one the other day about sleep—apparently, we’ve all been going about bedtime wrong.      Oh really? That sounds like one of those discoveries that makes you lie in bed and think, “So I’ve been doing this all wrong?” What did they say?      Turns out, it’s not just about hitting the sack at 10. It’s about aligning it with your innate body rhythms. They call it the 'chronotype'—whether you’re a lark or an owl. I’m an owl through and through, and I’ve only ever had trouble in the mornings.      I’m the same. It’s ridiculous how early some people seem to function. But I’d rather sleep in and be up late most days, thank you very much. Still, if researchers are saying that this matters, maybe I should be thinking about adjusting the kids' bedtimes too.      Yeah, the study actually suggested staggered bedtimes for different household members—personally, I’d be fine with that. Like a sleep timetable for the house. You sleep early, I go on a walk, read, and then in when I’m ready. Though I can’t imagine dragging myself out of bed early, that’s for sure.      It would be bizarre, but at least everyone gets the sleep they need! Though, let’s be honest, someone would eventually end up walking in on someone else in a very intimate moment.      Touché. Still, it’s interesting. Anyhow, speaking of sleep, we should take the kids camping soon. It’s always good for the mind—sleeping under the stars, no screens, just nature.      I know! I love it. There was one time we got lost in York for hours looking for the guesthouse. Eventually had to follow a friendly local into a pub. She told us stories all night and gave us a map. It was mad, but we ended up having a great time anyway.      Oh, we need more of that—getting lost and finding our way. Still, I’m a bit nervous about navigating the city by myself. I really need to figure out a good route into Cambridge. I swear, the more I’m here, the less I understand how the roads work.      It’s like the city was built by Romans one day and then aliens the next.

Rather annoying when a hamster takes off wi’ the bedding an’ sticks it in the middle o’ the floor, innit? I jist tried skypin’ it back an’ now it’s a mad hooman with whiskers. Look at it—gettin’ all riled up ’cause I breathed on it wrong!           Lissen, luv, you’ve only got yourself to blame fer that! I got me one once an’ she’d chuck the wee balls o’ wool out the wheel an’ demand me chase em, but the worst was when she decided the wires o’ me hair乾 made a good chew toy. Took six months to grow out.           Yeah, no’ just the mess they make, their personalities are wild, innit? My cousin screamed her head off when hers started creepin’ up her breakfast, lik’ it was this cute wee robber or sumthin’. But what’s even weirder is that m’ gran’s always sayin’ that ginger folk attract red squirrels. I swear she believes it.      I mean, don’t ye both ken readin’ the hobbit an’ thinkin’ summate like that might be true? Beaky got ginger eyes, after –?      Right cheery memory, Haylie! Anyway, I reckon gingers attract summat else as well. If I go out in a park with no sunscreen and daft enough someone starts gawpin’ at me. Not like a red squirrel’s gonna start a conversation with you over the weather.           No, naah! Although it might about daftness. My dad used to swear redheads were sunburn incarnate. "Jus’ take one look at ‘im and ye know it's a sunny day," he'd joke.      Ennn, if that’s true, sods law meus the one time I was sunbathin’ I ended up with a little beetle on me arm. Feckin’ yellow sprite of evil, if you ask me. No sunscreen and na warning—was like he ran a red alert for trouble.      I told ye folks, goin’ on pond life about your antecedents or pets is loosin’ the plot. I had a goldfish, bloomin’ disappeared. ‘Bec’s he doesn’t like you,’ me mum said. An’ I was startin’ to believe her, honest to God.      Yeah, why not? A goldfish that hates the vibe of one of us. Nawk, the universe is weird. Least me hamster, once it backs down from the madness, could be the next great Yorkshire adventurer.      As long as it doesn’t go off startin’ on the cat.

Rather annoyingly, I just got my fifth request for support from a promising student. Should I reallocate reinforcements... or focus on building maps for the next phase?      Maps, eh? You wouldn’t have said that as a lad, now would you? Back when I was your age, I used to think the only good maps were the ones on your back from a round of cards.      Oh, come now, John. That’s hardly relevant to the game. But speaking of strategy, Alice, how's your glass of sherry holding up? Still mostly full, I hope.      My turkey still walks unscathed. And the chocolate is fortified. Probably. I’ve been lucky, really, this whole game. A bit of playing cards luck, perhaps?      Well, with a bit of luck and a bit of science, you can get far in this game. Just like the old Chinese legends told by my Mum—about Genghis Khan, and how he'd always take two wives out of luck to balance the grief of one death.      Well, John, if you’re comparing ancient tales to modern board games, I might actually take you seriously if you stopped muttering about “chocolate,” “alcohol,” and “Christmas” in the same breath.      Hey, a bit of nostalgia is allowed. Besides, Christmas had the best cookies. Or at least the prettiest sprinkled ones.      Sprinkle or not, talking of cookies makes me think of my cooking. My last fails were because I trusted the new updated version of the recipe, not my own. My kids had to correct me.      Kids sure know it all these days, don’t they? I tried to play Risk when I was your age. Back then, we just followed the instructions. No faff with mispronouncing the place names!      You're just mad you couldn’t pronounce “environment” on your own if your life depended on it.      That might be true, but your mother still calls it “En-voyrun-ment” and I live with that knowledge every Saturday afternoon.      Look, we can debate semantics all we want, but my next move is to consolidate my power. My sixth wave starts once I can record it clearly on camera.      Ah, you won’t make it without another glass of sherry first, now will you? The night's young. And someone who enjoys good music and good company has to have their wings once in a while.      Well, if my wings are recreational, then I suppose it counts.

Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, I thought I’d love it here, but it’s just like... got to wake up at six every morning because my lectures start at seven, and I dunno, it just doesn’t feel quite right. Was I mad to ditch Falmouth all for this?      I understand that, yeah. I feel the same sometimes. Coming straight from Liverpool—it’s such a big shift. I thought I’d be loving the uni vibe but honestly, half the time I feel like a goldfish in a bowl. Like, where even are the kids with brains?      Oh,  yes . I talked to someone the other night and they mentioned some Nobel Prize winner type lectures, and I was like, “Blimey, I’m gon nap through the whole thing.” But I dunno, I just don’t know if uni was the right move for me. I see all these celebrities at home just doing their thing and being like “I’d be fine not having a 9 to 5.”      Yeah, I mean I do like the idea of going into acting—everyone I know in Liverpool says it’s bound to be a pip for me. But then there’s this reality thing, like, “Do you really want to be broke at 30 with no pension?” So I think I might do a bit of media and communications instead.      That sounds super pragmatic. I don’t even know what I’m doing yet. I’m just trying to enjoy it while it lasts, I guess. I mean, one day you’ll be out there with a mansion and a baby, and I’ll be stuck with my cats watching you on telly.      Haha! Only if I finally get over my fear of IVF! I know that sounds silly, but I’m just scared of not being able to do it ‘the natural way’ or whatever. Though I heard about this new celebrity couple—they used a surrogate or something. I think it sounds very intense but way too modern for me.      Yeah, I think I’d go mad trying to do all of that stuff while balancing work and life and, ugh,  babies . But then again, maybe it’s something I’d really get into. I dunno though, maybe I should focus on just not tripping over between my room and the kitchen until next year.      That sounds like a solid life plan to me.

: You think the teacher’s gonna be impressed with our project on poverty? I mean, it’s not like it’s the most popular topic in the class.     : I dunno, it is kinda controversial, honestly. But the data we’ve got on income inequality in Slough is pretty shocking. I read somewhere that more than one in five kids here live in households where they don’t have a clean fridge. That’s nuts, right?     : Yeah, I mean, you’d think in 2025, nobody should be in that situation. But then again, my cousin’s family had to move into a hostel last year because their rent spiked, and they couldn’t afford it anymore.     : That’s brutal. I suppose that’s why I like working on this project—it makes you think about the real consequences of politics and consumerism. Like, if we’re all just buying more and more stuff, is that actually helping people live better, or is it just benefitting the big companies?     : Honestly, I think it’s the big companies who win. My dad says people don’t even care about where their clothes come from anymore, as long as they’re on sale. But what if the workers in the factories got paid properly? Yeah, that would help with the poverty stuff.     : Yeah, and it’s not just about what you wear. If we could redistribute wealth a bit more, like through fair taxes, someone wouldn’t have to choose between feeding themselves and paying the electricity bill. I mean, that’s not something we think about when we’re buying the latest phone.     : True. Kinda sad how rich people walk past homeless folks every day without noticing. We were talking about this in history class—hearing about how life was in the 19th century, and how similar some of the problems are.     : I know. It just shows me that the system is broken.
