Rather than chuck a frozen lasagne in the oven, I thought we could knock up a bit ‘o spaghetti Bolognese, eh? Y’know, proper one, not that casserole dish type off the shelf. Although, fair play, homemade lasagne  is  like cheating MyFavSunday, but Bolognese’s a bit of a win. I’ll help, if you pick the wine. I don’t trust your taste in additives.      I see what you’re doin’ here, alright. Attempted bribery with vino and sarcasm hides deepest, darkest fear of stove-top ambitions. Fry a bit of onion, chuck the tins in, add garlic, spices, and let it be ‘neath a lid all  cosy . Meanwhile, we boil about five billion noodles. I’ll be browning the meat now, then you chuck th’ pasta into the pan. Let that go on while the sauce bubbles. Quick, efficient, and most importantly,  not  baked. Unless you fancy burning down Cambridge.      Sounds solid. Mince? Done. I once used ketchup as Bolognese. My flatmate said it was  bold , but academically interesting. Do people not add wine to this?      Classy touch, innit? You fancy a splash? That’ll add goenvironmental smogge if you ask me. Just don’t go adding mint in, like that  one  person did last TimeOf.      So, red wine, or ketchup, or mint—I’d say those three are solid descriptors of your life to date. For clarity, ‘dumped in the food and shrugged’ is that description. I’ll add the wine. Always better to drink it with it in, rather than later, right?      Laugh, and the whole oven’s on fire, you’ll be in it with me, yeah? Pass the bottle over, then.

Rather annoying when a horror film tries to do too much, innit? Like, jumping between jump scares and... proper plotlines, it just muddies things up. I mean, sure,  Insidious  is creepy, but honestly, sometimes the plot feels like it's been shuffled through a washing machine and eeny weeny  not  the one you want handed over if you're looking for self-respecting narratives.      Ay, that's a fair point. But y'know what, there's something to be said for the classics. You can't chase the Goosebumps factor with some modern horror like, say,  The Nun —that's worse than the Goosebumps books. On the other hand, you look at films like  The Omen —classic stuff! I mean, whoa, them films pick and stick in the head for a lifetime!      Oh definitely, I'm more of a 'look for quality over quantity' in films. When I watched  The Devil’s Dictionary , even though it's old, the way they explored themes and layered character relationships—it just jumps off screen, y'know? I mean, puts modern twists as to shame. And the real cherry on the top is how they managed to build that whole rhythm in storytelling without falling into clichés or pretentiousness.      Yeah, really, there's something about a tight narrative. Like,  The Ghost Silhouette  is iconic, and you can see the principles they follow in modern work—but in an age of binge-watching, unfortunately a lot of them just end up being— retch —90-minute stretchers and being filled with plot holes big enough to horse ride through.      Ah, I prefer the bangers! Give me something chaotic but vibes. I absolutely lost my mind at  The Possession of Sukey Spence . No plot, just screaming and eyeliner for 90 minutes. But you can’t deny the vibe. It's trashy, but it's got soul! Whereas some of these modern stuff, all flash, no stick. Feels as wholesome as sprite being called lemon water.      Grmmh! My nan took me to see  The Ghoulstones . It was like the worst film ever. Mournfully paced, about a family haunted by real estate ghosts—no line in quality. I was genuinely wishing the box office would jump through the plot to fast-forward to the ending. The only plus side was the roles costumes had amazing hours—there was even belly dancing ghosts!      Hah, imagine the box office jumping! It would have been a ghostly horror to watch.

She's good, thanks. Just had another kid, bless her. Crazy as it is, I still find it hard to believe she’s my sister. I mean, I was a control freak, but she just jumps into everything head first.      Oh that sounds like her. I have a cousin up in Leeds that’s just like that. Unfazed by anything.      I have one too. I'm told it's all in the genes. Guess we're just waiting for them to come out to our side and become middle of the road!      That would be a dream, wouldn't it? Anyway, let’s speak of something cheerful. Have you tried the new go-to skin serum that everyone's raving about?      Oh, no, I haven’t. But I'm on high alert due to my skin. Rather annoying to be honest. My gran keeps kosher, so I have to stick to it for Seder. It’s alright I guess—just means I’m more conscious about what I’m eating. How about you, Steph?      Oh I love being at Seder. We usually make my mum’s Italian version at home, with a bit of a twist. She uses kosher salt and everything. Though I once tried making latkes and set the kitchen on fire. Still, we eat loads of gefilte fish and it always smells amazing in the flat for days.      Mm, reminds me of the time I baked a  kugel  with my cousin in Italy. Her family had migrated there in the 50s, you see. They put a bit of nutmeg in the sweet version, which is a bit of a twist. I tried to take photos for my blog, but the kugel was practically gone before I could publish!      Blooming hell, is that what I ate in New York and didn’t know? I spent a summer working in Brooklyn and had the best plate of matzah ball soup I’ve ever had. It was like comfort food from another century. Have you tried properly simmering the soup for hours? That’s the trick.      I’m with you, Dan. My sister tried making her own matzah balls once and thought they were like dumplings. She put in egg yolks and it ended up being kind of like someone made chicken croquettes. My gran didn’t speak to her for weeks.      Ah, some family traditions can be… rigid. I remember trying to make a new sabra chicken recipe in Paris and mispronouncing a Hebrew word so the waiter just gave me this look. It was absolutely mortifying! Still, that place had the best wine to go with the food.      Oh I baked something for Passover last year too. A honey cake, with a bit of cinnamon and something I think was called cardamom. Everyone loved it. I told them the recipe had been passed down for generations. No one asked questions.      At least someone got their culinary oedipal complex in check around the table. I once tried to explain gochujang to my Irish cousin and he thought it was a form of dentistry.      You’re all hopeless. A bit of research and you could at least maintain fluency in your own culinary heritage. I once taught a kid to read Hebrew so they could say the  haggadah  prononcipally correctly.

Rather annoying this, innit? These bloomin’ phones. I blame Nokia for making ‘em so hard to unpack and set up. You used to just press a button, and it worked! Now, you’ve got to fumble about with PINs and Wi-Fi!      Yeah, I know what you mean, love. It was ridiculous at first, honestly. I had to read most of the manual just to turn this one on! I’m no phone expert, obviously, even though I have a doctoral thesis to finish, mind!      Aah, I’ve dealt with these ruddy things quite a bit in Germany. I tell ya, it still trips me up sometimes—what with all the little settings and services. You want me to look at it with you right now, or would you prefer to wait until we’ve had sommat to eat?      No, no—let’s get it sorted now. Our food won’t come in for ten minutes yet. Besides, I can just imagine Professor Hughes at the Uni flapping about this if my phone doesn’t work here. I had one of them ‘fore they rebranded it. All right, switch it on and wait for the main menu. Let me know when it shows up, luv.      Here it is—main menu. Right. And what now? Do I need a new SIM card or anything?      Not necessarily—depends if it’s unlocked. Let me check. Mm, says it’s factory unlocked. Good sign. Let’s go to settings, password, enter. And go from there. You’ll need your initial PIN code. It should’ve come with the box, though I reckon you lost those leaflets by now like I did.      Oh, I did—those things were like confetti the moment I opened the box.

Rather annoying when the beer’s warm, innit? Me an’ the lads always take a crate up to the park an’ chunder it on a Saturday afternoo’. But sure, over Christmas, we’d always do somethin’ bit different. Maa used to make the biggest mince pies y’could imagine, like plates big with pastry all thick an’ sticky.      Aww, now I feel like I got this all wrong, Miss Furness. In me nan’s place it was always Christmas pudding and brandy and stuff. An’ if the kids went near the tangerines, they were out!  laughs  But me nan was half-Philippino, so we had that pininyapp, marzipan an’ stuff. It was like a mash-up of the world, really, if y’know what I mean.      Mm, back when I was a girl, Christmases were a bit more... ornate, you might say! We used to have carol singers lining up the street, and we’d serve mulled wine, not lager, mind you—there I go with my dram! Here, let me share a story. One year we had this neighbor—very continental, used to mix up all sorts of foreign spices—he gave me a recipe for a cinnamon fig and orange cake, and it became a sort of tradition in our home to have it alongside the usual turkey and all the trimmings.      Aye, now that’s a bit more posh than me lot, love. I was raised out in Bognor—nothing fancy, but practical. The most excitement we got was whether the gravy would come out right, and who’d walk in with feathers still on! But we had this lass from Barnstaple—granddaughter of a schoolteacher—used to bring a kind of saffron bread, ‘cos her family were into that. All very proper, really. And I remember once the biscuits went a bit too greasy, cos I tried using too much butter. The missus was not pleased!      Yeah but wait—what about the  cultural  side of things? We always had that guy from Spain—his name was like ‘Pepe’, or go on then, ‘Django’ or something—brought in some bratwurst and that green stuff with the olive thing—what’s it called?      Oh, you mean pesto? Yeah, I think that was it. And then there was this lass from Glasgow, she brought this haggis and neeps and tatties... my jaw dropped like it was butterflied. Honestly, once you try haggis, you never go back.

Rather annoying the new recording software they've given us at work. Keeps transcribing her 'th' sounds like 'f's. Never mind, it is Friday yet. I’ve had a bit of toast with a little jam—nothing exciting, I know, but it does the trick.      Got eeny weeny bit of egg on toast for me. Watched an episode of  Luther  last night. A lot of shouting and cunning villains this time. Still, Iadmire how he manages to be both physically and mentally intense in the role. Funny you're talking about recording—it's a bit like listening in to peoples' secrets, isn't it?      I only grabbed a scone this morning—plain, no jam, just a bit of butter. Honestly, I was too engrossed in my Kindle this morning I forgot to even properly make breakfast. I was about a third of the way through  The Guest List , this new thriller with a twist in every chapter. It’s the kind of thing I can devour in one go when I’m not actually writing deadlines.      Oh yes, I’d heard good things about that one. A dinner party gone wrong, and only ten guests? Sounds like a classic whodunit—and it’s always been a staple of crime fans. I remember reading Agatha Christie fairly hungrily in my teens, though I’ve been into more sombre detective series these days like  Broadchurch . I might have to decide whether to digitise the lot, but for the time being, I've started scanning some of the novels I used for research a while back.      That’s a good idea, especially since I’m working on my next story and could use some of that old material as inspiration. I keep meaning to do the same with some of my published works for reflection, but somehow it never fits into the schedule. Anyway, work-wise I'm mostly plugging away at a new short story—still line edits, but I suppose it could go further if the publisher’s editor can get back to me soon.

Rather chilly this morning, isn't it? I needed me a decent cup of tea to get through it. I got the electric fire on now—keeps things warm enough, though I've been told it's a bit of a £soap killer.      Aye, it's beginning to bite, I'll say that for 'im. I’ve just had a cuppa too—it hit the spot after I got up early to do a spot of ironing. The grandson was in a reasonable state. I don’t mind the early start, but the bloke won’t fetch the tea tray! Probably woke up with the cat on his chest and thought: "Right, I'll spend the morning blinking at the wall." But no—tea’s good, everyone. Just keep in the cups. I’ve got meetings later, but you two wind up the day how you like.      Meetings, you say? Well, listen老爷, I don’t know what your world looks like, but I'd rather iron someone’s cravat than sit through one of them Zoom thingies again. All right, I still don’t know what a cravat is, but don’t start with me.      Cravats are for people who want to look important. I’m not trying to be a prat, George. Just a bit of negotiating over the new contract terms. You know the drill—meetings, negotiations, cups of lukewarm coffee in about five different countries.      Sounds different to this place. I can tell you this—once you've got the cold dishes and no kettle, meetings are quickly forgotten. My day’s planning is baked beans, guest list , and the telly on the side.      Same with me, really. You don’t get much choice when you’re retired. Though I’ve taken to bird-watching recently—only the big one outside the window, mind. Then again, if it's watching me back, that’s my day well spent.      You’re a dream, George. You ought to go further, then. A bit of colouring, gardening—something that’s better than staring at ducks and thinking: “Not much, not much.”      Why not embrace the quiet, Sally? It's rare these days. You work so hard that when you’re done, the only kind of rush you need is to see your tea steaming on the table.

Rather annoying that the recording of  Horace  cut out just as the main character finds the spider in the hedge, don’t you think? I was really invested in that narrative arc by the time the last twenty minutes rolled in. Not to mention we have to review those scenes for the annotations in the new edition. Has anyone else got a mirrored copy?      I’ve got the next-to-last section on paper—a transcription from when we last met in the project booth, but we’d only watched up to the hedge scene. We can pause the group meeting and screen the missing bit, but the studio has some conflict with the prior arrangement ofTomorrow’s  Variation on a Theme  screening. Would you rather do it in the archive room this afternoon?      Yeah, we could rally the team to the back room, assuming they pick up the snacks. I screamed at the screen when the spider nearly died from the hedge trimmer—relieved when it happened. Honestly, I’d throw a dinner party for the production team that saved that bug’s life. Should we pencil in time for that?      A dinner party is a nice touch, I mean if we land a permit from Print House and the catering budget allows. I’ve got a plus-one slot for Liverpool rhythm and blues from the 80s – Mate’s been bugging me to take him somewhere with  real  ambience.      Speaking of which, saving the spider—was that a directorial metaphor, or did they just want to cast an arachnid star? Either way, it made for oddly satisfying viewing. Some folks were saying at the meeting break that the pause in the music at that point  literally stopped us in our tracks , metaphorically speaking.      Oh, definitely a metaphor—coupled with what we found out yesterday in that data comparison. The spider survived not just as a plot device, but as proof that the ecosystem within the film’s narrative can  heal . And if we’re talking dinner parties, any event with scientists and artists is bound to have some wild stories. My postgrad seminar had a  field  day with that film.      Gracious, I do like your take, Speaker 5. But where do we host this? The Print House function goers are on pond life if you don’t get a two-week lead. Is the café below the archive space any good with big groups?

Rather annoying to be honest, I've just dealt with a mountain of tax forms for my account. But first... how was your week? Hope you didn’t run into any problems at work.      Oh, I’m quite alright. Was a busy week at work, truth be told — we had a bit of a backlog of paperwork to sort through, and I had to clean up all the mess after a recent party at one of the houses I work at. But honestly, easier said than done. I couldn’t believe the amount of wine bottles I collected from under the sofa!      You poor thing! It's enough to make  me  throw a party just to justify all the wine consumption. But seriously, what’s going on with your daughter? I heard she got detention last week, is that right?      I wish it were just detention. It turns out she’s been sneaking out to see her friends at weekends — happened twice already this term. And she was lucky not to get expelled — just a week’s worth of after-school detention. I’m at my wits’ end.      Oh, I hear you. Teenagers are as much trouble as grief. My son tried to hide a failed essay on the Tudors by hiding it in the bin. I found it – twice. But at least I didn’t have to visit the school for a meeting. You really take it on the chin. I’ve been trying not to worry about anything too dramatic, but it is a reminder not to sweat the small stuff. How are the treatments going? I tried to arrange some overtime at work to cover the visits, as I can’t afford to lose income right now with lunches, school trips, and all the various extra-curricular costs that just  seem  to pop up.      Look, I know life is suffocating at the moment, but I really appreciate you cleaning my house. And if you ever need someone to run your errands at the bank or planning work for a week, just say the word.

If I could manage that, I wouldn’t be stuck on this draft essay, I’ll tell ye!      Aye, I’d have forgotten I ever had a pen in me hand if I’d been cooped up like this. But I’ll talk to ye ‘bout this job when I’m not on shift. Now go get ‘at essay done, luv!      Thanks, Jo! I’ll try, honest!      Just make sure when ye do ‘ave to work, ye pick a decent employer.

Rather annoying I had to cancel my trip to the Lake District. My sister had her baby, and I couldn’t miss the blessing. Maybe next year I’ll just take a long weekend by myself      Aye, we had a bit o' rain at the weekend. We were gonna visit Halifax eeny friend’s, but we decided against it 'cos o’ the weather. Proper miserable up there.      Ay, that sounds like a top reason to stay home. I just came back from a nice trip to the Aran Islands. Didn’t even want to leave. Tose islands are like a miniature slice of heaven.      What, no chance to do some real wild camping?      Ha! Toldin me breakfasts—bacon and soda bread are still haunting me in the best possible way.      Ah, I see the Real Irish Good Life is still alive and kickin’ then, eh? Nothing exciting happened except me trying to phone home and spotting a seagull with more fashion sense than me in a coastal town near Folkestone.      That sounds oddly British. Tapas and champagne, it all sounds like your kind of holiday.      I’d say enjoy it, but I’m surprised nobody else   from Salford is trying to stop you.      That's the magic of it, innit? Different taste for different folks, I guess.      Aye, long as we all enjoy ourselves, eh? Just don’t ever lose out.

Rather annoying isn't it, how supermarkets are pushing all this scan-as-you-go nonsense these days. The first time I used it, I ended up scanning a loaf of bread three times by accident! Back then, you couldn't even buy seeds in February, let alone expect them to grow in this damp climate. But now with global warming, who knows? It snowed oddly late last week out in the garden!      And what about this driverless car business people are going on about? I heard on the news a while back that the government is testing them on the A38 now. Can you imagine? When I had my first flight, the pilot gave goody bags with sweets and a safety manual that was longer than the flight! Still, I’m glad to see we’ve progressed, even if it means your mother forgets to put the seatbelt sign up on the stairs of the pushchair when we go out!

Rather annoying when the cat’s been scratching the sofa again, isn’t it? I swear, that moggie thinks it’s some sort of scratching post contest.      Oh, don’t start again, love. I mean, the cat’s got an agenda, and let’s be honest, breakfast, bedtime and belly rubs are all requests she makes in her own language, using the odd stare or loudly repositioning herself onto the most coveted cushion.      I tell you what, we’d listen more if I understood two words out of one from her. Although I’d have to say, given the state of our finances, we’d probably all be doing belly-flops off the back deck if it were up to the cat to manage everything.

My nan used to mix cake ingredients by hand — no spoons?      Right cheffy, weren’t ya? So, somethin’ to eat and somethin’ to travel toward? When d’ya reckon we should go out? This thing is plug-in hybrid and it drives like a dream.      A plug-in? What do they do? Plug it in somewhere and it charges?      Yeah, it does. You just plug it into the wall or a stick. It’s clever.      Sounds faffy. I keep thinkin’ I’ve left the kettle oan when I’m out.      Don’t worry — goenvironmental map says it’s rated over 300 miles wi’ just a sniff of fuel. It’s the boxy one y’saw in th’ ad with all the white paint.      Oh, that one! I never had one of them, but me old van used to overheat if we went oan a long string. Served me right for buyin' a Renault.      Listen, let’s get th’ mince sorted. I’m starving, and I wanna hit the road before it’s light out. Movin' outta this place feels nae like home ever since Gran passed. It’s time fer a change.      Aye, that’s the spirit.

Rather annoyingly, I haven't even started sorting out my lecture plan yet this week. I've been so busy with the kids, and now I've got that meeting about student feedback on Monday. How are you getting on with your physics classes?      Honestly, it's gone better than I expected. The students seem quite engaged with the new material on thermodynamics. I think it helps that they're a smaller group this year, which tends to encourage more questions. Still, I'm rushing into it, pulling together videos and handouts last minute like I always do.      You really should start earlier like I do. I block out a whole Sunday morning to plan the upcoming week's lectures. It's like forcing Myself into a bit of routine. I left the house this morning to go to the supermarket and picked up some pickled egg snacks—remember how we had those in Norwich?      Oh, yes! My mum hated them. "Pickled in brine and regret," she always said. But you indulged me. Still, the memories. Speaking of food—after I finish this, maybe we can try out that new Sichuan restaurant your colleague recommended. I've been craving real heat since November.      That's a good idea, but only if we take the kids. I spoke with Lily this morning and she's really keen on learning more about spices and cooking. It might be a bit messy, but what the hell—Chinese spices seem to live up to their name. By the way, did you see the new series they just put out on the streaming service? The one with the detectives in the 1980s—I binged it in a day because it was about as exciting as solving a murder using a typewriter.      No, I haven’t! Add it to the list. I've been stuck watching classic superhero films to fill the hour before the lectures. There's something oddly soothing about watching a man in spandex save the world. It's probably giving my students the wrong impression of academic enthusiasm, though.      Well, we can’t all academically dissect thermodynamic equations with a little dramatic flair. But seriously, schedule a night when you can get serious about your classes. I’ll drag you away from the movie marathon for it if I have to.      Deal. Just no pickled egg snacks during the planning—unleash your academic self on me, but keep the brine out.

Rather annoying this new coffee machine, isn't it? Seems like everything sticks and it's always coughing up bits of debris. Never had such luck as a teacher with my own espresso machine.      Honestly, I should have gone for the manual one instead. Just like the cafes use. Got a bit carried away with the idea of one that makes proper cappuccinos.      I don’t know. If you’re this confused by it, imagine how the kids would fare pulling coffee with a hand pump. You’re the one always talking about simplifying things. Still, looks like we'll have to bear with it.      What’s worse is thinking about the removal cost if it ever breaks. You’ve already got to pay for fitting, and replacing, and now who knows what for taking the whole thing away.      That’s the problem with buying anything nowadays, isn’t it? Everything has hidden charges after the shiny packaging. When’s the last time you thought, “Right, I’ll get a new one for £50,” only to find out you need a specialist to move it for three times that?      And while we’re on the topic of hidden costs—have you seen the state of our services lately? Every national service – healthcare, transport, planning—has shifted towards profit models. It’s like the government is set up for companies to profit and the public to suffer.      It’s all very well someone like you saying that, Gary. You read books and have your opinions, but do you think the Labour Party is going to fix it overnight?      I don’t expect miracles, but I do expect honesty. Right now, everything feels like it’s built around this distorted idealism where what's good for business is suddenly good for society. Doesn’t sound logical to me.      And the new Labour leader—they promise all this, but actions are more important than words. If you ask me, it sounds very similar to what we’ve had for years. We need to trust someone who can actually make things work again.      Well, I’ve had enough of politics in any case. I’m off to make a coffee the old-fashioned way. Mugs on the counter if anyone needs one. And with that, the kettle whistles, the bench moves with a thump, and the conversation gently dissolves into the rhythm of a morning kitchen.

Rather annoying when a condiment is called something different in other places. I was in Birmingham and they said pâté, and I had no idea what they meant. I thought it was like pesto or something.      No, I mean pesto is one of the better-known ones. I saw an Italian restaurant last weekend that claimed they didn’t use any microwaves — like that’s a big claim. What’s next, they’re not going to use knives or forks?      Pfft, no, I get what they’re going for, but still. You can’t just not use a microwave. I mean, I don’t, but the people who work in cafés and restaurants probably have to use them for warming up stuff. Microwaves are just life, right?      Eww, no. I mean, if you’re cooking a nice sauce or something, you don’t stick it in a microwave. You’d be lucky if it’s even edible by the end, you know? I had a microwave burn once. I still can’t look at mine the same way.      I think we’re getting off-topic. We were talking about pâté versus something else…      Oh yeah, I said pâté and it turned out to be something different. I asked the other day, “You mean like the liver stuff,” and he was like, “No, no, no! That’s pâté!” So someone said chicken pâté.      That’s oddly specific. You can just say chicken liver. It’s not like the name is confusing otherwise. I mean, come on!      I know! And then there are these weird pseudonyms for rivers. I was reading about this canal system in East London and it mentioned the Regent’s Canal, but that’s just a river for all intents and purposes.      Yeah, but canals and rivers are a bit different. I mean, I’ve seen them on little boats. My mate Casey has one of those canal boats as a home. He calls it his “floating apartment.” It’s the weirdest thing.      I’d love to live on a boat. I bet it’s got a nice view of the river or whatever it runs into. I just don’t know if I could deal with the rules. I saw some thing about kosher law and canals and all that.      Oh, don’t even get me started on kosher law. I went to this club the other day and they said they wouldn’t serve my sandwich unless it was “kosher-friendly.”

: Right lasses, I’ve been doin’ me Tinder profile ages and still no luck. Honestly, it’s so annoying! It’s like they haven’t even bothered to read your bio, has they? A lot o’ blokes in this area just want a quick date, not a relationship worth talkin’ about.     : Didn’t your profile get buried after a while? I heard you’ve gotta keep updating it to stay on top, otherwise the algorithm just moves you down. I put a new photo on mine the other day an’ got a bit more interest. I’m from Derby, so I dunno how much of a difference that makes here in Chester, but better than nothin’!     : Fair point, Hattie. Me and Loretta moved in together, so we both have the same address. One time, we noticed lads would slide into Loretta’s DMs just ‘cause I’m from Wakefield as well and she’s only ten miles away. Geographical bias much?     : Oh, I swear it's all about proximity. Tinder gives you people in checsies, but if you’ve got a tight set of housemates already, it’s hard to make time for datein’. I been so distracted lyin’ about uni in Sheffield. Honestly, I’d rather just stay home and have a night in with me hotter housemates than meet a random!     : Awe, speakin’ of, how’s about we make our conversation group a date night? Loads of lads in the Midlands are into meetin’ other blokes on campus, why not try attractin’ the lasses too!     : Yeah, Gem, maybe even put in a bit more onlin’ or ‘open-minded’ vibes. Rather annoying this new eligibility criteria for universal credit, isn't it? I was just reading it in the  Eastern Daily Press , and they’re sifting through more and more requirements before they’ll give you a penny. Seems like they expect us to read the rules in our sleep by now!      I'm with you there, George. It was bad enough when we had to prove all that employment history a decade ago, but now they're asking for this and that, like we're hiding bank accounts in Antigua or something! My neighbour was turned down for a month 'cause he couldn't prove he'd paid a utility three months in a row. Absurd!      Honestly, I think it's like that new turkey TV programme I saw last night—it left me more confused than ever, and I watched the whole thing! They used to make programmes that screamed at you with rules, at least you knew what they were on about. Now they just want everyone to feel guilty in silence and wonder if you ever looked wrong at a passerby.      Good one, Nancy! I was watching it myself, and it reminded me of when I was in London with the council as a civil engineer supplying pipework and such. At least in local govern’ment, we dealt in black and white plans. Now it’s all shades of grey and political speeches!      And while the politicians promise the world, did you see the budget announced last week? They’re giving grants to universities, and the rest of us are expected to juggle two jobs and a side hustle just to qualify for a decent meal out.      That’s exactly the sort of thing that makes me think we need a Prime Minister who understands about people who don’t have the energy to do ten e-forms at 2am just to prove they're alive. I’m tired enough after laying out breakfast for the grandkids to do that nonsense!      True. All I know is, if I have to start measuring my sleep time for benefits, I might have to start using them schematics I drew out in the 70s. Though I’m not sure if they’d count dreaming of new bridge construction as "work-related activity."      You’re not wrong. I told the local MP go and live on benefits for a week and see how they manage it.

Rather skip the telly tonight, love. That drama on earlier was promising, but it’s not been on... got the kids arguing over who saw the last bit. I prefer a quiet evening after a long day. You?      That's a shame—we were supposed to catch it together. Got a bit busy at the community event last night, and I haven't had time to record it yet. Normally I'd just swap the programmes, but this one’s got me intrigued. If you watched it, I might just ask one of the kids to replay it later.      Mm, not sure I’ve got enough willpower to rewatch it with them.Been a long day, working on that project at the turkey farm. You know how it is—trying to sort out the compost system was like herding cats, and then I had to sort out a mess with one of the volunteers. Made it back when it was practically gone.      That's hard work. I imagine the mud doesn’t help, even in this time of year. Good job you’ve got that strong back, love, otherwise we’d be in trouble up here! Anyway, your mother called earlier. She and dad are coming for Sunday lunch—if that’s okay. They asked extra nicely this time, probably because she mentioned the new Baptists are coming to town, and dad swears he’s not interested unless there's cake involved.      Should be fine. Last time they came, we had those mince pies someone brought in an airtight container. Perfectly normal, just thought we’d opened an ancient tomb when we took a bite. You can’t be surprised I still dream about that.      I about did fall off the chair when you mentioned the smell the first time. Still, they’re family, and not often you get to see them. I'll just need to run in to the office tomorrow for a few hours. Got that meeting with the new charity. They want to expand to the Midlands, and I was asked to represent us.      You’ll be all day, then? Right. Well, if you’re not here with lunches, I might have to start cooking again instead of going out. Still, I did try this new recipe for the dinner the other night—cod with lemon and rosemary. If it survives one of your meetings, it’s edible, I promise.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh? You know, I do love the mountains around Tarnow when they're got the sun, but with the rain like this it's just a bit grey and gloomy.      Aw, yeah, I know what you mean. I hate it when the sun’s just trapped behind a curtain of grey. I was just on Facebook earlier and saw all these sunlit shots of Cambridge — all golden and blissful — and I got a bit homesick. It was quite a slap in the face, to be honest.      Oh dear, I know what you mean. I haven't been back in ages. I was in the north, near Manchester last winter for my sister’s funeral, and I must say, it left quite a lump in my throat to be back in the cold, grey north of England again.      Gosh, I'm so sorry, I didn’t know. That’s awful... I suppose it’s hard, being back in places that have such deep memories for you. I mean, I like teaching, but I get the strange feeling sometimes that I’d rather be back in Bury — even if it’s still drizzly.      Funny, I always considered Cambridge my home, but now I find it hard to see it as such any more. I mean, I’ve lived in places like Poland and all around Europe for so long now. I still consider the UK ‘home’ in a way, but the old life just feels... distant.      Yeah, I get that. I teach abroad a fair bit, and when I come back to Britain, I still feel like I'm in a different version of home. It's like the social media photos make the place feel different — shiny and unrealistic. I suppose that’s why I ended up becoming a TEFL teacher. The freedom, the nomadic lifestyle... It suits me better than being stuck in a high-rise office in Bury.      I admire that, love. I haven't stepped too far into the professional world again. I did a bit of private teaching of adults once in Brighton, but to be honest, I’m more of a ‘lounger’ these days. I’ve tried online therapy, though — it's helped a little with the melancholy of not feeling settled.      I think therapy's a good idea, especially when moving around your whole life. So, have you made any plans for the future?

Rather annoying the queue bar here, isn't it? Seems like we've been waiting forever for two mugs of tea and a couple of scones.      Yeah, I mean, it is a cash-and-carry spot, but still—  Lottie   gets it much worse at her job. She’s constantly waiting on clients for ridiculous amounts of time. But at least she gets a free latte every now and then for the stress!      Lottie deserves it, honestly. Admin and customer support are the most underrated jobs. Do you want to know what I hate? Pressing three times on a system just to speak to a human. It’s like they can't even be bothered to employ enough people anymore.      Oh, I  hate  the IVR systems too. It’s not even the queueing— it’s knowing there’s someone better waiting  on the other end and you’re likely stuck with some poorly trained intern. I pity the poor sods, though. My part-time gig working on survey software is  boring —but at least I know what I’m doing!      Still, you’re supplying the real stats for someone, aren’t you? I just churn out words in a sea of hashtags. It’s copywriting—isn't it supposed to be inspiring? Sometimes I feel like I'm just selling flat white filters to people who can’t use a toaster.      Haha, fair point. But at least your work gets you out of the chaos of academia for now. I  should  finish my thesis before Christmas, and then… here’s hoping for something more  exciting  than spreadsheets and about five survey questions.      Fingers crossed! Both our paths are  so  different, but I love that we've stayed tight. You remember when we used to come here for Burgers and Banter guest speaker nights? I think the last one was about  metaphors in surf culture —I still haven't got it out of my head.      Oh god,  the Metaphor with Turquoise Hair and the Driftwood Stick . Wasn’t that guy  mentally unwell  or something? That was one go-to event on your life if you ever wanted to feel inferior in your college line of work.       Totally  what your research was leading to at the time. Surveys on how un-understood driftwood can be, right?       Very  meta, very experimental. At least I landed a job. You haven’t been shortlisted for anything yet, have you?

Rather annoying to be woken up by two young people running around like they've got a schedule they need to meet, don’t you know?      We need to be excited, Mummy! There's the Neon Moon event tonight, and we're going to ride like the clowns in a circus!      I'm going to juggle fire like Ully Wally! I saw that on Telly. Do you have a flaming ring, Miss Mummy?      Well, we'll just see about that. Didn’t your father get the tickets for the show? Right, let's get you two sorted. First, breakfast. What would you like?      I want eggs, but you have to say it in Australian. My teacher said Aussies say 'arvo' and I think they say 'Bikkie' for biscuit.      Alright then, I shall say "arvo eggs," and pour us some tea as well, shall I? Now, have you got the colour-changing wand from that party shop? The one you wrapped up for your dad's birthday last week?      Yes! It’s in my pirates' gear bag… You can't miss it, it's all sparkly.      Mummy, can I wear my dragon cape tonight? The one with the neon eyes?      If the dragon can wear sensible shoes and not step on the PlayStation cords. Now, before we race off to the Neon Moon, have you thought about doing a bit of maths?      Not really… but I will if you make it exciting, Miss Mummy.      Oh, very well. How about this: if you can solve five sums and not spill your water, you get a taste of the glowing lollies that the circus people hand out.      I can do that! I’m nearly a mathematician!      Good, good. I rather like the sound of a mathematical dragon. Now, let’s get dressed, and don’t forget your circus boots. They're in the shed, next to the old skip.      Mummy, can Dad go as a jester? His tie's blue and silver.      Yes, if he promises not to juggle the remote control. Now, you two run along and get changed. I'm off to boil some eggs for your arvo feast.      I’m going to be the best rider at the cir-cus! Like a neon knight!      Just make sure you ride safely, my bright knight, and don't forget the colour-changing wand. We’re going to make some magical memories tonight.      I feel like I'm on the edge of a movie.

Rather annoying this new road tax policy, isn't it? I've been trying to get my head around it all weekend and I'm not sure I've fully understood it yet!      I'll say it's baffling alright. Look, when we were our children's age, it was so much simpler. I remember my father used to say 'you just paid it and that was that'. Now? A whole industry built around mitigating the costs! I don’t much like it, mind you.      Honestly, I don’t get the fuss. It's just another tax isn’t it? It's like council tax or income tax. I mean, the government needs the money for something, right? My lectures on economics seem to suggest that it's all part of the system, albeit wildly inefficient.      I think the real issue is how the rules keep changing every few years! You get used to one structure and then they restructure it for no obvious reason. It’s like they’re testing us, to see if we can keep up.      Indeed, and if you're not on top of the changes, you're quite literally paying to be penalised. For instance, my father used to live in Nantyglo, and when he got caught out with an old-style vehicle tax disc he was absolutely furious. It was a long time ago, but he still tells the tale as if it were yesterday.      That's actually kind of funny. My grandad in Aberystwyth had a similar story. He thought he had a week’s notice before the law changed, but the real notice was only 24 hours! He had a good rant about it about forty times.      Oh, my mother-in-law lives near Treffort and she once forgot that she had to notify the DVLC about a change in her address. She got visited by someone from the tax office in the middle of tea. Rather surprising, to say the least.      I wonder if it's regional? I could see the differences in bureaucratic efficiency. Though being from Wales myself, I've always thought our systems are just as good as anywhere else.      I'd say it's the system's fault as much as the individuals. I mean, there are so many forms and procedures to follow, it becomes a game of luck whether you stay on top of your paperwork.

Rather than share a new sentence, I'll request a more significant contribution from you. Please write a response that is ≥400 words long. Otherwise, I cannot proceed. Let's aim for a proper and meaningful discussion. Let me know when you're ready.      Actually, if it's easier, I can go ahead and start the conversation. Just let me know how you'd like to proceed.      Fair enough! I'll continue.      It's interesting you mentioned the Linton Book Festival, Sarah. I was thinking about it the other day. You remember those little handmade miniature books we used to make? I still keep one at home, actually!      My turkey! Ooh, did you make the one with the flamingo cover? I still have that!      That's the one! It must be about 20 years old. I can't believe I've held onto it all this time. It was during the Helen Moss awards we used to do back when the kids were small. I remember we had to write one of her stories and perform it in class—Sarah got stuck in the cow scene as the farmer's wife. Hilarious!      Was I in that one?      Oh yes – you were the farmer’s dog, and you barked  throughout  the entire story. It was brilliant.      I still can’t read the original story properly without laughing. You always said the dog was the real star of the show.      I  should  know—there are a fair few stories and mouths to feed at our house! Look, are you thinking of bringing about five copies to the festival this year? I know the stall is chaotic, but they said they need more interactive projects for the under-tens.      Maybe we could do something like ‘Animal Tales’ like the ones we did at home. Parents can read while the kids become the animals. You know, it would get them involved and make them little performance stars!      That sounds amazing. With a bit of ribbons and headbands, it could be the hit of the festival. The kids  love  getting into characters. I’ll get the parents go along with it too—let’s start planning.      Can I be the bear again?      You’ll be the biggest bear at the festival, I promise! Alright, how about we meet next week and start sketching some stories together? I’ve got some old Helen Moss stuff I can digitise and use as inspiration.

Rather annoyingly, I haven't been able to get hold of decent cruelty-free vitamins in the usual chemist... got to go elsewhere or maybe check online.      Yeah, sometimes that's where it gets tricky with certain things. Look, I bet you can get them through a few vegan companies on Etsy or Amazon, I used to use one and it worked out well.      Online might be your only bet if you're too far from a conventional shop. I started ordering some stuff like that a while ago.      Do you want to test out vegan meat too? I brought some of that synthetic stuff—called "shmeat"—back from the shop. It's like that Mycoprotein one, but new.      Oh, I'd like to try it, but I’ve been thinking the other day—Don't you think the idea of synthetic meat is, um… kind of clever in some ways? I mean, at least it means no animals are hurt, you know?      Yeah, I mean—there's still controversy, but for some people, especially vegetarians or people with strong feelings about animal cruelty, it could be a gift.      Exactly. But it’s such a sensitive topic. I remember my nan once talking about the difference between hunting and abattoirs—it used to drive her nuts because of the idea of "natural" slaughter.      She made sense in a way, someone said in one of those Curb Your Enthusiasm episodes once—don’t do things out of principle if you’re not consistent with your ethics. Still, it’s all complicated.      I mean, I get where the controversy is from—but the fact is, the meat industry as it exists is not good for the planet. I've read it contributes a lot to environmental issues. My sister once tried cutting out processing stuff completely for a month and said it was easier than expected.      Do you think we could start something like that here? I could stick to one synthetic meat night a week as a trial. Then we’d be contributing a little to lowering the impact.      That would be amazing. Plus, it's good to set an example. I remember someone I used to work with was into that—no red meat, no dairy, but still tried to keep the diet varied.      That sounds like it requires a bit of attention, but it can be really rewarding. You might find your recipes improve too.

Rather annoying this new washing machine, isn't it? Seems like everything sticks to it—the buttons, the p... What was I saying? Oh, the buttons, the switches! You'd think after all this time they'd make it a bit more simple, like the old one.      Aye, I know exactly what you mean. I 'ad to phone the bloke in town not too long ago. A right nutter he was, too—talking 'bout cycles and load sizes, like it was a physics lesson or sommat. Still, it does the job, I s'pose. Get the laundry decent enough.      Honestly, the only reason I can manage mine is because my Mycroft keeps an eye on it. He left it on spin last night, and I came home to a puddle and sad clothes. Honestly, I swear he enjoys making my life difficult sometimes. Wait, does anyone actually know how to read a manual these days?      Good grief, no, not if you can get a machine to do it for you—vast majority do, don’t they? Anyways, I don’t think your Mycroft’s the only grief. For instance, my sister’s in a right state 'cos she’s been chucking out clothes she loves at the very thought of sorting through them, and now she wants to go clothes shopping. Again.      Oh, here we're go again! When I 'ad a younger sister, she'd do the same. Go through a pile of stuff, throw half out, and then buy all the same ones at half price in the charity shop. Typical.      Oh, come on, I mean, I get it. I did the same the other day. Gave away a top that was barely worn because I thought it barely fitted me any more. Then went online to buy something, ‘cos I was feeling rather less motivated after that purging.      Oh, I was just saying to Terry last week that we need to tidy up the garage again. There's stuff in that place as old as our grandkid. 'Cept the grandkid’s younger than the washing machine.      You're like a man with a pickaxe in a china shop, if you ask me.      Wait, do I wanna know what happens when you two start arguing about your garage?      Oh, we never argue, we just go quiet and then send someone else in to fight for us. Last time ‘Terry asked the boys to do it while I was out...

Rather annoying isn't it, these butterfly forks? I remember when we had a proper fork with tines like everyone else. I don't know why dining has to be so complicated these days.      I don’t really get it either, like, what even is a butterfly fork for? Is it for fish? Or is it like a knife you can open and close?      No, you’ve got it wrong. I think it's just a funny-looking thing that makes you feel fancy, like it’s from some old fancy dinner service and now everyone’s copying it but nobody knows what to do with it.      Precisely! All we need is a normal fork and a knife. But Myra, you seem to have an ear for these kinds of things – how do you know what the butterfly fork is used for?      Well, it was a bit of a big breakfast, and we actually watched this documentary about historic dining customs in Russia. They showed different silverware and how they ate in royal courts. Butterfly forks weren’t excluded, but they were more for spreading things, maybe for buttering toast or salad greens.      Buttering toast with a butterfly fork? That sounds like it’d be disastrous! You'd slash the toast all up.      Exactly! And I’m not sure I take comfort in thinking that Russia had a history of dining oddities. Russia and their tea ceremonies, their big parties, their strange forks...      Well, speaking of Russia, I read somewhere that a lot of European customs were influenced by what they did, at some point or another. Maybe being fancy at dinner started there?      Kind of about time we stopped worrying about the forks, the silence starts in two minutes. I wonder if we should observe it inside or outside.      The garden, for sure. It’s a bit overcast, but quiet enough. Though I don’t see how just standing around in the garden is going to make all that much of a difference, you know.      It’s more about remembering than being loud or anything. It gives people a moment to think about things. Not just the war in Ukraine – but everything.      Yeah, I reckon. It’s one of those things you don’t get properly appreciated until you’re an adult, I think.      Time to lay the plates out. Cheeseboard at 19:00, champagne at 19:15. Just like your birthday to be on the same day as the silence, but I think the champagne will override the solemnity.

Rather than going up north this year, do you think we could do something closer to home, like a family staycation in Cornwall? I've been reading about the new Adventure Island visitor centre, and it sounds a bit more interactive than the usual beach days.      Oh, Cornwall sounds lovely! We always go to the north of the country with the grandparents. But if it's not too far from Dartford, that would be amazing. Do you have a specific place in mind?      There's a place just outside of St Ives that has a few caravan parks and some rented cottages. I like the idea of being near the coast so we can walk short distances easily, especially with the kids and everyone’s food sensitivities. I’ve already sketched out a week-long plan involving short beach trips, exploring St Ives, and I think the kids might enjoy the V&A museum at the weekend.      Can we go to Adventure Island, though? The book series my teacher read to us in school talked about building sandcastles the size of towers and finding real-life treasures. I want to see if it's like in the books!      Of course! We’ll visit Adventure Island for a couple of days and maybe even build a sandcastle together, like the one in the book – just don’t expect it to last longer than the tide, okay?      It won’t? Why not?      Nature has a way of bringing those kind of things back into the sea. But if you're quick, you can always build another! It’s all part of the fun.      I’m just curious – where are your colleague and I in all of this planning? I know you’re used to marking exams and planning, but have you thought about what you and I need to be doing to make the week run smoothly?      Honestly, I realized I need you for that. I can sort out the accommodation and maybe even a scenic day trip for us two as well. Perhaps I’ll look for a little boat tour or a quiet café with a view. You being involved with the booking will make lunches and bedtime routines much easier to handle.      That sounds perfect. Then we can truly make the most of it as a family without stressing over if something breaks or if one of the kids has an allergy flare-up again.

: You lot in Wembley must’ve got easier teachers. My history teacher just gave us  another  20-page essay on the Industrial Revolution. I don’t even know what specific angle he wants us to approach it from now.     : Lmao, it’s not that bad here. Yeah, history’s a pain, but at least he gives examples of how to structure it. You should come round, I can walk you through my essay on Boudicca. It might not be super relevant, but the structure’s the same. Didn’t your class get the coursework guide yet?     : Not really helpful. I skimmed the thing, and it was just like, "Show understanding!" as if that means anything to someone who’s allergic to wool, ink, and their own thoughts, let alone historical interpretation.     : Fair enough. I still remember when I tried to write an essay while sneezing for hours — ended up looking like some oversized raccoon, dabbing tissues everywhere. Worst essay I’ve ever written too. You need to do something about those allergies, man.     : Yeah, I might mention it to the school nurse today. She was on about medication last week. Honestly, I just got distracted by the new movie about dinosaurs — you saw it, right? It was  insane  the amount of set pieces they did.     : Oh yeah, I loved the creature effects. Our group of friends are gonna dress up as dinosaurs for the Halloween party this Friday. You should definitely come — you’ll get to pretend to roar and not get told off. Not like in school, where even breathing too loudly in about five minutes results in a prefect giving you the talking to.     : True. Speaking of, that new prefect barely left me alone yesterday after sending a meme to the class group. She thought it was funny, but I passed it off as 'suspicious behavior'. I'm still waiting to see if it gets reported or not.     : She sounds as overzealous as the prefects here. One of them tried to give me a detention for wearing the wrong tint of jeans. I had to show them the uniform policy four times before they gave up. But yeah, you've got to go to that Halloween party. I’ll even lend you a tie-dyed bandana if you promise to cause some mischief.     : Sold. I’ll bring those essays, maybe even finish half of one before we go.

Rather annoying this new road layout eh? You can’t even get past the roundabout in Chester-le-Street without feelin' like you’re in a bloody obstacle course. I swear, someone needs to give the planners a crash course in proper logic.      Haha, it’s a real eeny-meeny-miny-mo if you ask me. I passed it on the way in and nearly missed the junction by five seconds. Proper adrenaline stuff. Still, easier than driving into central London, ain't it?      Oh don’t even get me started on central London. I like to think of it as nature’s version of a dodgem car—everyone's tryin’ to go in the same direction, but only seven vehicles are allowed on the road at once. Speaking of dodging, d’you catch the cricket match the other night? It was a proper rollickin’ game.      Mate, cricket? I only watched the highlights, thanks to work! That team of yours showed some guts out there. Good to see Sam Curran actually standin’ up and being counted this time—bit of a flair with the ball. But let's be serious, can we still say it was a proper test if it rains half the time and ends in a draw?      I know, I know, but there’s something about a tight chase in the last over. You don't get that in one-dayers every week. Anyway, enough of cricket. Let’s talk bikes—what's new with yours? Still workin’ on that old Triumph you had?      Hey, she’s a classic! I’ve been giving her a bit of love—changed the carburetor and polished the tank. Might take her for a run this weekend if the weather holds. Proper scenic route up the A1. You up for it?      I might need a sit down after that, but yeah, I could do a day trip. Just don’t expect me to weave around bikes like a pro—I’ll be stickin' to the inside of the lane. No chance of me doin' a wheelie or anything.      Fair play, I won’t make you! Still, a day goin' on two wheels, a bit of countryside, and maybe even a pint in a pub that actually serves real ale—sounds better than arguing with your average roundabout.      You and your pubs. I'm startin' to think you've been to more of them than the Ministry of Defence.

Okay, I just called the Chinese takeaway on High Street, but they said they can't take orders before 6 p.m. What do you want to do? Maybe we can order something else now and wait for this one later?      Ugh, that’s annoying. I was really looking forward to the sweet and sour chicken. Do they take online orders at least? Maybe we can place it a bit earlier through their website? I know that helps sometimes.      Let me check their Facebook. Sometimes they post opening times or order windows. Here it says: "Evening orders only accepted from 6 p.m." So, dead line. Should we just order from Gold Dragon instead? They always deliver what you expect. I had melon and brie last time and it was decent—even for Chinese food.      Gold Dragon’s fine, but it’s a bit pricier. I was trying to save money since everyone has a spare in their budget this week. Do you remember that little new takeaway on Cowgate Road? They were offering 20% off for first timers, and the reviews on TripAdvisor were really good.      Cowgate Dragon? Hmmm... I might’ve read something about it disappearing because of licensing issues. Let me check. No, actually it’s been rebranded, and now it's called Blue Phoenix. Let me call them.      You know what, let’s just grab our orders from the two places at different times. I can get the pho from Gold Dragon now, and we can order the chicken and lobster from High Street later. Split order and double the fun!      Ooh, lobsters with medley of vegetables—that sounds good. Do we all agree on splitting the order? I can help write down the pickups and times. I’m better at organisation anyway, being a bid writer, you know.      As long as you don't have me writing a bid for a takeaway package, I'm in. Let me just pop out and grab some egg rolls from Gold Dragon. I’ll meet you back here with snacks and gossip to keep you entertained while we wait for the other meats.      Smart idea. I’ll get the sauces ready so everything can be enjoyed fresh. This does sound like a better plan than just relying on one takeaway. Never assume they’re open until the minutes tick your way.      Honestly, I think we’ve turned takeaway ordering into an actual project team effort.

Rather annoying the new folk next door, innit? Seems they’ve got a budgie squawkin’ all hours and a toddler who’s never seen a nap. I’ve asked their landlord if he might knock on their door… politely, of course… but he looks at me like I’m mad.  "That’s not the sort of thing we do,"  he says. Ridiculous.      Aye, I hear you. Got one too—new place, new mess. It was bad enough with the clatter of cutlery at 2 a.m. from the flat above. You'd think the NHS would run some kind of campaign on landlord responsibility, given the state of mental health with stressed tenants like that. I work in the ER, you know. The week you haven't heard the shouting, you're on the picket lines in A&E by midnight.      Right you are. I see it in academia too, though. Less shouting and more silence at the wrong times. Entire corridors that used to buzz with intellectual debate—and now it’s just echoing off quad bikes and overpriced kebabs sold in the staff room. I’m a lecturer, as it happens. English and Literature, based out of Liverpool John Moores. Overqualified for this postcode, but got a good deal on the house. Bring any of my students here, they’d star in a film about urban decay set in the 90s.      You don’t say. I mean, Liverpool’s got its charm, but housing crisis? That’s real. It just feels like folks are squeezed out hotter each year. I did a stretch in Finland with Erasmus—university education over there is free, and people about half as stressed. I sometimes wonder if the English lit students had time to read  Pride and Prejudice  without being late for their next housing interview.      My, you've thought about it. To be fair, I did my B.A. in Germany. Literature there is something you write  about  rather than write. Studying Kafka or Goethe while my flatmate was holed up doing a PhD in functional materials. Boring and brilliant in equal measure.      Still, I bet it’s better than my place—shift work goin’ on seven days a week. If I don’t see sunlight until six in the evening, I dream in blood trolleys. Family says I’m losing my touch at the piano. Touch, innit? Must be some steel in your blood to choose this life.

Rather annoying this new welfare cap they've introduced, eh, Bill? I was just reading about it in  The Guardian  and it doesn't bode well for people already scraping by on the breadline.      Aye, seems like the kind of thing our MPs like to hide behind jargon and then blame the  bobbies  for when it goes wrong. I reckon it all stems from laziness—no will to actually  teach  these kids a trade. Not like thirty years ago, when you learned a skill and had sommat to fall back on.      You’re probably not far off. Still, I do notice a difference with the younger people I teach these days. They’ve got the education, but not always the  push . I find myself constantly persuading them to look beyond the A-level Qualification bubble. A world beyond the classroom, if you will.      Aye, I've noticed that with the lads around here. I hear the  bobbies  out on the beat now—and I mean, I'm glad they're out—but it's often not for crimes, it's for immigration crackdowns. Like a week ago, I saw a van pull up near my gate, and three men grabbed a lad who looked about seventeen. You ever see anything like that down at your place, Mark?      Occasionally. Though I try not to comment to my students for obvious reasons. Still, it's worrying when our universities, which should be spaces of  enlightenment , are being pressured to exclude international students just to hit targets. You’d think the ones who ran these places cared about  education  over ideology.      Haha, I about blocked you there— enlightenment ! Sounds like something out of a dusty old history book. No wonder you’re better off barely speaking to your sister-in-law these days—she claimed her ‘ coding ’ job was her expressing herself better than any poem.      [laughing] I once joked I tried to write a poem about a spoon and lost my good side over that. Let’s just say, trying to find common ground with someone who plays  Fortnite  14 hours a day for a living is like talking to a wall made of Wi-Fi signals.      Roars. But in all seriousness, I’m just wondering… with the rate things are going, what your lot of lecturers are planting seeds in the heads of those students, it’d better be good ones. Because I don’t fancy a future made of rust and overcooked sausages and them lads I tell you I see all over the place, acting like the  university  is their Grandmother who gave them everything.

Rather annoying the queue at the canteen today, innit? Took me ten minutes just t' get a bacon sarnie an' a tea.      I feel you, I was just about t' give up an' grab a sandwich from the deli across the road. Got eeny weeny appetite left after that. Not 'cos I didn’t work up an appetite, mind. I’ve transcription notes piled up to the ceiling this week.      Honestly, dump the queue. We can just pop down the street later. Looks like it's gonna be a long lunch anyway. I’ve got some . . .  dramatic pause  . . . rather exciting news from the linguistics department. They seem to be revising the criteria for dialect markers in their latest corpus. You're all gonna be very sad to know the little local sayings everyone uses aren’t actually ‘influencing’ the data as much as they’d like to think.       laughs  Oh, that’s always the story isn't it? You collect all this data and it doesn’t tell the story you hoped for. I mean, we did a similar thing with learner English last quarter, and half the results looked like they were grabbed by chance. Have you all got dialect zones coded yet –?      Yeah, actually, just about to finish. Though I have to say, working out what gets logged for a Northern or Yorkshire accent is a nightmare. Like, what's the difference between ‘p’t’ing’ and ‘p’t’ not-ing’? I’m outta my depth half the time.      That’s where  you  are out of your depth, doll. I know a lad from Barnsley who speaks like this [mimics Northern accent], and he’ll be telling you ‘innit’ is a  full sentence .      Po-faced he was. All passed out after a kebab at 6pm. Doesn't do ‘innit’ very well stone dead, though.      Ugh, that lad again. Always getting into some trouble.      Okay, but seriously, back to you, Speaker_5. Are you working on the corpus as go-to or on sub-volumes? I mean, you're in publishing, so it’s interesting that you're working on a big publishing press’s linguistic tools.      I am, but it’s more about formatting and cleaning up the data than linguistics per se. Just made sure that every transcript is in the right section and everything's tagged. Slightly mind-numbing to be honest.      That's the magic, though, innit?

Rather annoying when the barista at John Lewis swears in Norwegian. I was just trying to order a flat white, and she said she wasn’t  farte  about it. I had to double-check with her that it was £2.80 and not some kind of Scandinavian satire on coffee pricing. Got a bit confused there, honestly.      Oh, that's easy.  Farte  is like a mild swear word in Norwegian—somewhat equivalent to ‘bloody’ in British English. I’ve heard her say it a few times when the espresso machine misbehaves. She’s not a native speaker herself, even! Spoke to her last week—turns out she trained in Vienna and now she jokes that she's "half melanger, half melange." Ten out of ten for coffee puns. But I digress. Do you still take soy milk in your flat white?      Yes, I do. Anglophile vegetarians apparently need their dairy substitutes. I remember once, back in Bath, a local took great exception to my substitution and said I was "compromising the integrity of the drink." I calmly replied that cow’s milk compromises the integrity of the atmosphere, and that ended the debate… plus, I got extra sugar in it from the barista. Small victories.      Ha, that's a good one. You and your PhD must be clashing quite a bit with British sensibilities. You ever bring your postgrad students out for this kind of thing?      Oh, absolutely. One came here a week ago and had the most adorable panic attack over the term  flat white . Said she had to Google it because it didn’t exist in her university cafeteria back in Hull. Interesting thing, language. You grow up with a phrase, and then you are suddenly explaining it like it's a dialectal species of whale to someone 200 miles up the road.      A bit like me trying to explain  Damage  was my first love song. My students are all into Arlo Parks these days, and I had to do this awkward walk-through of "well, back in the early 2000s, no one knew what a 'tinden' was either." They stared at me like I had time-voyaged or something.      I think they’re wondering if we were all just infatuated with one-eyed virtual men. It’s a cultural abyss, really.      On that note—should we go to that new talk on language and identity this Friday? I heard the keynote speaker is a Sámi linguist.

Rather annoying this newfit in the boiler innit? Seems like everything sticks on an’ it’s makin’ a right racket!      Blimey, I've heard about that! Got to be the £2000 one wi’ wi-fi, eh? Seems a bit flashy een? I thought Newtons used to be good 'ere.      Nonsense. A few A listing certifications and some gimmicks from a laddie in a suit, an’ suddenly you're a modern household. Back mey day, me 'n Alice 'ad a ’ose holdin' three kids on six quid a week. Now, we’ve got a boiler that blinks anditunes apps My turkey on Christmas. Ridiculous!      I ain’t the one complainin’ abou’ boilers, love! But if you lot was about t’bother me breakfast, I’d be 'appy! Brian here thinks I only like toast! I said five o’clock, Ken, not five minutes past!      Alice, I told thee, I didn’t say nothin’ about toast! You’re the one with the high and mighty hob, remember?      Right, right, both o’ you lot. Let’s just calm down. We’re not in Hull, it’s Malton today. Let’s try an’ enjoy ourselves.      Oi, don’t talk to me! I 'ave someone at school called Alice too. Alice Manning. Hair like a sheep’s bottom. Funny thing—looked like this fluffy cloud in the wind and still got detention for leavin’ jelly in the library!      That’s the spirit, love! She’s got taste an’ th’spark o’ mischief. Just like yi’Grans.      Oi, nonsense. Burgundy hair like yours was mischief enough. I was cuttin’ turf in the allotment while you was ‘avin’ bets with the witches at Queen’s Gardens!      Witches? You mean the lady in the yellow with 'Erneys on the nose? Perle? Wasn’t that you once, love?      Oh please go on then, recount it if you like. But for God’s sake, just leave the hob alone between now an’ boxin’ day. I can’t be facin’ both o’ you and a kettlin’ kettle!      It’s alright for you talkin’. You lot never had to walk to school! It rained so much my shoes looked like ducks!      Right, right, always somethin’, innit? First the power’s out, now she’s talkin’ abou’ ducks. Movin’ on—Ken, you're on teapot night, remember.      And you ken’ goat milk, Brian. The new one’s herbal.      Herbal, certainly. That stuff’s bitterer than a Liam Neeson film.

Rather lovely to sit out here on this evening, ay? The garden looks nice after the rain. The peas and chips still warm, mind you. I’m more than happy to take a second helping if you’re alright with it. Not often I get the chance to cook such a treat now that I’ve retired.      I don’t mind one bit. I reckon it’s about time we all chilled a bit. A lot’s been going on since this morning, honestly. Oh, and Grandmother is pulling her hat strings together to come and visit us for the weekend. Apparently, she wants to see how we’ve been doing without her around! Not that I complain, mind you. I do miss her company.      That’s grand! I’m curious to know what specific arrangements she has made. I mean, with the recent array of football games she screamed about—especially FIFA, by the way—she'll need somewhere to sit and watch this weekend. Not that I mind providing a spot, but the TV in the living room might not cut the mustard with the rest of the gang that often.      Oh, I’m sure she’ll settle in with a good seat to watch the games. For heavens’ sake, she probably even brought her FIFA stickers. She’s always been proud of her collection. But speaking of football, I heard last night's match ended in a huge upset. I reckon the pundits thought that team would lose their first game, but no—FIFA might as well have written in chalk someone else altogether.      Precisely! That's oddly satisfying. Now, shifting gears—there's a matter I need to be asking you two: I had to transcribe a heap of statements about oil company developments. Seems the entire story of blame and culpability is back in the news. Some old fails from the oil industry are coming up again. The regulator issued a report that names and shames for their poor development planning. Honestly, I'm starting to feel like I'm decoding a thriller script.      That’s no surprise. I had a bit of a crack at such planning in my time as well. The game’s changed a lot, and it's probably time someone took the bull by the horns and held the companies truly accountable. I sometimes think the technical goings-on were as confusing as FIFA's transfer market.

Rather annoying when the laptop won't shut down properly, isn't it? Mine just cranked itself off like it got scared of the dark or something while I was trying to finish a few emails      Yeah, that can drive you nuts. Is it overheating or something? Mine was doing that during the heatwave, and I had to leave it open on the desk just so it could breathe a bit      If I had a laptop, it'd probably be broken into a thousand pieces by now. Too many buttons and too few instructions. Didn’t even want to touch it at my granddaughter’s place, honestly      Classic! Some of the older models are easier to use, like that BlackBerry you still keep talking about, Grandma. I heard they tried to bring it back – would you use it again?      You know what, darling? I might. The last one, the old-fashioned one with the keypad, was much easier than all this touchscreen nonsense. Just press a button, not swipe this way and that. Good for texting your gran like you should do more often      Yeah I mean if we’re on the topic of high-tech things, setting that up sounds like its own kind of engineering. But I’m curious – what about the tap water – do you prefer bottled or filtered, like, because I swear mine tastes like the tap is saying goodbye      Honestly, I just boil mine and leave it in a jug for a bit. Takes the nastiness out. And God knows what the water companies are doing around here – with the bin strikes and everything else, I’m amazed they haven’t run out of chemicals      I about blocked the kettle after a bad coffee spill the other week. Another mishap and I might be handing this flat over to the manager with barely a week's notice      My, my! You need to calm that kettle down before it takes over. And have you been out walking round Brighton? I hear it's very flat but there are some little pockets with nice views      We did walk a bit yesterday – the seafront was lovely but the heat was insane. We almost passed out near the park where they had that festival setup the other month      If I had the energy, I'd go out more. But after work, between the train ride home and the dinner chore, your legs forget you even have feet sometimes

Rather annoying that the barista was rather slow with the coffee. Still, it's a beautiful place, don't you think? I often miss the hustle and bustle back home in Cambridge, but this has a lovely, quaint charm. Have you checked the football results?      Actually, I haven't—football never really interested me that much. But I did see on social media that Liverpool won their last match. A shame I can't get invested these days. The whole idea of watching Premier League while abroad just reminds me of how far I’ve come from home. Do you get the SAD feeling too?      Oh, brutally. I always get it when the sun sets before six. It's like that old turkey on Christmas dinner—just sits in the stomach, you know? I had a student the other day, a very sad young man. He came to me in a state, really. He hadn’t prepared enough for his IELTS. Reminded me of my early days, being unprepared for what lies ahead in life. Have you ever worked on a farm?      Funny you mention that—yes, I did one summer in Cumbria as part of my studies. It was awful, honestly. I much prefer working with teenagers. Still, it gave me a good reason to avoid doing estate agency work. I love working with my students, but the pressure of preparing them for exams is exhausting.      I understand completely. When I teach, which is very part-time these days, I always remember the importance of knowing what's coming next. I had a friend email me about the weather—she says I should bring an umbrella next time I come up to Manchester. Honestly, most people about as prepared as a bird trying to bumble through the rain without one.      At least you know that Bury barely sees the sun anyway. Still, I'd rather be here in Tarnow with good coffee than back home mucking cows. I have been reading a lot lately too. It's my escape, I suppose. I miss shopping too, honestly—who knew you could miss supermarket shopping?      Yes, but I keep meaning to message my younger cousins—maybe next weekend. Still, I did run into an old classmate the other day. We had a lovely chat about dogs. He has a beautiful Springer Spaniel. I always wished I had a dog of my own.      That’s the life.

Rather annoying the new event planning software, innit? Seems like everything wants to be digital these days. We had to shift our whole team onto it this week, and I’ve had more emails than usual about people getting lost in the system.
