Me and the lads just use spreadsheets and a mates’ WhatsApp group to sort stuff out.      Honestly, I like to think of it as  efficient  rather than  fancy . I only started working in production control a few months ago, and I’m still getting used to the specific systems they use. It’s not as bad as Speaker_1’s, but there’s quite a learning curve.      Aye, it’s just a bit of a pain in the backside, you know? I thought I’d be looking forward to the new year, but I’ve had to cancel one date already because of work. I’m starting to worry I’m going to turn into a hermit who only knows how to use modules and spreadsheets.      Be fair, you’re not the only one. I’ve had to cancel dates, too, what with the night shifts and tight deadlines. But to be honest, I’d rather work hard and date properly when I can, than fake interest just because I’m low on dates.      That’s oddly mature of you, Speek 3. For a while I thought being single was just because no one fancied me, but maybe I’ve just been daft about the whole thing. Haven’t had a proper date in… I don’t even know how long.      You should come out more! I mean,  you  baked the cake, didn’t you? So you’ve got to have  some  talent for something besides manual work.      You mad? That was just my grandad’s recipe. I just threw it in the oven.      That’s the difference between class and effort, then. Some people are just born with the skills, go to university, get well-paid jobs and  still  manage to flirt better than the rest of us.      Oh, stop your moaning! You all have things you’re good at. You, Speek 2, are great with your hands. And I expect you can charm a few people with the food, innit?

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? That lime tree near the fountain was in full bloom when I first came in. I always take a detour through here after my thesis session at the library. The birds are singing rather sweetly too.      It truly is. And it was only yesterday I saw a boy catch a pigeon while feeding the ducks by the bandstand. Almost as if they were a character from Aesop. By the way, I heard from Tim; he’s started teaching English in Tibet. Sounds a world away from Yorkshire, doesn’t it?      Yes, reminds me of when I lived in rural Devon—those winding roads, the peace, and only the occasional trinket stall at the market. I wonder how his students are responding to him. Probably, they're obsessed with mobiles and WECHAT.      Haha, oh definitely. Cats are better than breakfast, and pigeons better than tea. Reminds me—before I forget, have you considered taking that trip to the Isle of Wight? They say driving there is nothing like driving through the Thames Valley.      I might take you up on that. But let's not forget about our old friend, the death penalty—it always comes up in conversations about China. I find it intriguing how sensitive that topic is with some students, and how it really divides opinion in classrooms.      You're quite the expert on navigating cultural nuance in the education sector. Speaking of which, what did your consultant in London suggest about making the landscape of a typical class more inclusive for Chinese guests—especially when it comes to discussing controversial subjects?      A good supervisor insists on context and sensitivity. I was told that asking about a Chinese friend's birthday without the lunar calendar is an oversight. To be fair, even the coffee culture is different—more coconut cake, less salt in the crust.      That’s quite observational of you. On a tangent, have you been keeping up with West Ham United? I watched a match yesterday, and oh, it was a wild game!      Rather busy with the panda documentary I’m watching on Netflix, to be honest. Was going to visit Paris this summer for a teaching conference. I wonder how the tourists go about it with all their chuggers and elaborate parks.      Imagine that, between Tibet and the Seine—what a change your research will bring. I have to get going to meet my colleague, we're going for coffee, maybe even take in a concert nearby.

Rather annoying this, innit? Traffic’s mental again, even at this time. Should’ve walked, like I always say. But nooo, you lot always argue I’d murder me feet      Aye, we wouldn’t have got here faster if you’d walked, would we? Got een quarter to be there and we’re still ten minutes out. Ay, just tryna enjoy the drive a bit. A lot worse this would be in a train or bus.      Fair 'nuff. Just feels like me feet and shoes could run it faster than this glorified car choked with fookin’ lorries.      What I tell you, eh? You like that My boot still smells after that chemical experiment I left on the shelf last month, ain’t I? D’you think I’d risk sitting in that? Nah, nah, far sooner wait ‘nש breakfast, no doubt.      Ick, don’t remind me. I remember that felling -- chemical’s dead but the stank ain’t. It like crept into me jumpsuit for a day. Y’changing it in the lande as usual?      Ay, gear room’s free. They asked me if I was from the utility crew. Looking for a duck gee with a toolbox, like, because they thought I was a maintenance man.      Lmao. Dinna blame ‘em! Y’lookin’ like a someone who fixes elevators or something. All my uncles work in building management, I know what you mean.      Hey, look at it this way: We get a free pass past security about half the time. Just play along, man.      Shrugs. Maybe this failsafe is better than trying to convince me it is a ‘smart choice to do something, ‘cos I just like arguing.      Aye, me too. I’d told you ‘get me sjipboard yesterday, you just had to argue. We lost two good hours over that.      Because 'splitboard' wears out! They're not indestructible, you know. You run ‘em like a man with a grudge every time on them slab-and-snow runs, so of course they’re going in the bin.      Time to lay off your hobby preaching, innit. I can look after me own tools, thank you.      It's not preaching, it’s conse ‘nש advice. C'mon, you know what the team reckons I'm for if they ever do an opinion poll.      Right backs out of the car. Let’s roll, then. We’re here and before me slippers melt in this weather, I’d better get my jacket on, for goodness’ sakes.

Rather annoying I caught flu last week. You know, me being a conference co-ordinator, it kills me when I’m off sick mid-event. I’m more used to stress than lying in bed, eh?      Aw, don’t I know it! I wouldn’t say I’ve been ill een, but my back’s been playing up sorely from all the moving I’ve been doing. Labourer life’s tough on your bones, yeah? Proper ache, even after a stretch.      Oh, I’ve been stuck with a cold. Didn’t even want to leave the sofa some days. Not to mention, my brother’s been driving me mad with his new girlfriend, bless him. Constant updates like I’m a bloody therapist now.      Oh, boys and their new relationships, eh Darcy? Always dragging you in. I had a bloke in my flat the other week who honestly looked at me like I was a tour guide for Huddersfield. Blooming tourist!      Ha bloody ha. I mean, why would you expect that? I went with me mate up North once and ended up asking him how to get out of a bus without falling into the canal, for God’s sake. It was like the Northern Question game.      Oh come on Mateo, at least you didn’t try to cook parsnips while the gas wasn’t working! I nearly flooded the whole kitchen. Still, Rhys, at least you’re back now. Proper someone to chat to who doesn’t just say “Av aye, love.”      Speak for yourself, Lisa. I can talk being posh at times, but when I’m tired, it nearly about comes out like I’m trying to win the English lit prize or something. Honestly, I’ve lost my lilt entirely when I’m barely awake.      Nah man, you’re ‘ardly bloomin’ posh. I mean, you were born in Doncaster, right? That was bloody nice pottery once, I hear. I bet your mad nan could stick it to mine in terms of swearing as well.      Oh mate, speaking of mads—my nan still thinks ghastly is something you serve in a pie. She called my goth roommate “ghastly” like it was a brand of custard.      Honestly, I’ve got plans to visit my cousin in Brighton at the end of the month. If any of you want to come, you’re all invited. Unless, of course, you’re still curing ‘flu or walking up walls to avoid a headache.

: "Liz, can you pass the tea, love? I need a bit of time to process today... It was  honestly  the most chaotic project meeting I’ve ever been in. Didn’t your director get the memo about not yelling at each other in corporate spaces?  God , I get enough shouting at work, only it’s on the other end of a calm voice saying, 'I know you’re overwhelmed, let’s talk this through.' Our new intern, Jack—lovely lad, but ever so slightly hides behind his phone during group calls—and I swear he overheard something that wasn’t meant for him, and now he’s acting all awkward around me. Last week, one of my clients lashed out—thought I’d betrayed them because they believed I was favoring another nurse. Turns out, it was a misunderstanding over a shared Google Doc. I just wish, Chi, that professionals could remember how to be human when the pressure hits. It’s all so...  relatable , and yet, we act like it’s all or nothing."     : "Tell me about it.

Rather than share a specific sentence, I'll describe a scene. A teacher, her voice calm and measured, stands in the kitchen of their home in Comberton. She talks to their two young children, a girl and a boy, who sit at the wooden table, eager and wide-eyed. The children lean forward on their chairs as she gestures with her hands, telling them a tale about good and evil, making it a learning moment through stories rooted in British folk tales from her childhood.      [With a spark of curiosity in her voice] So the wicked witch never won in the end? But what if someone saw the story from her side?      [Nods, encouraging the child's thoughts] That's what’s great about stories, love—you get to reflect on different points of view. Good and evil aren’t always clear cut. The witch might have been misunderstood, or perhaps driven by pain.      [Chimes in, wide-eyed] I don’t like the bad guys ever! They hurt people, even if they say they’re sad. I like the hero—especially when they tell the bad guy what they’ve done wrong!      [Smiling warmly] And that, love, is a very important part of the moral. Heroes don’t just win by being stronger—they win by standing up for what's right and treating others with kindness, even when the others try to make life hard.      [Thoughtful] Like the knight who let the dragon go because someone said the dragon was also scared?      [Encouraging a deeper connection] Exactly! Some of my favorite folk stories from here—like the legend of the Bury St Edmunds dragon or about Lady Godiva—have all sorts of layers. People were scared once, just like we sometimes are. The important thing is learning to be brave and handle fears the right way.      [With interest] What was her name? Lady Godiva?      Yes! And she was quite famous. People still tell stories about her in Bury St Edmunds to this day.      [Nods with dreamy enthusiasm] So stories are like magic? They let us see things from a different side.      Oh yes, love. Stories are magic if you let them be. And they help us remember how to be kind, brave, and strong—even when the world feels a bit scary. So, shall we make up a new one tonight? [The children both jump up from their seats, grinning excitedly.]

Rather annoying this school trip’s on a weekend, isn’t it? I was hoping to spend a bit more time in the gym, really get the running machines sorted after my football weekend.      It is a bit, honestly. But the film trip sounds interesting for them. We haven’t had many opportunities to do anything like that with the kids. Which one is he on again?      The one with all the cameras and the old canal stuff. They’re going to make a documentary, or something like that. You’d be amazed how into it the kids are, even with all the walking around.      I’m sure so. I remember when the school had that photography day; the kids came back with a camera roll full of jelly babies left on the grass. Probably the highlights of the trip, from their perspective.      But I saw a seagull and filmed it for breakfast, Mummy! It was proper scary with a big beak and everything!      Oh, brave explorer! Well done, then. Did you enjoy it overall?      Yeah, I got to be one of the crew! Miss Davis said I did a good job, even though I dropped the camera once. It was shaking quite a lot after.      Mate, I got a doughnut and then it was  crushed  into my foot by someone’s camera bag. Not fair.      Oi, we’d better check in on someone who might be having a bit more of a tricky day. Your brother came back limping earlier, did the kid fall over or stretch his leg?      I think it was just a pulled muscle about half way through. They’re used to the walking, but this was an all-day trip. Maybe they should’ve done that easier path.      Yeah, I’ll have a word with the teacher about it. Doesn’t do much for morale when a bloke can’t even hobble back for afternoon tea.      I’ll pop in there later with the leg compress and some of these doughnuts we picked up from the shop. I think someone told me the chocolate ones ran out.      Then we best get moving on the gym plans goin’ on for tomorrow if we don’t want to be stuck with jelly baby documentaries and cramp between us. Who’s in?      Me! I want to go on the running machine and see if it’s better than seagull dodging!

Rather lovely to be out here, isn't it, old chap? The view from this restaurant always does something for me, and with this change in the weather, it's all the more welcome. How are you holding up with everything these days?      Aye, can't complain much. Got a bit of a cold last week that kept me under the covers for three days, but better now, I reckon. A shame, but I needed the rest after a rather busy few months. Things in the shop are getting a bit slow, and I've had to lay off a bit of the overtime. You'd think the economy was on its knees.      That's a pity to hear. I've noticed that the boot sales around town are thriving, though. I dropped off some clothes I didn't need the other weekend, and was paid in cash straight away. Living with cash again is a bit of a novelty. Health-wise, I've started cycling more frequently after I spoke to a friend from the Green Party last month, you remember Heather?      Ah yes, that Heather! I do recall, a pleasant enough lass. What about it? Did she convince you to go green and bike off into the wild?      Well, not quite "wild," but she's helped me see that it's better for my asthma and, let's be honest, my weight. I’m quite taken with the idea that I can help the environment and myself at the same time. There are also these group bike rides in the mornings. I might even coax a few colleagues at the school into joining—get them all out of their cars and into the fresh air.      That’s good of you, about the colleagues. I remember the days when the school still had a bike rack. Must be twenty years gone! Going back to the shop—truth be told, the boot sales are stealing quite a few customers from local stores like mine. People are more cautious about their spending now, and they don't mind a few holes in their jeans if it means saving a tenner.      Yes, and that brings me to relationships—perhaps you've noticed the same in your work? People today are far more practical when it comes to where they spend their money and the relationships they cultivate. It's not just about buying something or hiring someone for a job; it's about trust and connection now.

Rather annoying when the barista at my local café misses the pronunciation of the pasty recipe I always get. It’s "pas-tee," not "pas-ty," innit? Mind you, gotta give 'em a break, can’t blame 'em for being confused.      Aye, I get that. Down in Brum, people just call it a pie all the same most days. But I love a decent pasty when I get one, especially with a touch of leek and mash. You can blame the Americans for the "pas-ty" mispronunciation, truth be told. Bit ironic when they even make  pizza pasties .      Haha, yeah, that one’s a bit madness, innit? Speaking of Americans, did you hear the news about Trump running for president again? I swear he turned into a character in one of his own dodgy slogans. "Make America Great Again" – again. Honestly, I’m starting to wonder if planting some oversized American flags on his lawn’s the only original idea he’s had since 2016.      I mean, he might as well legislate a new currency with golden donuts for all the good it’s going to do. Doesn’t seem to be paying attention to how the national finances – or for that matter, his own – actually work. You'd think a bloke with a failed poker face would know when to fold.      Absolutely. It’s daft how someone who seemingly misunderstands the basics of bookkeeping ends up dictating global economics. I remember talking to a mate who ran a retail business in Cheltenham – said Trump’s tax policies are like trying to wear flammable trousers to a bonfire night. Eventually, the market’s just gonna set it all on fire and not know why.      Aye, and I bet the flares they use for the burners will be imported from China, with tax breaks at 60% off – probably docked straight into his offshore bank account. Honestly, I’d rather stick to my budget spreadsheet and shopping list than invest a single brass penny with that lot.      Some people still want to invest in a  tweed blazer with the points  as go-to fashion on the world stage. It’s like walking around in a very specific kind of failure that’s tailored.      Haha, fair one. I’m with you – if I had a quid for every cheap copy of a vintage.Percent of this to a farm in Cumbria where they grow the food that ends up in our pasties...

Rather annoying the new TV schedule, isn't it? Seems like everything promising ends up being some kind of violent drama or crime thriller these days. I was watching one last night, and by the time the credits rolled, I was wondering how we ever let this sort of thing on our living room screens.      I know exactly what you mean. I find it hard to justify watching it all unless it's a comedy. A lot of programmes just serve one purpose — to scare you or make you hyper-analyse someone's journey. It's not like the good old days of Blue Peter or anything. Remember how you used to collect those badges?      Oh, God! I had the one with the blue whale and the turkey on it. Still somewhere in my childhood bedroom, I suppose. I always wanted the one with the microchip and the robot, but my mum had an in with the vet and managed to get a dog badge for me instead!      Ha! That was lucky. I always wondered what happened to the badge I won when I went to the Great Ormond Street Water Feature with my class—personally signed by老爷爷 Peter himself! Felt quite elite to be honest.      You were probably much better behaved during those things than I was. I remember once we were doing this project on killer whales, and I ended up getting really involved in a documentary and didn't want to go to bed for days. Still, it got me into biology and made me want to be a teacher — full circle, right?      It's amazing how those early interests affect our lives, is it not? I started collecting bottle tops as a kid — I was obsessed with how you could reuse them. I'm still a bit of a maniac for that green bin. Funny how a childhood habit turned into part of my academic work now.      Definitely. I do think, though, part of being a guest lecturer is passed on from growing up and discovering new passions. I remember a time when my pottery project with the clay lizard led me to study art theory in the first place.      And we've both been lucky to keep that wonder from childhood alive. Some people lose it when they grow up.      True. Oh, go on then, another glass of wine?      You read my mind, love. Or maybe we were just both thinking about the same thing all along.

Rather annoying this new hostel’s set up, isn’t it? I mean, it's supposed to save costs, but the rooms are so cramped. I’m more used to the old days when we’d have a little more elbow room. Mind you, the view from my window is nice.      Oh dear, yes, cramped is one word for it! I’ve seen quite a few of these places in my time, when I was still doing the childminding. Oh, and bless me, there's that same Mrs. Johnson from the community centre who runs the place, don't you know? Still hasn’t changed her hairstyle since the Eighties! I popped in the other day, and she was stressed about the photo wall — no one under fifty seems to know left from right when it comes to printing photos now.      I think it's ironic. Living with young people while still having to explain how a digital camera works. I've been helping with a bit in the evenings. I showed her how to set up a gallery online for the old-timers to share photographs. It helps everyone feel included, you know? Speaking of which, I dropped in on old Mr. Davis from the shop early last week, he's in the hospital again. Poor fellow, workin' too hard again.      Oh, he was always like that — slap on his apron at six and not off till ten. Hard as nails, was his mam, from what I heard. She owned the corner shop before him. That reminds me, I still can't get over how bad that new abattoir smells. It's a proper nightmare if you live within two miles! I don’t see why it had to be built so close.      Oh, the smell is awful, I agree — what an eyesore too. But I shouldn’t complain, it is a proper job for some. My sister’s nephew works the processing line there. All that machinery, you know. He told me the whole place is run on engineering principles he used to hear about at school. I always envied the ones who could figure that out.      Family stories of hard work do tend to impress, don’t they? Still, I’m more interested in how things work than the actual goings-on in abattoirs. I had a real science bug as a lad. Used to study it at university, but I eventually went into teaching — better pay and more holidays.

Rather annoying to say the least. I remember sorting through applications for a few years in my previous role. It’s got to be far more rewarding to be back in academia, don’t you think?      Yeah, honestly, recruitment was a wild ride! I worked with a university for a while on their staff hiring, mostly lecturers and research associates. I reckon it was challenging in its own way. You’ve got to balance HR policy with the academic’s social quirks. Some people just can’t function in interviews.      Oh, I can imagine. I remember one guy came in with like three degrees, published in  Nature , no less, and the moment I asked him how he managed his time… he just sat there, blinking. Eventually left the room. Ten minutes later, I got an email from him pasting the entire CV back at me.      Classic! That doesn’t happen in academia much anymore, but still... I suppose part of the issue is the evaluation side of things, right? With the academic literacy frameworks, I mean. It’s not just about what you know—it’s about how you articulate your knowledge in a scholarly way.      Exactly. I’ve been marking essay drafts for the new intake, and it’s got me thinking. Some students have strong content but their structure, grammar, and citation styles are all over the place. It’s not that they’re not bright—it’s more about how they’ve been taught to write up to this point.      Completely. I was a bit conflicted when I started teaching—should I focus more on content or form? But being an associate lecturer, I had to come up with a middle ground. I actually ran an exercise where I split the class into different areas: literature review, methodology, analysis—that kind of thing. Let each group rewrite the same section using a different framework to see how the tone and clarity changed.      Oh, that’s a clever way to show the differences. I think it would help them understand why academic writing isn’t just “big words.” It’s  purposeful  structure.      Yeah, and it’s also helped me spot whose work might be beyond their capability level. Not that I’m accusing anyone of goosing it, but it’s a risk, isn’t it? Especially when you’re in a field like education.      God, yes. It’s why I sometimes get lost in the jargon roles we had in recruitment—there was always that line between fitting the job description and the “culture fit.”

: Right lads and lasses, I think it's time we all had a chinwag 'n got to know our new friend here. I’m Chloe by the way, by the by Bradford born and bred, and I’m reading sociology at the uni. You lot fancy a chat?     : Aye, I'm Liam. Not born in Bradford if that's what yer thinking, but I've been living up these parts for a few years now. I’m a bit of a shopkeeper, or as you might call it, a sales assistant at the mall in Salford. Tore my jeans like three times already trying to act posh. Bit of a struggle, but I’m working on it.     : Hi! I'm Sophie. From Bolton, over the road if you ask me. I’m also a student—fashion design—so I’m about as posh as Liam when it comes to fancy shops. Fair dinkum I’d walk in there, touch the clothes and say, “Right, I’ll make a dress like that, but with less price and more kicks, luv” and walk out proudly!     : Oh, hi there. I’m Priya. I was born in India, but I’ve been in the UK longer than most of my memories. I’m fairly new to Salford myself—only been studying here a couple of months. I’m taking business studies. Still getting the hang of everything, especially the dialects. Like what someone said in Bradford last week: “She’s gone a bit ratty.” I thought someone’s pet had escaped!     : Oh, that’s a good one. Yeah, "ratty” about means mad or annoyed up here. But the thing is, we chuck in vibes and stuff like that and make it sound like we're barely speaking English. But Priya, welcome to the jungle, I mean the North! Got a lotta slang here, but once you learn it, you can really show off how proper you are.     : Aye, stick to my story as being from—"South of here" always comes with a bit of a lie, but the laughs are worth it. Though you don't get laughs with the instructors if you turn up late goin' on about "fine weather or not" or whatever they expect us to say in lectures.     : Time to lay the proper English on them. I once tried to speak to a tutor like someone in London would. “Er, could I, perhaps, obtain a copy of that article?”

Rather annoying this newfit military type stuff innit? Me aunt’s still trying her best to ‘normalise’ things and all, she’s been reading up more than I can take on the War Memoirs type articles in them fancy £6 mags.      Yeah, I know what y’mean—mind you, I don’t read the 'War Memoir' section so much… been more into the sci-fi films stuff. Got this one from my nan, 'The Last Outpost'—glitchy as heck, but the story’s okay. Didn’t even want to touch it at first, but the graphics sort of drew you in.      What’s it about then? I like a bit of turkey on a screen, especially if it got bursts of neon and dramatic bits.      It's basically about a unit of soldiers stranded in an alien jungle—kinda forget what it was called—anyhoo, they’ve got a glitch in their heads-up display, and it messes with their ordering of command. Pretty shouty, actually, but that’s why I like it, maybe.      I mean if it’s a bit shouty and griefy, sounds like my type of sh t—mind you, I’m not sure how much longer I’m gonna put up with these newfangled, cheery military bios in them magazines. Feels like they don’t even know what they’re trying to say anymore.      True dat. Like what’s the point in glorifying the boring bits? Should focus more on the actual ops or the funny floring ones, like when the tech goes all bonkers and you're stuck analysing ballet as part of your orders about cosmic command structures. That type of story's better than all this “pride and glory” cliché.      Ehh, it is a bit strange how much the system’s ‘cosmicifying’ stuff. Like my cousin’s been working on some Signals Teams where the higher ups told him he was part of a ‘reality-based scheming unit’. Sounds all cracky if you ask me.      Mate, that’s a new one on me. I do the simulation work, you know, where they re-spin the old directives into newfangled protocols. I swear it’s like trying to get a ram to solve a line of poetry. Gets you nowhere.      Aye, well maybe you could sum it all up better than them conference gents in Cambridge. Next one I’m doing is on ‘Strategic Platforms: Future or Failure?’—might just start quoting them ram poems at them.

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know what they do. Just arrive in our town like it's all got to adapt to them. I was at the café on Saturday and saw someone nearly spill a latte on a cash register because they didn't know how things work here.      Got eeny weeny passive-aggressive messages from one bloke saying he expected more of a "vibe." As if our town is some kind of theme park and not a real place with people who live here.      It was ridiculous. My sister met someone when he was staying with us and he asked if we had a "authentic English" pub. We live half a mile from one of the oldest ale houses in the county. You don't get more authentic than that!      I mean, I can see how they think it's exotic. Living in London, everything’s so fast-paced and loud, and then suddenly you’re in some historic Hertfordshire village. It’s like time travel but without the planning.      One guy even asked me if I worked with "typical northern" builders. Like he expected someone in a flat cap with a donkey and a hobnail boot. Good on me I didn't correct him straight away, but I nearly said "actually – no."      Honestly, it's not all that bad. I reckon some of them are just trying their best. Still, it's funny when they say things like "this is just someone's garden and they also sell tea." Yeah, a garden that's been around since the 18th century.      Anyways, enough moaning about London posh people. What have we been up to? I’ve had a mammoth week at the firm. We’re designing what might be the greenest building in the city. It's got a lot of local materials, and we're planning on reusing construction waste. Super exciting.      That’s the future, mate. I think I might get involved in something like that when I sort out this indie movie project I'm working on. Maybe a short about climate change but not too preaching.      Was going to say – remember when we used to travel to London for the weekend and go out? I think it was more our idea of fun than anyone else's.      Never could beat a night in Shoreditch. Even with the tourists and the noise, it was something to see.

Rather exciting to have your parents over for the first time, isn't it? I hope they like the flat... got the kettle on, shall I brew some more tea? I know their previous stay over at Brighton was a hit. Not quite as spread out as this place, but well enough.      Oh dear, yes, we do hope they like it here. Their last trip to Brighton was adorable. I’ve been listing all the provisions needed in this flat, including a few more plastic bags as storage; you know, just in case. I also set up the outside pots, but the garden's not too... wild, is it?      I've been to Brighton once before, many decades ago now. My visit then was unforgettable, especially the eccentricities of the locals and the seafront – I still remember them proudly pronouncing "scones" differently. It must be far more modern now. And breakfast, no doubt more... extravagant.      Oh, the seafront remains as lively as ever, even if many of the people aren't quite the same. I grew up not far, and I loved taking trips to the town in my twenties. What did you think of the food then, by the way? Cream tea is always fun to trot out in discussions. Mind you, I remember my first master's degree fairly interfered with my metabolism, and I'm still trying to sort out my cholesterol.      If I understand correctly, you juggled your studies and your health at that time. That’s admirable. I often read about centenarians and their so-called "bad habits" – plenty of spices, tea, and being able to maintain social ties with your friends are all factors most people ignore. I try to incorporate all of these, though the window cleaning is an afterthought.      Oh that's right! I've heard of a few people in my old age group living over 100, often attributing it to sundry health philosophies. Senescence – it's quite an interesting field, though I suppose I haven't studied it much. As for friends and travel, being in a sustained space like this flat requires a new kind of balancing act.      Still, I think the flat is a good place for that balance. We really need to figure out our utility bills, though. I made a dent in the password list by borrowing from the box, but we're already due to pay for the electricity invoice.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh? You’d think in Cambridge we’d know if it’s ‘goin’ to stop or not by now. I’m more used to the blasts of wind we get in Sunderland, but this… this is just soggy and boring!      Can’t argue there! I moved from Kent to Cambridge just ‘cause I thought the weather might be drier, but I’ve been more soaked by this damp air than I ever got in Pembury. Mind you, it’s given me a good excuse to test out the new coffee shop by the library. That Moka Joe reminds me of the cafes in Berlin!      Oh right, I’d forgotten you’re half-German. Any plans to go back for a holiday anytime soon? I’ve never been to Germany, but I’d love to see the old cities.      Yeah, eventually. The last trip, I was actually working on a bridge design near Köln—civil engineering over there’s ever so slightly different, you know? More red tape, but also more funding for sustainability projects. I do miss the efficiency of some of their systems. I mean, we’re stuck in the UK trying to get house prices under control while they’re investing in communal housing.      You’re telling me – Mate of mine got knocked back on a house because the deposit was short by ten grand. He’s a teacher, for goodness’ sake! It’s just not sensible anymore. And the internet debates about this? Honestly, it’s more entertaining than useful.      Tell me about it. Just the other day, I was stewing a pot of lamb and lentils when I looked online and found a recipe with miso in it. Decided to try it out, and man, did it turn into a failsafe. I’m still trying to get it outta the walls in my kitchen!      Oh no! I passed that Miso Bazzar in Cambridge the other week – was thinking about trying it in a stew meself. You’d think with all the fancy recipes online, they’d also say, “Avoid trying with your landlords watching.”      Exactly. My landlord’s been asking after the smell by the way. That and the govt’s new health tax on sugary food. Just don’t ask me to give up biscuits, will you?      Speak for yerself. I’ve been cutting back to afford this flat’s rent.

Rather annoying the new bank manager we've got, isn't it? Handles money alright, but can't get a proper word out without contradicting herself. I had her on the phone today, trying to sort a direct debit error. Not only couldn’t she sort it, she managed to ring the wrong account in again. Right mess!      Honestly, I reckon it's not all their fault, is it? A lot of these places are so understaffed, especially with all the bank holidays coming up. I had a chat with my aunt the other day—she works in HR at a big office in Maidstone—and she said even they're scratching their heads trying to keep the rotas full.      It's not just the banks. I left my last care home job earlier this year because the manager wouldn’t pick up the phone half the time. I remember one morning, there were three shifts waiting breakfast, and no one showed up. I had a right grumble at the time, and not wrong, if you ask me.      I feel that—especially with the lack of cover for sick leave. I work occasional shifts in Farnborough as a carer and only last week, I got a call at three in the morning saying I needed to cover a last-minute booking. My shift had been planned two weeks in advance, but they just dropped it on the cheapest available staff.      You know what I blame? The education system. I mean, people just aren’t sticking in for degrees or proper qualifications like they used to. I came out of school with A-levels and got a nursing job straightaway. Now I see young people leaving school, doing apprenticeships or gap years, and then suddenly want to be head of nursing the next year. It’s just not realistic.      That’s a fair point, but there’s more to it. A lot of us just burn out, you know? I did a BSc at uni, finished it in three years, but I wouldn’t go back there for all the tea in the world. It was exhausting and I ended up doing a different job entirely after that.      I took the easy way out—did a couple of courses and got into the care sector as go. Worked for years, but after a few years of trying to get line manager status, I had to give it up because the hours were eating into my family time.
